## Exploring the Anticancer Potential of Novel Piperidine-Embedded Isoxazol-Triazole Conjugates Against MCF-7 Human Breast Adenocarcinoma Cell Line: Design, Synthesis, In Silico, and In Vitro Investigations.

**PMID**: 42763920 · **Journal**: Chemistry & biodiversity · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1002/cbdv.71702

**Authors**: Ghonia Jay R, Parikh Jigisha, Dholakiya Bharatkumar Z

**Types**: Journal Article

Cancer remains a major global health challenge, particularly as several tumors develop resistance to current therapies. Although doxorubicin is widely used to treat various cancers, its effectiveness is often limited by adverse effects, including cardiotoxicity and nephrotoxicity, which restrict its dosing. In search of safer and more effective options, a series of novel piperidine-embedded isoxazol-triazole conjugates (6a-6o) were designed, synthesized, and biologically evaluated against the MCF-7 cell line in this study. The synthesized compounds 6a-6o were characterized using FTIR, HRMS, and 1H and 13C NMR spectroscopy analysis to confirm their structure and verify successful synthesis. The GI50 (Growth Inhibition 50%) values of synthesized compounds 6a-6o were determined using the SRB assay. Among all synthesized compounds, 6m exhibited the most potent antiproliferative activity against MCF-7 cells, having GI50 <10 µg/mL (SI >5), comparable to adriamycin (doxorubicin, GI50 <10 µg/mL). Overall, 6m is a novel anticancer agent with promising abilities against MCF-7 human breast cancer. The results support the compounds relevance as a biologically active agent with effective proliferation-suppressive properties.

## A Greek Real-World Experience With the Implementation of the EndoPredict Gene Signature in a Cohort of Pre-menopausal and Post-menopausal Patients With ER+/HER2- Breast Cancer.

**PMID**: 42763779 · **Journal**: Cureus · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.7759/cureus.114838 · **PMCID**: PMC13589637

**Authors**: Pantazidis George, Sourla Antigoni, Vasiageorgi Aggeliki, Yfanti Christina, Alisandrou Anna-Maria, Stefanou Giasemi, Petsavas Aggelos, Pavlidou Fotini, Parpoudi Styliani, Alexandrou Dimitrios, Sachoulidou Anna, Marinatou Annezo, Kalogridaki Evgenia, Kontoulis Theodoros, Daskalakis Panagiotis E, Tsantilas Vlassios, Chatzopoulos Stavros, Kanistras Christos, Argyriou Theodoros, Dragoumis Dimitrios, Stafyla Vaia, Louis Konstantinos, Kouloura Andriana, Galanou Ioanna, Papazoglou Georgios, Grosomanidis Dimitrios, Chatzopoulos Konstantinos, Pasaskevakou Georgia, Varnava Panagiota, Giannopoulou Anna, Xenakis Xenofon, Mpakogiannis Apostolos, Flessas Ioannis, Nasikas Dimitrios, Koronarchis Dimitrios, Douvetzemis Stergios, Fyssas Ioannis, Spanopoulos Christos, Baltas Dimosthenis, Keramopoulos Dimitrios, Bouloukos Konstantinos, Gaki Vilma, Dimas Dionysios T, Missitzis Ioannis L, Rigas Georgios, Kalyvopoulos Christos, Intzes Stavros, Zervoudis Stefanos, Michailidou Europi, Katsourakis Anastasios, Thanos Markos, Zavos Apostolos, Boutsikos George, Kanara Maria, Rousogiannis Sotirios Α, Charatsaris Panagiotis, Lampropoulos Pavlos, Papadopoulos Sarantos, Solakis Evangelos P, Askoxylakis Ioannis, Kakoulaki Sofia, Sfakianakis Eleftherios, Vrentzos Nikolaos, Milonaki Despoina, Kyriasanos Ioannis, Irakleidis Foivos, Iosifidou Rodoniki

**Types**: Journal Article

Background EndoPredict® is a guideline-recommended gene signature assay guiding whether adjuvant treatment should include chemotherapy or not. The EndoPredict® Clinical (EPclin) Risk Score combines molecular and clinical data to predict the distant recurrence of breast cancer, providing valuable information about the prognosis and chemotherapy benefit in both pre- and post-menopausal patients. Methodology This is a real-world, retrospective study aiming to characterize the EPclin Risk Score's utility in 200 consecutively selected Greek patients with estrogen receptor positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative (ER+/HER2-) breast cancer, enrolled in a single institution, considering their clinicopathological features and menopausal status, with emphasis on its role in identifying patients suitable for treatment de-escalation. Results In this study, 100 pre-menopausal and 100 post-menopausal ER+/HER2- breast cancer patients were included. Among the pre-menopausal subgroup, 65% of the patients were classified as low risk and the other 35% as high risk, while among the post-menopausal subgroup, the low-risk and high-risk patients were 66% and 34%, respectively. A notable 30% of node-positive premenopausal patients were characterized by EPclin as at a low risk of breast cancer. Conclusions The EPclin Risk score has the ability to stratify and guide therapy decisions in ER+/HER2- breast cancer patients. It classifies the recurrence risk differently from traditional assessments and identifies low-risk premenopausal patients with node-positive disease. This may provide a de-escalation treatment pathway for such patients but requires further clinical validation.

Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed malignancy worldwide and remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. According to the World Health Organization (WHO, 2020) [ 1 ], it ranks as the fifth leading cause of cancer death globally, while more recent data indicate that it is the second most frequently diagnosed cancer and the fourth leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide (WHO, 2022) [ 2 ].

Breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease classified according to the molecular expression of hormone receptors (HR), namely estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR), as well as the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). Based on these biomarkers, tumors are categorized as the following subtypes: HR-positive/HER2-negative, HER2-positive, and triple-negative (HR-negative/HER2-negative). Among these, patients with HR-positive/HER2-negative tumors (invasive breast cancer) generally demonstrate the best prognosis, followed by those with HER2-positive disease, while triple-negative breast cancer is associated with the least favorable outcomes [ 3 ].

Early ER-positive, HER2-negative tumors are a heterogeneous group of tumors with variable prognosis. Although patients with this type of tumor derive substantial benefit from endocrine therapy, only a subset experience clinically meaningful improvement with adjuvant chemotherapy [ 4 ]. Consequently, an accurate risk stratification is essential to optimize treatment selection and avoid unnecessary toxicity for patients with localized ER+/HER2- breast cancer.

A number of commercially available prognostic and predictive assays are routinely used in clinical practice to inform the risk of recurrence and the benefit of chemotherapy for such patients. Their performance may differ depending on the patient's menopausal status [ 5 ]. While their clinical utility is well established in node-negative and post-menopausal patients, their value in pre-menopausal, node-positive breast cancer remains a controversial field in molecular oncology. Recent prospective randomized studies, including the Oncotype DX TAILORx (Trial Assigning Individualized Options for Treatment (Rx)), RxPonder trials, and the Mammaprint MINDACT (Microarray In Node negative Disease may Avoid ChemoTherapy) trial, have shown that molecular signatures in women differ in their prognostic ability and predictive power based on their menopausal status. The findings of these trials also suggest that the benefit of chemotherapy in pre-menopausal women may be related to chemotherapy-induced amenorrhea, which could potentially be achieved with ovarian function suppression (OFS). Ongoing trials, such as the OPTIMA (Optimal Personalised Treatment of early breast cancer using Multi-parameter Analysis) trial and the OFSET (Evaluating the Addition of Adjuvant Chemotherapy to Ovarian Function Suppression Plus Endocrine Therapy in Premenopausal Patients With pN0-1, ER-Positive/​HER2-Negative Breast Cancer and an Oncotype Recurrence Score Less Than or Equal to 25) study, which include OFS as part of the endocrine therapy in all pre-menopausal women, may clarify this question [ 6 ].

On the contrary, EndoPredict® (Myriad Genetics, Salt Lake City, UT) has been prognostic of 10-year distant recurrence in pre-menopausal women, independently of nodal status [ 5 ]. Overall, EndoPredict® is a validated multigene expression assay that identifies a substantial proportion of patients (approximately 55%-65% in clinical trials) with an excellent long-term prognosis who can safely forgo adjuvant chemotherapy. By integrating molecular and clinical parameters, EndoPredict® provides robust prognostic information regarding distant recurrence risk and predictive insight into chemotherapy benefit [ 7 - 10 ].

The test is supported by Level 1A evidence and is recommended in multiple national and international clinical practice guidelines, including those from the European Society for Medical Oncology [ 11 - 15 ]. Its use enables more precise, individualized treatment decisions by accurately predicting distant recurrence risk [ 7 , 16 ] and chemotherapy benefit [ 17 ]. Thus, it reduces both overtreatment and undertreatment, minimizing unnecessary adverse effects and improving patients’ quality of life.

The EndoPredict® Clinical (EPclin) Risk Score combines the 12-gene molecular score with key clinical variables, specifically tumor size and nodal status, and has been demonstrated to be an independent and clinically relevant predictor of distant recurrence. Importantly, it provides additional prognostic and predictive value beyond standard clinicopathological factors alone [ 7 ].

The objective of the present study was to evaluate the utility of the EPclin Risk Score in terms of how risk classification, recurrence estimates, and chemotherapy benefit estimates for a cohort of Greek patients with ER+/HER2- early breast cancer are contextualized to their clinicopathological features and menopausal status. The EPclin score’s potential to identify patients suitable for treatment de-escalation has been a key focus.

Study cohort

Samples from a total of 200 women with breast cancer were included in this study. This comprised a subgroup of 100 pre-menopausal and a subgroup of 100 post-menopausal patients who were tested consecutively from April 20, 2026, backward using the EPclin gene signature assay in a single laboratory until the desired number of 100 for each subgroup was reached.

Samples were eligible for inclusion in the study if the patient was of age >18 years, had a diagnosis of localized ER+/HER2- breast cancer, had the availability of a conclusive EPclin assessment, and had a date of EPclin testing prior to April 20, 2026. No exclusion criteria were applied to ensure the absence of selection bias.

Methods

Tumors were staged according to the TNM (tumor, node, metastasis) classification system, as defined by the American Joint Committee on Cancer and the Union for International Cancer Control [ 18 ].

Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue samples were sectioned at 5-10 μm thickness, depending on pathological assessment of tumor cellularity. Only samples with >30% tumor cell content were included, in accordance with the established guidelines.

RNA was extracted using the Maxwell® RSC RNA FFPE kit (Promega Corporation, Madison, WI). Following quality control (QC) assessment of RNA quantity and integrity, aliquots were used for EndoPredict® analysis.

Gene expression was quantified in triplicate using reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR). The assay measures eight cancer-related genes (AZGP1, BIRC5, DHCR7, IL6ST, MGP, RBBP8, STC2, UBE2C), three reference genes (CALM2, OAZ1, RPL37A), and one control gene to detect residual genomic DNA. Reactions were performed using EndoPredict® reagents (Myriad Genetics/Eurobio (Eurobio Scientific Service GmbH, Rheinbach-Allemagne, Germany)) on a QuantStudio™ 5 Dx Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems, Waltham, MA).

Raw RT-qPCR data were exported as .txt files and analyzed using the web-based EndoPredict® Report Generator (EPRG). The 12-gene molecular score (EPscore) was calculated from normalized gene expression values and subsequently combined with tumor size and nodal status to generate the EPclin Risk Score. The EPclin Risk Score provides: (i) 10-year risk of distant recurrence with endocrine therapy alone, (ii) risk of late recurrence (years five to 15) in patients free of distant recurrence after five years of endocrine therapy alone, and (iii) estimated absolute chemotherapy effect at 10 years [ 7 , 9 ].

Testing parameters

Both the 12-Gene Molecular Score and EPclin Risk Score were developed and trained in a multicenter cohort of 964 treatment-naive FFPE primary breast cancer samples [ 16 ]. A Cox proportional hazards model was used to derive the EPclin Risk Score as a linear combination of the molecular score, tumor size, and nodal status. According to the model, the EPclin Risk Score is calculated as:

\begin{document} \mathrm{EPclin\ Risk\ Score} = (0.35 \times \mathrm{Tumor\ Size}) + (0.64 \times \mathrm{Nodal\ Status}) + (0.28 \times \mathrm{EPscore}) \end{document}  [ 7 , 9 ].

Tumor size was categorized as: T1ab (≤1 cm), T1c (>1 but ≤2 cm), T2 (>2 but ≤5 cm), and T3 (>5 cm). Nodal status was categorized as: N0 (node-negative), N1 (one to three positive lymph nodes or micrometastases), and N2 (four to 10 positive lymph nodes).

Both the EPscore and EPclin Risk Score have been validated in multiple independent cohorts [ 7 , 9 ].

Interpretation of EPclin Risk Score

EPclin Risk Scores were interpreted according to predefined thresholds [ 7 , 9 ]:

Low risk (EPclin: 1.0-3.3): associated with a low 10-year risk of distant recurrence. This report states first the estimated 10-year risk of recurrence; second, the likelihood of distant recurrence five to 15 years after diagnosis; and finally, the estimated absolute benefit of chemotherapy at 10 years.

High risk (EPclin: 3.4-6.0): associated with a high 10-year risk of distant recurrence. This report includes the same results as in the low risk.

Scores outside the validated range: Scores >6.0 (up to 8.2) are reported as high risk; however, quantitative estimates for recurrence risk and chemotherapy effect are not provided. Scores <1.0 are not reportable.

Statistics

This was a non-interventional study and therefore epidemiological methods were applied in the analysis, and no formal hypotheses were tested. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed for all study data. Continuous variables were summarized with the use of descriptive statistical measures (mean value, median value, minimum value and maximum value). Categorical/distinct variables were displayed as frequency tables (N, %).

Data collection and availability

All EPclin data were generated and collected in the laboratory of Bioiatriki S.A. All clinical and pathological data were collected from the pathology reports accompanying each patient sample included in the study. Only the information relevant to the study objectives was collected, completely anonymized.

The data generated in this study are available upon reasonable request from the corresponding author.

Ethical oversight

The Scientific Commission of Bioiatriki S.A. approved the protocol and granted a waiver of informed consent provided that all personal patient data were effectively anonymized in accordance with applicable laws and national regulations.

Disclaimer: The present study had no clinical implications and patient-related decisions were made routinely by the treating physicians and were not influenced by the study’s results.

This retrospective study analyzed data from a Greek cohort of 200 patients who underwent EndoPredict® testing between April 20, 2025 and April 20, 2026 at the Molecular Biology Laboratory of Bioiatriki S.A.

The baseline characteristics of the study cohort, including tumor size, nodal status, grade, and the distribution of Ki-67 expression are depicted in Table  1 . Ki-67 subgroups were defined as per Constantinidou et al. [ 5 ]. Among the pre-menopausal patients (n=100), there were 76 with T1 disease and 24 with T2; 77 were N0 and 23 were N1. Among the post-menopausal patients (n=100), there were 77 with T1 tumor, 22 with T2 and one patient with T3; 83 were N0 and 17 N1.

In the pre-menopausal group of patients, 65 subjects (65%) were classified as low risk (EPclin Risk Score <3.3) and 35 subjects (35%) as high risk (EPclin Risk Score >3.3). Respectively, in the post-menopausal group of patients, 66 subjects (66%) were classified as low risk and 34 subjects (34%) as high risk. Categorization per EPclin Risk score and TNM staging is summarized separately for the pre-menopausal and the post-menopausal subgroups in Table  2 .

The categorization as per EPclin Risk score and Ki-67 expression subgroups is summarized separately for the pre-menopausal and the post-menopausal subgroups in Table  3 .

The distribution of TNM staging versus EPclin Risk Score in the pre-menopausal subgroup is depicted in Figure  1A  and the respective distribution in the post-menopausal subgroup in Figure  1B . In the pre-menopausal subgroup, all TNM stages are represented in both high- and low-risk EPclin score groups, with the exception of patients with pT2N1 breast cancer, who were all identified as high risk (no pT3 pre-menopausal patients were available in our analysis). Of note, 7/16 (43.8%) among pre-menopausal patients with pT1N1 disease and 7/23 (30.4%) with node-positive disease overall were identified as having a low risk of recurrence. In the post-menopausal subgroup, all but one patient with pT2N1 disease were identified as patients with high risk of recurrence and the single patient with T3 disease was also reported to have a high risk.

Considering Ki-67 expression and grade and among patients with node-positive disease: in the pre-menopausal subgroup, 2/2 with grade 3 and 10/12 with Ki-67 ≥20% were allocated to EPclin high-risk, and 5/23 had EPclin ≥4.8, whilst in the post-menopausal subgroup, these numbers were 1/1, 3/3 and 2/17, respectively.

The distribution of early and late recurrence risk, as well as estimated chemotherapy benefit, separately in pre-menopausal and post-menopausal patients is shown in Figure  2 . Among low-risk patients, both pre-menopausal and post-menopausal groups cluster predominantly within the 5% (17 pre-menopausal and 27 post-menopausal patients) and 5%-7% (30 pre-menopausal and 27 post-menopausal patients) categories for 10-year distant recurrence risk. In terms of the risk of late recurrence (years five to 15), most patients (41 pre- and 42 post-menopausal patients) were allocated within the 3%-5% range, while the estimated absolute chemotherapy benefit is minimal, typically ranging from 0% to 3% (65 pre-menopausal and 66 post-menopausal patients).

Among high-risk patients, the distribution of early and late risks of distal recurrence demonstrates a greater tendency for the pre-menopausal cohort to report higher rates of these risks: Considering early recurrence, in the pre-menopausal cohort, 12 patients were reported to have a risk <15% and 23 patients a risk >15%. In the post-menopausal cohort, 17 patients were reported to have a risk <15% and 17 a risk >15%. Considering late recurrence, more patients in the pre-menopausal cohort were identified with risk >15% (20 out of a total of 35) whilst most post-menopausal patients were allocated to the <15% risk group (26 out of a total of 33). Similarly, a marked difference in the estimated absolute chemotherapy benefit of >15% is observed with more pre-menopausal patients being allocated to that group than the post-menopausal group (seven vs three patients).

Since Greece introduced a systematic breast cancer screening program five years ago, early diagnoses have increased, reducing the number of patients with advanced stages of breast cancer. Gene expression signatures are included in international treatment guidelines to support and optimize decision-making in adjuvant systemic therapy for ER+/HER2- early breast cancer patients. These genomic tools identify patients for whom chemotherapy is beneficial and those with a low risk of recurrence and excellent prognosis who could avoid undergoing chemotherapy [ 6 ].

EndoPredict®, a second-generation genetic signature test, combines gene expression levels of 12 genes with tumor size and nodal status to predict the probability of late distant recurrence 0-10 years after diagnosis and five to 15 years after diagnosis for patients free of disease and after five-year endocrine therapy alone. It also estimates the 10-year absolute benefit of chemotherapy.

Overall, EndoPredict allocated 65%/66% in the low-risk group (in the pre-/post-menopausal subgroups) and 35%/34% in the high-risk group (respectively). These rates are similar to the ones reported by Klein et al. [ 19 ].

Considering tumor size and nodal status information, the parameters incorporated in the EPclin algorithm, the majority of breast-cancer patients with small tumor size (T1a, T1b, T1c) and negative nodal status (N0) were indeed identified as low risk based on EndoPredict® testing. However, a marked percentage (11%) of both pre- and post-menopausal women, with specific TNM staging classification, were reported with an EPclin Score >3.3 (high risk). This is in line with the main EndoPredict validation report by Filipits et al., where EPclin successfully provided additional prognostic information on the risk of distant recurrence of breast cancer patients, independently of clinicopathologic parameters [ 7 ].

Within the same context, EndoPredict® also identified a small percentage of patients (8%) with clinically high-risk characteristics (T2/N1 or T3/N0) who were characterized as low risk. Sestak et al. and Ettl et al. also demonstrated that EndoPredict classified patients with clinically high risk, tumors as low risk (EPclin Score<3.3) who either received unnecessary chemotherapy [ 17 ] or could safely forgo the use of chemotherapy [ 20 ].

Regarding the pre-menopausal subgroup, the specific low-risk rate (65%) also aligns with the respective rate reported in Constantinidou et al. [ 5 ], which only studied pre-menopausal patients. This low-risk subgroup includes patients with node-positive disease, with the present study reporting 30.4% of such patients being characterized as low risk, a rate higher than what Constantinidou et al. reported (19.4%) [ 5 ], but this difference may be attributed to the subgroup’s small sample size and the overall retrospective nature of the present study. This study therefore agrees with the previous reports of Constantinidou et al. [ 5 ] and Klein et al. [ 19 ], according to which EndoPredict has the ability to identify a specific subgroup of pre-menopausal ER+/HER2- early breast cancer patients with node-positive disease as low risk, therefore enabling treating physicians to de-escalate treatment and avoid chemotherapy. Conversely, the absence of follow-up information, including the level of adherence to the guidance of the EPclin score, deprives this study of more robust data compared to the aforementioned international literature.

No differences in the distribution of EPclin likelihoods of recurrence can be concluded between the two study subgroups mainly due to the small sample size of these groups. In the low-risk category, no considerable differences between the pre- and post-menopausal group were observed. More notable numerical differences were observed in the high-risk group, where patients from the pre-menopausal cohort were more frequently allocated to the higher-rated risk groups for both early and late recurrence and the highest estimated absolute chemotherapy benefit group. These findings, despite the small sample size of the study, are consistent with established knowledge that pre-menopausal women with ER+/HER2- often experience more aggressive disease, higher recurrence rates and lower survival [ 21 ]. Chemotherapy-induced amenorrhea via ovarian function suppression may be able to provide a significant survival benefit, a matter of extensive clinical research currently [ 6 , 21 ].

Last, but not least, the present study’s observations (albeit in small numbers) seem to be also in agreement with EPclin results from the UNIRAD (UNIversal RADiotherapy) trial [ 22 ], according to which the majority of node-positive patients with grade 3 and Ki-67 ≥20% were allocated to the high-risk EPclin subgroup. Furthermore, particularly for pre-menopausal patients, it is noteworthy that more than 20% of patients with node-positive disease had an EPclin score of ≥4.8. This threshold was the one assumed to define the benefit of a CDK4/6 inhibitor addition according to Penault-Llorca et al. [ 22 ].

Overall, our findings are in line with the previously published studies by Klein et al. [ 19 ] and Constantinidou et al. [ 5 ], which demonstrated that EndoPredict® can be performed both in pre- and post-menopausal ER-positive/HER2-negative early breast cancer patients and it has the ability to classify patients into either low or high risk of recurrence independently of their menopausal and nodal status and sometimes differently from what the standard clinicopathological features would impose [ 9 , 17 , 23 ].

Study limitations

This retrospective study was conducted on a cohort of 200 patients, leading to small subgroup sizes. The reports were consecutively selected for 100 pre-menopausal and 100 post-menopausal patients from a large group of ER-positive/HER2- breast-cancer patients who were tested in the Molecular Biology Laboratory of the Bioiatriki Group from April 20, 2026, backward. This study did not include the decision on any treatment protocol following the evaluation of the EndoPredict result, nor did it collect any patient follow-up information. Consequently, it presents an evaluation of predicted recurrence risks rather than any clinical outcomes of treatment decisions based on the EndoPredict result for patients. The study focused exclusively on the likelihood of distant recurrence within 0-10 and five to 15 years after five years of endocrine therapy alone and the absolute chemotherapy benefit. The study’s generalizability is therefore limited to these parameters and it is further restricted by the strictly descriptive statistical analysis performed.

Our findings underscore the ability of EPclin Risk score to stratify ER+/HER2- breast cancer patients independently of their menopausal and nodal status and classify patients’ recurrence risk differently than traditional clinicopathological assessment, involving tumor size, nodal status, Ki-67 expression, and grade. EPclin also demonstrated the ability to identify a subgroup of low-risk patients among the pre-menopausal patients with node-positive disease. This feature can provide treating physicians with the option to reassess the use of chemotherapy in selected pre-menopausal breast cancer patients. However, the lack of follow-up data and clinical outcomes limits conclusions about its clinical value and potential for treatment de-escalation. Larger cohort studies in the future will be able to address these questions.

## Glutathione-Responsive Disulfiram Delivery from Thiol-Functionalized N-Doped Carbon Nanodots: An in vitro Proof-of-Concept Study.

**PMID**: 42763685 · **Journal**: International journal of nanomedicine · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.2147/IJN.S637701 · **PMCID**: PMC13589579

**Authors**: Panaei Mohadese, Mahani Mohamad, Divsar Faten, Khakbaz Faeze

**Types**: Journal Article

**PURPOSE**: To develop and evaluate a glutathione (GSH)-responsive "Off-On" drug delivery system based on thiol-functionalized N-doped carbon dots (SNCDs) for controlled intracellular release of disulfiram (DSF).

**MATERIALS AND METHODS**: SNCDs were synthesized using a solvothermal technique and subsequently characterized using dynamic laser scattering, high-resolution electron imaging, UV-Vis spectrophotometry, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). DSF was immobilized onto SNCDs through redox-cleavable disulfide linkages, and loading efficiency was determined by UV-Vis analysis. The in vitro drug release kinetics were examined under simulated physiological (pH 7.4) and tumor-relevant acidic (pH 5.4) conditions, evaluating the impact of glutathione (GSH) by performing experiments with and without its inclusion. Cytotoxicity and compatibility studies in MCF-7 breast tumor cells, evaluated via MTT test, were used to investigate SNCD biocompatibility and the anticancer performance of DSF-SNCDs.

**RESULTS**: The FTIR spectra confirmed effective thiol functionalization and revealed oxygenated and nitrogenous groups on the particle surface suitable for disulfide linkage formation. DSF loading efficiency reached approximately 75%. Under non-reducing conditions, DSF-SNCDs exhibited minimal premature release (≤30% over 24 h at pH 7.4 and 5.4), demonstrating an "Off" state. In contrast, the presence of 5% (w/v) GSH at pH 5.4 triggered rapid DSF release, achieving approximately 80% cumulative release within 24 h, corresponding to the "On" state through reductive disulfide bond cleavage. Bare SNCDs showed high biocompatibility (>85% cell viability at 50 µg/mL), whereas DSF-SNCDs produced significantly enhanced cytotoxicity under GSH conditions, confirming redox-activated drug release.

**CONCLUSION**: SNCDs provide an effective GSH-responsive nanoplatform for DSF delivery, combining high drug loading, excellent stability under non-reducing conditions, and efficient intracellular drug release under reductive environments. This strategy minimizes premature drug leakage while enhancing anticancer activity, demonstrating strong potential for cancer therapy.

Globally, cancer remains a critical public health crisis, consistently ranking as a primary cause of mortality despite significant advancements in modern medicine. 1  Traditional chemotherapy is frequently constrained by a lack of selectivity, hindering its broader clinical utility. To overcome these limitations, targeting the tumor microenvironment (TME) offers a promising alternative. Unlike conventional methods, TME-responsive strategies enable more precise, localized drug delivery. This approach leverages the distinct physiological hallmarks of malignant cells—such as elevated concentrations of reactive oxygen species (ROS), increased glutathione (GSH) levels, acidic pH, and unique enzyme overexpression—to trigger drug release only within the pathological site, thereby distinguishing them from healthy tissues. 2 , 3  For instance, nanocarriers engineered with dual-responsive motifs can facilitate the controlled release of drug in response to specific redox potential (glutathione overexpression) and localized acidic environments. 4 , 5  In contrast to low-micromolar extracellular/plasma GSH in humans (typically about 1–6 μM, with a representative value of 2.8 ± 0.91 μM reported in healthy adults), intracellular GSH in tumor cells is generally in the millimolar range, commonly about 1–10 mM, ie, roughly 10 3 -fold higher than plasma and redox-sensitive advanced drug delivery systems were formulated by taking advantage of the elevated GSH concentration in tumor cells. 6–8

Clinicians have utilized disulfiram (DSF) to treat alcohol use disorder for more than half a century. 9  However, it has also shown promise as an anticancer agent due to its ability to inhibit multiple signaling pathways involved in cancer progression and metastasis. Numerous studies have demonstrated the strong anticancer potential of this compound against a broad spectrum of malignancies. 10  Despite these potential benefits, DSF’s clinical translation has been limited by poor solubility and low bioavailability. To overcome these challenges and enhance the therapeutic efficacy of DSF in cancer treatment, researchers have explored nanoparticle-based delivery systems. 11  Although encapsulating or conjugating DSF onto nanoparticles like polymer nanoparticles, liposomes, and nano-emulsions includes several advantages such as enhancing both the stability and solubility of DSF in physiological conditions, drug’s effectiveness, greater control over the release profile of the drug, prolonged circulation time within the body and provide opportunities for active targeting strategies by functionalizing their surfaces (this approach enables accumulation of DSF-loaded nanoparticles at tumor sites while minimizing off-target effects on healthy tissues) but many still suffer from premature leakage, poor aqueous dispersibility and…. 12 , 13  DSF can also encapsulated within carriers or nanoparticles through disulfide bridges. Hence, increased GSH levels inside cells can enhance the release of therapeutics from nanoparticles. 14

Fluorescent carbon dots (CDs) loaded with therapeutic agents have been developed for various applications, including drug delivery and cellular imaging. 15 , 16  This is mainly attributed to their biocompatibility and low toxicity, as well as distinctive optical properties, including remarkable photostability, and strong fluorescence emission that can be manipulated by adjusting particle size, surface chemistry, and excitation wavelength. 17  In contrast to many conventional polymeric or inorganic nanocarriers, carbon dots can simultaneously serve as nanoscale drug-delivery platforms and intrinsically fluorescent components, enabling monitoring of their physicochemical behavior and cellular interactions. Their biological performance is strongly governed by surface chemistry; therefore, rational surface functionalization is essential to control drug loading, colloidal stability, cellular uptake, and stimulus-responsive release. 18  Nitrogen doping was selected in the present study because incorporation of nitrogen-containing functionalities can modify the electronic structure, surface polarity, charge distribution, and density of reactive sites of carbon dots. These features may improve aqueous stability and provide additional hydrogen-bonding, electrostatic, and other noncovalent interactions with drug molecules. Nitrogen doping can also enhance the photoluminescence properties of carbon dots, thereby facilitating their characterization and potentially enabling optical tracking of the nanocarrier. Nevertheless, the contribution of nitrogen doping should be interpreted in the context of the whole surface structure, since the final properties of carbon dots depend on the introduction composition, reaction conditions, particle size, and distribution of surface groups. 19 , 20  CDs coated with amino and carboxyl groups have been used as a carrier for doxorubicin (DOX) as a model drug. 21  Pei et al 22  designed a carbon dot-templated star-like copolymer prodrug system that achieves tumor-specific delivery via pH- and reduction-sensitive dual-release mechanisms. Nair et al 23  reviewed the use of natural carbon-based quantum dots for drug delivery applications, highlighting their diverse functionality and biocompatibility. Wei et al 24  reported the synthesis of green-emitting carbon quantum dots co-doped with nitrogen and sulfur, and showed their suitability for cellular imaging applications. Chung et al 25  also designed nanoparticles composed of iron oxide and carbon dots that functioned as fluorescent agents for cancer imaging and drug delivery. Herein, the introduction of sulfur-containing or thiol-enriched surface functionalities was considered particularly relevant to the development of a redox-responsive disulfiram-delivery system. Thiol groups can alter the surface hydrophilicity, charge, and chemical reactivity of carbon dots and may provide additional interactions with disulfiram or with linker structures used for drug attachment. More importantly, thiol/disulfide chemistry used in intracellular redox-responsive delivery because the glutathione concentration is substantially higher in the cytosol than in the extracellular environment. In principle, GSH can participate in thiol–disulfide exchange reactions and destabilize disulfide-containing linkages, thereby promoting the release of a conjugated or associated payload. Thus, sulfur-containing surface modification was introduced to provide a chemically plausible basis for redox responsiveness, rather than merely to increase the loading capacity of the nanodots. Thus, thiol-functionalized nitrogen-doped carbon dots (SNCDs) were synthesized and conjugated with DSF. A GSH-triggered DSF-SNCD nano-delivery platform may improve the precision and release behavior of DSF in MCF-7 human tumor cells, ultimately enhancing its therapeutic potential. Under GSH-rich reducing conditions, the nanocarrier exhibited a stimulus-responsive release profile, with markedly accelerated DSF release compared with the GSH-free condition.

To our knowledge, this study presents the first GSH-responsive DSF-SNCD nanocarrier for targeted delivery of disulfiram to cells with increased GSH content. In addition, the anticancer toxicity of DSF-SNCDs was compared against the effect of unencapsulated DSF. This study highlights the versatility and potential of carbon dots as fluorescent probes for cell imaging and drug delivery applications.

The citric acid (98% purity), urea, glutathione, and phosphate buffered saline (PBS) were obtained from Merck Company (Merck, Germany) and used without any further purification. Culture medium (DMEM), fetal bovine serum (FBS), and trypsin-ethylenediamine tetra acetic acid X10 were prepared from Biosera Company (Biosera, England). Breast cancer cells MCF-7 cell were purchased from the National Cell Bank of Iran (Pasteur Institute, Tehran, Iran). Quinine hemisulfate (95% purity), disulfiram, dithiothreitol (DTT), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) (98% purity), and Thiazolyl blue tetrazolium bromide (MTT, 98% purity) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich, Germany. All chemicals were analytical grade and used as supplied. Deionized water was employed for preparing all aqueous solutions.

HRTEM images of the prepared SNCDs were obtained using a JEOL JEM-2100 instrument operated at 200 kV for structural characterization. The optical absorption spectra in the ultraviolet–visible region was recorded spectrophotometrically using an Agilent Cary 60 instrument (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, USA). Fluorescence spectra were measured by a spectrofluorometer (Carry Eclipse, Varian, Australia). FT-IR analysis was carried out on a TENSOR 27 instrument (Bruker, Germany) employing KBr pellets. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis by Zetasizer Nano S (Malvern Instruments Ltd., USA) was used to determine the average hydrodynamic particle size.

N-doped CDs were produced by dissolving citric acid (0.5 g) and urea (1.5 g) in 7 mL of dimethyl sulfoxide under constant stirring. The resulting uniform mixture was then poured into an autoclave lined with Teflon and subjected to heating at 160 °C for 4 h. The synthesis was accompanied by a pronounced color shift from colorless to dark brown, indicating the formation of nitrogen-doped carbon dots. Once cooling to ambient, the colloidal product was centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 20 minutes to remove large aggregates. The supernatant was collected and dialyzed against distilled water for 24 hours using a dialysis membrane with a molecular weight cut-off (MWCO) of 3.5 kDa to remove unreacted precursors and small molecular impurities. The purified product was freeze-dried using a vacuum freeze-dryer, yielding a dark brown powder of NCDs, which was stored for further use. For characterization and subsequent functionalization, the NCDs were redispersed in distilled water at the desired concentration.

To sulfur functionalize the synthesized NCDs, 0.08 g of dithiothreitol (DTT) was added to 3 mL of an aqueous NCD colloid. The mixture was stirred continuously at room temperature for 24 hours to ensure thorough functionalization. After the reaction, the sulfur-functionalized NCDs (SNCDs) were purified to remove unreacted DTT and other byproducts using a dialysis membrane (MWCO 3.5 kDa) against distilled water for 24 hours. After preparation, the SNCD colloid (10 mg/mL) was maintained at 4 °C for further studies.

The DSF-SNCDs were prepared by exploiting the formation of disulfide bonds between DSF and the thiol groups on the SNCDs. Specifically, 210 µL of the SNCDs colloid (10 mg/mL) was added dropwise to 3 mL of a DSF solution (250 µg/mL in distilled water) under vigorous stirring. The mixture was allowed to react for 24 hours at room temperature to ensure maximum loading of DSF onto the SNCDs. The colloid was then transferred into a dialysis membrane (MWCO 3.5 kDa) and dialyzed against distilled water overnight to remove unbound DSF. The concentration of free DSF in the dialysate was determined by measuring the absorbance at 280 nm spectrophotometrically, using a calibration curve constructed from standard DSF solutions in deionized water ( Figure S1 ). The drug loading efficiency (DLE) was calculated based on the initial and final concentrations of DSF.

A dialysis-based diffusion system was set up to track the release pattern of the DSF from the nanoparticles under simulated conditions. First, two milliliters of as prepared DSF-SNCDs colloid were transferred into a dialysis bag (MWCO 3.5 kDa), and then the dialysis bag was incubated in 20 mL of PBS buffer at pH 7.4 and 5.4 with or without GSH (5% w/v). Thermal and mechanical control was applied by keeping the release environment at 37 ± 1 °C under 100 rpm shaking for a 24 h period. To ensure the maintenance of sink conditions, 3 mL of the supernatant was periodically withdrawn and replaced with an identical volume of fresh PBS buffer over the duration of the experiment. The amount of DSF released from the nanocarrier was calculated using the calibration plot of DSF in PBS solution by measuring the absorbance at 280 nm. To monitor and eliminate any potential UV–Vis absorbance contribution arising from background S-NCD leaching, a parallel control experiment was conducted under identical conditions using 2.0 mL of pristine, drug-free S-NCDs inside a dialysis bag. To determine the profiles of DSF release from the SNCD nanoconjugates, the cumulative release fraction at successive intervals was calculated according to the following relation.

Cell viability was evaluated via the MTT reduction assay, following the established protocol. 26  Initially, MCF-7 cell suspensions were aliquoted into 96-well culture plates at a seeding density of 5 × 10 3  cells/well, utilizing high-glucose DMEM fortified with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% antibiotic/antimycotic reagents. The cultures were allowed to adhere for 24 h at 37 °C within a 5% CO 2  humidified incubator. Following this, the culture medium was exchanged for fresh medium incorporating varying concentrations of SNCDs, DSF-SNCDs, or pure DSF, and the plates were incubated for an additional 48 h. To quantify metabolic activity, the supernatant was removed, followed by a gentle PBS wash. Each well was then treated with 20 μL of MTT solution (5 mg/mL). Following a 4-hour incubation period at 37 °C, the MTT solution was aspirated, and 150 μL of DMSO was introduced to each well to facilitate the dissolution of the resulting formazan precipitates. After 10 minutes of mechanical agitation, the optical density was recorded at 570 nm utilizing a Wellscan Mk3 microplate reader (Labsystems Dragon Ltd, Finland).

It is well known that GSH plays a crucial role in the human body, where it can be oxidized to glutathione disulfide (GSSG) in a normal tissue microenvironment. In the presence of NADPH-dependent glutathione reductase, GSSG is regenerated to GSH, thereby supporting redox equilibrium essential for cellular function and survival. 27  By comparison, tumor cells generally maintain much higher intracellular GSH levels (approximately 2–20 mM) because of their altered microenvironment, growth-related nutrient demands, and genetic abnormalities. 4 , 28  The key goal of this work is to construct a nanocarrier that remains stable in non-reducing environments (“Off” state) while rapidly releasing DSF in reducing cancer cells media (“On” state).  Scheme 1  clearly depicts the release behavior of the redox-responsive drug delivery system. Thiol-functionalized N-doped carbon quantum dots (SNCDs) provide a multifunctional surface suitable for DSF immobilization through disulfide chemistry. In healthy tissues media (low reducing power), disulfide linkages remain intact, limiting DSF leakage. The nanocarrier accumulates in tumor tissues through the enhanced permeability and retention effect during prolonged blood circulation in the presence of strong redox potential, the responsive linker decomposes, resulting in the collapse of the nanocarrier structure and prompt liberation of the encapsulated drugs. This mechanism allows for precise delivery, rapid drug release, and minimal side effects, leveraging the reduction potential gradient between cancerous and healthy cells.
 Scheme 1 Redox-responsive system for drug delivery to cancer cells. A step-by-step schematic shows a nanoparticle labeled DSF-SNCD on the left with multiple disulfide (S to S) linkages highlighted in red and yellow, alongside scissors icons marking cleavage sites. A curved arrow labeled GSH points to the right toward a starburst reading High GSH, indicating an intracellular reducing environment. On the right, the particle is labeled SNCD, depicting the carrier after bond cleavage, with small molecular fragments shown as released cargo. A dotted blue bilayer labeled Tumor Cell represents the cell membrane and an oval labeled Nucleolus sits inside the cell to indicate the intracellular destination region. Schematic of disulfide-linked nanocarrier cleaved by glutathione inside a tumor cell.

We utilized a straightforward one-pot hydrothermal technique to produce NCDs, with citric acid serving as the primary carbon source, urea as the nitrogen source. For thiol functionalization of NCDs and facilitate their attachment to the drug via a covalent disulfide bond, DTT was utilized. NCDs typically exhibit significant ultraviolet absorption band with tails even reach into the visible spectrum. 29  When the SNCDs are exposed to light from a 365 nm lamp, they exhibit a distinct and vibrant blue color. The particle size, surface engineering, and heteroatom doping of SNCDs strongly influence their optical properties, thereby expanding their applicability. Among these factors, nitrogen doping is particularly beneficial because it enhances aqueous solubility without the need for additional agents and simultaneously improves the photoluminescence efficiency of carbon dots. 30  The UV-Vis spectrum of our SNCDs solution ( Figure 1 ) exhibits absorption band at wavelength of 240 nm, which can be attributed to the π-π* transition of the aromatic C=C sp 2  domains. 20  The other strong absorption peak at 340 is assigned to the n–π* transition of possible C=O or C=N groups present in SNCDs structure, and the shoulder around 480 nm is given to multiple surface defect states. 31  Similar to previous reports, 32 , 33  the peak at 620 nm shows that our SNCDs are in an oxidized state. It was observed that the optical features of the carbon dots are significantly dictated by the functional groups present on their surface.
 Figure 1 Electronic absorption spectrum of colloidal SNCDs. A line graph showing absorbance versus wavelength for a colloidal SNCDs.

Figure 2A  Shows that the SNCDs colloid can emit a bright blue fluorescence emission centered at 460 nm when excited at 365 nm. As shown in  Figure 2B , by increasing the excitation wavelengths from 345 nm to 375 nm, the emission peaks showed red-shift (~ 20 nm) to longer wavelengths owing to the varied band gaps from different surface states of CDs. 34  The SNCDs achieved their highest fluorescence intensity at an emission of 460 nm with 365 nm excitation. As documented in prior studies, the excitation-dependent emission observed in the synthesized SNCDs is primarily attributed to quantum confinement and surface-defect states. 35  Moreover,  Figure 2C  illustrates that the fluorescence intensity increases with the concentration of the aqueous SNCD colloid. Notably, the inset demonstrates a linear relationship between the fluorescence intensity at 460 nm and the SNCD concentration.

DLS measurements ( Figure 3A ) revealed a hydrodynamic size of 2 ± 1 nm. Furthermore, TEM imaging ( Figure 3B ) revealed spherical, uniformly dispersed SNCDs with an average diameter of approximately 3 nm.
 Figure 3 DLS analysis ( A ) and TEM image (scale bar: 5 nm) ( B ) of SNCDs. A line graph showing DLS analysis and a transmission electron microscopy micrograph showing SNCDs size characteristics.

The functional groups of the SNCDs were detected using FTIR analysis and presented in  Figure 4 . The FT-IR spectrum exhibits a prominent broad absorption band between 3000 and 3500 cm −1 , indicative of N–H and O–H stretching, which substantiates the incorporation of nitrogen within the SNCDs. Spectral features at 1673 cm −1 , 1622 cm −1 , and 1436 cm −1  are assigned to C=O stretching (carboxyl groups), N–H bending, and C–H bending modes, respectively. 36  Furthermore, the absorption at 1027 cm −1  represents C–O stretching, while the peak appearing at 1314 cm −1  is characteristic of C–N stretching. The signals at 2913 cm −1  and 2999 cm −1  arise from the symmetric and asymmetric stretching of CH 2  units. 37  C–S stretching vibrations are identified within the 703–785 cm −1  region, 38  and the bands noted between 2550 and 2600 cm −1  are attributed to the S–H stretching of thiol moieties. 39

To calculate the SNCD quantum yield, the slope of the integrated emission (λem = 460 nm) versus absorbance (λex = 365 nm) plot ( Figure 5A ) was calculated and compared to the reference data for quinine hemisulfate ( Figure 5B ) using the slope method. A quantum yield of 5.2% was obtained for the SNCDs. This level of photoluminescence, resulting from the urea/citric acid hydrothermal route and thiol modification, reflects an enhancement relative to various other carbon quantum dot systems documented in the literature. 26

Encouraged by the unique nanoscale structure and high specific surface area of SNCDs, DSF was chosen as a model anticancer agent and loaded onto SNCDs. To establish a reliable DSF quantification method for drug loading calculations, UV–Vis spectroscopy was used. DSF shows a strong characteristic absorption peak at 280 nm, which was selected as the analytical wavelength for concentration determination ( Figure S1A ). The LE was ~75%, indicating that SNCDs possess excellent drug loading capacity. This high LE is consistent with the presence of abundant surface functional groups and strong drug–carrier interactions, and it also supports the low premature release observed under non-reducing conditions ( Figure 6 ).

To evaluate controlled release behavior and stimulus responsiveness, cumulative DSF release from DSF‑SNCDs was investigated ( Figure 6 ). Free DSF exhibited a rapid burst release, with >90% diffusion into the medium within ~15 h, reflecting weak retention in the absence of a carrier. In contrast, DSF‑SNCDs displayed substantially suppressed release at both pH 7.4 and pH 5.4 in the absence of reductant, with cumulative release remaining ≤~30% after 24 h. The relatively small difference between pH 7.4 and 5.4 indicates that pH alone does not govern drug liberation, confirming that DSF is largely retained on the carrier (“Off” state) under non-reducing conditions.

Upon introduction of GSH (5% w/v in outside solution of dialysis bag) at pH 5.4, a pronounced increase in DSF release was observed, reaching ~80% at 24 h. This “On” state is attributed to GSH-mediated cleavage of disulfide linkages (reductive/thiol–disulfide exchange processes), enabling accelerated liberation of DSF in reducing environments. Collectively, these profiles demonstrate that DSF‑SNCDs behave primarily as a redox-responsive system rather than a purely pH-responsive carrier, thereby minimizing premature leakage while enabling intracellular activation.

The biocompatibility of the carrier and the redox-triggered therapeutic action were assessed by MTT assay on MCF‑7 cells ( Figure 7 ). Previous studies presented that nitrogen doped carbon dots were not cytotoxicity to MCF-7 cells. 20  As shown in  Figure 7 , Bare SNCDs (CQD) showed excellent cytocompatibility, maintaining near-normal cell viability across the tested concentrations and remaining >~85% viable at 50 µg/mL, indicating low inherent toxicity of the nanocarrier.
 Figure 7 Cytotoxicity of SNCDs with different concentrations for MCF-7 cells. (Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3)). A grouped bar graph showing cell viability for CQD, CQD and Drug, CQD and Drug in the presence of glutathione and Drug across concentration.

Free DSF exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, as expected. Notably, DSF‑loaded SNCDs (CQD‑D) in the absence of GSH caused lower cytotoxicity than free DSF, consistent with restricted DSF availability in the “Off” state. However, in the presence of GSH (CQD‑D + G), cell viability decreased sharply in a concentration-dependent manner; importantly, viability dropped to ~50% at 6.25 µg/mL, confirming that reducing conditions unlock the drug activity. This behavior directly supports the “Off–On” release mechanism observed in the release studies ( Figure 6 ) and indicates that SNCDs can effectively deliver DSF in a GSH-rich environment, potentially enhancing therapeutic selectivity.

In the in vitro release experiments, a reduced glutathione (GSH) concentration of 5% w/v (~163 mM) was introduced into the external release medium (outside the dialysis bag). While the effective local concentration experienced by the nanocarrier is modulated by the dialysis membrane molecular weight cut-off (MWCO), diffusion kinetics, and compartment volume ratios, we acknowledge that this represents a supranormal, accelerated reducing challenge rather than a direct simulation of the tumor microenvironment (TME). The release data presented herein should be interpreted as proof-of-concept evidence demonstrating the intrinsic redox responsiveness and cleavage kinetics of the nanocarrier under strong reducing stress, rather than as a direct quantitative prediction of in vivo drug release behavior. Future studies will systematically evaluate drug release and stability across a physiologically relevant GSH gradient to comprehensively elucidate the in vivo-mimicking release kinetics.

In conclusion, thiol-functionalized nitrogen-doped carbon quantum dots (SNCDs) were synthesized and evaluated as a glutathione (GSH)-responsive nanocarrier for disulfiram (DSF) delivery based on redox-cleavable linkages. Spectrophotometric analysis demonstrated an efficient drug loading capacity of ~75%. In vitro release profiles exhibited comparatively low drug liberation under non-reducing physiological and mildly acidic conditions (pH 7.4 and 5.4; ≤30% at 24 h), whereas the presence of GSH markedly triggered DSF release (~80% at 24 h). Cell viability assays indicated the cytocompatibility of blank SNCDs and demonstrated enhanced cytotoxicity of DSF-SNCDs against MCF-7 cells under redox-active conditions, which is consistent with the trigger-dependent release behavior observed in cell-free assays. Overall, these preliminary in vitro findings demonstrate the proof-of-concept potential of DSF-SNCDs for redox-responsive drug delivery with suppressed premature leakage. However, comprehensive cellular uptake studies, intracellular mechanistic analyses, and in vivo evaluations remain essential to fully determine their systemic biosafety, biodistribution, and therapeutic applicability.
