In this cross-sectional study, we assessed oncology patients’ awareness and knowledge of chemotherapy regimens and adverse events and explored their association with prior emergency visits and hospital admissions. In our cohort, the majority of patients (~69%) were classified as having moderate to high awareness based on self-report and concordance with EMR-verified information. This awareness classification was associated with greater knowledge of treatment goals, regimens, and side effects. Awareness was not independently associated with ED visits or hospital admissions. Instead, higher utilization was associated with limited English fluency for ED visits and with female gender for hospital admissions.

Comparable studies in different settings have reported variable levels of patient knowledge. In a Saudi study, only 8% of patients achieved high knowledge scores regarding chemotherapy and its side effects. 7  Similarly, a descriptive study from Pakistan reported that although patients expressed positive attitudes toward chemotherapy, their actual knowledge and practices were limited. 14  In Japan, educational level significantly influenced comprehension of chemotherapy among outpatients. 15  In contrast, Patients in our study report a higher self-perceived knowledge; however, discrepancies with EMR data suggest overestimation of awareness. These findings reinforce the notion that, while patients may appear to self-report high awareness, objective measurement in the EMR often reveals discrepancies.

Language proficiency and health communication are critical determinants of the quality of oncology care. In our study, limited English proficiency was independently associated with higher ED visits, with a similar but non-significant trend for hospital admissions, indicating that communication barriers may contribute to reactive rather than preventive healthcare use. This finding aligns with multiple lines of evidence. In a statewide telephone survey of 1,200 Californians, limited-English-proficient respondents were significantly more likely to report difficulties understanding medical information and adverse medication reactions, even when treated by language-concordant physicians (adjusted OR 3.2 and 2.3, respectively), underscoring persistent comprehension gaps despite interpreter or bilingual support. 16  Likewise, a study by Diamond et al systematically reviewed 33 studies and found that language-concordant care improved at least one clinical or communication outcome in 76% of studies, highlighting the protective effect of shared language on comprehension and adherence. 17  At the systems level, Chen et al demonstrated that non-English-speaking callers were far less likely to be provided access to cancer care than English-speaking callers, revealing structural communication barriers from the very first point of contact. 18  Collectively, these studies illustrate how language discordance operates throughout the cancer-care continuum, from access and comprehension to adherence and unplanned utilization, emphasizing the need for multilingual educational materials, interpreter integration, and culturally adapted counseling to reduce disparities and improve patient outcomes. 16–19

In our cohort, awareness was not independently associated with ED visits once demographic factors were accounted for, indicating that knowledge alone did not drive unplanned care. The frequency of ED visits and admissions may also be influenced by the quality of outpatient and discharge education provided to patients. Hence, education without clear symptom-triage guidance may increase cautious healthcare-seeking behavior. 20–23  These findings suggest that awareness alone may not translate into lower unplanned care without concurrent improvements in access to outpatient triage and same-day oncology review pathways.

Female gender was the principal correlate of hospital admission in our cohort, a finding aligned with reports that women often report symptoms earlier and utilize emergency services more frequently than men. 22  Together with language-related disparities, these findings highlight the complex social, behavioral, and system-level factors shaping oncology care and unplanned hospital use. Organizations should provide clear, well-structured, comprehensible, and language-appropriate education on chemotherapy regimens and their potential adverse effects. One study found that almost half of oncology patients’ ED visits and admissions are preventable. 23  Hence, integrating oncology pharmacists and patient educators to deliver reinforcement using visual aids, simplified language, and teach-back techniques can improve retention and decrease the risk of ED visits. 24 , 25  Oncology educational programs should also emphasize appropriate healthcare-seeking behaviors, clarifying which symptoms require urgent attention versus those that can be managed routinely, to avoid unnecessary ED visits. Interventions such as 24/7 nurse or pharmacist telephone triage, multilingual discharge materials, and culturally tailored counseling may help shift utilization from unplanned emergency care toward proactive outpatient management. Hence, the value of integration of organized patient education, especially those faced with language barriers could help manage their symptoms along with the assistance of outpatient triaging.

This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the cross-sectional design precludes establishing temporal or causal relationships between awareness and healthcare utilization. Because awareness showed no independent association with either outcome, reverse causation does not affect the study’s central findings, which instead identify female gender and limited English proficiency as the main correlates of higher utilization. Second, the study was conducted at a single center, which may limit generalizability to other settings within Saudi Arabia. Third, the questionnaire was investigator-developed and, although reviewed for face and content validity and pilot tested for clarity and feasibility, additional psychometric validation was not performed. Therefore, the awareness classification should be interpreted as an operational study-specific measure rather than a fully validated latent construct. Fourth, residual confounding by unmeasured clinical variables remains possible, including performance status, line of therapy, comorbidity burden, and regimen-specific toxicity risk. Fifth, self-reported responses are subject to recall and social desirability bias, and some participants may have overestimated their understanding of their diagnosis or treatment. Although EMR verification reduced some of this variability, discrepancies between self-report and documented information remained. Sixth, some ED visits or hospitalizations occurring outside the study institution may not have been fully captured. Finally, the heterogeneity of cancer types, treatment regimens, and disease stages in the sample may have influenced both awareness and healthcare utilization patterns.

Patient awareness of chemotherapy was generally high but uneven across domains, with gaps in identifying regimens and in defining treatment goals. Awareness was not independently associated with ED visits or hospital admissions; female gender and limited English proficiency were the principal correlates of higher utilization. Future studies should test whether integrating structured education with proactive symptom-management pathways can reduce unplanned care, particularly for patients with language barriers and those receiving high-toxicity regimens.

## Design, synthesis,

**PMID**: 42761633 · **Journal**: RSC advances · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1039/d6ra06404c · **PMCID**: PMC13588121

**Authors**: Said Gehad E, Samy Sonia, Abdel-Galil Ebrahim, Gaffer Hatem E, Abdel-Latif Ehab

**Types**: Journal Article

A novel series of thiazole, thiazolidin-4-one, and chromene derivatives incorporating a 4-methylbenzenesulfonate (tosylate) moiety were designed, synthesized, and evaluated for their anticancer potential. All structures were elucidated using IR, 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and MS spectroscopy. Anticancer potential was assessed by MTT assay against HepG-2 (hepatocellular carcinoma) and MCF-7 (breast cancer) cell lines, with doxorubicin as a reference. Against MCF-7, compounds 3d (IC50 = 28.2 ± 2.08 µM), 6a (30.0 ± 0.82 µM), and 8a (25.9 ± 1.35 µM) exhibited relatively enhanced cytotoxicity. For HepG-2, derivatives 3a (46.5 ± 1.23 µM), 3e (49.1 ± 0.95 µM), and 3d (54.6 ± 1.34 µM) showed moderate cytotoxic activity relative to doxorubicin. Also, all the synthesized compounds were subjected to molecular docking against the receptor (PDB ID: 1X7B) when compared with the standard drug doxorubicin. However, 3b had the best binding energy (6.4543 kcal mol-1), resulting in a π-cation interaction with phenyl and Lys471, and was closely followed by 3c (6.3568 kcal mol-1), 8c (6.3141 kcal mol-1), and 8b (6.3020 kcal mol-1). From DFT analysis on the most active molecules 3d, 6a, and 8a, it is clear that molecule 8a exhibits the lowest energy difference between its HOMO and LUMO orbitals (E gap = 3.39 eV) as well as highest molecular softness value (δ = 0.59), which may contribute to its enhanced chemical reactivity and observed biological activity compared to other molecules. Moreover, the pharmacokinetic characteristics of the thirteen synthesized analogues using SwissADME exhibited poor solubility, possessed low GI absorption, and unveiled no BBB permeability. The newly developed analogs possessed a high lipophilicity, larger polar surface area and poor predicted gastrointestinal absorption, mainly due to the presence of the sulfonamide/sulfonate-functionalized core structure. In addition to this, some of the compounds exhibited an inhibitory effect on some of the important CYP450 enzymes (CYP2C19, CYP2C9 and/or CYP3A4). The pharmacokinetic challenges pose a great need to optimize the structures before preclinical evaluation. Overall, this study provides integrated experimental and computational insights into the anticancer potential of tosylate-bearing heterocyclic scaffolds, addressing gaps in understanding their structure-activity relationships. The identified promising compounds may serve as useful starting points for further structural optimization and mechanistic studies toward the development of improved anticancer candidates.

Cancer is still a major public health problem throughout the world and remains one of the leading causes of death. According to recent global cancer statistics, approximately 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer-related deaths were reported worldwide in 2022, highlighting the urgent need for the development of more effective and safer anticancer agents. Furthermore, cancer is estimated to affect approximately one in five individuals during their lifetime, whereas nearly one in nine men and one in twelve women die from cancer-related causes worldwide. The global cancer burden is expected to increase substantially, reaching approximately 35 million new cases annually by 2050. 1  This growing global burden has driven intensive research toward more effective and safer therapeutic strategies, including targeted drug-delivery approaches and the design of novel anticancer agents with improved selectivity and reduced off-target toxicity. 2–8  Many anticancer drugs are heterocyclic compounds, which contain rings with atoms like nitrogen, oxygen, or sulfur. These compounds can mimic natural substrates and target enzymes or receptors in the cancer cells. They often show antiproliferative properties by inducing apoptosis or by inhibiting key pathways. 9–12

Thiazole derivatives are an important class of nitrogen–sulfur heterocycles that have attracted considerable interest because of the diverse chemical and functional properties associated with N- and S-containing compounds. 13  They exhibit a remarkably wide spectrum of biological activities, including anticancer, 14–16  antimicrobial, 17  anti-inflammatory, 18  antidiabetic, 19  antioxidant, 20  and anticonvulsant activity. 21  Recently, newly developed thiazole-based scaffolds have attracted considerable attention because of their strong antiproliferative effects against a variety of cancer cell lines. These compounds exert their anticancer activity through multiple mechanisms, including the induction of apoptosis, disruption of cell cycle progression, and inhibition of important molecular targets such as EGFR, VEGFR-2, topoisomerases, and Akt-associated signaling pathways. 22,23  Thiazole-based scaffolds are promising candidates for the development of next-generation therapeutic agents because of their broad spectrum of biological activities, such as antioxidant, cytotoxic, and antibacterial effects, as well as improved selectivity and reduced off-target toxicity. 24,25  The thiazole core is also found in many common and widely used anti-cancer drugs such as tiazofurin, bleomycin, and dasatinib ( Fig. 1 ).

Thiazolidine is an important and peculiar scaffold in medicinal chemistry containing a 5-membered heterocyclic ring system with the cyclic amide bond and sulfur. 26,27  Many studies have been performed to investigate the various biological activities of this nucleus, which may have therapeutic uses. 28–31  Thiazolidin-4-one is an effective scaffold for the development of drugs that inhibit the growth of cancer cells. 32,33  Development of innovative thiazolidin-4-one-containing drugs was established,  e.g. , etozolin (new diuretics), darbufelone (dual COX-2/5-LOX inhibitors), and hypoglycemic thiazolidinones (pioglitazone and its derivatives) 34–36  ( Fig. 1 ).

Chromene derivatives have a very wide range of biological, therapeutic, and pharmacological activities, such as hypolipidemic, 37  antioxidant, 38  antidiabetic, 39,40  antiviral activity against influenza viruses A and B, 41  antileishmanial, 42  anticancer, 43  antimicrobial, 44,45  anti-HIV, 46  and insecticidal properties. 47  Moreover, the introduction of hydrophobic substituents such as in benzo[ f ]chromene induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis by concurrent inhibition of the topoisomerases I and II. 48  Crolibulin, a 4-aryl-4 H -chromene derivative, is one of the most potent anticancer agents among the chromene analogs that have been reported recently 49  ( Fig. 1 ).

Interestingly, thiazole, thiazolidin-4-one, chromene, and tosylate derivatives represent privileged scaffolds known for their broad biological activities, including anticancer effects ( Fig. 1 ). It was reported that 3-(2-(1-((4-methoxy-3-(piperidin-1-ylsulfonyl)phenyl)ethylidene)hydrazineylidene)-2,3-dihydrothiazol-4-yl)-2 H -chromen-2-one (Compound I) ( Fig. 1 ) exhibited potent cytotoxicity against HepG2 and MCF-7 cell lines with IC 50  (6.35 and 7.70 µM), respectively in comparison to sorafenib with IC 50  (4 and 5.58 µM) and erlotinib with IC 50  (7.73 and 8.20 µM). 50  5-((5-Bromo-2-(3-bromo-2-(l3-methyl)phenoxy)phenyl)methylene)-2-thioxothiazolidin-4-one (Compound II) enhanced potency as a PRL-3 inhibitor with an IC 50  value of 0.9 µM in comparison to pentamidine (IC 50  = 53.6 µM). 51  Also, 2-imino-6-((3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)diazenyl)-2 H -chromene-3-carboxamide (Compound III) demonstrated high potency against MCF-7 with IC 50  = 7.82 µM in comparison to sorafenib (IC 50  = 7.26 µM). 52  Interestingly, sorafenib tosylate is approved by the USFDA to treat hepatocellular carcinoma, thyroid cancer, and kidney cancer 53  ( Fig. 1 ). Additionally, molecular hybridization through the incorporation of functional linkers, particularly amide, hydrazide-hydrazone, and azo moieties, has become a widely employed approach in anticancer drug discovery. These linkers not only connect two or more bioactive pharmacophores but also contribute directly to biological activity through hydrogen-bonding interactions, electronic modulation, and favorable spatial orientation of the pharmacophoric units. Consequently, numerous recent reports have revealed enhanced cytotoxic and target-specific anticancer activities for heterocyclic hybrids containing such linker functionalities 54,55  ( Fig. 1 ). Although the previously reported Compound I exhibited substantially higher cytotoxic potency than the newly synthesized derivatives, this comparison highlights that structural modification of the hybrid scaffold does not necessarily translate into enhanced activity and provides useful SAR information for further optimization.

Based on these considerations, we designed and synthesized novel tosylate-bearing thiazole, thiazolidin-4-one, and chromene derivatives incorporating selected linker functionalities to explore their anticancer potential. The synthesized compounds were evaluated against HepG2 and MCF-7 cell lines, with 3d, 6a, and 8a showing the highest cytotoxic activity within the synthesized series. These compounds were further investigated using DFT, while molecular docking and pharmacokinetic analyses were performed to provide complementary insights into their electronic properties, binding behavior, and drug-likeness. Overall, this integrated approach addresses the limited systematic investigation of these hybrid scaffolds and provides useful insights into their structure–activity relationships, supporting further structural optimization and biological evaluation toward improved anticancer candidates.

The present work was started from 4-formylphenyl 4-methylbenzenesulfonate (1) as the key starting material for the construction of the newly designed heterocyclic scaffolds ( Scheme 1 ). Compound 1 was prepared according to the literature-reported procedure, 56  providing a reliable and reproducible access to the required aldehyde-tosylate building block. Refluxing compound 1 with thiosemicarbazide in ethyl alcohol afforded the thiosemicarbazone derivative 2, as reported in the literature. 57  The intermediate 4-((2-carbamothioylhydrazono)methyl)phenyl 4-methylbenzenesulfonate (2) was used as the core precursor in the next heterocyclization step. The cyclization step represents a crucial transformation in the synthetic pathway, as it enables the construction of the thiazole ring, which constitutes one of the core structural motifs of the target compounds. The successful ring closure not only increases the molecular complexity but also introduces a biologically privileged heterocyclic scaffold known for its broad spectrum of pharmacological activities. Cyclization reactions were performed under reflux in absolute ethanol using anhydrous sodium acetate (AcONa) as a mild base to promote nucleophilic attack and deprotonation. The  α -halo carbonyl reagents 4-methylphenacyl bromide, 4-methoxyphenacyl bromide, 2-bromo-1-(naphthalen-2-yl)ethan-1-one, 3-(2-bromoacetyl)-2 H -chromen-2-one, and 6-bromo-3-(2-bromoacetyl)-2 H -chromen-2-one were added sequentially, each of them promoting the formation of one new thiazole ring, affording the corresponding thiazole derivatives 3a–e ( Scheme 1 ) according to Hantzsch thiazole synthesis and the reaction mechanism depicted in  Scheme 2 .

The chemical structures of compounds 3a–e were unambiguously assigned by their spectral data (IR,  1 H NMR,  13 C NMR, and MS) and elemental analysis, which were in full agreement with the proposed thiazole framework. Thus, the IR spectrum of compound 3a showed the disappearance of the NH 2  group absorption band and the appearance of a characteristic absorption band at 3151 cm −1  that was assigned to the NH stretching vibration. In the  1 H NMR spectrum, four singlet signals were detected at 2.29, 2.40, 7.23, and 12.22 ppm corresponding to two methyl groups (2CH 3 ), the thiazole ring CH proton, and the NH proton, respectively. The  13 C NMR spectrum further supported the proposed structure of 3a, as signals appeared at 20.81, 21.19, and 167.97 ppm, corresponding to the two methyl carbons and the   carbon atoms of the thiazole ring.

In an analogous manner, the arylazothiazole derivatives 4a,b were prepared by reacting compound 2 with different hydrazonyl halides, specifically 2-oxo- N ,2-diphenylacetohydrazonoyl bromide and  N -(4-methoxyphenyl)-2-oxo-2-phenylacetohydrazonoyl bromide, in absolute ethyl alcohol in the presence of anhydrous AcONa ( Scheme 1 ). It is worth noting that the hydrazonyl halides employed in this transformation were prepared according to the previously reported procedure in the literature. 58  The elemental analysis and spectral data fully matched the proposed molecular structures of compounds 4a and 4b (see Experimental section).

Additionally, the target thiazolidin-4-one derivatives 6a–c were synthesized in a single step  via  Knoevenagel condensation between 4-formylphenyl 4-methylbenzenesulfonate (1) and functionalized thiazolidin-4-one compounds 5a, 5b, and 5c, which were prepared according to literature methods 59,60  ( Scheme 3 ). The assigned structures of the new thiazolidin-4-ones 6a–c were fully corroborated by spectral and analytical data. For example, the IR spectrum of compound 6a exhibited characteristic bands at 3264, 1671, and 1633 cm −1 , corresponding to the NH, C

Specifically, Knoevenagel condensation of compound 7 (ref.  61 ) with the aldehyde groups of various salicylaldehyde derivatives, namely, 5-bromo-2-hydroxybenzaldehyde, 2-hydroxy-5-(phenyldiazenyl)benzaldehyde, and 4-((3-formyl-4-hydroxyphenyl)diazenyl)benzenesulfonamide, followed by intramolecular cyclization through nucleophilic addition of the OH group to the CN moiety, yielded the target 2-iminochromene derivatives 8a–c, respectively, instead of arylidenes 9a–c ( Scheme 4 ). Additional evidence was obtained from the corresponding  1 H NMR,  13 C NMR, mass spectra, and elemental analyses, all of which were consistent with the proposed chromene structures (8a–c) (see Experimental section). For 2-iminochromene 8a, the IR spectrum displayed bands at  ν  3303, 1676, and 1637 cm −1  due to 2NH, C O, and C N vibrations. **In vitro  anticancer activity**

The synthesized derivatives of thiazole (3a–e, 4a,b, 6a–c) and chromene (8a–c) were evaluated for anticancer activity by an  in vitro  method against 2 human cancer cell lines, HepG2 (liver carcinoma) and MCF-7 (breast adenocarcinoma), using the MTT assay, and the cytotoxicity was expressed as IC 50  values (µM), the concentration required to inhibit 50% of cell growth. Doxorubicin, a representative anthracycline chemotherapeutic drug, was used as the positive control and exerted strong activity with IC 50  values of 8.52 ± 0.29 µM against HepG2 and 11.37 ± 0.12 µM against MCF-7, which were consistent with its known mechanism of DNA intercalation, topoisomerase II inhibition, and induction of apoptosis.  Fig. 2  presents a preliminary comparison of the growth-inhibitory effects of the synthesized compounds at a fixed concentration of 500 µM against each cell line. The compounds exhibited varying degrees of growth inhibition under these conditions. Since this concentration is relatively high compared with the IC 50  values of several derivatives, the single-dose results are considered supportive screening data, while the IC 50  values presented in  Table 1  provide the primary basis for comparing cytotoxic potency. Certain tested compounds showed enhanced cytotoxic activity, especially against MCF-7 cells. Compounds 3d (28.2 ± 2.08 µM), 8a (25.9 ± 1.35 µM), and 6a (30.0 ± 0.82 µM) displayed moderate cytotoxicity toward MCF-7, outperforming several analogs and approaching the efficacy of doxorubicin in this cell line, while exhibiting weaker or negligible activity against HepG2 (>100 µM for 6a, 91.3 ± 0.22 for 8a, and 54.6 ± 1.34 µM for 3d). This differential profile suggests possible cell-type-specific mechanisms that may be related to structural features such as substituent differences on the thiazole or chromene scaffolds that enhance the targeting of breast cancer cells, possibly through improved interactions with estrogen receptor pathways or altered membrane permeability in MCF-7 cells.

In contrast, the HepG2 panel showed limited overall potency with no compound achieving an IC 50  below 46.5 µM. The best activity was found for the derivatives 3a (46.5 ± 1.23 µM), 3e (49.1 ± 0.95 µM), and 3d (54.6 ± 1.34 µM) from the thiazole and thiazole-chromene hybrid series. This may mean that the interaction with HepG2-specific targets such as topoisomerase enzymes or DNA repair pathways, usually present in hepatocellular carcinoma, could be stabilized by the presence of electron-withdrawing or hydrophobic substituents. However, compounds 4b, 6a–6c, and 8b, 8c were basically inactive (>100 µM), suggesting that the thiazolidin-4-one and chromene modifications or extended substitutions probably lead to a decrease in bioavailability or binding affinity in hepatic cells.

The normal human lung fibroblast cell line (WI38) was used to evaluate the selectivity of the most active scaffolds 3d, 6a, and 8a against two cancer cells. The examined scaffolds 3d, 6a, and 8a appeared to have low cytotoxicity toward the WI-38 normal cell line with IC 50  values of 62.5, 54.3, and 92.4 µM, respectively, compared to doxorubicin with a low value of IC 50  6.51 µM.

Based on the data presented in  Table 1  and illustrated in  Fig. 3 , the thiazole core in compounds 3a–e and 4a,b appears to contribute to their observed cytotoxic activity, potentially through its electronic characteristics, planarity, and ability to participate in hydrogen-bonding and π–π stacking interactions with biological targets. To further examine the structure–activity relationships within the synthesized series and assess the influence of different substituents, compounds bearing analogous substitution patterns were compared under the same criteria. This comparison provides a preliminary basis for relating the structural features of the synthesized derivatives to their observed cytotoxic profiles, while recognizing that the underlying biological interactions require further experimental investigation. In this regard, it appears that the increased activity of these analogs is linked to a substituted aryl or heteroaryl ring attached to the thiazole scaffold. Importantly, bulky aromatic substitutions improve π–π stacking and hydrogen bonding potentials, especially for MCF-7 and HepG2 cell lines. 62  Compound 3d, a thiazole–chromene hybrid, exhibited interesting cytotoxic activity against MCF-7 cells (IC 50  = 28.2 µM), which is probably due to the presence of two pharmacophoric heterocyclic motifs attached through a conjugated framework that may enhance molecular recognition and interaction with biological targets. 50  In addition, 4a and 4b have a more extended aromatic framework. The figure shows that the anticancer activity against both cell lines, MCF-7 and HepG2, is reduced by the presence of an electron-donating group (EDG) at the R position ( e.g. , methoxy (OCH 3 )). This might be due to EDGs increasing the electron density on the aromatic ring, which may influence the electronic and steric environment of the scaffold and, consequently, its ability to participate in favorable non-covalent interactions with biological macromolecules, and also reducing the planarity and binding affinity of the scaffold in comparison to electron-neutral or withdrawing substituents. 63  The reduced activity of these compounds on HepG2 cells suggests some selectivity, which may be related to differences in scaffold compatibility with breast- versus  liver-cancer-related molecular targets, as well as differences in cellular uptake or metabolic stability. Overall, these results underscore the importance of heterocyclic hybridization, halogen substitution and aryl appendage tuning for the regulation of anticancer activity. Compounds 6a–c demonstrated significant activity against MCF-7 cells, whereas they were nearly inactive against HepG2 cells. The selectivity could be due to the anticancer effects of thiazolidin-4-one derivatives, which are cell line specific and generally attributed to differences in molecular targets, receptor expression levels, metabolic characteristics, and intracellular signaling pathways between MCF-7 (breast adenocarcinoma) and HepG2 (hepatocellular carcinoma) cell lines. 64  Likewise, the thiazolidin-4-one compound 6a, having a phenyl substituent, showed remarkable cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cells (IC 50  = 30.0 µM), which is consistent with the anticancer properties of the thiazolidin-4-one core and the significance of aryl substitution for the bioactivity optimization. The anticancer activity order of compounds 6b and 6c on MCF-7 cells ( i.e. , 6c > 6b) indicated the important role of EWGs for the enhanced activity. In particular, the stepwise increase in the strength of EWG ( e.g. , sulfonamide) on the aryl ring, which may alter the electronic properties of the scaffold and potentially influence its non-covalent interactions with relevant biological targets, 63  although this hypothesis requires direct experimental validation.

Compound 8a, a brominated chromene derivative, showed the best activity against MCF-7 cells (IC 50  = 25.9 µM) with weak effects on HepG2 cells (IC 50  = 91.3 µM), suggesting that the bromine substituent may increase lipophilicity and facilitate favorable halogen bonding interactions, which may contribute to the observed cytotoxic profile; however, the contribution of halogen bonding, cellular uptake, 65  and target engagement remains to be experimentally established. Moreover, the presence of an electron withdrawing group (sulfonamide) in compound 8c enhanced its activity against MCF-7 cells (IC 50  = 36.0 µM) compared to 8b (IC 50  = 57.3 µM), probably due to increased lipophilicity and binding affinity to the target. 63  Importantly, the SAR interpretations presented herein should be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than definitive mechanistic conclusions. The proposed contributions of electronic effects and non-covalent interactions, including potential interactions with targets such as EGFR or ERα, are based on the observed cytotoxicity trends and structural features and require direct experimental validation. These findings therefore provide a basis for further structural optimization and mechanistic investigation.

The electronic properties and structural features of the most active scaffolds (3d, 6a, and 8a) were studied by DFT calculations. Reactivity, stability, and charge transfer are revealed  via  frontier molecular orbital (FMO) analysis by HOMO (electron-donating ability) and LUMO (electron-accepting capacity). The HOMO–LUMO gap ( E gap ) is a measure of charge transfer efficiency, and smaller gaps enhance the bioactivity. 61,66,67  The optimized geometries, FMO distributions, and molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) maps are displayed in  Fig. 4–6  and the main energy parameters are presented in  Table 2 . Global reactivity descriptors obtained from DFT calculations have been widely used for prediction of site selectivity and reactivity of the studied molecules. All theoretical calculations were performed using the Gaussian 09 software package with B3LYP functional and 6-311++G(d,p) basis set in the DFT framework. The biological reactivity of the most active synthesized compounds was evaluated by the key quantum chemical parameters such as energy gap ( E gap ), electronegativity ( χ ), global hardness ( η ), softness ( δ ), electrophilicity ( ω ), and dipole moment based on the known equations, where:

Molecules characterized by relatively narrow HOMO–LUMO energy gaps and higher softness may exhibit enhanced electronic reactivity and a greater tendency to participate in electron–transfer interactions. However, these descriptors should be regarded as supportive indicators rather than definitive predictors of biological activity. In the present study, the calculated electronic parameters showed a general consistency with the observed bioactivity, although the biological response is likely governed by multiple structural, electronic, and physicochemical factors. Notably, derivatives 3d, 6a, and 8a, which exhibited relatively lower energy gaps and higher softness, showed pronounced cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cells. These findings suggest that their electronic characteristics may contribute to their biological activity, while the observed activity cannot be attributed solely to the HOMO–LUMO energy gap.

From the docking experiment conducted using the MOE software on the active site of the target enzyme and using doxorubicin as the standard for comparison ( S  = −5.8426 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.6006, interacting with Glu474, Gly372, and Glu375 through three donating H-bonds at 2.79, 3.04, and 3.07 Å, respectively), had comparable or higher binding affinities than that of doxorubicin, indicating good accommodation in the enzyme active site; within the series of sulfonate-bearing molecules (Table S2 and Fig. S52). However, compound 3a had a binding energy ( S  = −6.1456 kcal mol −1  over RMSD = 1.3288 Å)  via  an interaction of the O19 sulfonate oxygen of compound 3a with His498 (3.48 Å) along with a π–H stacking of its phenyl ring with Arg329 (3.68 Å), whereas compound 3b had the highest negative value and thus the highest binding energy among all the series ( S  = −6.4543 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.8109), being stabilized only by the π–cation interaction of its phenyl ring with Lys471 (3.78 Å) ( Fig. 7 ). Meanwhile, compound 3c was also highly potent, displaying  S  = 6.3568 kcal mol −1  with RMSD = 1.2521 ( Fig. 7 ), the lowest RMSD value observed along with 8c and 6b, indicating a very reproducible pose), through a single H-acceptor bond between its O18 atom of the sulphonate group and Arg386 (at 3.17 Å), compound 3d ( S  = 6.0002 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.2936 Å) formed both H-acceptor and π–H interactions with Asn457 (3.15 Å) and Arg424 (4.66 Å, respectively), and compound 3e containing the chromenone functional group had the least binding energy amongst all tested compounds ( S  = −4.9930 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.8304), forming an H-acceptor bond (between O36 atom of the chromenone moiety and Asn431 at 3.08 Å) as well as a more distant π–cation bond (between the phenyl ring of the chromenone and Arg454 at 4.40 Å); amongst the thiazole/hydrazone-containing analogues. Moreover, compound 4a ( S  = −6.0522 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.7192) utilized only two π–H stackings (the thiazole ring with Leu324 at 3.99 Å and the phenyl ring with Thr611 at 4.53 Å), whereas the structure of compound 4b ( S  = −5.8649 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.6633), which formed three interactions (an H-donor) bond of the hydrazone moiety through its N6 atom with Cys481 at 3.51 Å and two π–H stackings (thiazole ring with Leu477 at 4.56 Å and phenyl ring with Leu500 at 4.68 Å), was characterized by a slightly smaller binding energy in comparison with doxorubicin, thus demonstrating that the larger number of weak, long distance contacts does not lead to an increased binding energy; the thiazolone/sulphonate containing compound 6a ( S  = −5.6315 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.4490) exhibited the most complex interaction network among all tested derivatives including an H-donor bond (the N4 atom of the thiazole ring with Glu389, 3.16 Å), two H-acceptor bonds due to its sulphonate oxygen atoms (O25 with Ser423, 3.30 Å and O26 with Arg424, 3.44 Å), as well as one π–H stacking (thiazolone ring with Leu390, 4.37 Å), however, the overall binding energy of this molecule was lower than doxorubicin. On the other hand, compound 6b exhibited a remarkably positive binding energy ( S  = −6.1069 kcal mol −1 ) along with the lowest RMSD value seen throughout the series, having one π–cation interaction through its phenyl ring with Arg386 (4.39 Å), while compound 6c ( S  = 5.9829 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.3666 Å) had a dual H-bonding arrangement through its sulphonamide group (N35 atom H-donor with Gln450 at 3.09 Å and O34 atom H-acceptor with Arg454 at 3.16 Å); among the amide/hydrazone containing compounds, 8a ( S  = −5.5964 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.8235) formed three bonds, two H-acceptor bonds (O5 atom of the amide moiety with Asn457 at 3.14 Å and phenyl ring with Ala427 at 3.61 Å) and one pi–H bond (pyran ring with Gln450, 4.08 Å). Alternatively, whereas compound 8b ( S  = −6.3020 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.1434) demonstrated an especially promising tight binding pose, forming H-acceptor bonds with Lys471 through two short bonds involving the N1 atom of the hydrazone moiety (3.28 Å) and the O5 atom of the amide group (2.75 Å) ( Fig. 7 ), the shortest bond length within the whole dataset), corresponding to a very stable double-anchor binding with one amino acid residue only, and compound 8c ( S  = −6.3141 kcal mol −1 , RMSD = 1.0088, the lowest RMSD of all compounds tested) ( Fig. 7 ), formed a combination of H-acceptor and π–cationic stackings between the N35 atom of the azo group and Lys443 (3.20 Å) and the phenyl ring with Lys443 (3.96 Å), respectively, revealing a cooperative bidentate-like binding of one lysine residue  via  two different kinds of interactions; thus, when ranking the molecules based on their binding energies we obtain: 3b > 3c > 8c > 8b > 3a > 6b > 4a > 3d > 6c > 4b > Dox. > 6a > 8a > 3e. It is possible to conclude that the hydrogen-bond formation through sulphonate, sulphonamide, amide, and hydrazone oxygen/nitrogen atoms and π–H and π–cation stackings involving phenyl and thiazole rings, play the key role in the binding of this compound class to the target protein, while the most often bound “hot spots” include residues Arg424, Arg454, Lys471, and Lys443, with RMSD lower than 2 Å for all compounds proving the reliability of docking procedure.

**In silico  drug-likeness assessment**

From the ADME prediction  in silico  of the thirteen synthesized derivatives, the pharmacokinetics associated showed major hindrances which limited their potential use as oral drugs (Table S3 and  Fig. 8 ). Lipophilic nature was noted to be one of the major constraints in many of the compounds in the series: 4a, 4b and 6a–c having very high log  P  values of 6.51–6.52, while compound 3c (log  P  = 5.83) and 8c (M. Wt. = 644.68 g mol −1 ) exceeded the acceptable levels of lipophilicity, each violating Lipinski rule in doing so. The high hydrophobicity caused by the presence of tosyl, naphthalene and extended aromatic substitution in the thiazole, thiazolidin-4-one and chromene structures translated to low predicted oral bioavailability; compounds 3e, 4a, 4b and 8c were in the lowest bioavailability level (0.17). Large topological polar surface area added to this constraint, especially for compounds 6c (TPSA = 187.05 Å 2 ) and 8c (TPSA = 223.46 Å 2 ), which contained more than one sulphonamide moiety which will affect passive membrane permeability leading to poor oral absorption and blood–brain penetration. Inhibition of CYPs  via  metabolism is another clinically important problem associated with this series of compounds. A number of structurally favorable and more lipophilic compounds, such as 3a, 3c, and 8a inhibited CYP450 enzymes including CYP2C19, CYP2C9 and/or CYP3A4, indicating the problem with drug–drug interaction and increased metabolic burden on liver if the compounds would be progressed. Importantly, the inverse correlation between CYP inhibition and lipophilicity was found in this series of analogues: the most hydrophobic compounds (4a, 4b, 6a–c, log  P  > 6.5) were always non-CYP-inhibitory, while the compounds with intermediate lipophilicity and favorable Lipinski compliance (3a, 3c, 8a) were still active CYP inhibitors. It should be noted that none of compounds in this series demonstrated the favorable profile for lipophilicity, absorption, and lack of metabolism problems at the same time, suggesting that further structure optimization will be required especially reducing aromatic fragments and sulfonamide/sulfonate polarity.

This study successfully synthesized novel thiazole (3a–e, 4a–b), thiazolidine-4-one (6a–c), and chromene (8a–c) derivatives incorporating the 4-methylbenzenesulfonate moiety. The structures were confirmed by detailed spectroscopic characterization. MTT assay results revealed promising anticancer activity, particularly in MCF-7 (breast cancer) and HepG-2 (hepatocellular carcinoma) cell lines. Notably, 3d emerged as a dual-active lead with IC 50  values of 28.2 ± 2.08 µM (MCF-7) and 54.6 ± 1.34 µM (HepG-2), while 6a and 8a showed selective MCF-7 potency, and 3a and 3e excelled against HepG-2. However, the best potential compound turned out to be Compound 3b, which provided good binding energy ( S  = −6.4543 kcal mol −1 ) through the formation of a strong π cation interaction with Lys471, with 3c, 8b, and 8c following in that order, which shows good docking poses. This reveals that sulfonate, sulfonamide, hydrazone, and amide functional groups work as essential hydrogen bond donor/acceptor pharmacophores, whereas phenyl and thiazole aromatic ring systems make good contributions to π–H and π–cation stabilization, and Arg424, Arg454, Lys471, and Lys443 are important hotspot residues. Despite the promising  in vitro  results, the synthesised compounds suffered from a number of important pharmacokinetic problems, such as being highly lipophilic, poor prediction for GI absorption and CYP450 inhibition in a few analogs, which limits the translational potential of the series of compounds. There was no one single compound from the series that offered a good balance between metabolic safety and absorption due to the intrinsic nature of the balance of lipophilicity and poor metabolism and CYP escape. Future efforts would need to focus on making appropriate structural changes to this structure. Collectively, this study expands the chemical space of sulfonate-containing heterocyclic scaffolds with anticancer potential and provides useful structure–activity insights for their further optimization. The promising profiles of 3a, 3c, 3d, and 3e identify these compounds as valuable starting points for future structural modification and biological validation. Further mechanistic, selectivity, and  in vivo  studies are warranted to clarify their therapeutic potential and advance these scaffolds toward anticancer drug discovery.

All chemicals and reagents used in this study were of analytical grade, purchased from commercial suppliers, and used without further purification. The supplementary data include all the instrumental information for the devices used in the chemistry section. Compounds 1, 56 2, 57  hydrazonyl halides, 58 5a–c, 59,60  and 7 (ref.  61 ) were prepared as reported.

An ethanolic solution of 0.01 mole of thiosemicarbazone 2 (3.49 g), sodium acetate (0.05 g), and 0.01 mole of  α -halo derivatives, namely; 4-methylphenacyl bromide (2.13 g), 4-methoxyphenacyl bromide (2.29 g), 2-bromo-1-(naphthalen-2-yl)ethan-1-one (2.49 g), 3-(2-bromoacetyl)-2 H -chromen-2-one (2.67 g), 6-bromo-3-(2-bromoacetyl)-2 H -chromen-2-one (3.46 g), 2-oxo- N ,2-diphenylacetohydrazonoyl bromide (3.03 g), and  N -(4-methoxyphenyl)-2-oxo-2-phenylacetohydrazonoyl bromide (3.33 g), was heated under reflux in 25 mL for 1 h. Upon completion of the reaction (monitored by TLC), the product precipitated directly from the hot ethanolic reaction medium. The solid was filtered while hot, washed several times with hot ethanol, and dried to afford the corresponding thiazole products 3a–e and 4a,b in pure form. No additional purification was required, as confirmed by TLC analysis and spectral characterization.

**In vitro  anticancer activities**

The cell lines MCF-7 and HepG2 were acquired from VACSERA in Cairo, Egypt. The cells were kept in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100 µg mL −1  streptomycin, and 100 units per mL penicillin. Cells were grown at 37 °C in a humidified environment with 5% CO 2 . After a few passes, the cells were planted in a 96-well plate after being cultivated in 75 cm 2  culture bottles with 15 mL DMEM. Cells at 70–80% confluence were used in all investigations.

Cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 10 000 cells per well. Following 24 h of incubation, the medium was replaced with 100 µL of fresh medium containing varying concentrations of the test compound (0, 62.5, 125, 250, 500, and 1000 µM) for 24 or 72 h, with untreated cells serving as the control. Cell viability was assessed  via  MTT assay after treatment. 68  This assay relies on the colorimetric reaction of mitochondrial dehydrogenases of viable cells with MTT. MTT (final concentration 5 mg mL −1  in PBS) was added to each well and plates were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO 2  for the last 2–4 h of the incubation period. The formazan crystals were dissolved in 150 µL DMSO, and the absorbance was read at 570 nm in a microplate reader. Cell proliferation was calculated as [(absorbance of treated cells/absorbance of control cells) × 100], expressed as a percentage. Then, the optical density was measured at 590 nm using a microplate reader (SunRise, TECAN, Inc., USA) to determine the number of viable cells. The percentage of cell viability was calculated using the following equation: cell viability (%) = (OD t /OD c ) × 100, where OD t  represents the mean optical density of wells treated with the tested sample and OD c  represents the mean optical density of untreated control cells. Each concentration was tested in three independent replicates ( n  = 3), and the results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). The relationship between cell viability and compound concentration was used to generate concentration–response curves for each tumor cell line. The 50% inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) was determined by nonlinear regression analysis of the concentration–response curves using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). The IC 50  value represents the concentration of the tested compound required to reduce cell viability by 50% relative to the untreated control (Mosmann, 1983). 69

DFT simulations confirmed the target geometries of the studied compounds using the Gaussian 09W software suite. Calculations employed the B3LYP exchange-correlation functional with the 6-311++G(d,p) basis set. HOMO–LUMO plots and molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) maps were generated  via  GaussView. 70–72
