## Training imaging professionals on transgender-inclusive breast cancer screening practices.

**PMID**: 42758345 · **Journal**: Cancer causes & control : CCC · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1007/s10552-026-02241-1 · **PMCID**: PMC13588859

**Authors**: Martinez Arielle, Whitton Sarah, Yokoyama Jonah, Madzia Jules, Hartlage Carson S, Kelly Elizabeth, Schumacher Madeline, Sosa Delia, Makkad Harsimran, Xu Catherine, Patel Rahul, Pickle Sarah, Stryker Shanna

**Types**: Journal Article

**PURPOSE**: Transgender/gender diverse (TGD) people are underscreened for breast cancer. A barrier to screening is anticipated discrimination during screening encounters. This pilot study evaluates a training session for breast imaging professionals (clinical support specialists, technologists, and radiologists) on LGBTQIA+-inclusive breast cancer screening visits.

**METHODS**: Training topics included terminology, an overview of the guidelines, principles of trauma-informed care, and strategies for creating a welcoming and inclusive environment. Pre- and post-surveys gathered participants' demographic information, frequency of LGBTQIA+ patient interactions, and previous exposure to LGBTQIA+ training and assessed changes in knowledge, self-reported knowledge, and attitudes toward gender diversity.

**RESULTS**: In pre-surveys, participants reported frequent interactions with LGBTQIA+ patients and little previous training. A 45-min didactic training that included storytelling of relevant experiences resulted in a significant increase in participants' self-reported knowledge of LGBTQIA+ terminology with a large effect size. After training, participants correctly answered more directly assessed knowledge questions (small effect size), with a trend toward attitudes more accepting of gender diversity (medium effect size), but neither reached statistical significance.

**CONCLUSION**: Continued efforts to implement and evaluate inclusive education for the entire clinical team are essential to enabling more inclusive and welcoming clinical encounters that will reduce the disparities in breast cancer screening for TGD populations.

Nearly 1 in 8 women in the U.S. will get breast cancer, which is the second-leading cause of cancer death in cisgender women [ 1 ]. Early detection is critical for decreasing mortality from breast cancer and is accomplished with screening using clinical breast examination, mammogram, molecular breast imaging, ultrasound, and/or magnetic resonance imaging.

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual, and other gender/sexual minority (LGBTQIA +) individuals, particularly transgender/gender diverse (TGD) individuals, have medication-related, behavioral, and reproductive risk factors for breast cancer (hereafter abbreviated BCC for ‘breast/chest cancer’ as a gender-inclusive term to refer to cancer which originates at the anatomic breast tissue; we intend this term as non-inclusive of thoracic cancers of the chest wall or of tissues or organs inside of the chest) [ 2 ]. While many reports of BCC in LGBTQIA+ individuals have been documented, the true prevalence remains unclear due to inconsistent and inaccurate collection of sexual orientation and gender identity data in clinical and cancer registries; data that are available show delays in BCC diagnosis and a 3-fold higher chance of recurrence [ 2 ,  3 ]. Contributing to these delays, LGBTQIA+ individuals, particularly TGD individuals, are underscreened for BCC due in part to low awareness about TGD BCC screening guidelines among primary care clinicians and gynecologists and, importantly, also due to anticipated discrimination [ 4 – 11 ].

Our study aims to evaluate the efficacy of a novel didactic training for imaging professionals on LGBTQIA+-inclusive screening encounters in improving participants' knowledge and attitudes toward gender diversity. Ultimately, such efforts could improve the BCC screening experience and thereby increase screening rates and lower BCC mortality.

A 45-min virtual training session was developed by students from the University of Cincinnati (UC) College of Medicine and the Gender-Affirming Care Clinical Specialist at Equitas Health, a community health center dedicated to serving the LGBTQIA+ community. The content was adapted from other cultural responsiveness trainings designed and led by the Gender-Affirming Care Clinical Specialist, a nurse with over a decade of experience training hundreds of medical professionals over the last decade and adapted to include content salient to an audience that included clinical service specialists involved in scheduling breast cancer screening imaging, radiology technologists, and radiologists. Most members of the team who developed the training content were inspired by their own lived experience as LGBTQIA+ community members, several of whom identified as TGD individuals. Content included terminology pertinent to the LGBTQIA+ community, the importance of inclusive communication and screening practices, an overview of current TGD BCC screening guidelines, and an emphasis on strategies to make the clinical space more inclusive for TGD patients. Specific content on respectful and inclusive care of TGD individuals was emphasized given the unique needs of the TGD community even within the larger LGBTQIA+ community related to BCC screening [ 12 ]. The presentation was delivered virtually to breast center team members at a large urban academic health center, including community-based team members working on mobile mammography units. The training used a slide deck and incorporated storytelling of relevant lived experiences. The presentation was offered over the lunch hour, with participants joining from a location that was convenient for them and leadership confirming that this was paid time in which there was not patient care duties; continuing education credit was offered upon completion, but participation in our evaluation surveys was not required for continuing education credit.

In this study, participants were given a QR code and link to complete an electronic survey via Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) immediately before (pre) and after (post) the training on their personal devices; participation was voluntary. This study was intended to improve the experiences of patients at our institution and was determined not to meet the criteria for human subjects research by the UC Institutional Review Board.

In the pre-intervention survey, participants reported cultural background, gender identity, and relationship to the LGBTQIA+ community (self-identity, family members, close friends, or none of the above). Participants also described their job title, the frequency with which they interacted with lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients, with transgender patients, with nonbinary patients, and if they had prior training in LGBTQIA+ patient care and felt that they had access to sufficient materials on LGBTQIA+ care. Participants were invited to share more information about why and how they would like more training in an open-response field.

Knowledge was assessed using two methods. First, participants were asked to self-rate their level of knowledge of five key learning objectives (definition of LGBTQIA+; the use of LGBTQIA+-inclusive terminology in a medical setting; current BCC guidelines and recommendations for LGBTQIA+ patients; ways to create a welcoming environment for LGBTQIA+ patients; and the difference between sex, gender, gender expression, and sexual orientation) using a four-point Likert scale (1 = Not knowledgeable; 4 = Very knowledgeable). Ratings were averaged across items (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.90 at pre, 0.91 at post).

Second, knowledge was evaluated with a series of eight multiple-choice questions that directly assessed the content covered in the training, including scenario-based questions where participants were asked to pick the best option(s) to respond to the situation. These questions were pilot-tested with five individuals prior to the study to optimize readability, flow, and a reasonable degree of difficulty that would be able to detect increases in relevant knowledge. They were developed based on the professional and lived experience of several team members, including the Gender-Affirming Clinical Care Specialist. Scenarios included calling a TGD patient from the waiting room, correcting a verbal pronoun mistake, and confirming a patient’s identity when the listed appointment name does not match the listed legal name. The remaining questions asked the participants to identify features of a welcoming environment and to describe a key feature of trauma-informed care covered in the training. For analyses, participant responses to each question were coded as correct (1) or incorrect (0); we summed these values across items to indicate the total number of items answered correctly (possible values from 0–12).

Finally, attitudes toward gender diversity were assessed using an adaptation of a transphobia scale developed by Stroumsa et al. in 2019 [ 13 ]. Participants were asked to rate how much they agreed with eight statements about gender (e.g., “It is important for me to be able to identify someone as only a man or only a woman upon meeting them”) on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Agree; 7 = Strongly Disagree). Ratings were averaged across items (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.85 at pre, 0.91 at post); higher scores reflect more accepting attitudes toward gender diversity.

Descriptive statistics were calculated to describe participants’ demographics and experience. Paired-samples  t -tests were used to assess within-person changes from pre- to post-intervention on key outcomes (self-reported knowledge, directly assessed knowledge, and attitudes toward gender diversity). Because this was a pilot study with a small sample, we focused on estimating effect sizes for pre-to-post changes to inform future larger-scale evaluations [ 14 ]. Effect sizes were estimated using Hedges’ g, which corrects for small sample size. Nevertheless, we also calculated statistical significance of pre-to-post changes.

There were 28 attendees, with 17 participants completing the pre-survey (61%) and 14 completing the post-survey (50%). Participant demographics are summarized in Table  1 . Slightly over half ( n =8, 53%) of our cohort were mammogram technologists; the others were ultrasound technologists, clinical support staff, radiologists, or managers. Table 1 Demographics of participants LGBTQIA+: lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual, and other gender/sexual minority

The relevance of this training was confirmed by our pre-intervention data showing that most ( n =13, 77%) of the participants reported sometimes, often, or very often working with TGD patients and almost all ( n =16, 94%) reported sometimes, often, or very often working with LGB patients. Despite this, only three participants had received LGBTQIA+-specific training (both radiologists and one mammography technologist), and only a third of participants ( n =6, 35.3%) felt they had adequate access to resources about LGBTQIA+ patients. In open-field responses, they described barriers to learning including discomfort about discussing this topic among others, not knowing where to start, and being unsure of how to support LGBTQIA+ patients without unintentionally singling them out.

Paired-samples t-tests revealed that self-reported knowledge increased from pre-intervention,  Mean  = 2.4 (SD = 0.75), to post-intervention,  Mean  = 3.13 (SD = 0.56), t = 4.39;  p  = 0.001. Hedges’ g = 1.1, indicating a large effect size. We also estimated pre- to post- changes on each of the five knowledge items separately, as seen in Fig.  1 ; self-reported level of knowledge on each of the five individual items increased at a statistically significant level (all  p s <0.02). As seen in Fig.  2 , the number of multiple-choice knowledge questions answered correctly increased slightly from pre-intervention,  Mean  = 8.08 (SD = 1.73), to post-intervention,  Mean  = 9.16 (SD = 2.12), with a small effect size (Hedges’  g  = 0.32). However, this increase was not statistically significant,  t  = 1.18;  p  = 0.26. As seen in Fig.  3 , Gender Attitudes Scale scores also increased from pre-intervention,  Mean  = 42.36 (SD = 9.15), to post-intervention,  Mean  = 44.36 (SD = 10.25), with a medium effect size (Hedges’  g  = 0.48), indicating a shift toward greater acceptance of gender diversity. However, this increase was not statistically significant,  t  = 1.71;  p  = 0.12. The full statistical output for these analyses is included in supplemental materials. Fig. 1 Self-reported knowledge pre- and post-intervention. LGBTQIA+: lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual, and other gender/sexual minority Fig. 2 Directly assessed knowledge Fig. 3 Gender attitudes scale scores

Our findings confirm that for many breast center team members, training opportunities in LGBTQIA+ care are rare despite frequent interactions with LGBTQIA+ patients. After a 45-min training, imaging professionals’ self-reported knowledge of the LGBTQIA+ community improved significantly. To our knowledge, this is the first published training aimed at the entire team of imaging professionals involved with BCC screening. Our team has previously received positive qualitative feedback from radiology residents on a transgender curriculum (not focused on BCC), but did not measure changes to knowledge [ 15 ].Clinical vignettes demonstrating inclusive terminology and evidence-based recommendations for TGD patients seeking breast imaging have been published to address a knowledge gap among physicians, and the authors emphasizes the need to educate all members of the imaging team [ 16 ]. To our knowledge, our work is the first that highlights the impact of education for all critical patient-facing team members, including technologists and clinical service specialists.

The improved self-reported understanding of the LGBTQIA+ community reported by our participants aligns with the findings from a study of interprofessional emergency department team members and with a review of brief training sessions for healthcare providers [ 17 ,  18 ]. Our training did not show improvement in gender attitudes and directly assessed knowledge, unlike other published studies with a similar training structure but larger and different participant groups [ 19 ,  20 ]. It is possible that we did not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in knowledge due to our smaller sample size.

In addition to sample size, another major limitation was our retention rate, which we attributed to insufficient time allocated for the surveys within the one-hour time slot due to participants needing to prepare to start patient care after the lunch hour. Important next steps include evaluating the training’s impact on patients, such as measuring changes in anticipated discrimination in patients who have experienced affirming BCC screening encounters. Participant feedback highlighted that the most valued component was storytelling of trainers’ lived experiences; therefore, incorporating additional narratives may strengthen the connection to the material. With these future steps, we aim to advance LGBTQIA+ cultural humility in cancer screening spaces and ultimately decrease BCC mortality.

## Fabrication and Characterization of Green-Synthesized Zinc Oxide Nanoparticles Loaded into Dissolving Microneedles: A Potential Delivery Platform for Breast Cancer Therapy.

**PMID**: 42757231 · **Journal**: ACS omega · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1021/acsomega.5c08765 · **PMCID**: PMC13584778

**Authors**: Al-Shawabkeh Haneen Faris, Aburayya Rafa, Basheer Haneen A, Zaid Alkilani Ahlam, Alhusban Maram A, Hamed Rania

**Types**: Journal Article

Green-synthesized zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) can be used to explore their anticancer applications. Therefore, this study aimed to synthesize ZnO NPs using an eco-friendly method by combining Phoenix dactylifera (P. dactylifera) root hair extract with 0.8 M zinc acetate dihydrate at a volume ratio of 4:1. The ZnO NPs had an average size of 24.01 ± 1.70 nm, a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.25 ± 0.02, and a zeta potential of -18.45 ± 1.80 mV. The X-ray diffraction analysis revealed the crystalline structure of ZnO NPs, and the energy-dispersive spectroscopy analysis showed zinc and oxygen compositions of 43.64% and 31.60%, respectively, confirming the formation of green-synthesized ZnO NPs. The ZnO NPs were then incorporated into dissolving microneedles (MNs) prepared using 10% sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (Na CMC). Additionally, doxorubicin hydrochloride (DOX), a chemotherapeutic agent used to treat breast cancer, was also loaded into MNs (DOX-loaded MNs). The ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs were evaluated for morphology, mechanical properties, needle insertion, dissolution rate, recovery of ZnO and DOX, FTIR, ex vivo permeation, and stability. Both types of MNs exhibited a pyramidal shape with a square base, were capable of withstanding a compression force of 32 N for 30 s, pierced the Parafilm M sheet at a depth of 378-504 μm, and dissolved completely within 30 min. The ZnO NP-loaded MNs remained stable for 2 weeks at room temperature and in the refrigerator. Whereas DOX-loaded MNs remained stable for up to 1 week at room temperature and 2 weeks in the refrigerator. In vitro cytotoxicity studies showed that green-synthesized ZnO NPs reduced the viability of breast cancer cells; however, these studies evaluated free ZnO NPs rather than the MN formulation itself. In conclusion, MNs demonstrated a promising platform for enhancing the transdermal delivery of green-synthesized ZnO NPs and DOX, representing a novel approach combining P. dactylifera-derived ZnO nanoparticles with dissolving microneedle-based delivery.

Breast cancer is a worldwide
health concern characterized by uncontrolled
and abnormal cellular proliferation, with a higher incidence found
among women.  Conventional chemotherapy,
surgery, radiotherapy, and other treatment modalities have been causing
severe adverse effects and sometimes involve invasive procedures that
affect the patient’s quality of life.  Therefore, scientists have been working to develop alternative approaches
to ensure effective treatment, minimize side effects, and enhance
patient compliance and safety.

Greenly synthesized ZnO NPs have
been used in various biomedical
applications due to their antibacterial, anticancer, antioxidant,
anti-inflammatory, and wound-healing properties.  George et al.  focused on green
synthesis of ZnO NPs from the root extract of  Rubus
fairholmianus  to evaluate their cytotoxic effects
on the MCF-7 breast cancer cell line. Cytotoxicity was evaluated by
assessing morphology, proliferation, apoptosis, and reactive oxygen
species (ROS) production. The results showed increased apoptosis,
as indicated by higher levels of apoptosis markers such as cytoplasmic
cytochrome C and caspases 3 and 7, which indicate cancer cell death,
along with decreased cellular proliferation. These findings collectively
demonstrate the potential of greenly synthesized ZnO NPs in breast
cancer therapy.  Moreover, the literature
reports the use of  Phoenix dactylifera  ( P. dactylifera ), commonly known
as the date palm, in the preparation of ZnO NPs due to the presence
of phytochemicals such as flavonoids, alkaloids, tannins, ellagic
acid, and others. 
 −

Doxorubicin hydrochloride (DOX) is a common chemotherapeutic
drug
for treating breast cancer.  It is administered
intravenously in clinical settings, and patients need to be monitored
for serious side effects like heart damage and hepatotoxicity.  To prevent such severe adverse events, the search
for safer agents with comparable efficacy is necessary. This has led
to the exploration of metal oxide nanoparticles, which have shown
promising potential as cytotoxic agents.

Microneedles (MNs) are a new minimally invasive drug delivery
system
made from tiny, fine, microsized needles designed to penetrate the
skin and improve drug permeability. MNs help avoid the invasiveness
and pain of injections and bypass the first-pass effect of oral formulations,
ensuring efficient and convenient drug administration.  The small size and length of MNs compared to
traditional hypodermic needles make them challenging to see with the
naked eye, which can alleviate patients’ needle phobia.  Dissolving microneedles (MNs) can puncture the
skin and penetrate the stratum corneum (SC) without leaving any waste,
as they disintegrate and degrade upon contact with skin fluids.  The materials used to make the needles must
provide sufficient strength to withstand the force without breaking,
and the proper length to deliver molecules without reaching the nerves,
thereby minimizing pain.  Advancements
in MNs fabrication have been achieved by combining desired polymers
and micro- or nanoparticles to deliver drugs through the skin for
various treatments.  One of the most commonly
used materials in fabricating dissolving MNs is carboxymethyl cellulose
(CMC).

The ongoing challenge of
finding alternative methods of administration
and potential therapies to replace conventional chemotherapy has driven
extensive research in this area. Therefore, this study aims to utilize
green-synthesized ZnO NPs loaded into dissolving MNs as a potential
transdermal delivery platform for anticancer agents. Instead of relying
on conventional chemical methods,  P. dactylifera  was used to prepare a plant extract containing reducing agents for
synthesizing eco-friendly ZnO NPs. The nanoscale size of ZnO NPs
may facilitate improved interactions with biological systems and enhance
their transdermal transport when delivered via MNs, compared to conventional
formulations. Additionally, loading ZnO NPs into dissolving MNs could
offer further benefits as these MNs enhance skin penetration and may
increase the local concentration of ZnO NPs at the site of application,
potentially improving their delivery across the skin barrier.

To our knowledge, this is the first study to utilize green-synthesized
ZnO NPs loaded into dissolving MNs to investigate their transdermal
delivery performance, while independently evaluating the cytotoxic
potential of the ZnO NPs  in vitro . However, this
study represents a preliminary investigation of delivery feasibility
and cytotoxic effects and does not establish direct therapeutic efficacy
at deep tumor sites. Remarkably, the use of green synthesis advances
the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by promoting
environmentally friendly and sustainable scientific approaches.  The ZnO NPs were characterized using UV–vis
spectral analysis, particle size analysis, polydispersity index measurement,
zeta potential determination, morphology studies, and stability tests.
Suitable matrices for preparing dissolving MNs were also evaluated.
Finally, ZnO NPs and DOX were loaded into dissolving MNs and characterized
for morphology, mechanical properties, needle insertion, dissolution
rate, FTIR,  ex vivo  permeation, and stability. Whereas
the  in vitro  cytotoxic and anticancer effects of
the green-synthesized ZnO NPs were assessed independently.

Sodium carboxymethyl cellulose
(Na CMC) (M.W 90 000 g/mol) was procured from Sigma-Aldrich
(St. Louis, MO, USA), doxorubicin hydrochloride (DOX) from Sigma-Aldrich
(Schnelldorf, Germany), zinc oxide nanopowder <100 nm from Sigma-Aldrich,
and zinc acetate (ZnC 4 H 6 O 4 ) from
Merck KGaA (Darmstadt, Germany). Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) pellets were
purchased from Fisher Scientific UK (Loughborough, UK). Ultrapure
water was supplied from the Millipore Direct-Q 5UV system (EMD Millipore,
MA, USA). Monobasic sodium phosphate (NaH 2 PO 4 ) and dibasic sodium phosphate (Na 2 HPO 4 ) were
purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Hydrochloric acid
(HCl) was purchased from Alpha Chemika (Mumbai, Maharashtra, India).
Glycerin (C 3 H 8 O 3 ) was purchased from
Sigma-Aldrich (Schnelldorf, Germany). All reagents were of analytical
grade and used without further purification.

**Preparation of Root Hair Extract of Phoenix dactylifera**

The root hair extract
of  Phoenix dactylifera  ( P. dactylifera ) was prepared as described in 
 , 
  with slight modifications. This slight modification involves increasing
the oven temperature for the root hair drying step from 40 to 50 °C
to ensure efficient moisture removal. Briefly, the root hair of  P. dactylifera  was collected from a date farm in
Al-Ghour, Jordan. The root hair was washed with distilled water and
left in the oven at 50 °C until completely dry. The dried root
hair was ground into a fine powder and then sieved through an 80-mesh
screen. In a 150 mL beaker containing 100 mL of distilled water, 2
g of ground root hair was added and heated to 40 °C for 30 min,
until a brownish-orange solution formed. The solution was then centrifuged
at 4000 rpm for 15 min and filtered through a 150 mm filter paper
to obtain the supernatant, which was stored at 4 °C for future
use.

ZnO NPs
were prepared as described in  with slight
modifications. Briefly, the aqueous root hair extract of  P. dactylifera  was combined with a 0.8 M ZnC 4 H 6 O 4  solution in a volume ratio of 4:1.
An NaOH solution was added dropwise until the pH reached a basic level
of ∼ 12. The mixture was then continuously stirred for 1 h
at 80 °C. The final solution was centrifuged for 15 min at 5000
rpm at 25 °C, then filtered to obtain a transparent yellow supernatant
for further studies. The yield percentage (%Yield) of ZnO NPs was
determined by dividing the mass of the ZnO NPs powder dried in the
oven at 40–60 °C overnight by the mass of zinc acetate
salt used, applying  eq  
 . Then the powder was calcined at 500 °C for 1 h.

Figure S1  illustrates the experimental flow of the green synthesis of ZnO

A UV–1800 spectrophotometer (Shimadzu,
Kyoto, Japan) was used to determine the maximum wavelengths (λ max ) of ZnO NPs and DOX. Standard solutions of 20 mg/mL ZnO
NPs in distilled water and 12 mg/mL DOX in phosphate buffer (PB, pH
6.2) were scanned from 200 to 800 nm to determine their respective
λ max  values. Distilled water and PB (pH 6.2) were
used as blanks to set the baseline for ZnO NPs and DOX, respectively.

The physical characteristics of ZnO NPs, including
particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), and zeta potential, were
evaluated using a Zetasizer analyzer (Nicomp Nano ZS3000, Santa Barbara,
CA, USA) with a particle size range of 0.3 nm to 10 μm. Measurements
were conducted at room temperature (∼23 °C) by scattering
light at a fixed angle of 90° with a viscosity of 0.933 cP. The
aqueous dispersions of ZnO NPs were prepared by diluting the ZnO NPs
sample 10-fold and mixing 50 μL of 20 mg/mL ZnO NPs dispersion
with 450 μL of ultrapure water to reduce multiple scattering
and ensure optimal particle concentration. For zeta potential measurements,
40 μL of ZnO NPs dispersion was diluted in 3 mL of ultrapure
water. The stability of ZnO NPs’ particle size, PDI, and zeta
potential was monitored over 60 days at room temperature. All measurements
were performed at least three times, and the mean and standard deviation
(SD) were calculated for each sample.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed to determine the crystallinity
of the green-synthesized ZnO NPs. The XRD patterns were acquired using
a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer (Karlsruhe, Germany) with
a Cu–Kα radiation source at a wavelength of 1.5406 Å.
Diffraction patterns were processed using Diffrac.EVA software. Background
correction and Kα 2  stripping were applied. Phase
identification was performed using the PDF-2 database. The diffractograms
were recorded over the 2θ range of 10–90° with a
step size of 0.005° at 1 s per step. The tube voltage was 40
kV, and the tube current was 40 mA.

The elemental composition of the green-synthesized ZnO NPs was
analyzed using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) coupled
with Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (Apreo 2S LoVac,
Thermo Fisher Scientific – FEI, Netherlands). EDS analysis
was performed using an UltraDry EDS detector (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
Madison, WI, USA) equipped with Silicon Drift Detector (SDD) technology,
providing high-resolution detection capabilities. EDS spectra were
acquired at an accelerating voltage of 30 kV to ensure sufficient
excitation of Zn K-lines.

The shape and size of the synthesized nanoparticles were determined
using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Morgani 268, Holland).
One drop of the ZnO NPs sample was added to a Formvar/Carbon-coated
copper grid and left to dry for 30 min before images were taken at
an accelerating voltage of 120 kV. The particle size distribution
of the green-synthesized ZnO NPs was determined from TEM images using
ImageJ (National Institutes of Health). The size of 65 nanoparticles
was measured, and the data were exported to Excel, where the particle
size distribution was plotted as a histogram to determine the average
particle size and size uniformity.

Initially, blank dissolving MNs were prepared using MPatch Microneedle
templates (Micropoint, Singapore) ( Figure S2 ). These silicone molds can be reused repeatedly without losing their
shape. To select the final matrix for fabricating MNs, four aqueous
Na CMC gel formulations (M1-M4) were prepared at concentrations of
6, 10, 12, and 14%  w/v , respectively. Additionally,
three potential covering layers (C1–C3) for MNs were examined
using 6% Na CMC, 6% Na CMC with 0.5% glycerin, and 6% Na CMC with
1% glycerin, respectively. The molds were filled with 85 μL
of M1-M4 formulations and then centrifuged in a Hermle Z326 K (Germany)
for 5 min at 1500 rpm. Afterward, they were left to dry for 2–3
h before adding 0.5 mL of the covering layer formulations (C1–C3).
The MNs were left overnight at room temperature until completely dry,
allowing for visual and mechanical evaluation to determine the best
MN formulations. A mechanical inspection was performed by measuring
the percentage of height reduction (%Height reduction) after applying
the compression force using the TA.XT2 Texture Analyzer.  Table  
  summarizes the composition
of the blank dissolving MNs.

To fabricate ZnO NP-loaded MNs, 1 mL of distilled water
was used to disperse 20 mg of dried ZnO NPs, resulting in a ZnO NP
solution. The ZnO NP dispersion was mixed with 10% Na CMC in a 1:1
volume ratio. The mixture was stirred until uniform, and 85 μL
was loaded into the MN molds. The molds were centrifuged for 5 min
at 1500 rpm and dried at room temperature for 2–3 h. Once dry,
0.5 mL of the covering layer, made of 6% Na CMC and 0.5% glycerin,
was poured on top and left to dry overnight at room temperature. The
following day, the ZnO NP-loaded MNs were carefully detached from
the molds and visually inspected.

To fabricate DOX-loaded MNs,
12 mg of DOX was dissolved in 1 mL of distilled water in a glass vial
wrapped in aluminum foil to prevent photodegradation. The DOX solution
was mixed with a 10% Na CMC gel at a 1:1 volume ratio. To prevent
photodegradation, the absence of light was assured until the mixture
was homogeneous, after which 85 μL was loaded into the MN molds.
The molds were centrifuged for 5 min at 1500 rpm and left to dry at
room temperature for 2–3 h. Once dried, 0.5 mL of the covering
material (6% CMC and 0.5% glycerin) was added. The molds were then
dried overnight at room temperature while covered with aluminum foil.
The next day, the DOX-loaded MNs were carefully detached from the
molds and visually inspected.  Figure S3  illustrates the fabrication steps of the ZnO NP-loaded MNs and DOX-loaded
MNs.

The viscosity of blank 10 and
12% Na CMC polymer solutions (prepared without adding ZnO NPs and
DOX) and 10% Na CMC polymer solutions loaded with 20 mg ZnO NPs and
12 mg DOX was measured using a controlled stress rheometer (CSR) (Anton
Paar, MCR 302; Graz, Austria). A cone and plate geometry with a 25
mm diameter and a 1.010° cone angle was used for viscosity measurement.
Before testing, 0.5 g of the polymer solution was placed on the plate
and allowed to relax for ∼ 1 min. Viscosity was measured at
a shear rate of 0.1 to 100 s –1 . The test was performed
in triplicate at 32 °C, and the results are presented as the
mean ± SD.

The height of needles and the shape of MNs were assessed
using a light-field microscope (B-190TBPL, OPTIKA Microscopes, Italy).

The TA.XT2 Texture Analyzer (Stable Micro
Systems, Haslemere, UK) was used in compression mode to evaluate the
mechanical properties of ZnO NPs- and DOX-loaded MNs as described
in Hamed et al.  The MNs were positioned
at the center of a 1.5 cm 2  diameter cylindrical probe,
which was pressed against a flat aluminum base as the texture analyzer
arm descended at 0.5 mm/sec. A 32 N force was applied for 30 s before
lifting the probe. The length of each needle was measured before and
after compression using a light-field microscope (B-190TBPL, OPTIKA
Microscopes, Italy). After applying the compression force, the percentage
height reduction (%Height reduction) was calculated using  eq  
 . This experiment was performed
in triplicate, and the %Height reduction was presented as mean ±
SD.

Parafilm M (Bemis Company Inc., Soignies, Belgium) was
used to evaluate the ability of ZnO NPs- and DOX-loaded MNs to penetrate
skin layers and withstand fractures as described in Hamed et al.  ZnO NPs and DOX-loaded MNs were pressed using
the thumb into an eight-layered thin sheet of Parafilm M for 30 s.
The thumb force simulates a 32 N force used in the texture analyzer.  Afterward, the MNs were carefully removed from
the Parafilm M, and the layers were separated to count the holes in
each layer and determine which layer the MNs could reach.

To validate the effective delivery of ZnO NPs and DOX
through the skin, the dissolution rate of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs
was investigated on rat skin as described in Hamed et al.  In this experiment, male Wistar rats weighing
180–200 g were housed at the animal care center of the Faculty
of Pharmacy at Al-Zaytoonah University of Jordan. The experiment was
conducted in accordance with the University’s Animal Welfare
Committee guidelines, as approved by the Institutional Review Board
(IRB) No. (01/10/2022–2023) dated 01/10/2023. Rats were anesthetized
using diethyl ether and sacrificed via cervical dislocation. Full-thickness
rat skin was cut into pieces after using potassium thioglycolate to
remove the hair from the abdomen, wrapped in aluminum foil, and stored
at −80 °C. Before use, each piece of skin was soaked and
cleaned in phosphate buffer (PB, pH 7.4) for 15 min. The MNs were
pressed into the skin using a Texture Analyzer that applied a 32 N
force for 30 s, simulating the force of thumb application. Then, MNs
were detached from the skin at 5-, 10-, 20-, 25-, and 30-min intervals.
Subsequently, a light-field microscope (B-190TBPL, OPTIKA Microscopes,
Italy) was used to examine the dissolution rate of MNs and to assess
their morphology, height, and %Height reduction.

The particle size and PDI of ZnO NPs,
after being loaded into MNs, were measured by dispersing the ZnO NP-loaded
MNs in 1 mL of ultrapure water. The dispersion was centrifuged for
3 min at 10000 rpm to separate the ZnO NPs from the Na CMC polymer
mixture. The particle size and PDI of the ZnO NPs were determined
using a Nicomp Nano ZS3000 (Santa Barbara, CA, USA).

The amount of ZnO recovered from loaded MNs
was determined by dispersing ZnO NP-loaded MNs in 1 mL of distilled
water and sonicating for 10 min at 37 °C. The ZnO concentration
was determined using a UV–vis spectrophotometer at 347 nm,
employing a calibration curve for ZnO NPs prepared over a concentration
range of 5–25 mg/mL. The DOX recovered from loaded MNs was
determined by dispersing DOX-loaded MNs in 5 mL of PB (pH 6.2) and
sonicating for 10 min at 37 °C. The recovered DOX was determined
using a UV–vis spectrophotometer at 480 nm, with a calibration
curve prepared over a concentration range of 5–50 μg/mL.

Samples of ZnO NPs, DOX, Na CMC, polymer mixtures
of (Na CMC and ZnO NPs) and (Na CMC and DOX), along with their corresponding
physical mixtures and ZnO NPs- and DOX-loaded MNs, were investigated
using FTIR analysis. The spectra were collected using FTIR spectroscopy
(Vertex 70 spectrometer, Bruker, Germany) with 10 scans at a resolution
of 4 cm –1 , spanning 3500–400 cm –1 . The obtained spectral data were then saved in CSV format and examined
using the software IRA FTIR Data Explorer V1.0.

**Ex vivo  Permeation Studies**

Ex vivo  permeation studies for ZnO NPs- and DOX-loaded
MNs were performed using Franz diffusion cells (PremeGear Inc., USA)
at 32 °C with an orifice diameter of 11.28 mm and a diffusion
surface area of 1 cm 2 . A full-thickness rat skin was obtained
from the back of the rat following a protocol approved by the Ethics
Committee for Scientific Research (IRB No. 01/10/2022–2023,
dated 01/10/2023). The rat skin was clamped between the donor and
receptor compartments, with the  SC  side facing the
donor. The ZnO NPs- and DOX-loaded MNs were manually pressed into
the rat skin in the donor compartment for 30 s. The receptor compartment
was filled with 8 mL of PB (pH 6.2). At 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 24 h,
1 mL samples were withdrawn from the receptor and replaced with 1
mL of fresh PB (pH 6.2) to maintain sink conditions. The concentrations
of ZnO and DOX in the samples were measured using a UV–vis
spectrophotometer at 347 and 480 nm, respectively. The cumulative
amount (%Q) of ZnO and DOX was plotted against time (t). The steady-state
flux (J ss , μg/cm 2  /h) was calculated from
the slope of the linear section of the plot of the cumulative amount
of ZnO and DOX permeated through skin per unit surface area (Q/A)
versus time (t). Additionally, the permeability coefficient (P, cm/h)
was computed using  eq  
 : 
 
 3 
 P = J s s C o 
 where P is the permeability coefficient, J ss  is the steady-state flux, and C 0  is the initial
concentration in the donor phase (assuming sink conditions).

**Ex vivo  Skin Deposition
Study**

The  ex vivo  skin deposition study
was performed to quantify the accumulation of green-synthesized ZnO
NPs and DOX within full-thickness rat skin following MN application,
as described in Ershaid et al.  After
completion of the 24-h  ex vivo  permeation experiment,
the skin samples were carefully removed from the Franz diffusion cells.
Any remaining undissolved MNs on the skin surface were gently wiped
off and discarded to avoid overestimation of drug content. The treated
skin was thoroughly rinsed with PBS (pH 6.2) to remove surface-adhered
formulation and cut into small sections. The samples were then transferred
to a beaker containing 15 mL PBS (pH 6.2) and sonicated for 1 h to
extract the deposited ZnO NPs and DOX from the skin. The resulting
dispersions were filtered through a 0.45 μm syringe filter to
remove tissue debris, and the filtrate was analyzed using a UV–visible
spectrophotometer at the λ max  of each compound. Skin
deposition was calculated using the constructed calibration curves
for ZnO NPs and DOX.

The MCF-7 cell line used in this study was obtained from the American
Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA, and the human dermal
fibroblast (HDF) cell line was donated by the Cancer Stem Research
Center in Amman, Jordan. The cell lines were cultivated and maintained
in a humidified 5% CO 2  atmosphere at 37 °C. The medium
used in this study was RPMI 1640, supplemented with 10%  v / v  fetal bovine serum (FBS), 2 mM  l -glutamine,
1 mM sodium pyruvate, and 1%  v / v  Penicillin (10,000 U/mL)Streptomycin (10 mg/mL).

MCF-7
and HDF cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 5 ×
10 3  cells per well and incubated overnight to allow for
attachment. The following day, cells were treated with various concentrations
(50, 25, 12.5, and 5 μg/mL) of synthetic ZnO nanoparticles (zinc
oxide nanopowder <100 nm from Sigma-Aldrich), green-synthesized
ZnO NPs, or zinc acetate for 72 h. Doxorubicin (DOX, 25 μM)
was used as a positive control and was not used for potency comparison
with ZnO NPs. Cell viability was assessed using the MTT assay (Sigma-Aldrich,
St. Louis, MO, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions
as previously reported.  Briefly, 20 μL
of MTT solution (5 mg/mL) was added to each well, and the plate was
incubated at 37 °C for 4 h. Following incubation, the medium
was aspirated, and the resulting formazan crystals were dissolved
in 150 μL of dimethyl sulfoxide. Absorbance was measured at
570 nm using a microplate reader. Cell viability was expressed as
a percentage relative to the untreated control group. The cytotoxicity
experiments were performed in triplicate, and data were analyzed using
Student’s  t  test to determine statistical
significance ( p  < 0.05).

ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs were assessed for moisture
content, %Height reduction, and needle insertion at 0, 1, 2, 4, and
8 weeks, both at room temperature and in the refrigerator (4 °C).
The difference between the initial and final weights of each microneedle
was recorded throughout the stability period to calculate the moisture
content percentage using  eq  
 . The %Height reduction and needle insertion were performed
as described in  Sections  
  and  , respectively.
All experiments were performed in triplicate, and the results are
presented as the mean ± SD.

The mean
and standard deviation were calculated for all experiments. Statistical

**Preparation of Root Hair Extract of  P. dactylifera**

The collected roots of  P. dactylifera  were approximately 30 cm long. This
length made handling the roots more difficult, so they were cut into
smaller pieces (∼2–3 cm) to ease drying and grinding
( Figure  
 A). The dried
roots were then ground and sieved through an 80-mesh screen.  Figure  
 B shows the brownish-orange
aqueous extract that was formed after centrifugation and filtration
of the boiled root hair.

P. dactylifera  plant extract was used in the synthesis
of ZnO NPs, where phytochemicals act as both reducing and stabilizing
agents, and ZnC 4 H 6 O 4  acts as a chemical
precursor and reducing agent. 
 P. dactylifera  root hair extract was chosen in our
study as the eco-friendly green reducing and stabilizing agent because
of its high content of polyphenols, flavonoids, tannins, and carbohydrates.
These compounds can efficiently donate electrons to reduce Zn 2+  ions to ZnO nuclei and simultaneously cap the formed nanoparticles,
thereby preventing agglomeration.  Additionally,  P. dactylifera  is a locally abundant plant in Jordan,
offering a sustainable and environmentally friendly alternative to
chemical synthesis methods. Its known antioxidant and anti-inflammatory
properties may also help improve the biological compatibility of the
resulting nanoparticles.

The mechanism
of ZnO NPs formation involves zinc acetate dihydrate dissociating
into Zn 2+  and acetate ions upon dissolution in an aqueous
medium. The released Zn 2+  ions serve as the central metal
source for nanoparticle formation. The aqueous extract of  P. dactylifera  is rich in phytochemicals containing
−OH, −COOH, and -NH2 groups, which act as both reducing
and stabilizing agents by donating electrons to facilitate the formation
of Zn­(OH) 2  intermediates. Additionally, the NaOH introduced
during synthesis provides hydroxide ions that react with Zn 2+ , further promoting Zn­(OH) 2  formation. Upon heating to
∼ 80 °C, Zn­(OH) 2  undergoes dehydration, promoting
the nucleation and growth of ZnO nanoparticles. During this process,
the phytochemicals adsorb onto the nanoparticle surface, acting as
capping and stabilizing agents that control particle size, prevent
agglomeration, and enhance colloidal stability. The combined action
of these phytochemicals and reaction conditions governs the nucleation
rate, particle growth, and final morphology of the ZnO NPs. 
 , 
  After 1 h of mixing, a yellowish, creamy solution formed, indicating
the formation of ZnO NPs. The solution was centrifuged at 5000 rpm
for 15 min at 25 °C to obtain a clear, yellow supernatant for
further studies ( Figure  
 C). The %Yield of ZnO NPs was 74.3 ± 0.32%, close to 72.7% reported
in.

Figure  
  illustrates the UV–vis spectra of ZnO NPs and DOX. The maximum
wavelength (λ max ) of ZnO NPs was observed at 347
nm. This finding aligns with that of Fouda et al.,  who reported a peak at 345 nm. The calibration curve of
ZnO NPs solutions, prepared using distilled water, at concentrations
ranging between 2.34 and 20 mg/mL, exhibited a linear regression equation
of y = 0.0288x + 0.1141 (R 2  = 0.9920) at λ max  348 nm ( Figure S4A ). Whereas the λ max  of DOX was observed at 480 nm, consistent with,  which reported a similar λ max  for DOX. The calibration curve of DOX solutions, prepared with PB
(pH 6.2), at concentrations ranging from 5 to 50 μg, showed
a linear equation of y = 0.0123x+0.0789 (R 2  = 0.9994) at
λ max  480 nm ( Figure S4B ).

Using a volume ratio of 4:1 of plant extract to 0.8
M ZnC 4 H 6 O 4  solution produced the
initial optimal particle size and PDI for ZnO NPs, at 24.01 ±
1.70 nm and 0.25 ± 0.02, respectively. The average particle size
of ZnO NPs was within the acceptable range for transdermally delivered
nanoparticles of 1–100 nm, as reported by Zhou et al.  Additionally, the smaller particle size of ZnO
NPs is associated with improved solubility, more precise targeting,
enhanced cellular uptake, and increased anticancer activity.

Figures  
 A and B illustrate the particle size and PDI of ZnO
NPs, respectively, upon storage at room temperature. After 7 days,
the particle size and PDI increased to 27.72 ± 0.41 nm and 0.35
± 0.04, respectively. After 14 days, particle size and PDI further
increased to 39.51 ± 1.57 nm and 0.42 ± 0.02, respectively.
After 30 days, the particle size increased to 70.39 ± 1.02 nm,
which falls within the acceptable range for nanoparticles intended
for transdermal drug delivery (<100 nm).  The PDI also increased to 0.48 ± 0.03, remaining within the
acceptable range of 0.01–0.5 for nanoparticles. 
 , 
  After 60 days, the size shifted toward larger particles, reaching
133.4 ± 0.84 nm ( p  = 0.14) with a PDI of 0.51
± 0.03 ( p  = 0.08). Although the particle size
of ZnO NPs increased from 24.01 ± 1.70 nm to 133.4 ± 0.84
nm after 60 days, they could still penetrate the skin through the
microchannels formed by the MNs, bypassing the  SC .

Figure  
 C illustrates
the zeta potential of ZnO NPs upon storage at room temperature. The
initial zeta potential of ZnO NPs was −18.45 ± 1.80 mV,
indicating that the nanoparticles may repel one another, thereby reducing
aggregation. This aligns with Faisal et al.,  who reported the formation of green-synthesized ZnO NPs using  Myristica fragrans  extract with a negative zeta potential
of −22.1 mV.

The zeta potential is a direct indicator
of the stability of colloidal
dispersions, where a high negative or positive charge on nanoparticles
indicates repulsion between them, decreasing the likelihood of aggregation.  After 30 days of storage, the zeta potential
decreased from −18.45 ± 1.80 mV to −10.28 ±
0.24 mV. Then, a statistically significant reduction to −6.55
± 0.55 mV ( p  < 0.05) was observed in the
zeta potential after 60 days. The change in zeta potential over time
might be attributed to changes in particle size during storage.  A larger size of ZnO NPs (133.4 ± 0.84
nm) led to a decrease in zeta potential after 60 days (−6.55
± 0.55 mV). John Malik  reported
that aggregation is the most likely factor influencing particle size
and zeta potential over time. The loss of surface charge on nanoparticles
due to adsorbed water molecules neutralizes the charge, leading to
aggregation and the formation of larger nanoparticles.  Additionally, the reduction in the zeta potential
of ZnO NPs, from −18.45 ± 1.80 mV to −6.55 ±
0.55 mV, may not significantly affect their stability. This is because
loading ZnO NPs into MNs further stabilizes the nanoparticles by physically
separating them, thereby preventing their aggregation.

The X-ray diffraction
pattern of the green-synthesized ZnO NPs showed distinct sharp peaks
observed at 2θ values of 31.91°, 34.56°, 36.39°,
47.67°, 56.72°, 62.97°, 68.08°, and 69.18°,
which are typical for the ZnO structure ( Figure  
 ). The diffraction pattern obtained was analyzed
and compared with the standard data from the International Center
for Diffraction Data (ICDD) to identify the crystal phase of the synthesized
material. The diffraction peaks were indexed to the (100), (002),
(101), (102), (110), (103), (112), and (201) crystallographic planes
of the hexagonal wurtzite structure of ZnO NPs, respectively.  The diffraction pattern corresponds to the P63mc
(No. 186) space group, in agreement with the reference data (ICDD
card no. 01–086–8817). These results are consistent
with, 
 − 
 
  which reported similar 2θ values for green-synthesized
ZnO NPs, confirming the successful formation of a crystalline ZnO
nanostructure.

NPs was calculated
using the Scherrer eq ( eq  
 ) for the most intense diffraction peak of the (101) plane and the
full width at half-maximum (FWHM) value of 0.6063° at 2θ
of 36.396°.

To further confirm the purity of the green-synthesized ZnO NPs,
elemental mapping was performed using EDS. The ZnO NPs samples showed
that the major chemical constituents were zinc (Zn) and oxygen (O),
with corresponding mass percentages of 42.02 ± 1.15% and 33.26
1.17%, respectively ( Table  
 ), confirming the presence of ZnO. The relatively high carbon
(C) content (16.55 ± 0.17%) is due to the sample grid holder
used for the measurements being covered with a carbon sticker and
the deposition of phytochemicals onto the ZnO NPs’ surfaces.  Additionally, elemental analysis detected silicon
(Si, 4.28 ± 0.12%) and phosphorus (P, 2.04 ± 0.05%), which
together accounted for approximately 6% of the total elemental mass.
The presence of these elements in the EDS spectrum of the green-synthesized
ZnO NPs might be attributed to residual phytochemicals from the plant
extracts that remain adsorbed on the nanoparticle surface. 
 , 
  Elements other than Zn and O, including phosphorus, silicon, sulfur,
and calcium, have been reported in the EDS spectrum of the green-synthesized
ZnO NPs, but at trace levels (<1.5% total).  Therefore, future studies should focus on minimizing these
elements by optimizing the synthesis protocol to ensure higher-purity
ZnO NPs.

The TEM images showed that the synthesized nanoparticles were spherical
and uniformly distributed with no significant agglomeration ( Figure  
 D). The particle-size
histogram ( Figure  
 E) of ZnO NPs indicates that particle sizes range from 20 to 50 nm,
with no particles smaller than 20 nm. The frequency distribution observed
from the histogram shows that about 46% of the particles fall within
the 20–30 nm range. These results are in agreement with the
initial particle size of ZnO NPs obtained by DLS measurements, which
was 24.01 ± 1.70 nm ( Figure  
 A). It has been shown that the shape and size of ZnO
NPs impact their ability to penetrate the skin,  with smaller ZnO NPs able to penetrate tumor cells more
deeply than larger nanoparticles.  TEM
is considered more accurate than DLS for determining the size of nanoparticles.  This is because TEM uses a high-voltage electron
beam that interacts with the sample to produce the final image. In
contrast, DLS estimates particle size by measuring the random variations
in light-scattering intensity resulting from the particles’
Brownian motion.

Dissolving MNs based on the “poke and dissolve” approach,
where drugs are loaded into biocompatible polymers that dissolve upon
puncturing the skin without leaving any traces.  Na CMC was selected as the primary polymeric matrix because
it is biocompatible, biodegradable, water-soluble, and mechanically
strong enough to penetrate the  SC  while rapidly dissolves
upon insertion. Na CMC offered a balance between mechanical integrity,
controlled dissolution rate, and compatibility with the green-synthesized
ZnO NPs, ensuring homogeneous dispersion without aggregation.

Four Na CMC gel formulations were used
to fabricate the MN matrices (M1-M4) ( Table  
 ). After allowing the molds to dry overnight,
the needles were carefully removed and examined both visually and
under a microscope to ensure proper filling. The inspection demonstrated
that M1-M3, composed of 6, 10, and 12% Na CMC, respectively, were
promising matrices for MNs. Conversely, M4, which contained 14% Na
CMC, had unpacked needles where the MN holes were empty, and air bubbles
were visible. This might be due to the high Na CMC concentration,
which increases the viscosity of the M4 gel formulation and hinders
the gel from filling the mold’s holes. Consequently, the M4
gel formulation was excluded from further testing. The mechanical
properties of M1-M3MNs were assessed by measuring the %Height reduction.
Each MN was subjected to a 32 N force for 30 s using a texture analyzer.
The difference in the needles’ height before and after applying
the force was calculated. M1, which comprises 6% Na CMC, exhibited
a %Height reduction of 16.73 ± 0.06%. According to Zaid Alkilani
et al.,  an acceptable %Height reduction
was reported to be ≤ 10%. This suggests that M1 was brittle
and prone to breakage during handling, making it unsuitable for fabricating
ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs. In contrast, M2 and M3, which contain
10 and 12% Na CMC, respectively, showed %Height reductions of 5.09
± 0.05 and 7.8 ± 0.1%, indicating that M2 and M3 were strong
enough to withstand a force of 32 N. Consequently, 10 and 12% Na CMC
were selected for further testing to identify the most suitable matrix.

The viscosities of 10% Na CMC (M2) and 12% Na CMC
(M3) were determined
to identify the best Na CMC gel formulation.  Figure  
  shows that M2 exhibited lower viscosity
than M3 due to its lower Na CMC concentration (10%) compared to M3
(12%), indicating fewer intermolecular interactions between Na CMC
molecules.  The viscosity curves of M2
and M3 display a plateau at shear rates below 1 s –1 , followed by shear-thinning behavior. This property is advantageous
for MN applications; when the MNs are pressed into the skin, the gel
becomes less viscous, making it easier to inject and deliver the cargo.  Therefore, 10% Na CMC (M2), with its lower viscosity,
was chosen as the MN matrix for loading either ZnO NPs or DOX.

Therefore, the choice of gel formulation was based
on the mechanical
properties of the MN matrices and the viscosity of their respective
polymeric mixtures. Since M2 and M3 exhibited shear-thinning behavior,
which facilitates injectability and drug delivery under pressure,
the MN matrix (M2) with lower height reduction and viscosity was selected
as the optimal MN matrix. Meanwhile, the best covering layer among
C1–C3 was chosen after pouring the gels into molds filled with
M2MN matrices ( Table  
 ). The covering layer (C2) comprises 6% Na CMC and 0.5% glycerin,
exhibiting optimal mechanical properties, including needle shape and
shape retention upon removal from the molds.

Dissolving MNs
are made of water-soluble polymers that carry drugs
within their MN arrays. These needles dissolve completely and rapidly
after skin insertion, leaving no biohazardous residues at the application
site.  The ability of MNs to improve transdermal
delivery is achieved by overcoming the complex  SC . 
 Figure  
 A and B illustrate the ZnO NP-loaded MNs and DOX-loaded
MNs.

The viscosity of the MN matrix (M2) might be altered after loading
ZnO NPs and DOX, which could impact the filling of the polymer mixtures
into the mold cavities during centrifugation.  Figure  
  compares the viscosity of the M2 matrix
(blank, 10% Na CMC) with its corresponding MN matrices loaded with
ZnO NPs and DOX. The viscosity of the blank 10% Na CMC (M2) was higher
than that of the polymer mixtures of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs. These
findings are consistent with Benchabane et al.,  who reported that Na CMC exhibits shear-thinning behavior,
with a plateau at medium shear rates (10° s –1 –10 2  s –1 ). The differences between
our results and those reported by Benchabane et al.  might be attributed to variations in the Na CMC concentration
used as the matrix in both studies. Hameed et al.  demonstrated that the decrease in Na CMC gel viscosity
when mixed with ZnO NPs is attributed to the interference of ZnO NPs
with Na CMC entanglement, disrupting the network and deterring its
entanglement, hence reducing the overall viscosity of the gel. Whereas
the viscosity of the polymer mixture of DOX-loaded MNs was higher
than that of the ZnO NPs-loaded MNs, suggesting a profound effect
of ZnO NPs on the viscosity of the Na CMC network compared to that
of DOX.

The morphology of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs is displayed in  Figure  
 . The needles had
a pyramidal shape with a square base. The molds used to fabricate
the MNs were a pyramidal MN master template with 15 × 15 MN arrays,
each measuring 300 × 800 μm (width × height).

MNs need to possess the optimal mechanical
properties to withstand handling, application pressure, and the delivery
of the loaded drug as intended. After determining the mechanical properties
of 10% Na CMC (M2) as a potential matrix for MNs, the effect of applying
a 32 N force for 30 s on ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs was quantitatively
assessed using a texture analyzer.  Figure  
  illustrates the ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs
before and after applying 32 N for 30 s with the texture analyzer.

The %Height reduction was calculated by measuring
needle heights
from the tip to the base before and after force application. The ZnO
NP-loaded MNs exhibited a %Height reduction of 5.08 ± 0.05% ( Figure  
 ), while DOX-loaded
MNs showed a %Height reduction of 5.05 ± 0.15%, with a slight
bending in the tips. None of the needles experienced shape deformity
or fracture.

Performing insertion studies using artificial membranes,
such as Parafilm M, offers an alternative to biological membranes,
which have drawbacks such as heterogeneity, instability, and complexity
that hinder standardization.  Parafilm
M is well-known for its ability to simulate skin during MN insertion.  The penetration depth into one layer of Parafilm
M is about 126 μm. ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs can pierce the
first three to four layers of Parafilm M, reaching approximately 378–504
μm ( Figure  
 A). For efficient drug delivery, the needle length should be sufficient
to create microchannels through the 130–180 μm-thick
viable epidermis and dissolve in the dermal layer.  Thus, ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs have demonstrated improved
mechanical properties and enhanced penetration efficiency. The number
of holes created by ZnO NP-loaded MNs and DOX-loaded MNs and their
corresponding perforated layers of Parafilm M are shown in  Figure  
 B and C.

Microneedles must have the perfect balance between their
ability to penetrate the skin and dissolve rapidly to deliver their
cargo effectively.  Based on applied force,
the dissolution rates of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs were determined
at 0, 5, 10, 20, and 30 min after insertion into rat skin, as illustrated
in  Table  
 . In the
first 5 min, 31.39% of ZnO NP-loaded MNs had dissolved, compared to
21.96% of DOX-loaded MNs. After 10 min of MNs’ application
into rat skin, 47.04 and 32.07% of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs had
dissolved, respectively. At 20 min of insertion, ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded
MNs dissolved at rates of 62.29 and 81.34%, respectively. DOX-loaded
MNs completely dissolved after 25 min, while at the same time point,
80.10% of ZnO NP-loaded MNs had dissolved, with complete dissolution
occurring at 30 min.

The particle size of ZnO NPs after casting the MNs
and dissolving them in ultrapure water was 63.14 ± 1.4 nm, and
the PDI was 0.48 ± 0.03. This indicates an increase in particle
size and PDI by 62 and 49%, respectively, compared to the initial
particle size and PDI of 24.01 ± 1.70 nm and 0.25 ± 0.02,
respectively. The larger size could be due to the coating of ZnO NPs
with the Na CMC polymer mixture. Nevertheless, the size of these ZnO
NPs remains within the acceptable range for transdermally delivered
nanoparticles, which is less than 100 nm.

ZnO NP-loaded MNs loaded with 0.85 mg ZnO NPs showed a recovery
of 101.8 ± 1.3%. Whereas DOX-loaded MNs loaded with 0.9 mg DOX
showed a recovery of 98.4 ± 0.0%. Therefore, the fabrication
process of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs and their composition did not
alter the drug content within the MN, indicating that the manufacturing
process was effective.

FTIR spectroscopy is a valuable tool for structural analysis, allowing
the assessment of ingredient incompatibility by studying their molecular
interactions. 
 Figure  
 A illustrates the FTIR spectra of Na CMC
powder, ZnO NPs powder, physical mixtures of ZnO NPs and Na CMC, polymeric
mixture of ZnO NPs and NA CMC, and ZnO NPs-loaded MNs.

The FTIR spectrum of Na CMC powder displayed a
peak at 2922 cm –1 , corresponding to the C–H
stretching vibrations,
and a broad peak between 3040 and 3506 cm –1 , corresponding
to O–H stretching of cellulose.  Peaks at 1414 and 1590 cm –1  correspond to the
symmetric and asymmetric stretching of the COO– group, respectively.
The peak at 1323 cm –1  corresponds to the O–H
bending vibrations.

The FTIR spectrum of the green-synthesized
ZnO NPs exhibited distinct
peaks at 645, 925, 1013, 1405, 1562, 1637, 1705, and 3417 cm –1 . The band at 645 cm –1  falls within the typical
Zn–O vibrational region (500–900 cm –1 ) as reported by Jaishi et al.,  whose
FTIR spectrum showed notable peaks at 877 and 520 cm –1 . Other studies on plant-mediated ZnO NPs showed similar features
in the range of 682–882 cm –1 .  and 517 cm –1 .  The peaks at 1014 and 1406 cm –1  correspond
to the C–O bond and the aromatic amine stretch C–N,
respectively. The peaks between 1560 and 1701 cm –1  correspond to C = O and C = C stretching vibrations in the aromatic
ring and polyphenols of the extract, respectively, confirming the
presence of the plant extract around the green-synthesized ZnO NPs.  The broad absorption peak at 3416 cm –1  corresponds to O–H groups, suggesting hydroxyl-containing
biomolecules adsorbed on the nanoparticle surface. A similar broad
O–H stretching peak was observed at 3417 cm –1  by Govahi et al.,  which corresponds
to the phenolic O–H functional group of the plant extract,
rich in phenolic and aromatic compounds.

The FTIR spectrum of
the physical mixture of ZnO NPs and Na CMC
shows the characteristic peaks of both ZnO NPs and Na CMC observed
in their respective pure spectra, but with reduced intensity. The
FTIR spectrum of the ZnO NPs and Na CMC polymer mixture showed no
new peaks, indicating no chemical interaction between the components.
Additionally, the broad peak observed in the 3400–3600 cm –1  range was more intense than the peak observed in
the FTIR spectrum of pure Na CMC, due to the abundance of O–H
groups from water.

The FTIR spectrum of ZnO NP-loaded MNs features
a characteristic
peak at 643 cm –1  associated with the ZnO NPs, though
it is less intense. Additionally, no new interactions are observed,
suggesting that the materials used to fabricate the MNs remain chemically
stable.

Figure  
 B shows
the FTIR spectrum of Na CMC discussed earlier. The FTIR spectrum of
DOX powder displayed peaks at 3527 and 3318 cm –1 , which correspond to the N–H stretching vibrations of the
primary amine group and O–H stretching, respectively. The peaks
at 2897 and 2932 cm –1  corresponded to the C–H
stretching. The peak at 1730 cm –1  corresponded to
the carbonyl group stretching in the anthracycline ring of DOX. Peaks
at 1615, 1580, 1525, and 1413 cm –1  are characteristic
of C = C ring stretching. Similar FTIR peaks for DOX powder were reported
by.

The FTIR spectrum of the physical
mixture of DOX and Na CMC showed
the characteristic peaks of both Na CMC and DOX powders, but at lower
intensities. The FTIR spectrum of the DOX and Na CMC polymer solution
showed several changes in the functional groups of both components.
The DOX peak around 1730 cm –1  was not prominent
due to dilution, as the amount of DOX in the gel formulation was lower
than that of Na CMC, resulting in more dominant Na CMC peaks. Additionally,
the disappearance of DOX peaks could be attributed to hydrogen bonding
between the amine groups of Na CMC and the carbonyl groups of DOX,
leading to their elimination and the formation of N–H stretching
bonds, and with the water molecules to form new hydrogen bonds. The
C–H stretching peaks were slightly shifted to 2883 and 2916
cm –1 . Furthermore, the peaks between 3000–3599
cm –1 , representing O–H and N–H bonds,
appeared broadened, indicating hydrogen-bond formation between Na
CMC, DOX, and water. The FITR spectrum of DOX-loaded MNs resembled
that of the polymer mixture, with peaks at 2917 and 2879 cm –1  corresponding to DOX loaded into MNs.

**Ex vivo  Permeation of ZnO
NP- and DOX-Loaded MNs**

To evaluate the permeation of ZnO
NPs and DOX into rat skin,  ex vivo  permeation studies
were conducted for ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs ( Figure  
 ). After 2 h, the cumulative amounts of
ZnO and DOX permeated from the loaded MNs per unit surface area were
44.23 ± 8.34 μg/cm 2  and 163.22 μg/cm 2 , respectively, corresponding to the percent amount permeated
(Q%) of 5.20 ± 0.98% for ZnO and 18.14 ± 3.05% for DOX.
After 5 h, the cumulative permeated amounts increased to 173.91 ±
22.84 μg/cm 2  for ZnO and 423.17 μg/cm 2  for DOX, corresponding to Q% values of 20.46 ± 2.69% and 47.02
± 7.66%, respectively. After 24 h, ZnO showed a cumulative amount
of 299.10 ± 43.22 μg/cm 2 , corresponding to a
35.19 ± 5.08% release, while DOX reached 604.28 ± 83.71
μg/cm 2 , representing a 67.14 ± 9.30% release.

Therefore, applying ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs
resulted in incomplete
skin permeation of the loaded ZnO NPs and DOX, with permeation rates
of 35.19 ± 5.08% and 67.14 ± 9.30% after 24 h, respectively.
This can be attributed to the fact that both ZnO NPs and DOX can form
chemical interactions with the CMC matrix. 
 − 
 
  ZnO NPs form
hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl groups of the CMC polymer chain
and the oxygen atoms of the ZnO NPs, as well as electrostatic interactions
between the Zn 2+  ions and the carboxylate groups of the
CMC matrix. 
 , 
  Whereas the hydroxyl and amino
groups of DOX can form hydrogen bonding with the carboxylate groups
of the CMC matrix.  This suggests a retardation
in the release of loaded ZnO NPs and DOX from the MN matrix. Nonetheless,
DOX exhibits a higher permeation rate than ZnO NPs. This is because
DOX, as hydrochloride, is a highly water-soluble small molecule  that can readily diffuse through the microchannels
created by microneedles. In contrast, ZnO NPs tend to interact strongly
with the CMC matrix through hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions,
and physical entrapment within the polymer network.  Additionally, the presence of ZnO NPs induces steric hindrance
and slower diffusion, further limiting their permeation compared to
free DOX.

Table  
  summarizes
the cumulative amounts of ZnO and DOX permeated per unit surface area
(Q/A), percent amount permeated (Q%), steady-state flux (J ss ), and permeability coefficient (P) across rat skin after 24 h. The
J ss  and permeability coefficient (P) for DOX-loaded MNs
were higher than those of ZnO NP-loaded MNs, in agreement with the  ex vivo  permeation results.

**Ex vivo  Skin Deposition Study**

The skin deposition results further support the permeation behavior
of ZnO NPs and DOX from the loaded MNs across the rat skin. Quantitative
analysis demonstrated that the amount of ZnO NPs retained within the
skin was 106.74 ± 3.86 μg, corresponding to 12.56 ±
0.45% of the total loaded amount of ZnO NPs. Whereas the deposition
of DOX within the skin was 237.85 ± 83.61 μg, corresponding
to 26.43 ± 3.21% of the total loaded amount of DOX. The accumulation
of ZnO NPs in the skin was low, owing to the chemical interactions
between ZnO NPs and the CMC matrix, 
 , 
  which hindered
their diffusion from the MN matrix and restricted the mobility of
ZnO NPs within the skin. Whereas DOX, with its relatively small molecule,
facilitates its diffusion through the aqueous microchannels created
by the microneedle.

The MTT assay was performed to evaluate the cytotoxic effect of synthetic
ZnO NPs, green-synthesized ZnO NPs, and zinc acetate on MCF-7 and
HDF cells. The results showed a concentration-dependent decrease in
cell viability for both cell lines after exposure to both synthetic
and plant-extract-derived ZnO NPs and zinc acetate. These findings
support the primary goal of this study, which is to explore the therapeutic
potential of green-synthesized ZnO NPs as a safer and more effective
alternative to conventional chemotherapeutics for breast cancer, delivered
via minimally invasive dissolving MNs.

As shown in  Figure  
 A, synthetic ZnO
NPs demonstrated a marked cytotoxic effect on MCF-7 cells at all tested
concentrations, with a dose-dependent decrease in cell viability.
At the highest concentration (50 μg/mL), the cell viability
declined significantly compared to the control, reaching approximately
15.64%. The green-synthesized ZnO NPs also reduced MCF-7 cell viability,
with an effect slightly higher than that of synthetic ZnO NPs. This
may be attributed to bioactive phytochemicals present in the plant
extract, which could interact synergistically with the ZnO core and
contribute to the observed cytotoxic activity. Zinc acetate exhibited
a cytotoxic effect comparable to that of synthetic ZnO NPs, with MCF-7
cell viability decreasing to 20.52%, 27.75%, and 37.51% following
treatment with 50, 25, and 12.5 μg/mL, respectively. The statistical
analysis revealed significant differences in cytotoxicity between
the treated and control groups ( p  < 0.05) for
most concentrations, indicating the cytotoxic potential of green
ZnO NPs against MCF-7 cells. These findings align with the literature,
which suggests that green ZnO NPs exhibit selective cytotoxicity toward
breast cancer cells through ROS-mediated apoptosis.  Moreover, Mongy et al.  demonstrated
that ZnO NPs synthesized using  Rhus coriaria  extract effectively inhibited MCF-7 cell proliferation in a concentration-dependent
manner. Similarly, George et al.  found
that ZnO NPs capped with  Rubus fairholmianus  extract induced apoptosis in breast cancer cells through a mitochondrial
pathway. This makes the green-synthesized ZnO NPs promising candidates
for incorporation into dissolving MNs, which offer localized delivery,
avoid hepatic metabolism, and enhance patient compliance through the
potential for self-administration.

Unlike MCF-7 cells, HDF cells demonstrated greater
resistance to
ZnO NP-induced cytotoxicity ( Figure  
 B). While higher concentrations (50 and 25 μg/mL)
of the synthetic ZnO NPs and zinc acetate induced a significant reduction
in cell viability, lower concentrations (12.5 and 5 μg/mL) resulted
in minimal cytotoxicity. Furthermore, the green-synthesized ZnO NPs
exhibited even lower toxicity toward HDF cells compared to synthetic
ZnO NPs, suggesting a potentially safer profile for biomedical applications.
These findings are consistent with those of Reis et al.,  who reported lower IC 50  values for
plant-derived ZnO NPs in HDF cells than for synthetic ZnO.

Taken
together, our results showed that green-synthesized ZnO NPs
can minimize damage to normal cells while preserving anticancer effectiveness,
an essential factor in developing less invasive and safer cancer treatments,
particularly when delivered transdermally via microneedles. This selectivity
supports the rationale for exploring plant-extract-derived ZnO NPs
as safer alternatives to conventional chemotherapeutics, particularly
when administered locally through MNs.

The stability of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs in terms
of moisture content, %Height reduction, and depth of needle insertion
was evaluated after 1, 2, 4, and 8 weeks at room temperature (22 °C)
and in the refrigerator (4 °C). To determine the moisture content
of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs,  Tables S1–S4  present the initial weight and the weight of MNs recorded after
8 weeks of storage at room temperature and in the refrigerator.

Overall, ZnO NP- and
DOX-loaded MNs showed better stability when
stored in the refrigerator (4 °C). Whereas signs of instability,
such as increased moisture content and %Height reduction, and decreased
needle insertion were more pronounced at room temperature.  Tables  
  and   summarize the moisture content, %Height reduction, and needle
insertion depth of ZnO NP- and DOX-loaded MNs at room temperature
and 4 °C after 1, 2, 4, and 8 weeks.

To overcome the limitations
of traditional methods for synthesizing
ZnO NPs, an environmentally safe, simple green synthesis method was
developed. The novelty of this study lies in combining three elements
that have not been previously combined.  P. dactylifera  root extract was used at an optimized 4:1 volume ratio with 0.8
M zinc acetate dihydrate to prepare eco-friendly, stable, and uniformly
spherical nanoparticles. The size of the green-synthesized ZnO NPs
was confirmed by DLS and TEM. Additionally, the crystalline nature
of ZnO NPs, their hexagonal shape, and the presence of ZnO were confirmed
by XRD and EDS analyses, respectively, demonstrating the success of
the green synthesis pathway. These green-synthesized ZnO NPs were
incorporated into dissolving MNs comprised of 10% Na CMC for potential
transdermal delivery in breast cancer-related applications. Furthermore,
the green-synthesized ZnO NPs demonstrated selectivity against MCF-7
breast cancer cells, with lower toxicity toward fibroblasts, indicating
promising cytotoxic potential compared to synthetic ZnO NPs. However,
it is important to emphasize that this biological activity was evaluated
using free ZnO NPs in solution and not from the MN formulation or
its released contents. Therefore, no direct conclusion can be drawn
regarding the anticancer efficacy of the MN-delivered system based
on the current data. Overall, the findings of this study demonstrate
the feasibility of combining green-synthesized ZnO NPs with dissolving
MNs as a promising, minimally invasive transdermal delivery approach.
Nevertheless, this work represents a preliminary investigation, and
further studies are still required to evaluate the cytotoxic effects
of ZnO NPs released from the MN system, as well as their  in
vivo  pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and ability to achieve
therapeutically relevant concentrations at target tumor sites, to
better understand their biological behavior, safety profile, and potential
applicability in breast cancer-related applications.
