## Outcomes of adult patients with Li-Fraumeni syndrome and myeloid neoplasms.

**PMID**: 42755391 · **Journal**: Cancer · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1002/cncr.70613 · **PMCID**: PMC13586844

**Authors**: Senapati Jayastu, Abdel-Salam Hiam M, Jdanov Vladislav D, Loghavi Sanam, Woodson Ashley, Corredor Jessica, Borthakur Gautam, Daver Naval G, Kadia Tapan M, Takahashi Koichi, Alvarado Yesid, Pemmaraju Naveen, Popat Uday R, Shpall Elizabeth J, Ravandi Farhad, McAllister Florencia, Daw Najat C, Garcia-Manero Guillermo, Arun Banu K, DiNardo Courtney D

**Types**: Journal Article

**BACKGROUND**: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is an inherited cancer predisposition syndrome. Hematologic malignancies are not considered LFS defining tumors, however, both acute lymphoblastic leukemia and therapy-related myeloid neoplasms (MNs) in LFS are described. Treatment approaches and outcomes of MN in LFS need further evaluation.

**METHODS**: The authors performed a retrospective analysis to understand treatment approaches and outcomes in patients with LFS who developed an MN.

**RESULTS**: Among 190 patients with LFS between February 2001 and February 2026 with a history of at least one neoplasm, 14 (7%) had an MN. Median age at MN diagnosis was 43 years (range, 25-73) and 11 (79%) patients were female. Overall, eight (57%) patients had myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), five (36%) had acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and one (7%) had T-myeloid mixed phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL). With frontline therapy, six (75%) patients with MDS and one (17%) patient with AML achieved an overall response. Considering all lines of therapy received, cumulatively six (75%) patients with MDS and five (83%) patients with AML/MPAL achieved an overall response. At a median follow-up of 28.8 months, the median overall survival (OS) was 18.2 months, and 1-year and 2-year OS rates were 77% and 17%, respectively. Five patients (two MDS, two AML, and one MPAL) underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation during their MN therapy with a median OS of 19.3 months.

**CONCLUSION**: Although short-lived responses to leukemia-directed therapy are common, long-term survival in most patients with LFS developing MN are poor. Additional research and understanding of the mechanisms to prevent MN and to improve MN treatment in LFS are needed.

Li Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder related to a germline  TP53  mutation, associated with high penetrance and a strong predisposition to multiple cancers. 
 1 
  The lifetime incidence of cancer ranges from 70% to 80% in men to almost 90%–100% in women. 
 2 
 ,  
 3 
  Although early onset breast cancer is the most common malignancy encountered in LFS, many patients experience multiple cancers through their life and certain rare cancers like adrenocortical carcinomas, recurrent osteosarcomas, choroid plexus carcinoma, etc. are strongly associated with LFS. Hematological neoplasms have been reported in approximately 10%–30% of patients across different LFS cohorts, with pediatric onset hypodiploid acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) being the most common type,. 
 4 
 ,  
 5 
  However, myeloid neoplasms (MNs), which are most often encountered as therapy‐related after exposure to cytotoxic therapy (chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy) for previous nonmyeloid cancers, are also described. The overall rarity of LFS and relative rarity of MNs in LFS means there are limited cohort data available and no clear treatment recommendations. Furthermore, assessment of therapy‐related myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)/acute myeloid leukemia (AML) versus de novo MDS/AML in LFS and outcomes with contemporary treatment options are needed to refine therapeutic decisions.

Somatic  TP53  mutations are common in MDS and AML, reported in ∼20% of patients, and associated with treatment resistance and dismal prognosis. Regardless of age and treatment pattern, the median overall survival is less than 1 year in patients with biallelic  TP53  aberrations. 
 6 
 ,  
 7 
 ,  
 8 
  Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in remission leads to long‐term survival in a small subset of patients. In patients with LFS who develops MDS/AML, heightened risks of organ toxicity from prior chemotherapy and HSCT conditioning, along with morbidities from prior nonmyeloid cancer therapy or residual nonmyeloid cancer, makes delivery of adequate MDS/AML therapy and HSCT challenging. 
 9 
 ,  
 10 
  Such challenges are also seen in therapy‐related MDS/AML without LFS, an entity enriched with  TP53  aberrations from chemotherapy‐/radiotherapy‐induced selection of  TP53  mutated myeloid clones. 
 11

To understand these issues further, we evaluated a cohort of adult patients with LFS who developed MDS/AML with or without exposure to prior nonmyeloid cancer therapy and assessed their trajectory of LFS and associated cancers, treatment regimens administered, and MDS/AML response and survival outcomes.

We identified patients with a confirmed diagnosis of a hematologic malignancy including MDS or AML from the full cohort of patients with LFS followed at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (MNs with germline  TP53  variant pathogenic/likely pathogenic, as per World Health Organization 2022). 
 12 
  The diagnosis of LFS was based on the identification of a pathogenic/likely pathogenic  TP53  mutation on germline testing with or without the fulfillment of the updated Chompret criteria. 
 13 
  Germline testing was completed on peripheral blood, saliva, buccal swab, or cultured fibroblasts. Patients with a suspected diagnosis of  TP53 ‐related clonal hematopoiesis based on variant detection below heterozygous variant allele frequency and negative ancillary testing on cultured fibroblasts were excluded. Electronic health records (EHR) were used to identify a diagnosis of MDS/AML (MN) and cross verified separately by two investigators.

Baseline characteristics of all patients with LFS were collected. For patients with a MN, baseline disease parameters, history of prior nonmyeloid cancer diagnosis, if any, and treatment details, concurrent genomics at time of MN diagnosis and therapy administered were extracted from EHR. Responses were annotated as per international working group (IWG) 2006 response criteria for MDS and European LeukemiaNet (ELN) 2022 response criteria for AML (including mixed phenotypic acute leukemia [MPAL]). 
 14 
 ,  
 15 
  Overall response includes complete remission (CR), marrow CR (mCR), partial response (PR), and hematological improvement for MDS and CR, CR with incomplete counts recovery (CRi) and morphological leukemia‐free state (MLFS) for AML/MPAL. Composite complete response included CR and CRi for AML/MPAL. Responses to frontline therapy as well as anytime during MDS/AML therapy were annotated. Diagnosis of MPAL was based on criteria as previously described. 
 16

All patients had a mutational assessment in 81 commonly mutated genes in myeloid neoplasms in our Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments–approved laboratory, including  TP53  gene (Table  S1 ). Cytogenetic evaluation included a combination of G‐banded karyotyping and fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH). Measurable residual disease (MRD) was assessed by multiparameter flow cytometry at a sensitivity of 1 in 10 4 . Duration of response (DOR) was calculated from the time point of achievement of an overall response to disease progression or death, whichever was earlier, and overall survival (OS) was calculated from the time of MN diagnosis to death. Both DOR and OS were censored for patients alive at last follow‐up and were not censored for HSCT. Kaplan–Meier estimation was used for calculation of DOR and OS.

Analysis was done on GraphPad Prism version 10.0.0 for Windows (GraphPad Software, Boston, Massachusetts,  www.graphpad ) and R Core Team ( https://www.R‐project.org/ ).

The study was approved by the institutional review board and research and reporting performed as per the Declaration of Helsinki.

From August 2001 to August 2025, 190 patients with LFS and a history of malignancy were identified. Most patients were female (141; 74.7%) and of White ethnicity (117; 61.6%). The median age at LFS diagnosis was 38 years (range, 3–98 years), and 98 patients (51.6%) fulfilled the modified Chompret criteria. The median age at diagnosis of first malignancy was 33 years (range, 2–72 years).

A total of 26 (13.7%) patients were diagnosed with hematological neoplasm anytime in their life, of whom 14 (7.4% of LFS cohort) had a diagnosis of a MN (Table  S2 ). The median age at diagnosis of MN was 42.8 years (range, 24.8–73.2 year), and 11 (78.6%) patients were female (Table  1 ). The diagnosis of MN included MDS in eight patients (57.1%) of whom five patients had MDS‐IB1 and three patients had MDS‐IB2 at diagnosis. Another five patients (35.7%) had AML, and one patient (7.1%) had T‐myeloid MPAL. Overall, MN was the primary presenting neoplasm in only three patients and for the remaining 11 patients, the MN was at median the third malignancy (range, 1–6). Among these 11 patients with prior nonmyeloid neoplasms who developed MDS/AML (therapy‐related MN), all patients had received prior chemotherapy, and five patients had also received prior radiotherapy.

At the time of MN diagnosis, 13 patients (92.9%) had a complex karyotype (three or more independent clonal chromosomal changes including a structural aberration) and only one patient (7.1%) had a diploid karyotype. Three patients had a secondary somatic  TP53  mutation identified, all with a small clone size (<5% variant allele fraction). Overall, the primary  TP53  mutation was a missense mutation in seven (50%) patients, truncating (nonsense) mutation in four (28.6%) patients, and one patient (7.1%) each with canonical splice site mutation, frameshift mutation, and synonymous mutation (Figure  1 ). The germline  TP53  mutation was considered pathogenic in 12 (85.7%%) patients and likely pathogenic in two (14.3%) patients.

Among eight patients diagnosed with MDS, six had therapy‐related MDS and two patients had de novo MDS. Among patients with therapy‐related MDS, the median time from first chemotherapy/radiotherapy exposure for prior neoplasm to MDS diagnosis was 11.9 years (range, 0.3–33.1 years). The time to development of MDS from treatment for prior nonmyeloid malignancy was ≥1 year in five patients and <1 year in one patient. All patients with MDS were initiated on hypomethylating agent (HMA)‐based therapy, which included HMA alone in six patients, HMA + venetoclax in one patient, and HMA + magrolimab in one patient. An overall response was achieved in six (75%) patients pre‐HSCT which included CR in two (25%) patients, mCR in two (25%) patients, and hematological improvement (HI) without mCR in two (25%) patients (Table  2 ). Among the four patients with CR/mCR, three patients had received HMA monotherapy, and one patient had received HMA + magrolimab; the median DOR was 5.6 months (range, 1.0–12.2 months). Both patients who achieved HI had received HMA monotherapy, one patient each with stable disease and no response had received HMA and HMA + venetoclax, respectively. Patients received a median of one line of MDS therapy (range, 1–3) (Figure  2 ).

Two (25%) patients with MDS were able to proceed to HSCT, one responder with CR after frontline therapy and one nonresponder with stable disease (pre‐HSCT bone marrow showed 10% blasts) after frontline therapy. The first patient relapsed 2.5 months after HSCT and died, whereas the second patient achieved CR after HSCT and remains alive in CR 28.8 months post‐MDS diagnosis and 24.3 months post‐HSCT. This patient received 12 months of oral decitabine‐cedazuridine as post‐HSCT maintenance. HSCT donor and conditioning details are mentioned in Table  S3 .

Among the responders who have died at last follow‐up ( n  = 5), two patients died after progression to AML and without any further response, one patient disease with persistent disease after relapse post‐HSCT and two patients (both with HI) had progression of prior nonmyeloid cancer and died in continued HI (nonrelapse mortality). At last follow‐up, three patients are alive. This included one patient post‐HSCT described above and two patients with persistent disease, one on second line decitabine therapy and one patient receiving supportive care alone. Among six patients with prior nonmyeloid cancers, three had progression of their solid cancer during MDS therapy, and three patients remained in remission from their previous nonmyeloid cancer. The median OS for the MDS cohort was 15.2 months (95% CI, 6.2–not estimable [NE]) (Figure  3A ).

Among the six patients with AML/MPAL, five had therapy‐related AML, and one patient with MPAL had de novo leukemia. AML developed at a median of 9.6 years (range, 1.9–25.2 years) from receipt of first chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy for prior neoplasms. The time to development of AML was ≥1 year in four patients and <1 year in one patient (patient with MPAL). Five patients received intensive chemotherapy, and two patients were treated with lower‐intensity therapy (LIT), consisting of decitabine in one patient and azacitidine with vorinostat on a clinical trial in one patient. Only one patient with a concurrent  IDH2  mutation achieved response with frontline therapy (MRD‐negative CR) to an intensive chemotherapy regimen with a DOR of 22.3 months. Three other patients had >50% blast reduction without blood count recovery with frontline therapy.

All patients received subsequent lines of therapy. Three patients achieved CR and one patient achieved MLFS with salvage therapy. One patient with no prior response with intensive chemotherapy + checkpoint inhibitor on a clinical trial received multiple further lines of therapy and eventually achieved MRD‐positive CR post fourth line decitabine monotherapy and proceeded with an HSCT. Another patient with >50% blast reduction, but no overall response with frontline decitabine monotherapy, achieved MRD‐positive CR with intensive chemotherapy, relapsed, and managed to re‐achieve CR with HMA + venetoclax. Following this, the patient relapsed again with no further response to therapy. Another patient who had received HMA + vorinostat on a clinical trial achieved >50% blast reduction but no overall response, eventually achieved an MLFS post‐intensive chemotherapy and was consolidated with decitabine monotherapy. Finally, one patient who achieved >50% blast reduction but no response to frontline intensive chemotherapy, achieved MRD‐positive CR with salvage intensive chemotherapy and venetoclax and was able to proceed to a consolidative HSCT. An overall response anytime during AML/MPAL therapy was thus achieved in five (83.3%) patients. Patients received a median of four lines of therapy (range, 1–8).

Three (50%) patients transitioned to allogeneic HSCT. This included one patient who achieved CR after frontline therapy described above, and two patients after later lines of therapy (second line and fourth line respectively). All transplanted patients unfortunately relapsed post HSCT, 5.6. 6.1, and 6.7 months post‐HSCT, and all received further salvage therapy without any response and died with persistent disease. With regard to previous and/or concurrent nonmyeloid cancers, only one patient, concurrently diagnosed with glioblastoma at the time of AML diagnosis, had progression of the glioblastoma during AML therapy. The previous nonmyeloid cancers remained in remission for the other patients with leukemia. The median OS of the patients was 18.8 months (95% CI, 3.8–NE) (Figure  3B ). At last follow‐up, none of the patients with AML/MPAL are alive. Four patients died with persistent disease after relapse (including two patients post‐HSCT), one patient died in continued MLFS with glioblastoma progression along with infectious complication and fungal pneumonia, and one patient died in ongoing remission after HSCT, from post‐HSCT complications. Thus, two patients had nonrelapse mortality.

Individual level patient treatment and outcomes details are provided in Table  S3 . For the full cohort of MN ( n  = 14) at a median estimated follow‐up of 28.8 months, the median OS was 18.2 months (95% CI, 8.1–19.7 months), and the 1‐year and 2‐year OS rates were 77.1% and 17.1%, respectively (Figure  3C ). Among 11 responders across the full cohort, the median OS was 18.3 months (95% CI, 8.1–NE), and 1‐year and 2‐year OS rates were 88.9% and 22.2%, respectively (Figure  3D ) . Finally, among the five patients who underwent an HSCT any time during their MN therapy, the median OS from MN diagnosis was 19.3 months (95% CI, 8.2–NE), and 1‐year and 2‐year OS rates were 80% and 40%, respectively (Figure  S1 ) .

Here, we present a cohort of patients with LFS who developed a MN, either de novo or therapy‐related. The majority of patients with prior exposure to cytotoxic chemotherapy developed MN with a ≥1‐year hiatus, although a few patients developed MN after a very short period, possibly from rapid progression of  TP53  mutant clonal hematopoiesis under therapy pressure, or possibly as a synchronous neoplasm not related to previous cytotoxic therapy. 
 17 
 ,  
 18

Compared with our previous report, the present analysis focused only on patients with LFS who developed a MN, with larger patient numbers and longer‐follow‐up, including patient level treatment and outcomes analysis. 
 19 
  Responses with MN‐directed therapy were common, however, responses were generally short lived. The 1‐year survival estimates of 77% for MDS and 83% for AML appear more favorable than the estimates in patients with MDS/AML associated with somatically acquired biallelic  TP53  aberrations and therapy‐related AML harboring  TP53  mutations. 
 6 
 ,  
 8 
 ,  
 11 
  Our study highlights that achieving remission and consideration of HSCT consolidation is feasible in a subset of patients with LFS and therapy related‐MN, although improved outcomes and novel treatment strategies are clearly needed.

Exposure to prior cytotoxic therapy is an important risk factor for MN in patients with LFS, however, a small percentage of patients with LFS (21% of the MN in our cohort) appeared to develop MN as the primary malignancy. Given the limited patient numbers, it was difficult to discern any divergent treatment trajectory and outcomes in the patients in our present analysis, and larger studies are needed to understand if therapy‐related MN have outcomes different to de novo MN in LFS. However, in patients with history of nonmyeloid cancers, morbidity from previous therapy and persistent disease status of previous cancers can add to the challenges of treating the MN, and progression of other cancers could also be seen during therapy for MN. 
 10 
  The additive concerns of cytopenia and cytopenia‐related infections during MN therapy might also hinder concurrent treatment of any nonmyeloid neoplasms. Consolidating such patients with HSCT is difficult even if some form of remission of the MN is achieved, given concerns of progression of the nonmyeloid cancer during post‐HSCT immunosuppression. Thus, although the impact of prior cytotoxic therapy on risk of MN is known in LFS, the impact of MN therapy on the course of previous nonmyeloid cancers directly or indirectly is not clearly elucidated and needs to be determined by specific cancer history in the individual. Additionally, uncommon toxicities can be encountered; in a small series of three patients with LFS and MDS/AML who underwent HSCT, exaggerated immune toxicities, including hyperacute graft versus host disease were encountered. 
 20 
  In our analysis, the majority of deaths were related to MN relapse/progression, however, progression of previous nonmyeloid cancer prevented further therapy for two patients with MDS and led to nonrelapse mortality.

Given the heterogenous treatment approaches in our analysis, it was not possible to understand the impact of different therapies or regimens on outcomes. However, at least in the MDS cohort, HMA‐based therapy induced response in six of eight (75%) patients and warrants consideration also in AML, given the limited efficacy of intensive chemotherapy in AML with high‐burden  TP53  aberrations. 
 6 
  Indeed, clinical trials should always be the first consideration for such patients given overall poor outcomes to standard of care therapy. In clinical practice, the optimal treatment approaches for patients with MDS/AML harboring high‐burden  TP53  aberrations remain debated, including the controversial role of venetoclax added to LIT. In LFS, these options have not been prospectively evaluated but are expected to yield similar results as in MDS/AML with somatically acquired  TP53  aberrations. Additionally, whether the recommended treatment should be different based on blast cutoff remains an area of debate. In recent years, there has been some consensus that the blast boundaries are less important than the burden of the  TP53  mutation, and AML‐directed intensive therapy might not necessarily be better based on retrospective observation, while HMA‐based therapy with early HSCT could be considered as one of the options.

Although there has been notable improvement in treatment options in some subtypes of AML that harbor targetable aberrations, this has trailed behind in  TP53 ‐mutated MDS/AML. Recent studies with magrolimab and eprenetapopt failed to show any improvement in outcomes. 
 21 
 ,  
 22 
  However, another recent study showed single‐agent efficacy with rezatapopt (a small molecule reactivator for mutated p53‐Y220C) in patients with solid neoplasms harboring the  TP53‐ Y220C mutation. 
 23 
  Further noncytotoxic approaches are clearly needed in these patients. Additionally, strategies for MN prevention in patients with LFS who received prior cytotoxic therapy for nonmyeloid neoplasms are also important. Limiting the exposure to chemotherapy/radiotherapy for solid organ neoplasms in LFS and use of immunotherapeutic strategies or noncytotoxic targeted therapies could be helpful, whenever feasible. Recently trilaciclib, a CDK4/6 inhibitor, was shown to reduce the rate of expansion of  TP53  clonal hematopoiesis in patients with solid organ neoplasms treated with trilaciclib and other cytotoxic chemotherapy. 
 24 
  Such approaches also warrant evaluation in patients with LFS who are receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy for CDK4/6‐independent tumors.

In summary, in a cohort of patients with LFS with MN, an overall response rate of 79% (11 of 14 patients) was achieved anytime during the course of MN therapy and with successful HSCT in 36% (5 of 14) patients for MN. Although long‐term survival (>2 years) was limited, a 1‐year OS rate of 77% in MDS and 83% in AML was achieved. Newer preventive strategies for MN in patients with LFS and targeted or noncytotoxic approaches for management of  TP53 ‐mutated MDS/AML are much needed to improve outcomes of these challenging hematological neoplasms. Lessons learned from prevention and management of MN in LFS can also be potentially used to halt clonal evolution in patients with  TP53  clonal hematopoiesis.

## E7389-LF as a first-line chemotherapy for patients with metastatic/advanced HER2-negative breast cancer: results from the phase 1 dose-expansion part of study 114.

**PMID**: 42754887 · **Journal**: Breast cancer research : BCR · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1186/s13058-026-02295-8 · **PMCID**: PMC13587422

**Authors**: Ishiguro Hiroshi, Miyoshi Yasuo, Yasojima Hiroyuki, Watanabe Junichiro, Takano Toshimi, Shimomura Akihiko, Tokunaga Eriko, Mukohara Toru, Naoi Yasuto, Matsuoka Daiko, Okumura Shiori, Otake Yohei, Suzuki Takuya, Takase Takao, Semba Taro, Zhao Ziming, Yonemori Kan

**Types**: Journal Article, Clinical Trial, Phase I, Multicenter Study

**BACKGROUND**: There is an ongoing need for first-line (1L) chemotherapies for metastatic HER2-negative breast cancer. This study evaluated the efficacy and safety profile of the dose-expansion part 6 of Study 114 in patients receiving E7389-LF as a 1L chemotherapy for metastatic/advanced HER2-negative breast cancer.

**METHODS**: Japanese patients (≥ 20 years of age) with confirmed HER2-negative breast cancer (HER2-0 or HER2-low) were enrolled; subgroup analyses included luminal-like and triple-negative breast cancer tumors. Eligible patients had ≥ 1 measurable lesion per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumor version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1) and had not received prior chemotherapy for advanced/metastatic disease. Objectives included safety, efficacy, and biomarker changes. Tumors were assessed by investigators per RECIST v1.1.

**RESULTS**: Twenty-six patients received E7389-LF. Overall, 24 patients (92.3%) had discontinued treatment by the data cutoff date (October 18, 2023). Most common treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) of any grade were alopecia (88.5%), neutropenia (88.5%; grade ≥ 3, 76.9%), and thrombocytopenia (84.6%; grade ≥ 3, 34.6%). Three patients discontinued due to TRAEs. No patient showed a complete response, and 8 (30.8%) had confirmed partial responses, for an objective response rate of 30.8%. Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 8.1 months overall (patients with luminal breast cancer [n = 22]: 8.1 months; triple-negative breast cancer [n = 4]: 9.8 months). Median overall survival was not reached at 22.7 months of follow-up. Median PFS on next-line therapy was 20.6 months. Changes in vasculature- and IFNγ-related biomarkers were observed in all patients who received E7389-LF.

**CONCLUSIONS**: These results highlight the antitumor activity and manageable safety profile of E7389-LF, indicating the potential of E7389-LF as a 1L treatment for patients with HER2-negative breast cancer, warranting further study.

**CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION**: NCT03207672. Registered 5 July 2017.

Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in women worldwide accounting for 11.6% of all new cancer diagnoses in women globally [ 1 ]. In 2018, there were > 400,000 cases of metastatic breast cancer in the European Union [ 2 ], and it was estimated that 169,347 patients will be living with metastatic breast cancer in the United States as of January 2025 [ 3 ]. In Japan, breast cancer accounts for approximately one-fifth of cancers in women, and has an age-standardized mortality of 9.7 per 100,000 [ 4 ].

Breast cancer is a biologically heterogeneous disease and is classified by the American Society of Clinical Oncology/College of American Pathologists based on the expression levels of different biomarkers such as hormone receptors (HRs), including estrogen and progesterone receptors, and the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) [ 5 ,  6 ]. HER2-negative breast cancers account for about 80% of breast cancers and can be further categorized into HER2-0 or HER2-low breast cancers [ 7 ,  8 ]. HER2-negative disease can also be categorized as luminal-like (positive for estrogen and/or progesterone receptors) or triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC; negative for estrogen and progesterone receptors) [ 9 ]. Approximately 80% of HER2-low breast cancers are luminal-like and 15–20% are TNBC [ 10 ].

Metastatic breast cancer remains incurable despite advances in understanding and classifying the disease [ 2 ]. Currently, systemic therapy is recommended [ 2 ]; however, prolonged treatment with taxane causes significant toxicities [ 11 ]. Bevacizumab combined with paclitaxel significantly prolonged median progression-free survival (PFS) compared with paclitaxel alone (11.8 months vs. 5.9 months;  P  < 0.001) [ 12 ]. Although bevacizumab plus paclitaxel received accelerated approval by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a first-line (1L) treatment for patients with HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, the approval was removed after widespread clinical uptake showed increased toxicity and no benefit to patient survival [ 13 ,  14 ]. Recently, the HER2-directed trastuzumab deruxtecan showed prolonged overall survival (OS) and PFS in previously treated metastatic HER2-low breast cancer and in untreated metastatic luminal HER2-low and ultralow (HER2-0 with membrane staining) breast cancer compared with the physician’s choice of chemotherapy [ 15 ,  16 ]. However, trastuzumab deruxtecan—a HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (ADC)—was not studied in patients with HER2-0 without membrane staining or HR-negative breast cancer in the 1L setting, which highlights the ongoing need for therapies that can be broadly used in the 1L treatment of HER2-negative breast cancer.

Eribulin mesylate (known as eribulin) is a nontaxane microtubule dynamics inhibitor [ 17 ] reported to induce a phenotypic reversal from epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) to mesenchymal–epithelial transition (MET) in breast cancer cells [ 18 ]. Eribulin mesylate has established efficacy in heavily pretreated patients with HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer. In the EMBRACE study, eribulin significantly increased the median OS in patients with locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer who received 2–5 prior lines of chemotherapy compared with treatment of physician’s choice, (median OS 13.1 vs. 10.6 months, respectively,  P  = 0.041, log-rank) [ 19 ]. Eribulin further demonstrated prolonged median OS (15.9 months) in patients with metastatic breast cancer who received ≤ 3 prior chemotherapy treatments, including an anthracycline and a taxane in Study 301 [ 20 ]. Notably, in a pooled analysis of EMBRACE and Study 301, wherein 11% of patients did not receive prior chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer, patients treated with eribulin had favorable OS results compared with the control arms [ 21 ].

Recently, E7389-LF was developed as a liposomal formulation of eribulin mesylate and is hypothesized to improve the accumulation of eribulin in tumor tissue. E7389-LF demonstrated improved antitumor activity compared with eribulin in a preclinical model [ 22 ] and was well tolerated in patients with solid tumors [ 23 ]. In the open-label phase 1 Study 114 of E7389-LF in Japanese patients with advanced solid tumors, a recommended regimen of 2.0 mg/m 2  as free eribulin once every 3 weeks (Q3W) was determined based on the dose-escalation part [ 24 ]. In the dose-expansion part 1 of Study 114 that examined Japanese patients with HER2-negative breast cancer who received prior chemotherapy of an anthracycline and a taxane and had ≤ 3 prior chemotherapy regimens for advanced/metastatic breast cancer, the overall objective response rate (ORR) was 35.7% (95% confidence interval [CI] 18.6–55.9). Notably, of the 7 patients without prior chemotherapy for advanced/metastatic breast cancer, 5 presented with a partial response (PR; ORR 71.4%) [ 25 ]. In addition to antitumor activity, previous reports of E7389-LF have shown increases in vascular- and immune-related biomarkers, suggesting that treatment contributes to remodeling of the tumor microenvironment [ 24 ,  25 ].

Here, we present the antitumor activity and safety data from the dose-expansion part 6 of Study 114 in Japanese patients with confirmed metastatic HER2-negative breast cancer who had not received prior chemotherapy for locally advanced/metastatic disease across molecular subtypes.

Study 114 ( NCT03207672 ) is an open-label phase 1 trial of E7389-LF, a liposomal formulation of eribulin, in patients with solid tumors. Study 114 consists of a previously reported dose-escalation part [ 24 ] and 6 dose-expansion cohorts conducted in patients with various solid tumors. Here, we focus on the dose-expansion part 6 of Study 114. This part included patients with breast cancer who received the recommended dose of E7389-LF free base intravenously at 2.0 mg/m 2  on day (D) 1 of a 21-day cycle (C), Q3W, until disease progression, development of unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent.

Japanese patients (≥ 20 years of age) were required to have a confirmed diagnosis of HER2-negative breast cancer as determined by an immunohistochemistry (IHC) score of 0 (HER2-0), or an IHC score of 1 + /2 + and a negative fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH; HER2-low). IHC tests were performed using FDA-approved HER2 testing kits as follows: Ventana Ultraview Pathway HER2 in 12 patients (46.2%), Ventana I-VIEW Pathway HER2 in 3 patients (11.5%), and the Bond polymer system HER2 test (CB11) in 1 patient (3.8%). Patients with TNBC were eligible if they were diagnosed as programmed cell-death ligand 1 (PD-L1)-negative per local testing or were clinically judged as not eligible for atezolizumab or another immuno-checkpoint inhibitor-containing regimen by their site investigator. Patients had to have at least 1 measurable lesion based on Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1); lesions previously treated with radiotherapy or loco-regional therapies must have shown evidence of progressive disease to be deemed measurable. Patients could not have received prior chemotherapy regimens for advanced or metastatic disease.

In addition, eligible patients must have had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1 and adequate organ function. Patients were excluded if they had a Child–Pugh score B or C indicating liver dysfunction, an active or acute oral infection requiring dental treatment, or a confirmed radiologic disease progression within 12 months after completing a taxane regimen in the neo- and/or adjuvant setting. Prior hormonal therapy including combination therapy (eg, containing a cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 [CDK4/6] inhibitor or everolimus) and bone-modifying agents (eg, bisphosphonates, denosumab) were not counted as prior therapies.

The primary objective of Study 114 was to determine the maximum tolerated dose of E7389-LF (previously reported to be 2.0 mg/m 2  Q3W) [ 24 ]. Secondary objectives assessed safety, pharmacokinetic parameters, ORR, and PFS. Exploratory endpoints included PFS on next-line therapy (PFS2) defined from the start of study treatment until disease progression on next-line therapy, OS, disease control rate (DCR), clinical benefit rate (CBR), and potential biomarkers of E7389-LF. DCR was defined as the proportion of patients who had a best overall response (BOR) of complete response (CR), PR, or stable disease (SD) (≥ 5 weeks after C1D1). CBR is the proportion of patients with a BOR of CR, PR, or durable SD (≥ 23 weeks of SD).

Exploratory subanalyses of tumor response endpoints were conducted by HER2 status (HER2-0 or HER2-low), disease type (luminal breast cancer or TNBC), and presence of visceral crisis (lung or liver) or nonvisceral metastases. Additionally, PFS2 was assessed according to second-line treatment (chemotherapy or endocrine therapy or ADC).

Tumors were assessed by investigators based on RECIST v1.1 at screening, every 6 weeks from C1D1, at discontinuation, and when clinically indicated. After week 24, tumor assessments were conducted every 12 weeks. CR and PR were to be confirmed by a subsequent evaluation at least 28 days later. During survival follow-up, survival status and subsequent anticancer therapy were collected every 3 months (± 2 weeks) or per request from the sponsor after discontinuation from study treatment; information on the reasons for discontinuing subsequent therapy was collected for PFS2 assessment. Safety assessments consisted of monitoring and recording all adverse events, including all grades according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events of the National Cancer Institute version 4.03 (for both increasing and decreasing severity), and serious adverse events. Of particular interest was febrile neutropenia, which was monitored and was considered for subanalyses; at the investigators’ discretion, pegfilgrastim agents could be administered for the prevention of febrile neutropenia. Premedication with antihistamines was instituted on C1D1, other prophylactic medications were further administered at the investigator’s discretion on C1D1.

Blood (serum) biomarker samples were collected from patients predose on D1 of each cycle (C1–C6) and on D8 of C1. Plasma concentrations of eribulin and biomarkers were measured by a validated liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry method. A total of 78 markers were planned for analysis to assess the tumor microenvironment, including tumor immunity and vascularization.

To test the null hypothesis that the true response rate is 21.2% based on the ORR of paclitaxel [ 12 ] against a 1-sided alternative, at least 22 patients are required to achieve a type I error rate of 5% and a power of 85% when the true response rate is 50.0%. Assuming that approximately 2 patients may not be appropriately assessed for tumors as scheduled and withdrawn from the study, the sample size needed was determined to be 24 patients. All safety and tumor response analyses were performed on the safety analysis set defined as all patients who received at least 1 dose of the study drug.

BOR was summarized and ORR, DCR, and CBR were provided with 95% and 90% (ORR in overall population only) CIs calculated with the Clopper-Pearson method. PFS, OS, and PFS2 were estimated and plotted over time using the Kaplan–Meier method. 95% CIs were calculated based on Greenwood formula and a generalized Brookmeyer and Crowley method with log–log transformation. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS software (version 9.2 or later, SAS Institute, Cary, NC).

Serum protein biomarkers were analyzed for biomarkers in which ≥ 70% of the samples demonstrated levels above the lower limit of quantification. Percent changes from C1D1 were assessed using the 1-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The cutoff value (33rd percentile) for serum biomarker percentage changes classified patients into a “low” group (with percentage change in serum biomarkers < cutoff value) and a “high” group (with percentage change in serum biomarkers ≥ cutoff value). Dichotomized analyses of each serum biomarker were performed at C1D8 and C5D1, and the hazard ratios of PFS were calculated using univariate Cox regression and a log-rank test to investigate possible prognostic biomarkers for PFS.

A total of 26 patients with breast cancer were included in the dose-expansion cohort 6 (Table  1 ). The median age was 59.0 years (range 35, 77). Of patients included in this analysis, 22 (84.6%) had luminal breast cancer and 4 (15.4%) had TNBC; 6 patients (23.1%) had de novo stage IV disease, and 19 (73.1%) had recurrent disease. Visceral (lung or liver) metastatic sites were observed in 20 patients (76.9%); 6 patients (23.1%) had nonvisceral metastatic sites. Fourteen patients (53.8%) received prior taxane or anthracycline regimens for adjuvant or neoadjuvant treatment of breast cancer, and 15 (57.7%) received a prior CDK4/6 inhibitor for metastatic disease (Table  1 ). Further details on prior anticancer therapies are summarized in Supplementary Table  S1 . At the data cutoff date (October 18, 2023), 2 (7.7%) of the 26 patients who received E7389-LF were undergoing treatment; 24 (92.3%) patients discontinued due to either progressive disease (19 [73.1%]), adverse events (3 [11.5%]), or patient choice (2 [7.7%]). Overall, 23 patients received second-line treatment (chemotherapy, n = 16; endocrine therapy, n = 6; ADC, n = 1) (Supplementary Table  S1 ). Baseline characteristics of patients by second-line treatment are reported in Supplementary Table  S2 .

A summary of treatment-related treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) is shown in Table  2 . Treatment-related TEAEs led to study drug discontinuation in 3 (11.5%) patients, reduction in 15 (57.7%) patients, and interruption in 3 (11.5%) patients; the 3 leading to drug discontinuation of E7389-LF were drug hypersensitivity, peripheral motor neuropathy, and interstitial lung disease (n = 1 each). Treatment-related TEAEs of any grade and grade ≥ 3 severity occurred in 100% and 96.2% of the 26 enrolled patients, respectively (Table  2 ). The most common treatment-related TEAEs of any grade (> 50%) were alopecia (88.5%), neutropenia (88.5%; grade ≥ 3, 76.9%), thrombocytopenia (84.6%; grade ≥ 3, 34.6%), leukopenia (73.1%; grade ≥ 3, 42.3%), aspartate aminotransferase increased (65.4%; grade ≥ 3, 7.7%), and alanine aminotransferase increased (57.7%; grade ≥ 3, 7.7%). Of note, febrile neutropenia was recorded in 3 patients (11.5%), 2 cases in C1 and 1 in C3. Hypersensitivity reaction of any grade was observed in 10 patients (38.5%): 7 (26.9%) patients developed drug hypersensitivity of grade 1, 2 (7.7%) developed drug hypersensitivity of grade 2, and 1 (3.9%) developed drug hypersensitivity of grade 3. All 26 patients were given prophylactic medication for hypersensitivity management during C1: 23 received an antihistamine alone and 3 received an antihistamine plus a steroid. During C1, 7 of 23 patients (30.4%) given prophylactic antihistamine and one (33.3%) of the 3 patients given both a prophylactic antihistamine and a steroid developed a drug hypersensitivity reaction, all hypersensitivity events were grade 1. Additionally, 7 of 26 patients received prophylactic pegylated granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (peg-GCSF) in C1, none of whom developed febrile neutropenia of any grade in C1. Febrile neutropenia was observed in 2 of 19 (10.5%) patients who did not receive prophylactic pegylated granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (peg-GCSF) in C1.

Among all 26 patients in the expansion cohort, no patient had a CR, and 8 (30.8%) had a confirmed PR, for an ORR of 30.8% (90% CI 16.3–48.7, 95% CI 14.3–51.8) (Table  3 ). The time to first objective response was 87 days (range 36, 121). ORR was 27.3% (n = 6/22; 95% CI 10.7–50.2) in patients with luminal breast cancer and 50% (n = 2/4; 95% CI 6.8–93.2) in patients with TNBC. Subgroup analyses of tumor response by patient characteristics are shown in Supplementary Table  S3 . Of note, 1 of 6 patients with de novo stage IV disease had an objective response (ORR: 16.7%; 95% CI 0.4–64.1) and ORR was 31.6% (n = 6/19; 95% CI 12.6–56.6) in patients with recurrent disease. ORR was 30.0% (n = 6/20; 95% CI 11.9–54.3) in patients with visceral metastases and 33.3% (n = 2/6; 95% CI 4.3–77.7) in patients without visceral metastases. ORR was 26.7% (n = 4/15; 95% CI 7.8–55.1) in patients who received CDK4/6 inhibitors for metastatic disease, and 28.6% (n = 2/7; 95% CI 3.7–71.0) in those who did not. ORR was 66.7% (n = 4/6; 95% CI 22.3–95.7) in patients with HER2-0 breast cancer and 20.0% (n = 4/20; 95% CI 5.7–43.7) in patients with HER2-low breast cancer.

Maximum reduction in the sum of target lesions was > 30% in 11 of 25 evaluable patients, including 8 patients with a confirmed PR (2 of whom had TNBC), 2 patients with SD (1 with TNBC), and 1 patient with progressive disease (Fig.  1 A). Reduction in target lesions were generally maintained over time (Fig.  1 B). Two patients were still receiving study treatment at the data cutoff date; the longest treatment period was nearly 2 years (Fig.  1 B). At 19.1 months (range 10.9, not estimable [NE]) median follow-up time for PFS, median PFS was 8.1 months (95% CI 5.5–11.1) in the overall population (Fig.  2 A), 8.1 months (95% CI 5.4–11.1) in patients with luminal breast cancer, and 9.8 months (95% CI 3.1–NE) in patients with TNBC (Fig.  2 B). Subgroup analyses of PFS indicate that median PFS was similar between patients with de novo stage IV and recurrent disease (7.4 months vs. 8.1 months), patients with visceral and nonvisceral metastases (8.1 months for both), and patients with HER2-0 breast cancer and HER2-low breast cancer (8.4 months vs. 8.1 months) (Supplementary Fig.  S1 , Supplementary Table  S4 ). Median PFS was 8.1 months (95% CI 4.4–8.5) in patients who had previously received metastatic CDK4/6 inhibitors, and 11.1 months (95% CI 4.2–NE) in those who did not.

At 22.7 months (95% CI 19.7–23.6) median follow-up time for OS, median OS was not reached in all patients irrespective of their luminal or TNBC status (Fig.  2 C and D). Of note, OS rate (95% CI) was 96.2% (75.7–99.4) at 12 months, 84.6% (64.0–93.9) at 18 months, and 75.7% (53.4–88.3) at 24 months.

Of the 26 patients evaluable for PFS2 analysis, 16 received chemotherapy, 6 received endocrine therapy, and 1 received an ADC (datopotamab deruxtecan) following study treatment. Overall median PFS2 was 20.6 months (95% CI 14.5–NE) (Fig.  3 A). Median PFS2 based on the type of second-line treatment was 16.2 months (95% CI 8.8–NE) for patients who received chemotherapy and NR (95% CI 18.9 months–NE) among patients who received endocrine therapy; PFS2 was 20.6 months in the one patient who received an ADC (Fig.  3 B). Notably, 6 of the 16 patients receiving chemotherapy and 3 of the 6 receiving endocrine were still undergoing treatment at data cutoff (Fig.  3 C). ADC, antibody-drug conjugate; AE adverse event; BSC, best supportive care; chemo, chemotherapy; ET, endocrine therapy; LF, liposomal formulation; NE, not estimable; NR, not reached; PD, progressive disease; PFS, progression-free survival; PFS2, progression-free survival on next-line therapy

Of the 78 biomarkers tested for serum biomarkers, 52 were considered evaluable, as ≥ 70% of their samples had levels above the lower limit of quantification for biomarker analyses. Vascular and interferon gamma (IFNγ)-related markers generally increased on C1D8 compared with C1D1, regardless of breast cancer subtype and BOR status (Fig.  4 ). The levels of vasculature-related markers (collagen IV, tyrosine kinase with immunoglobulin-like and EGF-like domains 2 [TIE2], and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 [ICAM1]) decreased slightly compared with those measured at C1D8 but remained elevated on D1 of each subsequent cycle, while platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule 1 (PECAM1) increased after C1D8 and remained elevated on D1 of each subsequent cycle. However, the levels of IFNγ-related markers (IFNγ and IFNγ-induced protein 10 [IP-10]) measured on D1 of subsequent cycles decreased compared with C1D8 and were similar to levels measured on C1D1 (Fig.  4 ). Furthermore, improved PFS was associated with a greater increase in the vasculature-related markers ICAM1 and PECAM1 at C5D1, and with IFNγ at C1D8 (Supplementary Fig.  S2 ). Improved PFS was also associated with a greater change in vasculature-related markers (endoglin and vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 1 [VEGFR1]) and in the IFNγ-related marker interferon-induced T-cell alpha chemoattract (ITAC) at C5D1 (Supplementary Table  S5 ). Here, we report results of the dose-expansion part 6 of Study 114 in Japanese patients with confirmed metastatic HER2-negative breast cancer (including HER2-0 and HER2-low breast cancer) who had not received prior chemotherapy for locally advanced/metastatic disease.

E7389-LF (2.0 mg/m 2  Q3W as a free base) was tolerated and had a manageable safety profile in patients with metastatic HER2-negative breast cancer and who did not receive prior metastatic chemotherapy regimens. E7389-LF showed antitumor activity in the 1L setting, similar to a previous report of E7389-LF that required prior treatment with an anthracycline and a taxane [ 25 ].

Adverse events developed in all patients and 3 patients discontinued treatment due to treatment-related TEAEs (drug hypersensitivity, peripheral motor neuropathy, and interstitial lung disease). The safety profile was consistent with the previous study of E7389-LF in cohort 1 of the dose-expansion part of Study 114 [ 25 ]. Febrile neutropenia in C1 was only observed in patients who did not receive peg-GCSF (n = 2). The use of prophylactic peg-GCSF might be considered to prevent febrile neutropenia in high-risk subpopulations including elderly patients or patients with a clinical history of febrile neutropenia developed on previous chemotherapies in perioperative settings.

Regarding hypersensitivity reactions, the importance of antihistamine premedication was suggested in a prior cohort of this study enrolling 34 patients with gastric cancer [ 26 ]. In that study, no infusion-related reactions were encountered in those who received a steroid and antihistamine (n = 3) or only an antihistamine (n = 10), while 6 (28.6%) had an infusion-related reaction among 21 patients who received no premedication with steroid or antihistamine [ 26 ]. Here, although hypersensitivity reactions during C1 were relatively common (30.4%) in patients who received prophylactic antihistamines, all events during C1 were grade 1 and most hypersensitivity events throughout the study were of grade 1–2. Thus, antihistamines may have some merit in preventing severe reactions, and should be investigated further. It remains unclear whether the addition of steroids provides any clinical benefit, as only 3 patients in this study received both antihistamines and steroids.

E7389-LF showed promising antitumor activity as a 1L chemotherapy treatment in patients with HER2-negative breast cancer; ORR was 30.8% and the median PFS was 8.1 months in the overall population. Median OS was not reached; thus, additional follow-up will be needed. Acknowledging the limitations of cross-study comparisons, E7389-LF showed a median PFS comparable to that of the historical data of paclitaxel administered in the 1L setting (median PFS 5.9–11.8 months) [ 12 ]. Moreover, in this study, E7389-LF showed favorable PFS compared with a historical analysis of eribulin in patients who had no prior chemotherapy for advanced/metastatic disease (8.1 months vs. 4.2 months, respectively) [ 27 ]. Considering the differences between E7389-LF and eribulin mesylate, liposomal encapsulation of eribulin may have contributed to an enhanced antitumor effect, resulting in prolonged PFS.

Recently, the ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan showed promising median PFS (13.2 months) in patients with HR-positive and HER2-low or HER2-ultralow metastatic breast cancer, but this treatment was not examined for patients with HR-positive HER2-0 or HR-negative HER2-low and HER2-0 metastatic breast cancer [ 15 ], thus cross-study comparisons between E7389-LF and trastuzumab deruxtecan are limited.

Given the known differences among subtypes of HER2-negative breast cancer, we explored antitumor activity outcomes across molecular subtype (luminal vs. TNBC), HER2-negative status (HER2-0 vs. HER2-low), and other disease characteristics. Median PFS was comparable between patients with luminal breast cancer (8.1 months) and TNBC (9.8 months). Similarities in PFS and OS among luminal breast cancer and TNBC subtypes observed in our metastatic patient population are consistent with those observed in a meta-analysis of patients with metastatic breast cancer treated with chemotherapy [ 28 ]. ORR appeared favorable in the HER2-0 group versus the HER2-low group (66.7% vs. 20.0%), however median PFS was similar between groups (8.4 months vs. 8.1 months, respectively).

Changes in vasculature- and IFNγ-related serum markers were observed in all patients who received E7389-LF, suggesting that they are pharmacodynamic. Per a previous study, E7389-LF may induce vascular remodeling and increase T-cell infiltration in the tumor tissue, either directly via cytotoxic effects on tubulin inhibition or indirectly by changing the tumor microenvironment [ 29 ]. Notably, our study suggests that changes in vascular and IFNγ-related markers appear to be associated with improved PFS. We also found the median PFS2 for patients who received subsequent chemotherapy (16.2 months) to be notable; thus, it is possible that changes observed in serum IFNγ and vascular markers indicate a change in the tumor microenvironment that persists after treatment discontinuation. Further studies are needed to explore the potential link between changes in serum biomarkers and the observed antitumor effect in the clinical setting.

This study has several limitations, such as the small sample size overall (particularly in patients with TNBC) and inclusion of Japanese patients only. Subgroup analyses of OS with longer follow-up are further needed. Biomarker analyses were performed in serum samples rather than tumor-specific samples and could indicate systemic changes rather than changes in the tumor microenvironment. Moreover, ADCs were not established as major therapeutic options in the first-line treatment of breast cancer at the time this study was initiated. However, later advances in the field have significantly changed the treatment landscape. In TNBC, sacituzumab govitecan [ 30 ] and datopotamab deruxtecan [ 31 ] have demonstrated superior efficacy compared with standard chemotherapy in the first-line setting, emerging as promising new standard-of-care candidates. Moreover, in HR-positive breast cancer, the introduction of novel HER2 classifications (such as HER2-low and HER2-ultralow) has facilitated the adoption of the ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan as treatment for patients with these HER2 profiles [ 32 ], further transforming current therapeutic strategies.

Despite these shifts in clinical practice, the present study demonstrates that E7389‑LF, which operates through mechanisms distinct from those of ADCs, exhibits meaningful clinical activity in patients with HER2‑negative breast cancer receiving first-line therapy. These findings suggest that E7389‑LF may continue to represent a potential therapeutic option within the modern and increasingly diversified treatment environment, especially for patients without target molecule expression corresponding to approved ADCs.

## The clinical and phenotypic spectrum of PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome: a retrospective cohort study.

**PMID**: 42753013 · **Journal**: Familial cancer · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1007/s10689-026-00604-w · **PMCID**: PMC13585824

**Authors**: Ritter Einat, Shtaya Aasem Abu, Kariv Revital, Lieberman Sari, Half Elizabeth, Postnikov Maria, Rosner Guy, Strul Hana, Gluck Nathan, Katz Lior, Levy-Lahad Ephrat, May Dalit, Laish Ido, Goldberg Yael, Vainer Elez, Levi Zohar, Golan Maya Aharoni

**Types**: Journal Article

PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome (PHTS) is a rare condition characterized by a complex phenotype including gastrointestinal hamartomas and increased lifetime malignancy risk. To characterize the clinical phenotype, genetic landscape, and spectrum of malignancies within a large cohort of adult PHTS carriers. A retrospective cohort study of adult patients (≥ 18 years) followed at specialized high-risk clinics who met PHTS diagnostic criteria based on either: (1) identification of a germline PTEN pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant, or (2) fulfillment of clinical criteria according to National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines. A total of 62 individuals were included (62.9% male; median age at inclusion 39.5, IQR, 28-52). All fulfilled diagnostic criteria for PHTS. PTEN pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant were identified in 50 individuals (80.6%). Colonic polyps were present in 40 patients. Malignancies were reported in 61% (n = 38), most frequently breast (n=13) and thyroid (n=7). Three individuals (4.8%) had rare soft tissue tumors: one with a desmoid tumor at age 18, one with concurrent axillary osteosarcoma and bilateral chest liposarcoma, and one with a skull-base sarcoma. Macrocephaly was observed in 33.8% (n = 21), and developmental delay, including autism spectrum disorder, in 8 patients (12.9%). One case of PTEN mosaicism was identified through tumor sequencing after negative blood genetic testing. Five individuals (8%) were treated with Sirolimus. This large cohort highlights the broad clinical spectrum and substantial cancer burden in PHTS, including rare soft tissue tumors. Constitutional mosaicism should be considered when clinical suspicion persists despite negative germline testing.

The PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS) encompasses a spectrum of rare disorders caused by a germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant (P/LP variant) within the phosphate and tensin homolog ( PTEN ) gene (MIM 601728).  PTEN , located on chromosome 10, functions as a tumor suppressor gene regulating cellular growth. Beyond its role in suppressing tumorigenesis,  PTEN  is crucial for normal embryonic development, particularly within the central nervous system where it orchestrates neural stem cell proliferation, cell migration, and synaptic plasticity. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variant leads to dysregulation of the mTOR pathway, which normally promotes cell growth, survival, and proliferation, thereby enhancing cell proliferation and inhibiting apoptosis [ 1 ]. In addition to its role in tumorigenesis,  PTEN  loss has been increasingly linked to immune dysregulation and chronic inflammatory processes. This is mediated through aberrant activation of the PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling pathway, which influences cytokine production, immune cell differentiation and the tumor microenvironment [ 2 ].

PHTS encompasses several historical clinical subtypes, such as Cowden syndrome and Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome, which are now recognized not as distinct syndromes, but as a single disease entity with age-dependent phenotypic presentations that can occur within the same family [ 3 ,  4 ]. The prevalence of PHTS is estimated at 1 in 100,000 to 200,000 individuals. While childhood presentations are typically dominated by macrocephaly, autism, developmental delay, vascular malformations, or benign intestinal polyposis, cancer-related features become prominent in adulthood. Adults with PHTS are highly predisposed to both benign and malignant tumors, most notably breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers, as well as renal cell carcinoma,colorectal cancer and melanoma. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variant in  PTEN  drives these diverse manifestations across the lifespan [ 5 – 7 ].

PHTS diagnosis is based upon diagnostic criteria, including the most recent National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines that recommend relying on a combination of major and minor clinical criteria or the detection of a  PTEN  pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant for definitive diagnosis [ 8 ]. Despite established diagnostic criteria, the wide phenotypic variability of PHTS poses significant challenges in identifying affected individuals. While some patients present with only mild or benign manifestations, others experience developmental delays, severe clinical symptoms, or life-threatening malignancies. Furthermore, uncommon or atypical features remain poorly characterized, complicating both diagnosis and counseling [ 9 ].

The aim of this study is to describe the spectrum of the clinical, endoscopic, and genetic characteristics of patients with PHTS with an emphasis on rare clinical findings and diagnostic approach.

This retrospective cohort study included adult patients (age ≥18 years) who were diagnosed with PHTSbased on either: [ 1 ] identification of a germline PTEN pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant, or [ 2 ] fulfillment of clinical criteria according to National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines.

A clinical diagnosis was established based on the presence of a combinations of major and minor criteria.[ 10 ] Patients were followed in six tertiary academic centers. Age at diagnosis was defined as the chronological age at which the patient was first clinically or genetically diagnosed with PHTS. Age at inclusion was defined as the age of the patient at the time of study initiation and cohort data collection.

Most patients carry a known  PTEN  P/LP variant, identified through Sanger sequencing or multigene next-generation sequencing (NGS) panels. A comprehensive chart review was performed extracting demographic, medical and genetic data, including age, biologic sex, follow-up duration,  PTEN  variant status and type, phenotypic features, family history of PHTS, occurrence of malignant and pre-malignant lesions and pharmacologic therapies received. Upper and lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy reports were reviewed for inflammatory findings, polyp burden and histology.  PTEN  pathogenic variants were documented by the precise Human Genome Variation Society nomenclature (HGVS) (Transcript NM_314.8). Variants were classified according to the ClinGen  PTEN  Expert Panel Specifications to the ACMG/AMP Variant Interpretation Guidelines. The study was approved by the Institutional review board in each medical center. Informed consent was waived.

Data were summarized using standard descriptive statistics. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages, and continuous variables are reported as medians with IQR.

Sixty-two patients were included in the study; 37.1% were female, the median age at diagnosis was 30 years (IQR 19–46), median follow-up time was 5.5 years (IQR 3–15), and 80% had at least one first-degree relative with PHTS diagnosis. The most common benign manifestations included colonic polyps (40 patients), macrocephaly (33.8%), benign thyroid disease and mucocutaneous lesions (29% and 26% respectively). Among the 12 patients who did not carry pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant in  PTEN  gene, the diagnosis was based on a combination of major and minor criteria according to NCCN guidelines[ 10 ]. Demographic characteristics and clinical findings are depicted in Table  1  and Supplementary Table  1 . Full endoscopic and pathologic reports were available for 48 subjects (77.4%).Overall, 40 patients (64.5% of total cohort) underwent colonoscopy, and 22 patients (35.5%) underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy. Patients without available endoscopic data were either under the recommended age threshold for screening initiation (e.g., age 35 years according to NCCN guidelines) or had procedures performed at outside institutions prior to specialized center follow-up. Most of the endoscopic findings were benign. One case of early-stage colorectal cancer was identified in a 44-year-old patient ( PTEN : c.53A>T). Polyps were observed throughout the digestive tract, most commonly in the colon (64.5%). In the colon, fourteen patients (22.6%) had less than 10 cumulative polyps, 14 patients had 11–100 polyps, and 8 patients had over 100 polyps. The most common histological type was hyperplastic polyps (n=20, 32.3%), followed by hamartomatous (n=13, 21%) and adenomatous polyps (n=5, 12.5%). Two patients demonstrated ulcerative colitis–like colonic inflammation, and one patient was diagnosed with celiac disease based on duodenal inflammation and supportive serologic findings. Sixteen patients had 11–100 gastric polyps, mostly hyperplastic. Sixteen patients had small bowel polyps, most commonly hyperplastic polyps located in the duodenum. A total of 38 patients (61%) had at least one malignancy, diagnosed at a median age of 45 years. Among them, 5 patients (13.1%) had two distinct cancers, and 3 patients (7.8%) had three different cancers. The most frequent malignancy was breast cancer, occurring in 13 patients which represents 56.5% of female participants (13/23) at a median diagnosis age of 47 years (IQR 25–58); three of these patients had bilateral breast cancer. One Ashkenazi Jewish female presented at the age of 47 with typical features of PHTS: mucosal papillomatosis and papillary thyroid cancer pre-malignant uterine polyp, despite the high probability of PHTS, genetic testing that included blood-based  PTEN  gene Sanger sequencing and subsequent  PTEN  promoter sequencing did not reveal any disease-causing variant.  PTEN  NGS of multiple tissue samples showed a variable expression of the  PTEN  pathogenic variant (c.445 C>T P.Q149X) as follows: 3% mosaicism in blood, 6% in saliva, 59% in endometrial polyp and 87% in thyroid lesion which suggest  PTEN  germline mosaicism. These findings along with the typical clinical manifestations established the diagnosis of PHTS. (Table  4 ).

Five patients (8%) were treated with the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus. Subject #2, who presented with a high burden of colonic polyps (> 100 polyps), was treated with sirolimus at a dose of 2 mg/day, and a reduction in polyp burden was noted on follow-up colonoscopies performed 1 and 2 years after treatment initiation. The remaining four patients were treated for large thyroid cysts, multinodular goiter, thyroid nodules, and astrocytoma. Disease burden remained stable throughout follow-up, and no adverse effects were reported.

In this multicenter cohort, we characterized the diverse and distinctive clinical manifestations, diagnostic approach, and treatment responses of individuals with PHTS. The malignancy spectrum observed in our cohort was largely consistent with that previously reported in PHTS [ 11 ,  12 ]. Overall, 61% of patients developed at least one malignancy, most commonly breast (uni or bilateral), and thyroid cancer. Notably, we also identified soft-tissue malignancies, osteosarcoma, and germ cell tumors in three patients. These uncommon cancers are not typically associated with PHTS, suggesting a potentially broader tumor spectrum in this condition. Notably,  PTEN  mosaicism was identified in an individual exhibiting classic PHTS symptoms despite negative blood-based  PTEN  sequencing.

Our cohort reinforces the clinical predictors established in the Tan et al. prospective study, although the study population was different. While the Tan study identified a 9.5% mutation yield among 3,042 probands satisfying relaxed PHTS clinical criteria, 80.6% of our cohort carried pathogenic variant. Compared with clinically based  PTEN  negative individuals, carriers of P/LP variant in  PTEN  gene had substantially higher frequencies of macrocephaly and gastrointestinal polyposis, similar to our cohort [ 13 ].In addition to the typical phenotype, our data highlights the wide and rare presentation spectrum of PHTS to include rare manifestations. While PHTS is characterized by well-established benign and malignant manifestations, individuals undergoing intensive surveillance or targeted cohort ascertainment frequently present with additional phenotypic findings. It remains crucial to differentiate true PHTS-driven spectrum features from coincidental events or ascertainment bias. Recent cohort data by Yehia et al. expanded the candidate tumor spectrum in PTEN carriers, suggesting an elevated risk for soft-tissue sarcomas [ 14 ]. Comprehensive molecular characterizations are essential to confirm whether these additional clinical observations are mechanistic features of PHTS or coincidental background events.

Notably, although soft tissue cancers are rare in the general population, with a lifetime risk of approximately 0.3% according to 2021–2023 SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results) data, they were identified in 4.8% of patients in our cohort [ 11 ,  15 ].

This observed occurrence of soft tissue cancer is particularly noteworthy. Previous case reports have described several cases of soft tissue sarcomas among individuals diagnosed with  PHTS  which include Ewing sarcoma [ 12 ], breast fibrosarcoma and femoral osteosarcoma [ 16 ]. Recent cohort data demonstrate that individuals with pathogenic  PTEN  variant have a higher risk of soft tissue sarcomas at younger ages compared to the general population, and these malignancies may occur alongside other PHTS component cancers such as breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers [ 14 ]. As to patient #5 who developed axillary sarcoma following breast cancer, while radiation therapy is a well-established risk factor for secondary sarcomagenesisn [ 17 ], we hypothesize that the co-existence of germline  PTEN  dysfunction and localized radiation exposure creates a synergistic, 'two-hit' effect. In this scenario, the underlying loss of  PTEN  tumor suppressor function provides a baseline genetic susceptibility, while radiation-induced DNA damage acts as a severe environmental trigger that accelerates malignant transformation.

The pathogenesis of soft tissue malignancies in PHTS is linked to the loss of tumor suppressor function, which disrupts PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling and impairs genomic stability, thereby facilitating malignant transformation in mesenchymal tissues and formation of soft tissue malignancies [ 18 ]. Our observations, together with those reported by others, support the concept that  PTEN  deficiency may broaden susceptibility to soft-tissue malignancies in PHTS and underscore the need for increased clinical awareness of atypical or mesenchymal tumors in this population.

Similarly, germ cell tumors are not traditionally considered part of the PHTS tumor spectrum, but growing evidence suggests a biologically plausible association.  PTEN  loss activates the PI3K/AKT pathway, promoting germ cell proliferation, and experimental models show that  PTEN  suppression contributes to germ cell tumor growth and progression [ 19 ,  20 ]. Several reports describe patients with P/LP variant  PTEN  s who developed germ cell tumors, including pediatric ovarian germ cell and cases in which germ cell tumors and acute megakaryoblastic leukemia shared  PTEN  and TP53 variants [ 21 ,  22 ].

Together, these findings support the possibility that, although rare, germ cell tumors may represent an underrecognized component of the PHTS-associated tumor spectrum.

The diagnosis of PHTS is based on clinical phenotype and identification of pathogenic change in  PTEN  gene. However, diagnosis is not always straightforward. We described a subject who had a typical clinical presentation for PHTS however, both Sanger sequencing of the  PTEN  coding region and NGS  PTEN  as well as promoter sequencing were negative. After examining affected tissues,  PTEN  mosaicism was noted and the diagnosis of PHTS was made. Several cases of mosaicism have been reported. One involved a 40-year-old woman with PHTS and Lhermitte-Duclos disease. Standard  PTEN  testing on blood DNA was negative, but a frameshift  PTEN  variant (c.767_768delAG) was later identified at full heterozygous levels in skin fibroblasts and cerebellar tumor tissue, and at ~25% in colonic and endocervical mucosa, confirming somatic mosaicism [ 23 ]. Similarly, two unrelated patients with juvenile polyposis, macrocephaly, intellectual disability, and hyperpigmented macules—consistent with BRRS—were reported. One carried a 10q23 deletion ( PTEN , BMPR1A, KLLN) in buccal mucosa, while the other showed high-level mosaicism for a 10q23.2q23.3 deletion and a somatic  PTEN  mutation in thyroid tissue, with low-level mosaicism in blood and buccal samples [ 24 ]. These findings highlight the importance of the clinical pretest probability that relies on PHTS characteristic phenotype and that  PTEN  mosaic expression can be the cause for blood based germinal testing. While this case of constitutional mosaicism highlights a key diagnostic pitfall, its prevalence in PHTS remains unclear. Given that up to 35% of clinically diagnosed patients lack germline P/LP variant, the theoretical potential for tissue-based testing is high, though the actual yield remains undetermined [ 25 ].As advanced genetic testing becomes more accessible, tissue-based analysis is likely to identify further cases and gain clinical significance.

Vascular anomalies are increasingly recognized as an integral, though heterogeneous, component of the PHTS phenotypic spectrum, largely attributed to the up-regulation of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway resulting from  PTEN  dysfunction, which alters normal angiogenesis. While literature commonly describes complex vascular malformations, including fast-flow arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) and deep intramuscular hemangiomas, our cohort primarily demonstrated localized hemangiomas. Notably, we also observed a rare manifestation of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) [ 26 ].

We further describe our observations regarding the use of mTOR inhibitor (Sirolimus) in 5 patients.

While Sirolimus is not FDA- approved specifically forPHTS, its use is supported by mechanistic rationale and clinical data. As  PTEN  deficiency results in dysregulated activation of the PI3K–Akt–mTOR pathway, driving excessive cell growth and hamartoma formation characteristic of  PTEN- related disorders, Sirolimus, through inhibition of mTOR complex 1, attenuates downstream signaling involved in protein synthesis and cell cycle regulation. By suppressing mTOR-mediated cellular proliferation, sirolimus provides a biologically rational therapeutic approach for mitigating disease manifestations in patients with  PTEN  loss [ 27 ]. mTOR inhibitor has shown clinical benefit in the management of vascular abnormalities and selected malignant manifestations, as well as regression of gastrointestinal lesions [ 5 ,  28 ].

In our cohort, sirolimus was not administered as a standard first-line therapy, but rather as an off-label, patient-tailored systemic intervention under the close monitoring of gastroenterology specialists working at a dedicated high-risk clinic. This targeted therapy was reserved for selected cases who had severe, progressive disease phenotypes and was administered in addition to standard endoscopic surveillance .  This included cases with an exceptionally high burden of colonic polyps  ( Subject #2, with >100 polyps) and large, progressive thyroid nodules.

A reduction in polyp burden was observed in one patient, while the remaining treated patients demonstrated overall disease stabilization, with a favorable safety profile. Although the small sample size and retrospective design preclude definitive conclusions regarding efficacy, these findings strongly align with a recent clinical trial by Stanich et al., which also demonstrated a reduction in colon polyp burden with sirolimus in PHTS patients, thereby reinforcing the therapeutic potential and value of further prospective evaluation of sirolimus in this setting [ 29 ].

This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, its retrospective design inherently limits data completeness and uniformity. Clinical, endoscopic, and pathologic evaluations were not performed according to a standardized protocol across the six participating centers, which may have introduced inter-institutional variability in phenotypic documentation, endoscopic surveillance intervals, and histological reporting.

Second, the cohort size was relatively small, reflecting the rarity of PHTS, and limits the statistical power to detect genotype–phenotype correlations or associations between specific  PTEN  variant classes and clinical outcomes, including malignancy risk and gastrointestinal burden. Consequently, analyses were primarily descriptive, and causal inferences cannot be drawn. In addition, the cohort is heterogeneous in both age and clinical presentation, which further complicates efforts to identify consistent patterns or establish meaningful genotype–phenotype correlations.

Despite these limitations, this multicenter cohort provides detailed phenotypic, endoscopic, and oncologic characterization of adult patients with PHTS, including rare manifestations, mosaicism, and real-world experience with mTOR inhibition. Notably, our study highlights significant clinical diversity across the adult lifespan. By capturing a broad age spectrum, we were able to observe distinct differences in disease expression between younger adults and older cohorts, particularly regarding the progressive severity and accumulation of symptoms over time. Importantly, patients were followed for a prolonged duration in specialized tertiary referral clinics with expertise in hereditary cancer syndromes, allowing for comprehensive longitudinal assessment.

In summary, our cohort underscores the marked clinical complexity and phenotypic variability of PHTS, as well as the risk of rare malignancies. Recognition of the potential unique phenotype and diagnostic challenges are important for PHTS surveillance. Future prospective studies with larger cohorts will be essential to refine surveillance guidelines, evaluate therapeutic options, and further clarify the natural history of this rare but clinically significant syndrome.
