## Suspected Brachial Plexus Neuropathy After Breast Reconstruction With Bilateral Deep Inferior Epigastric Perforator Flaps.

**PMID**: 42751689 · **Journal**: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1097/GOX.0000000000008062 · **PMCID**: PMC13581365

**Authors**: Miyazaki Shihori, Watanabe Shiho, Oka Aiko, Ochiai Hiroko

**Types**: Case Reports, Journal Article

Perioperative brachial plexus injury has become relatively rare, as preventive positioning strategies are now widely implemented. We report the case of a female patient who underwent bilateral breast reconstruction with bilateral deep inferior epigastric perforator flaps for bilateral breast cancer and developed left upper limb neuropathy, despite careful intraoperative positioning measures. General anesthesia was induced, and the operative time was 10 hours and 36 minutes. The patient was positioned supine, with both upper limbs abducted to approximately 90 degrees and secured to arm boards with the forearms extended. The head was stabilized on the operating table using adhesive tape and a pillow. The patient was temporarily placed in a sitting position for approximately 4 minutes to assess the breast shape. Immediately after emergence from anesthesia, the patient reported weakness in left elbow flexion and a sensory disturbance extending from the radial side of the upper arm to the forearm. Physical examination suggested an upper trunk (C5-C6) brachial plexus lesion. Cervical magnetic resonance imaging revealed no obvious brachial plexus abnormality; however, mild C5-C6 cervical disc herniation was noted. At discharge, only mild forearm numbness persisted, and the symptoms had nearly resolved by 6 months. Although double crush syndrome was considered as a possible patient-related contributing factor, careful positioning may have helped prevent progression to a more severe neurological deficit. This case underscores the importance of comprehensive preoperative risk assessment and meticulous intraoperative positioning through collaboration among surgeons, anesthesiologists, and operating room staff.

Postoperative upper limb motor and sensory disturbances may result from brachial plexus injury or peripheral neuropathies. 1  The brachial plexus, originating from the C5 to T1 nerve roots, is anatomically vulnerable to mechanical stress as it passes between the clavicle and the first rib (Fig.  1 ). Perioperative brachial plexus injury is uncommon, with an incidence of 0.02%–0.06%. 2  Intraoperative brachial plexus injury is caused by nerve overstretching or compression, leading to ischemia of the vasa nervorum. 1 , 3 , 4  Excessive arm abduction, external rotation, and neck traction due to head positioning can contribute to brachial plexus injury, particularly at the upper trunk (C5–C6), which is vulnerable to stretch during arm abduction and neck rotation. 1  Patient-related factors may increase susceptibility. Subclinical neuropathies may become symptomatic when additional stress, such as prolonged operative time or sustained arm traction, is imposed, a phenomenon known as double crush syndrome. 5  We report a case of suspected brachial plexus injury after breast reconstruction with bilateral deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) flaps, focusing on the clinical course and mechanisms.

A 50-year-old woman (height, 163 cm; weight, 49 kg) with invasive ductal carcinoma of both breasts underwent bilateral mastectomy at our institution. The pathological stage was pT1bN0M0 (stage I) for the right breast and pT1cN0M0 (stage I) for the left breast. She requested immediate single-stage autologous reconstruction, and bilateral DIEP flap reconstruction was performed. Written informed consent was obtained for the procedure and publication. Her medical history included dyslipidemia; her preoperative evaluation was unremarkable, and she had no smoking history.

General anesthesia was induced. The operative time was 10 hours and 36 minutes, with a blood loss of 496 mL. The patient was positioned supine, with upper limbs abducted to approximately 90 degrees and secured to arm boards, with the forearms extended. To allow temporary sitting intraoperatively, the head was fixed to the table with adhesive tape and a pillow. Bilateral internal mammary vessels were used as the recipient vessels. After vascular anastomosis, the patient was placed in a sitting position for approximately 4 minutes to assess the breast shape. To prevent sliding, the sitting angle was limited to approximately 80 degrees, with a cushion under the knees and a footboard supporting the soles. The surgery was completed uneventfully, and the flap survived without vascular compromise.

Immediately after emergence from anesthesia, the patient complained of difficulty flexing the left elbow and sensory disturbance from the radial side of the upper arm to that of the forearm. On postoperative day (POD) 1, orthopedic evaluation suggested that an isolated peripheral nerve injury was unlikely; therefore, brachial plexus injury involving the upper trunk (C5–C6) and a cervical spine lesion were considered. Oral pregabalin (150 mg/d) and mecobalamin (1500 µg/d) therapy was initiated per the orthopedic specialist’s recommendation. By POD 2, the symptoms had begun to improve. Cervical magnetic resonance imaging conducted on POD 2 showed symmetric visualization of the brachial plexus without clear evidence of injury; however, mild C5–C6 cervical disc herniation was observed (Fig.  2 ). By POD 3, the motor deficit had completely resolved. On POD 9, pregabalin was increased to 300 mg/d. At discharge, on POD 23, only mild radial forearm numbness remained. Pregabalin dosage was reduced after 1 month without worsening of symptoms. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies at 4 months showed no definitive brachial plexus injury but suggested neurogenic changes in the biceps brachii. Symptoms had nearly resolved by 6 months.

In this case, elbow flexion weakness and sensory disturbance along the lateral aspect of the upper arm and forearm could not be explained by isolated peripheral nerve injury, necessitating differentiation between a brachial plexus injury and cervical radiculopathy. Given the immediate postoperative onset, positioning-related brachial plexus injury was considered most likely. Although radiological and electrophysiological findings were inconclusive, electromyography performed at 4 months showed neurogenic changes in the biceps brachii, suggesting transient nerve injury, such as acute demyelination, followed by recovery.

Reported patient-related risk factors include lean body habitus, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and smoking. 1 , 3  Associated neuropathies can be classified as mechanical or metabolic/ischemic (Table  1 ). Additionally, intraoperative hypotension or hypothermia may also have contributed to the development of the condition by reducing perfusion of the vasa nervorum. 4  Subclinical preexisting neuropathies may become symptomatic postoperatively when additional mechanical stress is imposed, a phenomenon known as double crush syndrome. 5

Previous reports of brachial plexus injury after breast reconstruction are limited. Cases after reconstruction with latissimus dorsi or transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous flaps have been reported, 6 – 8  with most patients presenting with C5–C6 dominant symptoms, including impaired shoulder abduction, elbow flexion weakness, and radial forearm hypoesthesia. Most cases involved neuropraxia and recovery following conservative management. Preventive recommendations are represented by limiting arm abduction to less than 90 degrees, maintaining neutral head and neck alignment, and using adequate padding for upper limbs. 6 – 9  However, nerve injury may occur even with these measures, particularly with prolonged positioning or an increased abduction within 90 degrees. 4

In this case, although arm abduction was maintained within 90 degrees, nerve injury developed, suggesting additional contributing factors. Prolonged bilateral arm abduction and temporary intraoperative sitting may also have contributed. Additionally, the patient had a lean body habitus and dyslipidemia, and postoperative magnetic resonance imaging revealed mild C5–C6 disc herniation, suggesting possible involvement of double crush syndrome. These findings indicate that both positioning and patient-related factors were concomitant. Intraoperative hypotension and hypothermia were not unlikely to have contributed, as they were appropriately managed.

After this case, cushioned arm pads (Fig.  3 ) and routine positioning checks every 2 hours to maintain arm abduction at less than 90 degrees whenever possible were implemented, along with greater emphasis on preoperative risk assessment. No similar cases have occurred since.

We report a case of suspected brachial plexus injury after breast reconstruction using a bilateral DIEP flap, despite careful intraoperative positioning management. In addition to the known risk factors, including prolonged arm abduction and intraoperative position changes, double crush syndrome may have contributed to symptom development. Although the prognosis is generally favorable, postoperative neuropathy can significantly impair quality of life. This case highlights the importance of comprehensive preoperative risk assessment and meticulous intraoperative positioning through close collaboration among surgical and anesthetic teams.

The authors have no financial interest to declare in relation to the content of this article.

<!-- ===== PMID 42751599 ===== -->
## BET Protein Degrader ZBC260 Induces Tumor Vascular Reprogramming Through Endothelial Cell Remodeling.

**PMID**: 42751599 · **Journal**: Breast cancer (Dove Medical Press) · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.2147/BCTT.S626513 · **PMCID**: PMC13580462

**Authors**: Sharma Deeksha, Hager Cody G, Wicha Max S, Burness Monika L

**Types**: Journal Article

**PURPOSE**: Endothelial cells regulate angiogenesis, matrix remodeling, and immune responses within the tumor microenvironment, yet endothelial cell heterogeneity across breast cancer subtypes and its regulation by bromodomain and extraterminal domain proteins remain unclear. This study profiled endothelial cells at single-cell resolution in two immunocompetent murine breast cancer models with distinct tumor immune microenvironments: PyMT_FVB/N and D2A1_BALB/c tumors.

**METHODS**: Mice were treated intravenously with the bromodomain and extraterminal domain degrader (ZBC260) at 10mg/kg 3 days/week until tumors reached humane endpoints and were harvested. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on vehicle and ZBC260 treated tumors (n=3 per condition), and endothelial cell populations were identified and analyzed using Seurat package in R.

**RESULTS**: Six transcriptionally distinct endothelial subpopulations were identified across both breast cancer models, with D2A1 tumors dominated by tip-like and proliferative endothelial cells with strong angiogenic and collagen-producing signatures. ZBC260 reprogrammed endothelial landscape by reducing proliferative, tip-like, and arterial endothelial cells while enriching venous and lymphatic endothelial cells. ZBC260 suppressed hypoxia, glycolysis, and mTORC1 signaling, downregulated angiogenesis and matrix associated pathways and was accompanied by reduced collagen signatures and increased leukocyte adhesion. Cell-cell communication analysis demonstrated that ZBC260 disrupted endothelial cells interactions with tumor and immune cells, by disrupting ligand-receptor communications and attenuating NOTCH, TGF-β, and VEGF signaling networks that sustain angiogenesis and immune suppression.

**CONCLUSION**: Together, these findings highlight endothelial diversity across breast cancer models and identify ZBC260 as a regulator of tumor endothelial states. ZBC260 reprograms endothelial heterogeneity and remodels the tumor vascular landscape. The transcriptomic and cell-cell communication changes observed are consistent with the establishment of a more immune-permissive tumor microenvironment, supporting the potential of BET degradation as a strategy to complement immunotherapy and improve therapeutic responsiveness in breast cancer.

Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women and is characterized by high heterogeneity, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. 1–3  Despite advances in treatment, patient outcomes remain poor due to the complex, diverse, and adaptive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME). 3  While immunotherapy has improved cancer treatment, its benefit is largely limited to patients with immunologically “hot” (immune-inflamed) tumors, whereas breast cancers with a “cold” (immune-desert) TME fail to support effective immune infiltration and activation. 4 , 5  The immune phenotype of the TME is determined by the composition and function of both immune and stromal cells, highlighting the importance of targeting not only the tumor cells but also the surrounding microenvironment to improve therapy responses. 6

Although precision oncology has advanced the identification of tumor-intrinsic therapeutic targets across breast cancer subtypes, these tumor-centered approaches may not fully address the contribution of the TME to disease progression and therapeutic resistance. 7 , 8  Among TME populations, endothelial cells (ECs) are critical yet understudied regulators of tumor progression and therapy resistance, forming abnormal tumor-associated vasculature that supports growth and metastasis, while limiting immune infiltration. 9 , 10  Beyond their structural role, ECs display significant phenotypic plasticity, undergoing endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) and acquiring immune-regulatory and pro-invasive functions. 11 , 12  Additionally, ECs modulate anti-tumor immunity through cytokine secretion, antigen presentation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. 13  Therapies targeting ECs, primarily via anti-angiogenic treatments (AATs), have achieved limited success due to EC heterogeneity and intrinsic plasticity. 14  In some preclinical models, AATs can paradoxically promote tumor invasion and metastasis, likely driven by hypoxia-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), activation of MET signaling, and stromal cell recruitment. 15

These limitations underscore the need to better define the functional diversity of tumor-associated ECs and the mechanisms that regulate their phenotypic states. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) have begun to resolve this complexity, revealing transcriptionally distinct EC subtypes with specialized roles in angiogenesis, vascular remodeling, leukocyte trafficking, and immune regulation. 16 , 17  In breast tumors, previously described EC populations include angiogenic, arterial, venous, and lymphatic ECs, with angiogenic ECs exhibiting transcriptional features associated with vascular sprouting and remodeling, while arterial and venous ECs reflect distinct vascular and inflammatory programs and lymphatic ECs contribute to lymphatic vascular function and immune interactions. 18  Within the angiogenic compartment, tip-like ECs represent a specialized state associated with active vessel sprouting. 17  Together, these findings highlight the diversity and plasticity of breast cancer endothelium. However, the molecular factors that regulate endothelial state transitions and the functional consequences of endothelial heterogeneity in breast cancer remain poorly understood. In particular, whether epigenetic regulators such as Bromodomain and extraterminal domain (BET) proteins contribute to the regulation of distinct endothelial states remains unknown.

BET proteins are epigenetic regulators of genes involved in cancer progression, stemness, inflammation, and angiogenesis 19 , 20  which has led to the development of BET inhibitors (BETi) and selective BET degraders (BETd), several of which are now in clinical trials. BET inhibition not only targets tumor cells but also enhances anti-tumor immunity by reprogramming immune cells and sensitizing immunologically cold tumors to immunotherapy. 21–25  Beyond tumor and immune cells, BET targeting can influence stromal cells of the TME. In cancer-associated fibroblasts, BET inhibition has been shown to suppress fibroblast activation and tumor-promoting functions. 26  In ECs, BET suppression inhibits VEGF-induced angiogenesis and vascular permeability through VEGFR2-mediated PAK1/eNOS signaling. 27  Similarly, BRD4 inhibition suppresses angiogenesis through regulation of AP-1 expression. 27 , 28  More recently transcriptomic analyses demonstrated that BET proteins regulate basal endothelial gene expression programs involved in migration, proliferation, and angiogenesis, further supporting a role for BET proteins in maintaining endothelial cell function. 29  Although these studies establish important roles for BET proteins in endothelial biology, their function within tumor-associated endothelial populations remains poorly defined. Whether BET proteins regulate ECs heterogeneity, endothelial state transitions, and interactions with tumor and immune cells remain largely unknown. In particular, it is unclear whether BET degradation can selectively reprogram tumor-associated endothelial populations to remodel the tumor vasculature and enhance anti-tumor immunity.

We hypothesized that BET protein degradation would reprogram ECs heterogeneity, reduce pro-tumor endothelial states, and remodel vascular–immune interactions to generate a more immune-permissive tumor microenvironment. To determine whether BET-dependent endothelial remodeling is conserved across distinct tumor contexts, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to profile ECs states in two complementary immunocompetent murine breast cancer models. MMTV-PyMT tumors develop spontaneously in the mammary gland through oncogene-driven tumorigenesis, whereas D2A1 tumors are established by orthotopic transplantation of a syngeneic mammary carcinoma cell line into BALB/c mice. These models differ in tumor origin, progression, and host context while preserving intact tumor–immune–stromal interactions. 30 , 31  To pharmacologically target BET proteins, we used the pan-BET degrader ZBC260, which has previously demonstrated anti-tumor efficacy in breast cancer models by suppressing tumor cell stemness and reprogramming inflammatory signaling. 20  Importantly, in the D2A1 model used in the present study, ZBC260 increased lymphoid infiltration while reducing fibroblast and endothelial populations. 32  Building on these findings, we investigated how BET degradation directly reprograms EC states and vascular–immune interactions.

We identified distinct EC subpopulations with diverse transcriptional and functional states. Treatment with the BET degrader ZBC260 reprogrammed EC heterogeneity, suppressed pro-tumor signaling, and disrupted EC-mediated key ligand–receptor interactions with tumor and immune cells. These findings highlight the complexity and plasticity of ECs in breast cancer and reveal a previously unrecognized role for BET proteins. BET degradation represents a promising strategy to remodel tumor vasculature and enhance immune responsiveness in breast cancer. By targeting endothelial plasticity and vascular states in addition to tumor-intrinsic pathways, this approach may complement current precision oncology strategies aimed at overcoming therapeutic resistance and improving responses to existing treatments.

All animal studies were approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) (PRO00011242, RRID:SCR_025789), conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines and the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, and conducted in a pathogen-free facility. 20  D2A1 cells (RRID#CVCL_0I90) were provided by the laboratory of Hunter Kent (National Cancer Institute, USA). PyMT cells were derived from a spontaneous MMTV-PyMT tumor in the laboratory of Max S Wicha (University of Michigan, USA) under IACUC approved protocols. The use of these murine cell lines was approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Biosafety Committee (IBCA00000534) and IACUC, and all studies were conducted in accordance with institutional animal care and use guidelines. Female six-week-old FVBN (Cat#001800, RRID: IMSR_JAX:001800, Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, Maine, USA) and BALB/c mice (Cat#000651, RRID#IMSR_JAX:000651, Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, Maine, USA) were anesthetized using inhaled isoflurane (delivered via precision vaporizer at 4–5% for induction and 1–2% for maintenance) and orthotopically injected with 5×10 5  PyMT or D2A1 cells into the fourth left mammary fat pad. Once tumors reached approximately 200 mm 3 , mice (n = 10 per group) were randomized to receive ZBC260 (10 mg/kg) (provided by Dr. Shaomeng Wang Lab (Department of Pharmacology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA) and purchased (Cat#HY-101519, MedChemExpress, Monmouth Junction, NJ, USA) or vehicle (20% PEG400, 6% Cremophor EL) intravenously three times per week. Tumor size and body weight were monitored twice weekly. Once any tumor within a given murine model (PyMT or D2A1) reached 2cm in any direction, the experiment was terminated. Mice were euthanized by carbon dioxide inhalation (gradual fill rate of 40% chamber volume displacement per minute) consistent with AVMA guidelines. Bilateral pneumothorax was used as secondary physical method to ensure death. Treatment duration prior to euthanasia was 35 days for the PyMT model and 19 days for the D2A1 model. Tumors were excised under aseptic conditions and processed for formalin fixed paraffin embedding (FFPE). FFPE blocks were submitted for subsequent Single-cell RNA sequencing (n=3). In vivo experiments included 10 biological replicates per experimental group. Three independent tumor samples per condition were randomly selected for single-cell RNA sequencing (n = 3/group), with each sample analyzed individually without pooling, consistent with commonly used scRNA-seq study designs for characterization of cellular heterogeneity and cellular states.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed at the Advanced Genomics Core, University of Michigan, using the 10x Genomics Chromium platform with Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits v3. Libraries were converted with the MGIEasy Universal Library Conversion Kit for sequencing on the MGISEQ-2000 platform (RRID:SCR_017980, MGI Tech Co., Shenzhen, Guangdong, China). Raw sequencing data was processed by the Advanced Genomics Core. Gene expression matrices were generated using Cell Ranger, with reads aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10, v8.0.1, RRID:SCR_023221). Sequencing quality metrics, including the number of recovered cells per sample, sequencing depth, median reads per cell, median genes detected per cell, and median unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) per cell, were used to evaluate sequencing quality and overall dataset robustness.

Data analysis was performed in Seurat (v5.2.0, RRID:SCR_016341) following the Seurat vignette ( https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/pbmc3k_tutorial ). The cell-by-gene count metrices obtained from CellRanger’s output were subsequently imported into R (v4.3.30) with Seurat package (v5.4.0) for downstream analyses. Quality control was performed to filter out low-quality cells with fewer than 200 detected genes or >10% mitochondrial genes contents were excluded. The filtered count matrices were integrated and processed mainly with Seurat package. Potential batch effects between sequencing runs and samples were assessed and corrected using the Seurat integration workflow. Integration anchors were identified using FindIntegrationAnchors, followed by dataset integration using IntegrateData.

Data were log-normalized by scaling counts and log-transforming values. Dimensionality reduction was conducted using principal component analysis (PCA), retaining 20 principal components for further steps. Clustering was performed via FindNeighbors to construct a k-nearest neighbor graph, followed by FindClusters with a resolution of 0.2. Clusters were visualized using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). Differential gene expression analysis across clusters was conducted with FindAllMarkers and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, considering adjusted p-values < 0.05 as significant. 33

All major cell populations were initially annotated based on cluster-specific differentially expressed genes together with established canonical marker genes reported in the literature. Major cellular populations were identified using their characteristic marker expression profiles. 34  Following initial clustering and annotation, ECs were identified and extracted for independent processing. The endothelial subset was re-normalized, reclustered, and subclusters were annotated using cluster-specific differentially expressed genes, canonical endothelial markers, and established endothelial transcriptomic classifications from published single-cell studies 18 , 34 , 35  to resolve endothelial heterogeneity.

Pathway enrichment analysis was performed using the clusterProfiler R package. Gene Ontology Biological Process (GO-BP), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and the Hallmark gene set collection from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB; mouse Hallmark collection, mh.all.v2025.1mm.entrez.gmt) were used for enrichment analyses. Enrichment significance was assessed using statistical testing implemented in clusterProfiler, and multiple comparisons were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method. Pathways with adjusted P values <0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

Angiogenesis, collagen formation, and leukocyte adhesion scores were calculated using the Seurat AddModuleScore function based on predefined gene signatures. 36  Module scores were used to evaluate endothelial functional scores in both tumor models (PyMT and D2A1) and to assess differences associated with ZBC260 treatment compared with vehicle treatment.

Cell-cell communication analysis was performed using the CellChat R package (v1.1.3). 37  For mouse datasets, ligand-receptor interactions were inferred using the CellChatDB.mouse reference database. The input dataset consisted of annotated cell populations generated from the Seurat analysis. Genes were screened for overexpression using identifyOverExpressedGenes with a significance threshold of  P  <0.05, followed by identification of overexpressed ligand-receptor interactions using identifyOverExpressedInteractions. Communication probabilities were calculated using computeCommunProb based on CellChat’s permutation-based statistical framework. Significant signaling pathways were identified using computeCommunProbPathway (threshold = 0.05), and interaction networks were summarized using aggregateNet (threshold = 0.05). Multiple testing correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and ligand-receptor interactions with adjusted  P  <0.05 were considered significant.

The KM Plotter online tool ( http://www.kmplot.com ), a publicly available database, was used to study the relationship between the expression of tip-like EC markers and overall survival in breast cancer patients. Patients were divided into two groups (high vs low expression) based on the median gene expression value.

All statistical analyses were performed using R (Version 4.3.0). Differential gene expression analyzed using the Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, with p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. A p-value threshold of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. For functional enrichment analyses, statistical significance was determined using Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted  P  values, with an adjusted  P  value <0.05 considered significant. For module score analyses, comparisons were performed to evaluate differences between the PyMT and D2A1 tumor models, as well as differences between ZBC260-treated and vehicle-treated groups. Statistical comparisons were performed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s  t -test. Individual biological replicates were considered the experimental unit, and a  P  value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Schematic figures created using BioRender.com (no version number available); no generative AI features were used.

To characterize ECs heterogeneity across breast cancer models, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of tumors from two immunocompetent murine breast cancer models, PyMT_FVB/N and D2A1_BALB/c ( Figure 1A ). Sequencing metrics are summarized in  Supplementary Table S1 . Initial unsupervised clustering identified the major cellular compartments in the PyMT_FVB/N model, including tumor (Krt18), myeloid (Ptprc, Csf1r), lymphoid (Ptprc, Cd3e, Cd19), fibroblast (Col3a1, Col1a1), and endothelial cells (Eng, Cdh5) 34  ( Figure 1B  and  C ;  Supplemental Figure S1A ). Following initial clustering and annotation of the whole-tumor scRNA-seq datasets, 3,611 ECs were identified, of which 3,435 cells were retained for EC-specific analysis. These cells were subsequently subsetted from the integrated Seurat object for endothelial-specific analysis.

Unsupervised dimensional reduction revealed a clear separation of endothelial populations derived from D2A1 and PyMT tumors, with minimal overlap in the UMAP projection ( Figure 1D ). Differential gene expression analysis identified 4,120 significantly differentially expressed genes between PyMT- and D2A1-derived ECs, including 3,201 upregulated and 919 downregulated genes. Hierarchical clustering based on the differentially expressed endothelial genes further demonstrated distinct transcriptional profiles between the two models. D2A1-derived ECs exhibited higher expression of Cfl1, Vim, Lgals1, and Set, among other genes whereas PyMT-derived ECs showed higher expression of Chil1, Ly6e, Col9a2, Sox10, Tmc4, Cdh1, and Elf5 ( Figure 1E ;  Supplemental Figure S1B  and  C ). These findings suggest model-specific differences in endothelial gene expression profiles.

Pathway enrichment analysis identified 51 significantly enriched pathways, with the top pathways shown in  Figure 1F . D2A1-derived ECs were enriched for epithelial–mesenchymal transition, MYC target, and TGF-β signaling pathways, whereas PyMT-derived ECs showed enrichment for hypoxia, p53, and TNFα signaling pathways. Consistent with these transcriptional differences, module scores for angiogenesis and collagen formation further highlighted functional distinctions: D2A1-derived ECs exhibited higher angiogenic activity, while PyMT-derived ECs showed increased collagen formation scores ( Figure 1G  and  H ). Together, these findings demonstrate pronounced model-specific endothelial transcriptional heterogeneity, with distinct molecular and functional programs across D2A1 and PyMT tumors.

To build on our understanding of EC heterogeneity in these two diverse models, we integrated scRNA-seq data from both PyMT_FVB/N and D2A1_BALB/c tumor models and performed unsupervised clustering specifically on ECs. Subclustering revealed six transcriptionally distinct ECs populations, visualized using UMAP ( Figure 2A ). Endothelial subtypes were annotated using both unbiased approaches and canonical differential markers. 18 , 34–36  The identified EC subtypes included Arap3⁺ (expressing  Rgcc, Arap3, Jak3 ), proliferative (pECs; expressing  Mki67, Top2a, Pcna ), tip-like (expressing  Cxcr4, Col4a1, Mcam ), arterial (expressing  Gja5, Gja4, Fbln5 ), venous (expressing  Ackr1, Selp, Clu ), and lymphatic (expressing  Prox1, Lyve1, Vcam ) ( Figure 2B–D ). DEGs for each subtype were analyzed for pathway enrichment, and Gene Ontology (GO) analysis indicated that each subtype was enriched for distinct biological pathways, highlighting their functional specialization ( Supplemental Figure S2A – F ).

Breast cancer endothelial cell subtypes: clustering, markers, proportions, survival analysis.

Comparative analysis revealed distinct endothelial state distributions between PyMT and D2A1 tumors ( Figure 2E ). PyMT tumors exhibited a broader distribution of EC states. Arap3⁺ ECs constituted the largest proportion (0.417%), followed by pECs (0.257%) and tip-like ECs (0.251%), whereas arterial, venous, and lymphatic ECs represented smaller proportions (0.052%, 0.013%, and 0.010% respectively). In contrast, D2A1 tumors were predominantly composed of tip-like ECs (0.792%) and proliferative ECs (0.184%), while Arap3⁺ and arterial ECs represented only 0.010% and 0.014% of the EC cells respectively ( Figure 2F ). Together, these findings highlight differences in endothelial heterogeneity and vascular phenotype between the two tumor models.

To further assess functional specialization inferred from transcriptional profiles, we calculated angiogenesis, collagen formation, and leukocyte-endothelial adhesion scores. Ridge plot analyses showed higher leukocyte adhesion signatures in venous ECs, while tip-like ECs displayed elevated collagen formation and angiogenesis scores ( Figure 2G ). To determine the prognostic relevance of tip-like EC marker genes in breast cancer patients, we performed Kaplan–Meier survival analysis using TCGA breast cancer data. High expression levels of ESM1 and ANGPT2 were correlated with worse overall survival compared to low expression levels ( Figure 2H  and  I ). Because these analyses were performed using bulk tumor transcriptomic data, expression of these genes may reflect contributions from multiple cellular compartments in addition to tip-like ECs. This correlation supports the clinical relevance of tip-like EC-associated signatures. Overall, our findings suggest that tip-like ECs may play a central role in extracellular matrix remodeling and angiogenic activity, potentially supporting tumor growth and vascular remodeling.

To assess the effects of ZBC260 on tumor ECs, we analyzed ECs from the PyMT and D2A1 tumor models and integrated the datasets for visualization. The integrated UMAP showed marked differences in the distribution of EC populations following ZBC260 treatment ( Figure 3A ). Quantitative analysis revealed a shift in EC subtype distribution following ZBC260 treatment, characterized by reductions in the proportion of proliferative, tip-like, and arterial ECs and enrichment of lymphatic and venous ECs ( Figure 3B ). These findings indicate that ZBC260 selectively alters EC phenotypes.

To determine whether the effects of ZBC260 were conserved across tumor models, we compared EC populations in PyMT and D2A1 tumors. The most consistent change was observed in tip-like ECs, which decreased by approximately 50% following ZBC260 treatment in both models, from 69.1% to 30.9% in PyMT tumors and from 66.5% to 33.5% in D2A1 tumors. In contrast, the effect on pECs was model-dependent. In PyMT tumors, pECs decreased substantially from 73.3% to 26.7%, whereas in D2A1 tumors pECs remained unchanged, representing approximately 50% of the EC compartment in both vehicle and treatment groups. Arap3+ and arterial ECs represented relatively small populations in D2A1 tumors, limiting interpretation of treatment-associated changes in these subsets ( Supplemental Figure S3A  and  B ).

Some differences are likely reflects the distinct baseline endothelial composition of the two tumor models. Six EC populations were identified in PyMT tumors, including venous and lymphatic ECs, both of which increased following ZBC260 treatment. In contrast, these populations were not detected in D2A1 tumors. Together, these findings indicate that ZBC260 consistently depleted tip-like ECs across tumor models while producing model-specific changes in other endothelial populations, underscoring both conserved and context-dependent regulation of endothelial heterogeneity within the tumor microenvironment.

Differential gene expression analysis revealed widespread transcriptional changes in ECs following ZBC260 treatment. A volcano plot illustrated differential gene expression between vehicle and ZBC260 treated ECs, with  Glycam1  upregulated ( Supplemental Figure S4A ). GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses of upregulated genes indicated activation of immune-related pathways, including antigen presentation, lymphocyte-mediated immunity, leukocyte adhesion, and positive regulation of adaptive immune responses. Conversely, downregulated pathways were primarily associated with HIF-1 signaling and carbohydrate metabolism ( Supplemental Figure 4B – E ).

Given that tip-like ECs are a predominant population in both tumor models and exhibit elevated collagen formation and angiogenesis scores, we further analyzed their functional and transcriptional changes following ZBC260 treatment. In tip-like ECs, ZBC260 treatment significantly downregulated 10 hallmark pathways, including hypoxia, glycolysis, and mTORC1 signaling, with no hallmark pathways significantly upregulated ( Figure 3C ). GO analysis revealed suppression of the epithelial cell migration pathway, accompanied by upregulation of leukocyte migration–related pathways ( Figure 3D  and  E ). Analysis of the top 20 downregulated genes highlighted suppression of critical regulators of tumor vascular remodeling, including  Lox, Perp , and  Nrg1  ( Figure 3F ). Additionally, collagen formation score was reduced, leukocyte adhesion score was enhanced, and angiogenesis score remained unchanged following treatment ( Figure 3G ). Together, these results demonstrate that ZBC260 remodels ECs, selectively reprogramming tip-like ECs and suppressing tumor-supportive transcriptional pathways.

To investigate interactions between EC subtypes and other cells within the TME, we performed cell–cell communication analysis using CellChat. 37  Interaction strength analysis revealed that tip-like ECs exhibited the highest overall interaction strength, predominantly interacting with tumor and immune cells (myeloid and lymphoid) ( Figure 4A ). Arap⁺ and arterial ECs also demonstrated preferential signaling with myeloid cells in untreated tumors. ZBC260 treatment significantly reduced the overall interaction strength of ECs, with tip-like ECs showing the most pronounced decrease in signaling with both immune and tumor cells, decreasing to nearly half of control levels ( Figure 4B ).

Bubble plots of ligand–receptor interactions between tip-like ECs and ( C ) Tumor cells, ( D ) Fibroblast cells, ( E ) Myeloid cells, and ( F ) Lymphoid cells with and without ZBC260 treatment. Circos plots illustrating endothelial-mediated ( G ) Notch, ( H ) TGFb, and ( I ) VEGF signaling pathways in vehicle-treated (top) and ZBC260-treated (bottom) conditions. Consistent with the reduction in overall interaction strength, ZBC260 also altered the number and distribution of predicted EC interactions. The total number of predicted interactions decreased modestly from 1,146 to 1,102. However, this limited overall change masked substantial subtype-specific remodeling of the predicted communication network ( Supplementary Table S2 ). The largest reduction in predicted interactions was observed for tip-like ECs, which decreased from 286 to 189 total interactions, including marked reductions in predicted interactions with lymphoid (64 to 20) and myeloid (77 to 42) cell populations. Decreases in the number of predicted interactions were also observed for arterial, proliferative, Arap3⁺, and lymphatic ECs. In contrast, predicted interactions involving venous ECs were detected only in ZBC260 treated tumors. Additionally, the number of predicted interactions between tumor cells and both lymphatic and venous ECs increased following treatment. Together, these findings indicate that BET degradation has a limited effect on the overall number of predicted EC interactions but is associated with substantial redistribution of predicted EC–TME communication across endothelial subtypes and interacting cell populations.

Ligand–receptor analysis identified the COL4A1–SDC4 axis as one of the most prominent interactions across all EC subtypes, which was significantly (p<0.05) reduced following treatment. In addition, multiple collagen- and integrin-mediated interactions between ECs and tumor cells, as well as between ECs and fibroblasts, were disrupted. Interactions between ECs and myeloid cells exhibited subtype-specific patterns. However, SPP1-mediated signaling, which is a shared axis across EC subsets, was completely abolished after treatment. Communication with lymphoid cells was broadly reduced, with the notable exception of APP–CD74 signaling, which was increased following treatment. In tip-like ECs in particular, several signaling interactions were differentially affected. Notably, DLL4–NOTCH1 and HSP2–DAG1 signaling between ECs and lymphoid cells were disrupted, while APP-mediated interactions (including APP–SORL1 and APP–TNFRSF21) showed altered activity. In myeloid cell interactions, F11R–F11R, APP–TREM2–TYROBP, and SPP1–ITGA9–ITGB4 signaling axes were completely disrupted following treatment ( Figure 4C–F ;  Supplemental Figures S5A – H ,  S6A – H  and  S7A – D ).

Pathway-level analysis showed strong suppression of NOTCH, TGFb and VEGF signaling with arterial and tip-like ECs primarily mediating communications with tumor and immune cells ( Figure 4G–I ). Collectively, these findings indicate that BET degradation reprograms endothelial communication within the TME, dampening angiogenic and immunosuppressive networks that support tumor progression.

Overall, our data demonstrates that BETd reshapes endothelial heterogeneity at multiple levels suppressing pathological hypoxic, metabolic, and MYC-driven signaling while enhancing immune-supportive features and weakening tumor–endothelial–immune suppressive interactions. These integrated results highlight a unifying mechanism through which BETd remodels the vascular niche toward a less immunosuppressive and more therapeutically responsive state ( Figure 5 ).
 Figure 5 BETd-driven remodeling of endothelial heterogeneity and communication across breast cancer models. Baseline endothelial programs in PyMT_FVB/N and D2A1_BALB/c tumors displayed distinct, model-specific enrichment patterns. BETd treatment broadly reduced most EC subtypes while selectively expanding lymphatic and venous subtypes. Tip-like ECs, present in both models, exhibited high angiogenesis and collagen-formation scores and were reprogrammed by BETd, showing reduced hypoxia, glycolysis, MTORC1 and MYC-target signaling. BETd further enhanced EC immunostimulatory features, including lymphocyte migration, proliferation, adhesion, and antigen-presentation signatures. Cell–cell communication analysis highlighted significant disruption of tumor–EC–immune immunosuppressive axes, accompanied by decreased overall interaction strength and suppression of NOTCH, TGFβ, and VEGF signaling pathways. In both models, BETd treatment reduces most EC populations while increasing lymphatic and venous ECs. The treatment enhances lymphocyte migration, proliferation, adhesion and antigen presentation. Tip-like ECs in both models show enriched angiogenesis and collagen-formation scores. BETd decreases glycolysis, MTORC1, ROS and PI3K-AKT-MTOR signaling in metabolic pathways. It also reduces hypoxia, MYC targets, TNF signaling via NF-kB and cell growth regulation in regulatory signaling. Key elements include tumor cells, tip-like ECs and immune cells, with disrupted communication pathways highlighted. Diagram of BETd effects on endothelial cells in breast cancer models.

Breast cancers with aggressive phenotypes and treatment resistance remain a major clinical challenge. 1 , 2  The TME, particularly ECs, contributes to therapeutic failure by promoting angiogenesis, immune evasion, and metastasis. 9 , 10  Traditional anti-angiogenic therapies have demonstrated limited and often transient benefits, largely because they fail to address the heterogeneity and plasticity of EC populations. 14  In this study, single-cell analyses revealed distinct EC subpopulations across breast cancer models and demonstrated that BET protein degradation reprograms EC transcriptional states, suppresses tumor-promoting signaling, and disrupts key intercellular communication networks. Together, these findings highlight endothelial state remodeling as a potential mechanism for reshaping the TME and suggest new therapeutic opportunities to overcome resistance in aggressive breast cancers.

The distinct model-specific distribution of endothelial populations between D2A1 and PyMT tumors suggests that endothelial transcriptional states are strongly influenced by the tumor context in which they develop. Although both models represent mammary carcinoma, they differ substantially in tumor biology, including oncogenic drivers, tumor architecture, growth kinetics, and interaction with the surrounding microenvironment. 30 , 31 , 38  Therefore, the observed endothelial heterogeneity may reflect differences in tumor-derived signals, rather than representing a single conserved tumor endothelial phenotype. Differences in tumor progression and treatment duration may also contribute to the distinct EC states observed between the models, although inherent tumor- and host-specific differences cannot be excluded. 39

Our results demonstrate that ECs are not a homogeneous population but instead comprise multiple subtypes with specialized functional properties. Similar EC diversity has been reported in human breast cancer, 40  in murine endothelial cell atlases, 34  and across several other cancer types. 36 , 41–43  Consistent with these observations, our findings indicate that EC composition and function vary depending on the TME. Specifically, MMTV-PyMT tumors exhibited a diverse array of EC subtypes, whereas D2A1 tumors were enriched for pro-angiogenic, tip-like EC states. 43 , 44  Previous studies have identified tip-like ECs as a key subtype distinguishing tumor tissue from normal tissue, associated with tumor angiogenesis and immune-suppressive features, and a high proportion of tip-like ECs has been correlated with poor clinical outcomes across multiple cancer types. 43  These findings provide a context for interpreting the preferential remodeling of tip-like ECs following BET protein degradation in our models.

BET protein degradation by ZBC260 reshaped endothelial transcriptional states by shifting the balance toward venous and lymphatic phenotypes while depleting proliferative, arterial, and tip-like EC populations involved in angiogenesis and extracellular. This shift is particularly important for tip-like ECs, which are characterized by high expression of ESM1 and COL4A1 and have been associated with M2-like macrophage and regulatory T-cell enrichment, increased tumor proliferation, and poor clinical outcomes in breast cancer Tip-like ECs are also enriched within tumor cores and closely associated with malignant epithelial cells, consistent with their proposed role in supporting a tumor-promoting vascular niche. 17 , 45  In contrast, venous ECs display distinct spatial distributions and have been associated with increased T-cell infiltration, and antigen presentation suggesting a potentially more immune-permissive vascular context. 18 , 46  Together, these observations suggest that BET degradation may selectively reduce endothelial states associated with angiogenesis and tumor progression while promoting a shift toward alternative endothelial phenotypes.

Mechanistically, ZBC260 induces endothelial transcriptional changes consistent with an immunostimulatory EC phenotype, characterized by upregulation of lymphocyte-associated signaling, and immune activation pathway. 13  Concurrently, it downregulates hypoxia and HIF-1 signaling. 47  Collectively, these results suggest that BET protein degradation remodels hypoxia- and metabolism-driven programs in ECs and may promote a more immune-permissive vascular environment; however, the functional consequences of these transcriptional changes require further validation. 48–50

Cell–cell interaction analyses revealed that tip-like ECs exhibited the highest number of interactions within the TME, and that these interactions were markedly reduced following BETd treatment. Consistent with prior observations, tip-like ECs in untreated tumors demonstrated extensive crosstalk with both immune and tumor cells through extracellular matrix–mediated interactions, including COL4A1/COL4A2 and laminins (LAMC1, LAMB1/2, LAMA4/5) engaging integrin receptors (ITGA/ITGB). 51  Notably, the COL4A1–SDC4 axis, a key mediator of ECM signaling implicated in pro-angiogenic and mesenchymal-like programs, was significantly diminished after treatment, suggesting that BET degradation may suppress pro-tumorigenic endothelial reprogramming and matrix-driven signaling. 51  SPP1-mediated interactions, prominent across EC subsets and myeloid cells at baseline, were completely abolished following treatment. SPP1 (osteopontin), an integrin-binding matricellular protein, has been implicated in M2-like macrophage polarization and the formation of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment; 52  thus, loss of SPP1–integrin signaling (eg, SPP1–ITGA9–ITGB4) following BET degradation may indicate reduced endothelial–myeloid crosstalk associated with tumor-promoting signaling. Consistently, APP–TREM2–TYROBP signaling between ECs and myeloid cells was also completely disrupted. TREM2⁺ macrophages represent immunosuppressive TAM populations associated with CD8⁺ T cell dysfunction and impaired immunotherapy response, 53  and the disruption of this signaling axis may reflect attenuation of endothelial-myeloid interactions associated with immunosuppressive TME following BET degradation. Moreover, pathways central to angiogenesis, immunosuppression, and tumor progression including NOTCH, TGFβ, and VEGF were significantly attenuated. 13  However, these ligand-receptor interactions represent computational predictions and require experimental validation. In contrast, APP–CD74 signaling with lymphoid cells was upregulated following BET protein degradation. Although APP–CD74 interactions have primarily been described in myeloid cells, 54  CD74 broadly regulates antigen presentation and immune activation. The increased APP–CD74 signaling may reflect enhanced antigen-presenting activity, although this interpretation requires functional validation. 55

Beyond conventional anti-angiogenic approaches, recent strategies have focused on vascular normalization and modulation of endothelial function to improve tumor microenvironment organization. 56 , 57  Vascular normalization strategies targeting pathways such as VEGF/VEGFR and ANG2/Tie2 aim to stabilize abnormal tumor vessels, improve perfusion, and enhance immune-cell infiltration. 14 , 58  In contrast, our findings suggest that BET degradation represents a distinct approach to endothelial remodeling by altering multiple transcriptional programs and endothelial states rather than simply suppressing angiogenesis. By reducing tip-like and proliferative endothelial states and altering tumor-associated communication networks, ZBC260 may promote a less tumor-supportive and potentially more immune-permissive vascular phenotype. Although these findings require functional validation, they suggest that BET-mediated endothelial reprogramming may complement conventional vascular normalization strategies and expand the concept of vascular targeting beyond vessel inhibition.

Within the TME, interactions among ECs, immune cells, stromal components, and cytokines critically influence tumor progression and immunotherapy response. 2 , 56 , 59  ECs are particularly important in regulating immune-cell trafficking and activation through vascular permeability, adhesion molecules, and intercellular communication. 60  Our findings suggest that the observed endothelial remodeling and altered communication networks may contribute to a less tumor-supportive and more immune-permissive TME. Whether these changes translate into improved immunotherapy responses requires further functional and combination studies.

Despite these findings, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study was conducted exclusively in murine breast cancer models, and validation in human tumors will be necessary to establish clinical relevance. In addition, the predicted ligand–receptor interactions and functional pathway analyses are based on computational inference from single-cell transcriptomic data and therefore require functional validation. Finally, although our analyses provide insights into endothelial heterogeneity and BET degrader-induced vascular remodeling, complementary functional studies will be important to confirm the biological consequences of these transcriptional changes. Future studies integrating orthogonal validation approaches, including protein-level analyses, functional angiogenesis essays, and human clinical specimens, will be essential to further define the role of BET degradation in endothelial reprogramming and tumor vascular remodeling.

Collectively, these findings indicate that BET protein degradation broadly reshapes endothelial heterogeneity within the breast cancer tumor microenvironment by reducing tumor-associated endothelial states, altering endothelial transcriptional programs, and remodeling predicted intercellular communication networks. These changes are consistent with suppression of pro-angiogenic and immunoregulatory endothelial pathways and support a role for BET degradation in endothelial remodeling. These findings are consistent with prior evidence identifying ECs as central regulators of immune exclusion and further support the concept that EC cell states are therapeutic targets within the TME. 13  Together, our findings identify endothelial plasticity as a potential therapeutic vulnerability and suggest that targeting BET-dependent endothelial reprogramming may represent a promising strategy for tumor microenvironment remodeling in breast cancer. Future studies should evaluate BET degraders in combination with immunotherapy or other targeted therapies and validate these findings in human breast cancer specimens to determine their translational potential.

## Added value of serial troponin I and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide for early detection of cardiotoxicity in breast cancer: A three-year retrospective cohort study.

**PMID**: 42751596 · **Journal**: Qatar medical journal · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.5339/qmj.2026.60 · **PMCID**: PMC13580469

**Authors**: Shehu Benard, Shehu Klerida, Kraja Bledar, Kraja Fatjona

**Types**: Journal Article

**BACKGROUND**: Cardiotoxicity remains a major limitation in breast cancer treatment, especially with anthracyclines and radiotherapy. Early biomarkers may improve risk stratification.

**METHODS**: This retrospective cohort study included breast cancer patients treated between 2020 and 2023 with chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy. Troponin I (TPI) and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) were measured at baseline and at three, six, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 36 months. Cardiotoxicity was defined per European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines as a ≥10% drop in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) to <53% or >15% relative reduction in global longitudinal strain (GLS). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, logistic regression, and mixed-effects models assessed associations.

**RESULTS**: A total of 190 patients were included; 141 patients (74.2%) developed cardiotoxicity within 12 months. At six months, NT-proBNP (median: 212.6 pg/mL) and TPI (0.038 ng/mL) were significantly higher in the cardiotoxic group (p < 0.01). ROC area under the curve (AUC) for NT-proBNP at six months was 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77-0.89); for TPI, AUC = 0.79 (95% CI: 0.73-0.86). Multivariable regression showed both biomarkers remained independent predictors of cardiotoxicity after adjustment for GLS and cumulative anthracycline dose (NT-proBNP: OR 1.78 [95% CI 1.22-2.61], p = 0.003).

**CONCLUSION**: In this real-world breast cancer cohort, serial NT-proBNP and TPI monitoring, particularly at 3 and 6 months, provided meaningful early prognostic information for subsequent cardiotoxicity beyond baseline assessment alone. When integrated with echocardiographic surveillance, these biomarkers may support earlier identification of high-risk patients, more tailored cardio-oncology follow-up, and timely cardioprotective intervention, although prospective external validation is required before routine implementation.

Anthracycline-based chemotherapy and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted agents have significantly improved survival in breast cancer, but their use is limited by potential cardiotoxicity. Cardiac dysfunction may develop insidiously and progress to symptomatic heart failure, even years after therapy. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) defines cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) as a ≥10% decline in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) to <53%, or a >15% reduction in global longitudinal strain (GLS).Traditional imaging markers may not detect subclinical injury in time to enable preventive strategies. 1

Cardiac biomarkers such as troponin I (TPI), which reflects cardiomyocyte necrosis, and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), which indicates myocardial stress, have emerged as adjunctive tools for early detection. 2  Previous studies have suggested that elevations in these markers during chemotherapy are associated with future left ventricular dysfunction. 3 – 6  However, prospective data evaluating the additive prognostic value of serial biomarker trends in real-world populations remain limited. While such biomarker associations are increasingly reported, there is limited real-world evidence on their incremental value in routine clinical practice. 7 , 8  This study aimed to assess whether NT-proBNP and TPI predict cardiotoxicity more effectively than baseline values alone, and whether they add independent prognostic information to standard echocardiographic monitoring using GLS and LVEF. We hypothesize that early elevations in these biomarkers during treatment are predictive of both early and persistent myocardial dysfunction.

This retrospective cohort study was conducted at the University Hospital Center “Mother Teresa,” Tirana, Albania, between January 2020 and December 2023, and included breast cancer patients treated with chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy.

Inclusion criteria were adult female patients (≥18 years) with histologically confirmed breast cancer treated with anthracyclines and/or radiotherapy and with serial TPI and NT-proBNP measurements available during follow-up.

Exclusion criteria were incomplete biomarker data, uncontrolled arrhythmia, recent myocardial infarction, and pre-existing heart failure (baseline LVEF <50%).

GLS was defined as the echocardiographic measure of myocardial deformation. Cardiotoxicity was defined as an LVEF decline ≥10% to <53% and/or a >15% relative reduction in GLS from baseline, in line with ESC cardio-oncology guidance.

The primary outcome was cardiotoxicity at 12 months, defined by ESC 2022 cardio-oncology guidelines 1  as: LVEF decline ≥10% to a value <53% or GLS relative reduction >15% from baseline. Secondary outcomes included persistent cardiotoxicity at 36 months and hospitalization for heart failure.

Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± SD or median (IQR), and categorical data as counts (%). Group comparisons used Student’s t-test, Mann–Whitney U, or Chi-square tests. Receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) analysis calculated the area under the curve (AUC) for NT-proBNP and TPI at three and six months to predict one-year cardiotoxicity. Logistic regression models were used to determine independent predictors, adjusted for age, GLS, anthracycline dose, and baseline EF. Longitudinal biomarker trends were assessed with mixed-effects linear models. Statistical significance was set at  p  < 0.05. Analyses were performed using SPSS v27 and R v4. three.

Among the 190 breast cancer patients included, the mean age was 56.3 ± 8.2 years, with a predominance of cardiovascular comorbidities, including hypertension (45.8%), diabetes mellitus (14.7%), and chronic kidney disease (10%). Anthracycline-based chemotherapy was administered to all patients, and 61.1% also received chest radiotherapy, primarily on the left side (62.1%). Patients who developed cardiotoxicity ( n  = 141, 74.2%) were significantly older ( p  = 0.014) and more frequently had hypertension ( p  = 0.034), diabetes ( p  = 0.045), and received higher cumulative anthracycline doses ( p  = 0.021), as shown in  Table 1 .

Cardiotoxicity occurred in 141 patients (74.2%) during the first year of follow-up. A GLS decline >15% was the most common criterion (64%), while a reduction in LVEF below 53% accounted for 36% of cases. At 36 months, 25.3% ( n  = 48) had persistent cardiac dysfunction.

By the six-month mark, both biomarkers showed significant differences between groups. Patients with cardiotoxicity had higher NT-proBNP (212.6 pg/mL vs. 129.1 pg/mL,  p  < 0.001) and TPI (0.038 ng/mL vs. 0.021 ng/mL,  p  = 0.003). ROC analysis ( Table 2 ) demonstrated high diagnostic performance: AUC for NT-proBNP was 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77–0.89) and for TPI was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.73–0.86) at six months. These findings are illustrated in  Figure 1 .

In logistic regression models adjusted for clinical and treatment-related variables, both NT-proBNP and TPI retained independent predictive value. As shown in  Table 3 , a 100 pg/mL increase in NT-proBNP was associated with 1.78-fold higher odds (95% CI: 1.22–2.61,  p  = 0.003) of cardiotoxicity, while each 0.01 ng/mL rise in TPI conferred a 44% increased risk (OR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.11–1.87,  p  = 0.009). Additionally, anthracycline dose ≥250 mg/m 2  was a significant covariate (OR = 1.92,  p  = 0.021).

As shown in  Table 4  and visualized in  Figures 2 – 4 , NT-proBNP and TPI increased steadily in the cardiotoxicity group over the 12-month period, while levels remained comparatively stable in the non-cardiotoxic group ( p  < 0.001) for time-by-group interaction. NT-proBNP rose from 86.5 pg/mL to 256.2 pg/mL in the affected group, while TPI increased from 0.017 to 0.042 ng/mL, showing progressive biomarker elevation over time.

At six months, NT-proBNP levels inversely correlated with GLS ( r  = –0.48,  p  < 0.001), suggesting that elevated biomarker values reflect impaired myocardial deformation. This association is detailed in  Table 5  and illustrated in  Figure 5 .

Exploratory ROC analyses using optimized cut-offs, including Youden’s index and relative changes from baseline, showed similar diagnostic accuracy to the primary analysis. These analyses showed similar diagnostic performance to the primary analysis, as shown in  Figure 6 .

Our results align with those reported by Cardinale et al. 4  who first demonstrated that troponin elevation predicts left ventricular dysfunction in breast cancer patients undergoing anthracyclines and trastuzumab therapy. Similarly, Ky et al. 5  confirmed that early biomarker rise correlates with later cardiotoxicity. In contrast to those prospective cohort studies, our retrospective real-world data reaffirm the prognostic strength of troponin I and NT-proBNP. Strain imaging via GLS, as advocated by Thavendiranathan et al. 6  remains a cornerstone of early dysfunction assessment; however, our findings show that NT-proBNP independently correlates with GLS, echoing the mechanistic insights of Michel et al. 7  The superiority of NT-proBNP over TPI in our ROC analysis supports observations by Putt et al. 8  who showed longitudinal NT-proBNP elevations more closely track with structural dysfunction. Finally, the complementary utility of echocardiography and biomarkers is consistent with the integrative surveillance models proposed by Sawaya et al. 9

The present study provides robust evidence supporting the clinical value of serial TPI and NT-proBNP measurements for the early identification of cardiotoxicity in breast cancer patients undergoing anthracycline-based chemotherapy and/or chest radiotherapy. Our results corroborate prior findings from smaller prospective cohorts but expand the evidence by demonstrating that serial rather than isolated biomarker measurements enhance predictive accuracy, particularly when integrated with imaging modalities like GLS. 10

The high incidence of cardiotoxicity observed in our cohort (74.2%; Table 1 ) reflects both the aggressive oncologic regimens used and the rigorous definition of subclinical myocardial dysfunction according to ESC 2022 guidelines. 1  Importantly, over one quarter of patients exhibited persistent cardiac dysfunction at 36 months, underscoring the clinical relevance of long-term cardiac surveillance beyond the acute treatment window.

NT-proBNP emerged as the most reliable early predictor of cardiotoxicity, with an AUC of 0.83 at six months ( Table 2 ,  Figure 1 ). This finding aligns with its established role in detecting myocardial wall stress and subclinical diastolic dysfunction, often preceding systolic decline. Our study strengthens its application in cardio-oncology by demonstrating its longitudinal association with GLS reduction, a sensitive echocardiographic marker of myocardial deformation. 11

Similarly, the role of TPI in reflecting cardiomyocyte necrosis was confirmed through its moderate discriminative ability (AUC = 0.79;  Table 2 ,  Figure 1 ), consistent with prior trials such as the OVERCOME study (prevention of left ventricular dysfunction with enalapril and carvedilol in patients submitted to intensive chemotherapy for the treatment of malignant hemopathies). 12  Interestingly, TPI and NT-proBNP showed complementary value, supporting the hypothesis that combining necrotic and hemodynamic markers yields superior risk stratification.

Our multivariate models confirm that biomarker dynamics remain independently associated with cardiotoxicity even after adjusting for known confounders including baseline GLS and cumulative anthracycline dose ( Table 3 ). 13  Furthermore, the significance of the mixed-effects model in revealing time–treatment interactions illustrates the dynamic evolution of cardiac injury, which might be overlooked by conventional cross-sectional assessments.

The progressive biomarker elevation over 12 months observed in the cardiotoxicity group ( Table 4 ;  Figures 2 – 4 ) supports the concept of ongoing myocardial stress/injury during and after treatment and provides a mechanistic rationale for closer follow-up in higher-risk patients.

Our findings suggest that routine serial monitoring of NT-proBNP and TPI can enhance the early detection of cardiotoxicity in breast cancer patients receiving anthracycline-based therapy. Incorporating these biomarkers alongside GLS assessment may facilitate timely risk stratification and targeted cardio-oncology interventions in line with ESC recommendations.

In our cohort, diagnostic performance at 6 months is summarised in  Table 2  and  Figures 1  and  6 , while longitudinal biomarker trajectories are reported in  Table 4  and  Figures 2 – 4 ; the association between NT-proBNP and GLS is shown in  Figure 5 .

In clinical terms, our findings advocate for the integration of serial biomarker monitoring into existing imaging-based protocols. 14  This is particularly relevant in settings where GLS assessment is technically limited or resource-constrained. Incorporating threshold-based decision-making for NT-proBNP and TPI may enable earlier cardioprotective interventions such as the administration of ACE inhibitors or beta-blockers. 15 , 16

Considering our study, however, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the retrospective design may introduce selection bias, although uniform treatment protocols and centralized biomarker testing mitigate this risk. Second, the study population was limited to a single institution, potentially affecting generalizability. Third, biomarker thresholds were not pre-specified but derived empirically, warranting validation in external cohorts.

Future research should aim at prospective external validation in multi-center cohorts, including predefined sampling timepoints and assay standardization. Studies should also test whether biomarker-guided surveillance and early cardioprotective management improve clinically relevant outcomes (e.g., fewer treatment interruptions, fewer heart failure admissions, and better preservation of left ventricular function). Finally, comparative work combining biomarkers with echocardiographic strain and clinical risk scores could support practical, resource-sensitive prediction models.

In this Albanian breast cancer cohort, serial TPI and NT-proBNP—particularly at 3 and 6 months—were independently associated with subsequent cardiotoxicity. These findings support a pragmatic biomarker-based monitoring strategy to identify higher-risk patients earlier and to trigger intensified echocardiographic surveillance and timely cardio-protective management when indicated, to preserve cardiac function and avoid treatment interruptions. Prospective external validation is needed before routine implementation.

The authors thank the clinical staff involved in patient care and data collection.
