Among the 83 breasts that developed acute edema, edema was first detected on the second pretreatment CBCT in 80 cases (96.4%), on the third CBCT in 2 cases (2.4%), and on the fourth CBCT in 1 case (1.2%), respectively. In 42 swelling breasts (50.6%), the edema reached its peak severity after the first fraction, which remained stable or improved at the subsequent CBCT scans, while in 18 (21.7%), 14 (16.9%), and 9 (10.8%) breasts, edema peaked after the second, third, and fourth fractions, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 1). Overall, following the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th fractions (i.e., at the 2nd to 5th CBCT scans), edema was present in 80 (35.7%), 82 (36.6%), 83 (37.1%), and 79 (35.3%) breasts, respectively.

Clinically, only 12 of the 83 edematous breasts (14.5%) had detectable mild breast swelling on physical examination, all classified as CTCAE grade 1. No grade ≥ 2 acute edema was observed. No patients underwent adaptive replanning. Two patients with edema >8 mm received a 1-day treatment interval and symptomatic anti-edema treatment; all other patients completed the full 5-fraction course without interruption.

In terms of all CBCT scans, the maximum swelling thickness value of edematous breasts was 11.2 mm, with a median of 3.3 mm (IQR, 2.5–4.2 mm). In terms of all breasts, the median of the maximum swelling thickness values (DD max ) was 4.1 mm (IQR, 3.3–5.2 mm). Among the CBCT scans for the 2nd to 5th fraction, the maximum swelling thickness values were 11.2 mm, 9.6 mm, 10.5 mm, and 9.6 mm, respectively; the corresponding medians were 3.4 mm (IQR, 2.5–5.0 mm), 3.4 mm (IQR, 2.8–4.6 mm), 3.2 mm (IQR, 2.5–4.1 mm), and 2.9 mm (IQR, 2.2–3.8 mm), respectively. A total of 65 breasts (78.3%) had a DD max  > 3 mm, and 22 breasts (26.5%) had a DD max  > 5 mm. The distribution of DD max  for each breast is detailed in  Table 2 . Based on the breast subregion analysis, after layer-by-layer review of axial CBCT images, the maximum swelling poles were located at the slices corresponding to the middle-breast region in 75 cases (90.4% of the 83 edematous breasts), with 38.6% cases in the central region and 38.6% cases in the middle-outer region, respectively. (distribution detailed in  Fig. 2 ). This highly concentrated distribution confirms that the nipple-level axial plane is a representative and reliable region for standardized edema quantification, supporting its use as the primary measurement plane in this study. Since breast edema was not uniformly distributed across the breast, for the convenience of physicians' intuition as well as inter-patient comparability, we furtherly measured the swelling thickness at the axial nipple plane—where the maximum swelling pole most frequently occurred. On the 332 sets of CBCT images during the 2nd to 5th fractions for the 83 edematous breasts, the swelling thicknesses were defined as D tc , D tl , and D tm , representing the central, lateral quarter, and medial quarter of the breast, respectively ( Table 3 ). In the central zone, 12.6% of CBCT slices presented swelling thickness values over 5 mm, and 37.3% showed thickness values ranging from 3 to 5 mm. The mid-lateral area was mostly affected by mild swelling ≤3 mm, yet around 15% of scans displayed thickness values above 3 mm. By contrast, the mid-medial region had the least pronounced edema: only 9.6% of scans exceeded 3 mm, with almost no cases surpassing 5 mm. To identify factors associated with clinically significant acute breast edema (defined as D max  ≥ 3 mm), variables including age, body mass index (BMI), primary tumor location and size, lymph node status, molecular types, axillary surgery types, systemic therapy, treatment field, target volumes, treatment break after the 1st fraction, L PTV , L CW , D Breast , and so on were included in analyses. Univariate analysis revealed that age was a significant factor affecting swelling thickness ≥ 3 mm ( P  = 0.020), while D Breast  ( P  = 0.055) and ALND ( P  = 0.068) showed a trend toward significance ( Table 4 ). Variables with  P  < 0.10 in the univariate analysis were incorporated into a multivariate logistic regression model. The results demonstrated that age and D Breast  were independent risk factors for breast edema ≥3 mm. Specifically, for every 1-year increase in age, the risk decreased by 4.2% (OR = 0.958,  P  = 0.009); for every 1-cm increase in breast thickness, the risk increased by almost 26% (OR = 1.255,  P  = 0.036). To further identify factors associated with the severity of acute breast edema, a multiple linear regression model was constructed using swelling thickness as a continuous variable for breasts that developed edema. Both univariate and multivariate analyses indicated that D Breast  was the only independent risk factor determining edema severity ( P  = 0.047), for every 1-cm increase in breast thickness, swelling thickness increased by 6.8%.

Breast edema is a frequent multimodal breast cancer treatment adverse event with widely variable reported incidences (5%–100%), impairing cosmetic results and quality of life, yet it is frequently overlooked clinically  [5] ,  [6] . Most prior studies focus on post-radiotherapy (post-RT) edema, whereas acute intra-treatment edema remains poorly described. One-week uHFRT is now widely adopted, and FAST-Forward trial 10-year data verified its non-inferiority versus mHFRT  [2] . To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically analyze acute intra-treatment breast edema in BCS patients receiving 5-fraction uHFRT. We detail its incidence, dynamic evolution and risk factors, providing clinical evidence to optimize accurate uHFRT delivery and guide intra-treatment edema prevention and intervention.

Unlike skin desquamation and breast pain, breast edema presents subtly and is often underappreciated clinically. Typical signs include peau d’ orange, erythema, pitting edema, breast enlargement, dermal thickening and dilated pigmented pores; prevalent symptoms comprise breast heaviness, numbness, tingling, stabbing pain and cutaneous twitching. Assessment strategies for breast edema vary greatly, ranging from subjective patient reports and physical examination to telephone surveys, questionnaires and radiological evaluation. Such methodological heterogeneity, together with inconsistent assessment timing (pre-, intra- or post-RT), yields widely divergent reported edema incidences across studies. Colciago et al. ( n  = 425) reported an 11% rate of grade 1–2 breast edema at RT completion via RTOG scoring, falling to 8.5% at 5 years  [7] . In contrast, Grann et al. observed a far higher 72% edema rate during 3-year follow-up of 56 patients  [6] . Using the LENT-SOMA scale, Hille-Betz et al. found only 5% grade 1–2 edema beyond 3 months post-RT among 158 patients  [8] . Young-Afat et al. applied the EORTC QLQ-BR23 to 836 patients, with edema incidences of 7.1%, 12.4%, 8.1% and 5.5% at 3, 6, 12 and 18 months post-RT  [5] . Lee et al. recorded a 74.8% in-treatment edema rate in 173 patients with their self-designed RADA-11 BCE questionnaire  [9] . For 1156 patients, Oyur et al. reported 17% post-RT edema per CTCAE v2.0 versus 37% using their proprietary Westerstede classification  [10] . Collectively, these discrepancies hinder reliable cross-study comparisons, highlighting an unmet need for objective, accurate, and highly reproducible assessment tools for breast edema.

CBCT enables intuitive, convenient, reproducible observation of breast edema independent of patients' subjective reports. Registration outcomes can quantify delivery accuracy and guide decisions to continue or interrupt radiotherapy. In the present study, after rigid image registration, the proportions of breasts with swelling exceeding 1 mm, 3 mm, 5 mm, and 8 mm were 37.1%, 29.1%, 9.8%, and 2.7%, respectively, relative to baseline planning CT images. At our institution, the PTV margin for uHFRT is set at 3–5 mm. This indicates that ruffly 10%–30% of patients may develop breast swelling exceeding the predefined margin, which could compromise planned dose coverage. Phantom studies by Klepper demonstrated that breast edema with a 5-mm outward contour expansion reduced PTV surface dose to 71.3%  [4] . Rossi et al. analyzed breast cancer treatment plans and showed that edema reduced PTV surface dose by 0.4–1.6 Gy across various VMAT plans. Plans incorporating Auto Skin Flash were particularly susceptible to such dose perturbations, requiring an additional 8-mm tissue bolus to ensure adequate target coverage  [11] . The topographic distribution of edema further informs clinical optimization: since maximum swelling predominantly occurs in the central and mid-lateral breast, which correspond to the steepest dose gradient region in tangential and VMAT plans, outward expansion in this area is most likely to cause insufficient lateral PTV margin coverage. For high-risk patients, targeted expansion of the lateral PTV margin or additional skin flash during initial planning can more efficiently offset potential dose loss than uniform whole-breast margin expansion. In our cohort, edema developed immediately after the first fraction in 96.4%, peaked after the first fraction in 50.6% and persisted at the final fraction in 95.2% of affected breasts. Without timely intervention, this early-onset, persistent edema may compromise the efficacy of the remaining few fractions. Notably, the majority of CBCT-detected edema in this cohort was subclinical and unrecognizable on routine physical examination, which further increases the risk of unrecognized target dose deviation. Accordingly, in-treatment breast edema associated with 5-fraction uHFRT merits considerable clinical attention.

Data regarding in-treatment breast edema are scarce. Morakkabati et al. assessed 72 BCS patients receiving CFRT via MRI, reporting 84% skin edema and 73% parenchymal edema without clear diagnostic thresholds  [12] . Johansson et al. quantified interstitial fluid in 118 patients by measuring the 2.5 mm subcutaneous tissue dielectric constant (TDC); edema was defined as an ipsilateral/contralateral TDC ratio > 1.4, yielding incidences of 47.3%, 47.3% and 45.9% at RT weeks 1, 2 and 3  [13] .

Seldom studies have evaluated in-treatment breast edema via CBCT. Seppälä et al. analyzed 93 BCS patients receiving mHFRT. After global and breast-specific CBCT-planning CT registration, they quantified edema using magnitude of breast surface excursion (MBSE); 62%, 34% and 13% of patients had MBSE >3 mm, ≥5 mm and ≥ 8 mm, respectively  [14] . Unlike their 3D vector-based metric, our study measured contour deviations directly, partially accounting for our lower edema incidence. Sang et al. compared tissue thickness on CBCT (fractions 1, 6, 11) with baseline CT among 144 mHFRT patients. Thickness differences >5 mm occurred in 8%, 16% and 17.4% of patients, with a cumulative edema rate of 24.3%  [15] . Only 9.8% (22 breasts) in our cohort showed swelling over 5 mm. This discrepancy may stem from divergent measurement workflows and registration variations. Sang's patients had a younger median age (43.7 vs. 49 years), and younger individuals face higher edema risk, consistent with our risk factor results. Additionally, 5-fraction uHFRT may intrinsically produce milder peak acute edema than mHFRT.

Data on intra-treatment breast edema for 5-fraction uHFRT are sparse. This scarcity partly arises from primary attention to radiodermatitis during early clinical implementation of this regimen. Additionally, breast edema has been categorized as grade 3 and grade 2 cutaneous toxicity under RTOG and CTCAE criteria, respectively, so it has been often pooled with other skin toxicities instead of analyzed independently. The FAST-Forward trial summarized acute toxicities up to 4 weeks post-RT. According to CTCAE criteria, grade 2 breast edema occurred in 1 patient (2%) in the 26 Gy/5-fraction arm  [16] . Other cohort studies, with sample sizes ranging from 70 to 400 patients, have reported acute breast edema incidences of 0.8% to 10%  [17] ,  [18] ,  [19] . In the HAI-5 trial, patients received WBI (28.5 Gy/5 fractions), with a SIB of 32.5–34.5 Gy delivered on alternate days. At 1-week post-RT, the incidences of grade 1 and grade 2 acute edema were 38% and 12% (read from figures), respectively  [20] . A Spanish cohort of 160 patients treated with WBI (26 Gy/5 fractions), RNI, and a SIB of 30 Gy/5 fractions, the overall incidence of grade 1–2 acute edema at 3 months post-RT was 3.3%  [22] . Another Spanish study of 383 patients used WBI (28.5 Gy/5 fractions) with or without RNI, plus a SIB of 29–31 Gy/5 fractions. According to RTOG criteria, the incidences of grade 1 and grade 2 acute edema at 3 months post-RT were 2% and 0.5%, respectively  [21] . The 9.8% incidence of contour swelling >5 mm during RT in our cohort is broadly consistent with published literature. CBCT-based measurement offers high sensitivity and objectivity, with the ability to detect contour changes as small as 1 mm, achieving a higher detection rate than physical examination.

Multivariate analysis identified younger age and greater breast thickness (D Breast ) as independent risk factors for breast edema with contour swelling ≥3 mm. In contrast, BMI, ALND and target volume parameters showed no significant association with edema. Findings regarding risk factors for radiation-induced breast edema remain inconsistent across the literature, and several investigations have even found no significant factors  [23] . Elevated BMI has been reported as an independent risk factor in some cohorts  [14] ,  [24] , whereas no association has been observed in others  [25] . ALND has been associated with increased edema risk in multiple studies  [8] ,  [10] ,  [26] , but it did not reach statistical significance in our cohort ( P  = 0.068) or in several prior reports  [25] ,  [27] ,  [28] . Larger breast size has been consistently identified as an independent risk factor  [27] ,  [28] , and our D Breast  finding supports this conclusion. Notably, whole-breast CTV, another metric of breast size, was not associated with edema risk in our analysis, nor was larger breast volume in several other studies  [23] ,  [29] . This suggests that breast thickness or cup size may represent a more sensitive marker than total volume. The higher edema susceptibility observed in younger patients is consistent with clinical observations. Younger breast tissue contains abundant fibroglandular parenchyma, which may elicit a more pronounced inflammatory response to RT-induced tissue injury. Tanwiwat et al. evaluated the correlation between breast density and post-RT toxicities in 922 patients and concluded that dense breast tissue confers greater vulnerability to edema  [30] . Nevertheless, conflicting data exist, with some studies reporting higher edema incidence in older patients  [7] . In two large-scale cohorts each including over 1000 patients, Oyur et al. identified ALND and RNI as independent risk factors for post-RT breast edema  [10] , while Yono et al. reported preoperative breast volume ≥ 1500 cm 3 , Black patients, chemotherapy, cellulitis, and post-RT upper limb lymphedema as relevant predictors  [27] . As noted above, heterogeneity in assessment methods, diagnostic definitions, and monitoring time points, combined with variations in patient demographics, surgical techniques, and RT fractionation schedules, precludes consistent, generalizable conclusions across studies.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to characterize acute in-treatment breast edema in patients treated with 5-fraction uHFRT after BCS. Using objective serial CBCT measurements, our findings provide a clinical basis for predicting and monitoring acute edema during delivery of this and analogous RT regimens. This study has several limitations. First, comprehensive dosimetric analysis was not performed. Nevertheless, all treatment plans strictly adhered to protocol-specified dose constraints, including target conformity index, homogeneity index, V107 and V110 limits, and intermediate high dose constraints for the non-boost PTV region. Thus, PTV and PTV boost volumes served as reasonable surrogates for overall dose distribution. Second, our analysis was limited to linear measurements of acute breast edema; volumetric swelling quantification and systematic assessment of dosimetric coverage degradation were not performed. Subsequent research will recalculate treatment plans from sequential CBCT scans to accurately quantify edema-related changes in target dose coverage.

In conclusion, in-treatment breast edema occurred in 37.1% of patients who underwent BSC followed by uHFRT. Among affected breasts, swelling emerged immediately after the first fraction in 96.4% of cases, and edema peaked at this timepoint in 50.6%, with a maximum thickness increment of 11.2 mm. Contour expansion exceeding 5 mm was observed in 9.8% of all breasts. The central middle region was most susceptible to edema development. Given its possible detrimental effect on RT efficacy, for patients at elevated risk, rigorous monitoring and timely management are warranted.

Yanxin Zhang, Wei Zhang, Hao Jing and Junlin Yi designed the study, analyzed the data and wrote the manuscript; Yanxin Zhang and Hao Jing contributed to the study concept; Yanxin Zhang, Hao Jing and Junlin Yi contributed to the study coordination; Yanxin Zhang, Wei Zhang, Hao Jing and Junlin Yi performed the statistical analysis; and all authors contributed to patient enrollment, data collection and interpretation, and finally approved the manuscript.

## Integrated transcriptomics approach identifies the upregulated SLC7A5, and associated pathways across different thyroid cancer cell types.

**PMID**: 42751400 · **Journal**: Frontiers in genetics · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.3389/fgene.2026.1890433 · **PMCID**: PMC13581278

**Authors**: Naeem Muhammad, Wu Nan, Wu Yang, Nawaz Shahid, Jing Ren, Luo Yuanbin, Yi Shijian

**Types**: Journal Article

Thyroid cancer is the most common type of endocrine malignancy, and its aggressive types are diagnosed at advanced stage due to limited treatment options. This study aimed to identify upregulated SLC7A5 across thyroid cancer cell types using an integrated transcriptomics approach. Total RNA was extracted from different samples. Differential expression analysis was performed through DESeq2. Functional enrichment analyses were performed to explore key pathways. The PPI network was built using the STRING database to investigate the functional relationships among significantly differentially expressed genes. Differential expression analysis revealed that SLC7A5 was significantly upregulated in KTC-1. GO and KEGG analyses were enriched with cell adhesion, protein binding, extracellular exosome, RNA processing, ECM-receptor interactions, and focal adhesion. The PPI network analysis showed the interaction of SLC7A5 with TERF1, CARD10, PSAT1, SIRPA, and MYC. Western blot analysis revealed that expression of mTOR was not elevated in KTC-1. Overall, these results could provide valuable insights for further validation in thyroid cancer therapy.

Thyroid cancer is the most common type of endocrine malignancy, and more than 237,000 cases were reported worldwide in 2022. It has become a global health issue due to the increasing number of cases in recent years ( Li et al., 2026 ). Limited treatment options are available for early-stage detection of thyroid cancer ( Lee et al., 2026 ). However, the risk of complications increases due to limited treatments. Based on histological features and cell origin, it is classified into different types, such as papillary, anaplastic, and follicular thyroid cancers. It was observed that patients with anaplastic thyroid cancer were diagnosed at an advanced stage, with a median 1-year survival rate about 10–20% ( Moreno et al., 2022 ). Some patients with advanced stages of differentiated thyroid cancers could develop radioiodine-refractory disease (RAIR) ( Hosseinzadeh et al., 2025 ). Therefore, early stage detection and precise treatment are crucial for improving survival rates in thyroid cancer patients ( Codrich et al., 2025 ).

Previous literature reported that some genes have been identified in the development of thyroid cancer ( Vaio et al., 2026 ). Mutations in the  RAS  (rat sarcoma virus) and  BRAF  (v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B) genes had been reported in papillary thyroid cancer ( Moposita Molina et al., 2025 ).  PLAU  (Plasminogen activator),  COL1A1  (Alpha type I collagen protein),  RRM2  (Ribonucleoside reductase subunit M2), and  LGALS3  (Galectin-3) had reported in papillary thyroid cancer ( Sarin et al., 2022 ;  Qiu et al., 2016 ).  HRAS  (Harvey rat sarcoma homolog) , KRAS  (Kirsten rat sarcoma homolog), and  NRAS  (neuroblastoma proto-oncogene) genes were observed in the progression of follicular thyroid cancer ( Chiba, 2024 ). Moreover,  TERT  (telomerase reverse transcriptase),  PIK3CA  (phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase catalytic subunit alpha), and  PTEN  (phosphatase and tensin homolog) also reported in anaplastic thyroid cancer ( Cleere et al., 2024 ).

SLC7A5 is a membrane transporter involved in cellular signaling, protein synthesis, amino acid transport, and physiological processes ( Jeckelmann et al., 2022 ). Different roles of SLC7A1, SLC7A5, SLC7A7, and SLC7A11 observed in breast, thyroid, and ovarian cancers. SLC7A1 was reported in arginine uptake for promoting the tumor growth in patients with ovarian cancer. Its expression was high in tumor tissues relative to the control group ( Gong et al., 2021 ). SLC7A5 participates in leucine uptake, which is involved in the mTOR signaling pathway ( Sokolov et al., 2020 ).  Wang et al. (2024)  reported that SLC7A7 stimulates cell growth and proliferation in colorectal cancer ( Wang et al., 2024 ). SLC7A11 stimulates glutathione (GSH) synthesis via cystine-glutamine exchange and protects thyroid cancer cells from ferroptosis ( Wang et al., 2021 ). However, limited literature is available on the role of SLC7A5 in thyroid cancer.

RNA sequencing technology is used to identify novel genes, alternative splicing events, and gene alterations. This approach provides the precise measurement of transcript expression analysis ( Pan et al., 2024 ). Integration of RNA sequencing data with clinical datasets could provide a platform for categorizing the novel DEGs into biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions associated with cell cycle regulation, metabolic reprogramming, DNA replication and RNA processing, mTOR signaling, biosynthetic metabolism, and cellular growth. However, the upregulation of SLC7A5 and its involvement in cellular processes and signaling pathways remain unclear ( Byun et al., 2025 ;  Xu T. et al., 2025 ).

SLC7A5 is a membrane transporter involved in mTOR signaling, supporting its biological and translational relevance for prioritizing significantly differentially expressed genes. In this study, we performed an integrated RNA-seq analysis to identify SLC7A5 upregulation across different thyroid cancer cell lines. We also performed functional enrichment analyses to identify the biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions. The PPI network was built to investigate the functional relationships among differentially expressed genes. Western blot analysis was performed to evaluate expression levels.

RPMI-1640 was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific (New York, USA). Trizol was purchased from Apexbio Technology (Houston, USA). Fetal bovine serum (FBS) was utilized for cell growth and supplied by Excell Biotechnology (Suzhou, China). HRP secondary antibody was obtained from Jackson ImmunoResearch Company (Pennsylvania, USA). Phosphate-buffered saline (pH∼7.4) was used for cell washing and obtained from Biyun Tian Biotechnology (Shanghai, China).

KTC-1 cells (Catalog No. ZQ0318) were purchased from Zhong Qiao Xin Zhou Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. These cells referred to a well-characterized human thyroid cancer cell model derived from an adult patient with poorly differentiated papillary thyroid cancer and originated from the site of metastatic pleural effusion. ATC, FTC, KTC-1, and Nthy-ori 3-1 were cultured in RMIP-1640 with the addition of 10% FBS and 1% penicillin. The reaction mixture was incubated with 5% CO 2  at 37 °C for 24 h. Trizol reagent was added for total RNA extraction, and samples were stored at −80 °C for further analysis.

Total RNA was extracted from ATC, FTC, and KTC-1 using an RNA extraction kit, and purity was determined using the Agilent 5300 Fragment Analyzer (Agilent, CA, USA). Capture beads were used for mRNA purification, and fragmentation was performed at 94 °C in the presence of magnesium ions (cat. no. 12340ES97; Shanghai Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd). The cleaved RNA fragments were reverse-transcribed to produce the first cDNA strand. Each strand was modified by adding an A base pair to an adapter containing a T base pair. Amplification was performed using a thermocycler, and PCR products were purified with Hieff NGSDNA selection beads. Sequencing analysis was performed using the Illumina Novaseq™ X Plus (LC-Bio Technology CO., Ltd., Hangzhou, China).

Raw sequencing reads were evaluated for quality control, followed by the removal of low-quality reads, reference genome alignment, transcript reconstruction, gene expression quantification, differential gene expression analysis, and functional enrichment analysis ( Figure 1 ).

FastQC (v0.11.9) was used for assessment of GC content, sequence quality, adapters contamination, and sequence repetition. MultiQC (v1.14) was used to summarize the quality control reports. Reads having a minimum length were eliminated after trimming. This process ensured that only high-quality and sufficient reads were retained for downstream analysis.

HISAT2 (version 2.2.1) was used for mapping the post-processed data into the human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38). Alignment files were generated in BAM format using HISAT2. Alignment quality was evaluated by measuring key metrics and the total number of reads.

StringTie (version 2.1.6) was used for transcript reconstruction and expression measurement. Gffcompare tool (version 0.9.8) was used for construction of comprehensive transcriptome across samples. Levels of gene expression were assessed in FPKM units for normalization of sequencing depth, and transcript length. StringTie software was used for calculation of the FPKM values.

Quantification was performed at the gene level, and reads counts were independently normalized to obtain the FPKM. The transcript-level expression data were analyzed using isoform-specific information, and downstream analyses in the present study were focused on gene-level expression, which was sufficient to address the biological questions of interest.

Oligo(dT) enrichments were performed for the generation of sequencing libraries. Each gene has annotation information, location of chromosome, codon positions, read counts, GO, and KEGG. Other classes of RNAs were further investigated using transcript-type annotations in the reference genome.

DESeq2 (v1.38.3) was used to perform differential gene expression analysis. The low-expressed genes were removed due to weak expression signals. Wald test was applied for differential gene expression analysis. Genes that passed the |log 2 FC| ≥1, and q-value <0.05 (the q-value is the adjusted p-value) were considered differentially expressed.

Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed for assessment of transcriptomics correlations of different samples. The heatmap of top 100 DEGs was constructed using the pheatmap (v1.0.12). Normalization was performed using Z-score, and Euclidean distance was used for hierarchical clustering analysis.

ClusterProfiler (v4.6.2) was used for assessment of GO and KEGG analyses of DEGs. Benjamini-Hochberg method was used for determination of enrichment significance. Reactome pathways were analyzed using the ReactomePA (v1.42.0). Gene sets (upregulated and downregulated) were examined independently to identify key pathways in thyroid cancer cells.

The protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis was constructed using the STRING database to investigate the functional relationships among differentially expressed genes.

Total proteins were extracted in the presence of RIPA lysis buffer and separated by SDS-PAGE. The PVDF membranes were used for transferring the resolved proteins, blocked with 5% skimmed milk, and incubated with primary and secondary antibodies. The phospho-mTOR antibody was used to detect the phosphorylation site at Ser2481.Western blot experiments were performed with three biological replicates, and data were presented as mean ± SD. ImageJ software was used for densitometry analysis of blots ( Supplementary Table 1 ). Relative protein expression was normalized to GAPDH. Statistical analysis was performed using the Sidak test, and significance was set as p < 0.05. The expression profiles of different proteins were evaluated using a high-sensitivity chemiluminescence kit (Kangwei, Beijing, China). Different antibodies were used, such as p-mTOR (Catalog No: bs-3495r, Bioss, Woburn, United States), mTOR (Catalog No: 66888-1-Ig, Proteintech, Wuhan, China), SLC7A5 (Catalog No: YP-mAb- 09823, UpingBio, Hangzhou, China ), GAPDH (Catalog No: ET1601-4, Huabio, Massachusetts, USA), and HRP-Goat anti Rabbit (Catalog No: 111-035-003, Jackson, Pennsylvania, United States).

Benjamini-Hochberg method was used for determination of enrichment significance. Functional enrichment analyses were performed for the identification of key pathways using the false discovery rate (FDR) method. Sidak test was performed for multiple comparisons.

Principal component analysis (PCA) of the top variable genes revealed distinct differences between thyroid cancer and normal cells along PCA1 and PCA2, indicating extensive transcriptomic reprogramming ( Figure 2A ). ATC cells were furthest from normal human thyroid epithelial cells along the principal components. FTC and KTC-1 cells were separated into intermediate clusters between ATC and normal cells. The sample-to-sample distance heatmap shows strong clustering within biological replicates and clear separation between thyroid cancer cells and normal human thyroid epithelial cells ( Figure 2B ).

The volcano plot for each thyroid cancer cell shows upregulated and downregulated genes. The volcano plot of KTC-1 shows 2716 upregulated and 4332 downregulated genes. PLP2, ST3GAL1, TGFB2, CDH4, DNAJC15, UNC5B, and ALDH1L2, were significantly upregulated. The volcano plot for ATC-8350C shows 3935 upregulated and 5167 downregulated genes. SPRED2, IGBP1, MAP3K5, SPOCD1, and TLE3 were significantly upregulated. Moreover, the volcano plot for FTC shows 3622 upregulated and 5118 downregulated genes. SOX9, LBH, FNDC1, BHLHE41, ADAM12, and PORCN genes were significantly upregulated ( Figures 3A–D ).

The top 100 significantly differentially expressed genes were converted into a heatmap showing expression patterns. Upregulated SLC7A5 was highlighted in a circle as shown in  Figure 4A . Therefore, its differential expression analysis was discussed in the next section.

Using the criteria of |log 2 FC| ≥ 1, and q-value <0.05 (the q-value is the adjusted p-value), we found that SLC7A5 gene expression was significantly upregulated in KTC-1. Therefore, SLC7A5 was selected for further study due to its significant expression ( Figure 4A ;  Supplementary Table 2 ). Differential expression of SLC7A5 was not observed in ATC and FTC as compared to normal human thyroid epithelial cells ( Figures 4B–D ).

Enrichment analyses were performed to identify biological processes and associated pathways ( Figures 5A–D ,  6A–D ,  7A–D ). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis in KTC-1 showed that biological processes enriched with cell adhesion, protein binding, extracellular exosome, RNA processing, and transmembrane transport. KEGG analysis showed key pathways enriched with ECM-receptor interactions, focal adhesion, and PI3K-Akt. These analyses were performed on the complete set of differentially expressed genes, and SLC7A5 was associated with these biological processes and pathways. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses in ATC and FTC did not reveal pathways similar to those for SLC7A5 ( Figures 5A–D ,  6A–D ). Reactome enrichment profiles further emphasize the type-specific pathway activation and transciptomics involvment ( Figures 7A–D ).

A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was built using the STRING database and functionally coordinated by forming a dense core through interconnected nodes. SLC7A5 was located within the network and interacted with various proteins, including TERF1, CARD10, PSAT1, SIRPA, and MYC ( Figure 8 ). Cell adhesion and extracellular matrix organization proteins, such as VCAN, COL4A1, THBS3, FBLN5, ALCAM, and CD44 also interacted in KTC-1. The resultant network depicts the numerous interrelations among different proteins involved in cellular processes.

On the basis of the previously reported association between SLC7A5 and mTOR, Western blot analysis was performed to evaluate the expression profiles. The results revealed that expression of mTOR was not elevated in KTC-1. SLC7A5 and p-mTOR were also assessed, and the results suggested an association that requires further validation ( Figures 9A,B ).

In this study, we performed an integrated transcriptomic analysis across different thyroid cancer cell lines. The expression patterns revealed the distinct transcriptional profiles for cell type. Limited treatment options are available for early-stage detection of thyroid cancer ( Gil-Bernabé et al., 2025 ).  Sun et al. (2021)  reported that ENTPD1, RUNX1, THRSP, KLK10, and MIR31HG were upregulated in papillary thyroid cancer ( Sun et al., 2021 ). Another study by  Fan et al. (2021)  identified the hub genes LPAR5, TFPI and ENTPD1 in papillary thyroid cancer ( Fan et al., 2021 ). SPOCK1 is a multi-domain glycoprotein that is involved in extracellular matrix organization, and cell adhesion ( Karaman et al., 2025 ;  Xu et al., 2020 ). SCARF1 is a multilayer network of proteoglycans, and its altered expression has been observed in gastric cancer ( Patten, 2018 ). DCDC2 is a structural protein involved in microtubule localization process ( Dai et al., 2023 ). Our transcriptomic analysis revealed the significantly differentially expressed genes in KTC-1, including SPOCK1, SCARF1, and DCDC2. However, the role of these genes in thyroid cancer cells remains unclear, suggested further functional studies.

SLC7A5 is involved in cellular signaling, protein synthesis, energy metabolism, and physiological processes ( Jeckelmann et al., 2022 ).  Gong et al. (2021)  reported that SLC7A1 promoted tumor growth through activating the mTOR signaling pathway in ovarian cancer ( Gong et al., 2021 ).  Chen et al. (2022)  investigated that SLC7A6 contributed to angiogenesis and activated the mTORC1/S6K pathway in hepatocellular carcinoma ( Chen et al., 2022 ).  Dai et al. (2021)  investigated that SLC7A7 was involved in cell proliferation and PIK/AKT pathway in lung cancer ( Dai et al., 2021 ). Western blot analysis revealed that expression of mTOR was not elevated in KTC-1. However, expression profiles of SLC7A5 and p-mTOR were also assessed and suggested an association requiring further validation ( Dunlap et al., 2025 ;  Scalise et al., 2018 ).

GO analysis provides a framework for revealing the biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions. These processes are important for a better understanding the events occurred during thyroid cancer development ( Menyhart et al., 2025 ).  Sun et al. (2021)  performed GO analysis and reported that mitotic spindle organization and chromosome segregation were crucial for maintaining the genomic stability ( Sun et al., 2021 ).  Xue et al. (2020)  reported that DNA replication was involved in the genome duplication during the cell cycle. Our findings revealed that GO analysis in KTC-1 was associated with RNA processing, protein binding, cell adhesion, and extracellular exosome. These analyses were performed on the complete set of DEGs, and SLC7A5 was also associated with these biological processes. These findings could provide valuable insights for functional studies ( Xue et al., 2020 ;  Shen et al., 2020 ).

KEGG analysis is used to identify key pathways in thyroid cancer and metabolic diseases.  Zhao and Li (2018)  performed KEGG analysis and identified the ECM-receptor interaction pathways. These pathways were involved in regulating the cell-matrix adhesion ( Zhao and Li, 2018 ;  Xia et al., 2024 ).  Xu H. et al. (2025)  reported that PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and Ras signaling pathways were dysregulated in breast, gastric, colorectal, and thyroid cancers ( Xu H. et al., 2025 ;  Xia et al., 2024 ). Our KEGG analysis were enriched with focal adhesion, ECM-receptor interactions, and PI3K-Akt pathways ( Nashier et al., 2026 ). Previous studies reported that dysregulation of these oncogenic pathways could promote the signaling cascades. Therefore, these associated pathways revealed the transcriptional programs in thyroid cancer cells ( Derwich et al., 2023 ;  Leandro-García and Landa, 2023 ).

The protein-protein interaction (PPI) network is widely used to understand protein interactions that regulate biological functions ( Khalid et al., 2026 ). The PPI network was built using the STRING database.  Szklarczyk et al. (2025)  explored the functional relationships among different proteins through PPI network analysis ( Szklarczyk et al., 2025 ). SLC7A5 was located withthin the network and interacted with TERF1, CARD10, PSAT1, SIRPA, MYC and other different proteins. SPOCK1 showed interaction through mTOR signalling and SLC7A5 also involved in amino acid uptake ( Xu et al., 2020 ;  Dunlap et al., 2025 ). SCARF1 is a glycoprotein involved in disease pathology and SLC7A5 interacts with glycoproteins ( Patten, 2018 ;  Scalise et al., 2018 ). DCDC2 is involved in microtubule-organizing pathways and SL7A5 in tumor microenvironment. Disruption of these processes and pathways causes alterations in protein-protein interactions ( Dai et al., 2023 ;  Nachef et al., 2021 ). These genes interacted with SLC7A5 in the PPI network through regulatory networks. Therefore, these interactions could be helpful in exploring the functional roles of different proteins in biological processes.

This study has some limitations, such as a lack of gene expression validation by RT-qPCR. Patient sample validation and functional validation, such as SLC7A5 knockdown, proliferation assays, amino acid uptake, and mTOR pathway assessment, are further required to establish the biological and clinical significance of SLC7A5.

In this study, integrated transcriptomics approach revealed the SLC7A5 upregulation in KTC-1. Functional enrichment analyses identified the RNA processing, protein binding, ECM-receptor interactions, and PI3K-Akt. These analyses were performed on the complete set of DEGs, and SLC7A5 was also associated with these biological processes and pathways. Moreover, SLC7A5 showed interaction with different proteins in the PPI network. Future studies are required to explore the functional validation and targeted therapy.

## Editorial: Novel anti-cancer agents targeting triple-negative breast cancer.

**PMID**: 42751378 · **Journal**: Frontiers in oncology · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1906771 · **PMCID**: PMC13579636

**Authors**: Zhu Tong, Ding Baifang, Zhu Zhengnan, Bu Jiawen, Guo Tianyu, Jin Zhipeng, Zhu Xudong, Liu Yefu

**Types**: Editorial

[No abstract]

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) accounts for approximately 15%–20% of all breast cancer cases ( 1 – 3 ). Due to the lack of estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) expression, TNBC lacks well-defined and effective targeted therapeutic options ( 4 ). For decades, cytotoxic chemotherapy represented the mainstay of systemic treatment. In recent years, with the advancing research on immunotherapy, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), and molecular subtyping, the treatment landscape for TNBC has been undergoing significant changes. Nevertheless, challenges such as drug resistance, metastasis, and high tumor heterogeneity of TNBC remain major obstacles in current clinical practice ( 5 ). Consequently, deriving therapeutic strategies from real-world evidence, accelerating the translation of basic research into clinical applications and identifying novel therapeutic targets have become critical directions in the area of TNBC research.

This Research Topic aggregates a comprehensive array of studies spanning real-world clinical evidence, targeted ADC development, and fundamental mechanistic insights. It offers a comprehensive overview of the current therapeutic landscape of TNBC, as well as the evolving trends and future directions of anti-TNBC strategies ( Figure 1 ).

Before introducing additional therapeutic innovations, it is necessary to reconsider whether established treatment strategies provide consistent benefit across the biologically heterogeneous TNBC population. Patients with residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy represent a particularly high-risk subgroup, for whom the CREATE-X trial established adjuvant capecitabine as a standard therapeutic approach. However, in a real-world analysis by  Godoy-Ortiz et al. , involving 312 patients from two Spanish institutions, the clinical benefit of adjuvant capecitabine appeared more limited than expected. Although patients achieving pathological complete response (pCR) experienced substantially improved outcomes, those with residual disease did not demonstrate a significant improvement in disease-free survival or overall survival compared with observation alone ( P  = 0.94 and  P  = 0.34, respectively). These findings are consistent with observations from the CIBOMA trial, which suggested that capecitabine efficacy may vary according to molecular subtype, with potential benefit restricted to non-basal-like TNBC. Collectively, therapeutic decisions based solely on clinical classification may fail to capture the underlying biological diversity of TNBC. Even established regimens require molecular reassessment to define which patients are most likely to benefit. This principle provides an important foundation for determining the optimal clinical context in which ADCs and other emerging therapies should be incorporated.

Among the recent advances transforming TNBC treatment, ADCs represent one of the most clinically significant developments. Sacituzumab govitecan (SG), an anti-Trop-2 ADC, has become an established treatment option for patients with previously treated metastatic TNBC following the results of the ASCENT trial. In the SACISUR cohort,  Falcon-Gonzalez et al.  evaluated 159 patients from Southern Spain and reported real-world outcomes comparable to those observed in ASCENT, with median rwPFS and rwOS of 4.6 and 10.9 months, respectively. Notably, 13.8% of patients had brain metastases, which experienced poorer outcomes (rwPFS, 2.3 months), but the presence of measurable clinical activity suggests that SG may retain therapeutic potential in patients with central nervous system involvement. Therefore, emerging real-world evidence is extending our understanding of SG activity beyond the populations typically enrolled in randomized clinical trials.

Beyond conventional trial populations, preliminary evidence suggests that SG may also have activity in high-risk clinical presentations such as hepatic visceral crisis (HVC).  Ye et al.  reported a case of a patient with TNBC characterized by diffuse hepatic metastases and rapidly worsening liver function who achieved substantial regression of liver lesions after two cycles of SG, with a PFS of 16.3 months. Although limited to a single case, this observation provides a hypothesis-generating finding that ADC-based therapy may warrant consideration even in patients with severe tumor burden and restricted therapeutic options.

The expanding role of ADCs is further illustrated by the emergence of the HER2-low paradigm, which has challenged the traditional binary classification between HER2-positive and HER2-negative breast cancer.  Wu et al.  described a heavily pretreated patient with HER2-low metastatic breast cancer who achieved a favorable response to disitamab vedotin (RC-48), an anti-HER2 ADC developed in China. More importantly, serial evaluation revealed dynamic changes in HER2 expression throughout disease evolution: HER2-low at initial diagnosis, HER2–0 at first recurrence, and HER2-low again at subsequent progression. This expression shift highlights a fundamental aspect of tumor; biomarker expression can evolve under therapeutic pressure. Clinically, these findings support the consideration of repeat biomarker assessment at disease progression, as HER2 status may represent a dynamic therapeutic determinant rather than a fixed classification. Such an approach may help identify additional patients who could benefit from ADC strategies during the course of their disease.

The expanding use of immunotherapy and ADCs in TNBC underscores the need to maintain a parallel focus on safety, particularly for rare but potentially life-threatening adverse events.  Benkalfate et al.  described a case of pembrolizumab-associated capillary leak syndrome (CLS) accompanied by chylothorax in a patient receiving immunotherapy for early-stage TNBC. Following two cycles of adjuvant pembrolizumab, the patient developed diffuse subcutaneous edema, bilateral pleural effusions, and ascites despite having previously tolerated neoadjuvant exposure. A comprehensive evaluation excluded infectious, malignant, cardiac, and autoimmune causes, while pleural biopsy showed no evidence of malignant or inflammatory infiltration, suggesting an endothelial dysfunction–mediated mechanism. Rapid clinical improvement following corticosteroid therapy further supported the diagnosis. Although rare, such events highlight a critical consideration as immune checkpoint inhibitors move increasingly into curative-intent settings. Therapeutic success must be accompanied by vigilant toxicity surveillance. Early recognition, systematic evaluation, and timely intervention remain essential for minimizing the impact of severe immune-related adverse events.

Despite the clinical success of existing ADCs, the molecular heterogeneity of TNBC suggests that no single target will be sufficient to address the full spectrum of disease biology. Expanding the repertoire of actionable targets therefore remains a critical objective.  Zhou et al.  identified lipolysis-stimulated lipoprotein receptor (LSR) as a potential ADC target, demonstrating its overexpression in more than 60% of TNBC samples and its association with adverse clinical features. An LSR-directed ADC incorporating a DM1 payload showed substantial antitumor activity in animal models, including marked tumor reduction or complete regression, without apparent toxicity across major organs. Although these findings remain preclinical, they provide a rationale for further investigation of LSR as a candidate target beyond currently established ADC strategies.

Beyond surface antigens, tumor signaling networks represent another avenue for therapeutic exploration. The androgen receptor (AR) has emerged as a potential vulnerability in selected TNBC subsets, although its biological role remains incompletely defined.  Caceres et al.  demonstrated that AR promotes TNBC cell proliferation through EGFR upregulation and MAPK/PI3K pathway activation, while attenuating ERβ-mediated anti-proliferative effects. Their evaluation of AR antagonists identified ailanthone as a potent inhibitor of AR signaling, including suppression of AR full length and AR-V7, accompanied by reduced Src expression and impaired cellular migration.

In parallel, addressing metastatic dissemination remains essential for improving TNBC outcomes.  Deserti et al.  investigated gabexate mesylate (GM), an established protease inhibitor, and found that it restored expression of Raf kinase inhibitor protein (RKIP), thereby attenuating MAPK and NF-κB signaling and reversing epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT). The resulting reduction in migration, invasion, and MMP-2/MMP-9 activity suggests a potential role for drug repurposing approaches in targeting metastatic mechanisms. However, further validation is required to determine whether these preclinical observations can translate into clinically meaningful benefit.

Complementing target discovery and pathway modulation, advances in drug delivery may provide additional opportunities to improve therapeutic windows.  Zhang et al.  developed glycyrrhizic acid-modified liposomes for delivery of celastrol, a bioactive compound limited by systemic toxicity. This nanotechnology-based formulation enhanced tumor uptake, improved drug stability and loading capacity, and increased cytotoxic activity against TNBC cells while reducing effects on normal mammary epithelial cells. Such approaches exemplify how delivery engineering can transform biologically active but clinically constrained molecules into more viable therapeutic candidates.

Overall, the studies included in this Research Topic illustrate a significant shift occurring in the field of TNBC treatment. This shift is moving away from traditional empirical cytotoxic therapy toward a precision medicine approach based on the biological characteristics of the tumor. Whether through the discovery of novel molecular targets, the development of ADCs and nano delivery systems, or the accumulation of real-world clinical evidence, these studies indeed reflect the refinement of treatment strategies for TNBC. In the future, with further advances in patient stratification, biomarker screening, tumor microenvironment regulation, and combination therapy strategies, precision treatment of TNBC is expected to deliver more individualized and sustainable clinical benefits.

## Safety, treatment delivery, and pathological response before and after pembrolizumab implementation for early ER-negative, HER2-normal breast cancer.

**PMID**: 42751222 · **Journal**: ESMO real world data and digital oncology · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100769 · **PMCID**: PMC13579295

**Authors**: Henriksen A F, Lundgren A N H, Andersen M A, Gerds T A, Knop A S, Petersen T S, Lassen U, Bjerrum A

**Types**: Journal Article

**BACKGROUND**: Pembrolizumab has become standard neoadjuvant systemic therapy (NST) for early estrogen receptor (ER)-negative, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-normal early breast cancer (eBC). Electronic health record (EHR) data may support real-world assessment of its implementation in routine care.

**PATIENTS AND METHODS**: Using centralized EHR data from eastern Denmark, we identified adults with ER-negative, HER2-normal eBC receiving NST. Patients were grouped by treatment start before (April 2021-June 2022; comparator) or after (April 2023-June 2024; study) pembrolizumab implementation. We compared treatment exposure, adverse events (AEs) from laboratory data, clinical notes, and AE-indicating medications, and pathological complete response (pCR) from pathology records. Follow-up ended 200 days after surgery, progression, or death. Manual validation included 50 patients.

**RESULTS**: Among 210 included patients, 109 were in the study population and 101 in the comparator population. Baseline characteristics were broadly similar. Pembrolizumab was received by 77% versus 0% and carboplatin omission was less frequent after implementation (7% versus 47%). During NST, grade 3/4 AEs were observed in 77 study patients (71%) and 66 comparator patients (65%). Suspected grade 3/4 autoimmune disorders during NST occurred in 18 pembrolizumab-treated study patients (21%) and in no comparator patients, and no grade 5 AEs were identified. pCR was achieved in 74 study patients (68%) versus 49 comparator patients (49%). Manual validation showed high structured-data completeness after resolution of a small number of data processing errors but also identified missing data.

**CONCLUSION**: After introduction of pembrolizumab into NST, patients with early ER-negative, HER2-normal breast cancer (BC) had a higher pCR proportion, alongside a higher toxicity.

Higher rates of pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant systemic therapy (NST) have been associated with both better event-free survival and overall survival (OS) in early breast cancer (eBC), 1  and are used as a surrogate marker for long-term clinical outcomes in the treatment of estrogen receptor-negative (ER-negative), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 normal (HER2-normal) eBC. Based on a decision in April 2023 by the Danish Medicines Council, 2  current Danish national clinical guidelines recommend a regimen including epirubicin and cyclophosphamide (EC), paclitaxel, carboplatin, and pembrolizumab as NST in ER-negative, HER2-normal eBC. 3  EC can be prescribed every 2 weeks (q2w) as dose-dense (dd) or every 3 weeks (q3w) at an identical cumulative dose.

The addition of the programmed cell death protein 1 checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab to standard of care (SoC) was based on the results from the KEYNOTE-522 trial, 4 , 5  where both improvement of pCR rates and OS were seen in the pembrolizumab arm, accompanied by more frequent adverse events (AEs). Immune-related AEs (irAEs) in particular warrant close attention, as they may be severe and potentially long-lasting.

Because external validity of randomized controlled trial results might vary depending on study population selection, complementary real-world data (RWD) can be utilized to generate real-world evidence (RWE) on complete patient cohorts as seen in the clinic.

Utilizing RWE aligns with the wishes of the Danish Medicines Council, who advised that data be collected to monitor both pCR outcomes and safety postapproval of pembrolizumab. 2

Here, we present results from analyses of electronic health record (EHR) data, comparing safety and effectiveness outcomes of NST for ER-negative, HER2-normal eBC treatment in two periods: before (comparator population, SoC: q2w EC followed by carboplatin + paclitaxel) and after (study population, SoC: pembrolizumab alongside q2w EC followed by carboplatin + paclitaxel or pembrolizumab alongside carboplatin + paclitaxel followed by q3w EC) introducing pembrolizumab to SoC for ER-negative, HER2-normal eBC in Denmark.

The primary objective was to describe and compare AEs captured through structured data (laboratory results), unstructured EHR text (clinical notes), and prescription patterns of AE-indicating medications before, during, and after NST in the two populations.

The secondary objective was to describe proportions of pCR after NST treatment in the two populations.

We screened all adult patients who resided in Region Zealand or the Capital Region of Denmark and had an International Classification of Diseases-10 diagnosis code for breast cancer assigned between 1 January 2016 and 30 June 2024 and who had at least one hospital contact in an oncology department after the diagnosis code assignment.

We then identified patients who received at least one NST dose (outside clinical trials) in the Capital Region of Denmark for breast cancer between April 2021 and June 2024 and who had the ER-negative, HER2-normal pathological subtype. This cohort was divided into the study population (treatment initiation between 1 April 2023 and 30 June 2024) and the comparator population, defined over a temporally shifted, matched treatment initiation window (1 April 2021 to 30 June 2022). The study population eligibility period reflects the approval of pembrolizumab as SoC in Denmark (April 2023), with the end date being the approved inclusion cut-off date. The comparator window was selected to mirror the duration and calendar months of the study period, providing a similarly sized preimplementation cohort while keeping manual free-text AE review feasible.

EHR data were extracted on 11 April 2025 from a centralized database covering all public hospitals treating breast cancer in eastern Denmark. Pathology records were extracted on 3 February 2025, from the Danish national pathology database. Extracted data covered EHR records from January 2016 to March 2025 and pathology records from January 1978 to January 2025. Selected data from February to December 2025 were manually extracted. Data included structured records on antineoplastic treatments, selected supportive medications, treatment plan titles, laboratory results, and pathology records. Manual review of free-text clinical notes was used to ascertain menopause status and narratively documented AEs not captured in structured-data fields. Laboratory-defined AEs were obtained from structured laboratory data. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status was extracted by both manual review and a custom rule-based R function. Cause of death in deceased patients and possible cancer stage I misclassification were assessed by manual review. See  Supplementary Materials  (available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100769 ) for further details.

Index date was the first NST treatment day. The observation period started 90 days before the index date for manual record review. For baseline medications and pathology records, the observation period started 730 days before the index date and 1 January 1978, respectively. We followed patients for 200 days after eBC surgery or until cancer progression (documented in free-text notes) or death, whichever occurred first.

Baseline variables were ascertained from the most recent recorded measurement within 90 days before the index. Medication exposures were summarized from anatomical therapeutic chemical-coded prescriptions and administrations across prespecified pre-, peri-, and post-NST periods (from 730 days before the index to 200 days after breast cancer operation).

ER-negative was defined as ER 0% or ER 1%-9% with a nonluminal PAM50 subtype. In descriptive tables, ER status was defined as ER-low (ER 1%-9%) versus ER 0. HER2-normal was defined as immunohistochemistry (IHC) 0, 1+, or 2+ with negative  in situ  hybridization (ISH). In descriptive tables, HER2 status was defined as HER2-low (IHC 1+ or 2+ with negative ISH) versus HER2 0/ultralow. Modified Charlson Comorbidity Index excluding malignant diagnoses was reported. Clinical T and N stages were obtained from the most recently signed clinical cancer-staging record within 90 days before to 200 days after index, allowing for delayed structured registration of baseline stage.

Antineoplastic treatment exposure was summarized by drug relative to the Danish standard neoadjuvant regimen, with doses standardized to mg/m 2  or carboplatin area under the concentration-time curve. Drug-specific measures of treatment duration, dose cessations, dose reductions, relative cumulated dose (RCD), relative treatment time (RTT), dose intensity (DI), and relative dose intensity (RDI) were calculated from administered drug data. The EC values were calculated relative to the q3w regimen. See  Supplementary Materials  (available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100769 ) for details.

AEs were recorded throughout follow-up, including the adjuvant period where applicable. Events were graded according to National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI CTCAE), version 5.0, 6  and summarized as grades 1-2 and 3-4. For recurrent events, the highest grade per treatment cycle was used. Overlapping unstructured AE terms were consolidated into clinically coherent groupings based on shared or overlapping symptomatology and the highest grade within each group was registered. AE groups with a frequency of ≤5 patients and limited to grade 1-2 severity were not reported. Suspected autoimmune AEs were assigned a CTCAE-defined label according to the recorded organ-specific manifestation. A presumed immune-mediated label was added when the treating physician’s narrative note described the event as suspected autoimmune or immune-related toxicity. No independent adjudication was carried out. Available routine laboratory data included irAE-relevant tests such as thyroid-stimulating hormone, troponin, and cortisol as ordered by the treating physician. Laboratory markers without a clear CTCAE v5.0 grading cut-off were not tabulated as structured AE outcomes; for troponin, any value above the upper limit of normal was described instead of being assigned a CTCAE grade.

Selected supportive medications, including drugs recommended in regional guidelines for treatment of suspected immune-related toxicity, were summarized as indirect indicators of toxicity management and used to supplement laboratory- and free-text-based AE assessment.

pCR and tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) were defined according to Danish national clinical guidelines, 7  and both were extracted from breast cancer operation pathology records identified between the index date and 250 days after the index date.

Full definitions are provided in the  Supplementary Materials  (available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100769 ).

For baseline characteristics, percentage missing values were calculated for all variables, except for the Charlson index, in which the absence of a diagnosis code was interpreted as the absence of comorbidity. Structured laboratory AEs were summarized among patients with available values.

To verify concordance between values displayed in the EHR clinical interface and those extracted from the underlying source database, pragmatic targeted manual validation was carried out by AFH in 50 patients. Across 98 predefined variables and study-specific time windows, values obtained via manual chart review were compared with those derived from the source database; any discrepancy was classified as an error, regardless of its presumed origin. Each error was reviewed by AFH through cross-referencing of the clinical EHR interface, extracted source data, and derived analysis variables to identify the most likely explanation. A sample size of 50 observations per variable was chosen to achieve a high probability of detecting errors if the true error rate was ≥5% (92% probability of at least one observed error). In the absence of observed errors, the one-sided 95% upper confidence bound on the error rate is 5.8%. This sample size was chosen as a pragmatic variable-level error detection to identify potential issues across selected key variables. Validated variables included key demographic information, staging, laboratory results, BC subtype, treatments, surgery, and supportive medication variables. The custom R-based ECOG performance status extraction was also informally compared with manually abstracted values, with discordances adjudicated by AFH before analysis. See  Supplementary Materials  (available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100769 ) for details. Discrepancies identified during validation were corrected before final analyses.

All statistical analyses were conducted using R 8  (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) in RStudio within Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio, in which pseudonymized data were stored. Baseline covariates were compared using Welch’s two-sample  t  test for continuous variables and Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, applied to nonmissing values. Normality of body mass index and age was assessed by visual inspection of histograms, density curves, Q–Q plots, and boxplots. Variables satisfying the normality assumption are reported as mean (standard deviation), and nonnormal variables as median (interquartile range).

All included patients were female and approximately half were postmenopausal. In the comparator population, a higher proportion had low HER2 receptor expression. No other significant differences between the two groups were seen, although the different number of missing values for ECOG performance status, cancer stage, and hypoalbuminemia should be noted.

Nineteen patients were recorded as having stage I disease before the index date and were therefore outside the recommended target population for NST; most had tumor sizes close to 2 cm.

Pembrolizumab was administered to 84 patients (77%) in the study population and to none in the comparator population. The RDI for cyclophosphamide and epirubicin were comparable between the two populations and aligned closely with the q3w regimen standard, despite approximately half of patients being prescribed q2w EC. Paclitaxel and carboplatin both exhibited higher RDI in the study population, primarily driven by a higher RCD of both drugs. A marked difference in the proportion of patients not receiving any dose of carboplatin was observed (7% in the study population versus 47% in the comparator population).

In the study population, 36 patients (33%) received at least one dose of adjuvant therapy versus 44 patients (44%) in the comparator population. See  Supplementary Materials  (available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100769 ) for further details.

For structured AEs during NST, no values were missing for anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, or creatinine; missingness for alanine transaminase, bilirubin, and hypoalbuminemia was 1% versus 2%, 1% versus 3%, and 3% versus 20% in the study and comparator populations, respectively. Troponin measurements were available for 71% of the study population and 4% of the comparator population; among tested patients, elevated values occurred in 29% and 0%, respectively. A total of 18 (21%) pembrolizumab-treated study patients were suspected to have experienced a grade 3/4 autoimmune disorder during NST. These included patients with hepatitis (7), nephritis (3), pneumonitis (2), colitis + adrenitis (1), colitis (1), dermatitis (1), thyroiditis (1), elevated troponin (1), and one patient with both adrenitis, thyroiditis, stomatitis, arthritis, and dermatitis. No autoimmune events were recorded during the adjuvant period or reported in the comparator population; no grade 5 AEs were identified.

Seventy-four (68%) of the patients in the study population achieved pCR versus 49 (49%) in the comparator population. One patient in each group died due to rapid progression and did not undergo surgical resection of the breast tumor.

Surgery specimen TILs were assessed in 19 (17%) patients in the study population and 34 (34%) patients in the comparator population; among assessed reports, 5 (26%) and 4 (12%), respectively, showed stromal TIL levels of ≥30%.

Error numbers, categories, and resolution approaches are summarized in  Supplementary Table S6 , available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100769 . Separate from 147 initial discrepancies attributable to manual abstraction errors (typos), 70 errors were identified in the validation study comparing algorithmically derived variables with manual EHR review. Of these, 25 were errors introduced by incorrect implementation of the intended coding logic and were identified through the validation process (including four T/N stage errors caused by challenges in algorithmically assigning stage in patients with synchronous bilateral tumors). The remaining 45 errors were related to data availability or EHR interface limitations: 12 were attributable to incomplete availability of structured pathology data during the validation period, 8 reflected true extraction discordance for weight dates and values, 2 were due to incorrect filtering during manual extraction of dermatological drugs in the EHR interface, and 23 errors were caused by outpatient prescriptions not being visible in the summarized drug field of the clinical interface.

For ECOG performance status, the custom R function agreed with the initial manual abstraction for 206 of 210 patients (98%), including concordant identification of missing performance status values. The four discordant cases all represented errors in the manual abstraction.

In this real-world (RW) study of neoadjuvant systemic treatment for ER-negative, HER2-normal early breast cancer, the pCR rate was higher in the study population (68%) than in the comparator population (49%), indicating improved RW effectiveness following the introduction of pembrolizumab into standard NST. However, causal interpretation of these descriptive results is limited by differences in chemotherapy exposure and potential unmeasured period-related confounding from other changes in clinical practice.

We found a higher burden of toxicity after introducing pembrolizumab to SoC, with more grade 3/4 events experienced by more patients (74% versus 68% in the study and comparator populations, respectively) during or immediately after the neoadjuvant treatment. The distributions of most unstructured AEs were broadly comparable across the two populations; however, suspected severe irAEs represented a distinct toxicity signal in the study population.

Among the 84 pembrolizumab-treated patients in the study population, 18 (21%) experienced a suspected severe irAE compared with 13% in the intervention arm in KEYNOTE-522.

For severe AEs of any type, the distribution in the study population (74% during the complete follow-up period) was comparable to that reported in KEYNOTE-522, in which 77% of the intervention arm experienced a severe AE. 4

Of note, our study population was older (median age 56 versus 49) and included more postmenopausal women (55% versus 44%) with fewer stage III and more stage I BC, but similar ECOG performance status scores, compared with the intervention arm in KEYNOTE-522.

A strength of our study is the use of routinely collected EHR data from the same database that underpins clinical decision-making, extracted from the EHR system that covers all public hospital contacts for approximately half of the Danish population. Structured data had low missingness and detailed records of prescriptions, administrations, and laboratory results, enabling transparent and reproducible data flows and allowing us to report comprehensive treatment exposure estimation on an individual drug basis. Averaging treatment intensities across multiple drugs in a regimen is common and possibly reflects the combined effect of sequential and parallel drug exposures, but the transparency of summarizing individual drugs might be warranted, especially in case of toxicity reporting.

By triangulating three complementary AE assessment approaches, we aimed to reduce source-specific reporting bias and provide a more comprehensive representation of patients’ experience. Due to our approval with a waiver of individual consent, we present evidence on unselected RW cohorts from participating departments, including a substantial number of patients. The comparator population provides a clear reference for temporal interpretation and future causal analyses.

The validation highlights several considerations beyond identifying processing errors when using structured EHR data. Variables should be sought across relevant EHR structures, as illustrated by inconsistent weight capture in oncology-specific versus general forms. Manual review of the clinical interface is also not always an absolute reference standard, as structured EHR extracts may include data from dynamically updated fields not consistently visible during review. Finally, 147 of 217 initial discrepancies reflected manual transcription rather than extraction errors, underscoring that human review is itself error-prone. For future EHR-based RW studies, these findings highlight the need for validation across source tables, extraction logic, derivation code, and manual reference standards while distinguishing variables suited for structured extraction from those requiring curated manual review.

Several limitations merit consideration. Cohort identification in EHRs is inherently challenging: despite reliance on structured pathology and treatment data, misclassification or coding errors may exclude eligible patients and threaten internal validity. The reliability of unstructured data varies: ECOG performance status is usually well documented, whereas subjective AEs are incompletely and selectively recorded, with severe events more consistently captured than mild events, leading to potentially biased toxicity estimates. Prescription patterns should not directly equate to treatment toxicity. As seen, autoimmune disorders were only reported in the study population. This may reflect true toxicity introduced by pembrolizumab, but comparisons between periods are also vulnerable to differential ascertainment and reporting bias, as clinicians were likely more attentive to immune-related symptoms after pembrolizumab implementation. This also applies to troponin, where markedly different test availability limits between-period comparison. This bias may be even more pronounced in the adjuvant period, in which less frequent oncology contact may reduce the capture of immune-related as well as other symptoms. The value gained from extracting unstructured AE data from EHR notes should be considered against the time consumed for this task and weighed against the inevitable risk of misclassification and bias.

Importantly,  Supplementary Table S2 , available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmorw.2026.100769 , shows that pembrolizumab is not the only treatment exposure difference in the two populations: the study population received more carboplatin and paclitaxel as well as more pembrolizumab. This point reflects a previous finding, 9  in which low RDI, driven mainly by dose reductions or discontinuations of paclitaxel and carboplatin, was correlated with a lower chance of achieving pCR after NST in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Other unmeasured changes in clinical practice between the comparator and study periods may also have influenced treatment delivery, toxicity detection, and pCR. Thus, differences in effectiveness or toxicity should therefore be interpreted as period-based RW comparisons rather than causal estimates of pembrolizumab alone.

Two of the six patients in the study population who were prescribed systemic hydrocortisone had confirmed immune-mediated adrenitis (2.4% of pembrolizumab-treated patients). This is comparable to KEYNOTE-522, in which 1.3% in the intervention arm experienced adrenal insufficiency. A recent RW study on early TNBC 10  did, however, find 6% adrenal insufficiency in a cohort of patients treated with pembrolizumab, suggesting possible differences in populations, detection methods, or registration practices.

When adherence to recommended treatment protocols cannot be assumed, metrics like relative total DI 11  or RDI 9  may obscure differences in drug exposure. For example, omission of a planned fourth dose may reduce both RCD and RTT to 0.75, yielding an apparent RDI of 100% despite only 75% of the planned dose being administered. This consideration is particularly relevant in our setting, in which treatment discontinuations were observed in 13%-26% of patients receiving EC and 14%-50% of those receiving carboplatin–paclitaxel. We therefore report RDI as RCD/RTT, with RCD based on administered cumulative dose and RTT corrected for the actual number of administrations received.

Patients treated with NST for early ER-negative, HER2-normal breast cancer after introduction of pembrolizumab to SoC demonstrated a higher pCR rate alongside a higher burden of toxicity, including suspected immune-mediated AEs, relative to patients treated before the introduction of pembrolizumab. Because chemotherapy delivery also differed between periods, the higher pCR rate should be interpreted as reflecting the implemented treatment strategy rather than pembrolizumab alone.

This study shows that structured EHR and pathology data from hospitals treating breast cancer in eastern Denmark can support reproducible identification of patients with clearly defined clinical or pathological subtypes and detailed documentation of treatment delivery, supportive medications, laboratory-test–based AEs, and pathology-coded outcomes such as pCR. Keyword-based extraction can support simple character-string variables such as performance status and potentially menopausal status, whereas unstructured AE ascertainment remains labor-intensive and requires clinical curation.
