Although we profiled single-agent activity across multiple breast cancer cell lines, the comprehensive assessment and testing of drug combinations were performed primarily in SUM149, as it is a triple-negative/basal-like IBC model (ER/PR negative, HER2 not activated) [ 54 ,  156 ] that represents the most aggressive forms of IBC. This focus may limit the generalizability of our results as IBC is heterogeneous across receptor subtypes [ 140 ] and patient tumors; and thus, at this stage, our results should be interpreted as defining synergistic interactions and pathways in SUM149 rather than more broadly across all IBC subtypes. Nonetheless, we suggest that our findings support as proof-of-concept, that co-targeting the IGF-1R/EGFR/PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling axis can yield strong anti-proliferative and anti-motility effects in the SUM149 TN-IBC model, and future work will test the prioritized combinations (or clinically tractable analogs) in additional IBC models (e.g., HER2 + SUM190 and MDA-IBC-3), as molecular subtype differences may influence the degree to which co-targeting EGFR/IGF-1R and downstream PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling produces synergy. These combinations can also be assessed in patient-derived xenografts and/or primary patient material to more fully assess translational potential in models that better preserve IBC tissue architecture, tumor emboli, and microenvironmental ligand signaling. While our 3D spheroid results serve as an intermediate level of complexity, they do not capture stromal/immune contributions or systemic exposure constraints.

While we did not directly test our selected drug combinations in other IBC subtypes, we can propose how they might act. HER2 + disease represents a substantial subset of IBC and these tumors frequently signal through PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways that overlap with the targets of our prioritized combinations [ 157 ]. HER2 + IBC biopsied at progression on HER2-targeted therapy reported mTOR activation in 83% of cases, and also noted frequent co-activation of HER2 and mTOR signaling, consistent with PI3K/AKT/mTOR functioning as a bypass/resistance axis [ 158 ]. Hence, we anticipate that the downstream co-targeting combinations we identified (e.g., Akt + mTOR inhibition, or IGF-1R/IR + Akt inhibition) may remain relevant in HER2 + IBC, particularly where PI3K pathway activation is present. However, efficacy is expected to be context-dependent (e.g., EGFR dependence and HER-family expression) [ 159 ], and translation to HER2 + disease will likely require further investigation. IGF-1R can crosstalk with HER2 signaling; in trastuzumab-resistant HER2 + breast cancer models, co-targeting IGF-1R and HER2 reduced invasion and produced modest but significant growth effects, supporting IGF-1R/IR inhibition as a rational partner node when HER2 signaling is persistent [ 159 ]. These data suggest that our downstream-node combinations (e.g., Akt + mTOR or IGF-1R/IR + Akt) may be likely to retain activity in HER2 + IBC models, whereas the IGF-1R/IR + EGFR pair may be more context-dependent (e.g., influenced by EGFR/HER-family expression and compensatory HER2 signaling). In the HER2 + IBC cell line SUM190, mTORC1 inhibitors (rapamycin/everolimus) show only modest single-agent growth inhibition, supporting the need for combination strategies rather than mTOR blockade alone [ 158 ]. In the same SUM190 IBC model, the allosteric Akt inhibitor MK-2206 (1 µM) reduced Akt phosphorylation [ 160 ], while in another study, the IGF-axis–targeting compound KW-2450 inhibited growth with an IC₅₀ of 0.22 µM [ 161 ].

From a translational perspective, two compounds from the top GRR combinations (tyrphostin AG‑1478 and AKTIV) are widely used laboratory inhibitors and should be viewed primarily as chemical probes that help validate pathway co-targeting strategies, rather than as immediate clinical combination partners. Tyrphostin AG‑1478 has been described as discontinued from clinical development and used mainly as an experimental EGFR inhibitor, with preclinical studies reporting systemic effects (e.g., hypomagnesemia and cardiac dysfunction) with chronic exposure, underscoring the need for careful safety assessment when translating EGFR-pathway inhibition [ 162 – 164 ]. AKTIV also has limited clinical development information and as mentioned previously, is reported to accumulate in mitochondria and disrupt cellular bioenergetics, raising the possibility of off-target effects [ 92 ]. For both compounds, the established human pharmacokinetic and safety data are limited, which further constrains direct translational interpretation of these compounds. BMS-536924 is an orally active preclinical IGF-1R/IR inhibitor [ 68 ], but the broader class of dual IGF-1R/IR kinase inhibitors has been difficult to translate clinically because insulin receptor co-inhibition can produce metabolic toxicity, and later agents such as linsitinib [ 165 ] and BMS-754807 [ 166 ] did not advance successfully in breast cancer/solid tumor development. For our identified combinations, other inhibitors for the same targets are clinically advanced, including FDA-approved Akt inhibitor capivasertib [ 114 ], and approved mTOR inhibitor temsirolimus [ 167 ]. Future studies should therefore evaluate whether the synergy observed here can be reproduced with clinically tractable pathway inhibitors, while accounting for pharmacokinetic compatibility and overlapping mechanism-based toxicities common to EGFR and PI3K/Akt/mTOR axis inhibition [ 168 ].

An additional important translational consideration is whether the combination effects we observed  in vitro  can be achieved at clinically relevant drug exposures. Approved mTOR and Akt inhibitors achieve clinically relevant exposures at standard doses: temsirolimus (25 mg i.v. weekly) reaches a mean C max  of ~585 ng/mL (~sub-µM) in whole blood, and capivasertib, recently approved for HR + /HER2 − advanced breast cancer, achieves steady-state C max  values in the low-µM range (1,371 ng/mL (30%)) [ 113 ,  169 ]. Safety is also important for translating PI3K/Akt/mTOR-targeted combinations. Capivasertib was mainly associated with diarrhea and rash [ 117 ,  169 ], while everolimus was associated with stomatitis and other toxicities in BOLERO-2 [ 90 ]. Clinical studies of PI3Kα inhibitors such as alpelisib and inavolisib reported pathway-related adverse effects, including hyperglycemia, rash, diarrhea, and/or stomatitis [ 115 ,  169 ]. These findings highlight the need to optimize dose, schedule, and drug selection in any future IBC studies, especially when combining agents that may have overlapping toxicities. Future studies will employ clinically relevant agents (e.g., capivasertib, ipatasertib, and approved EGFR/HER-family inhibitors) and evaluate efficacy and tolerability in  in vivo  IBC and patient-derived models.

Together, our results highlight the therapeutic promise of the identified combinations for targeting IBC, and, to our knowledge, these specific combinations have not been reported previously in IBC. Because the three most effective combinations all came from the GRR-derived list, these findings also support the use of complementary computational approaches to identify effective novel combinations.

While these initial findings are promising, it should be noted that all efficacy data were generated  in vitro  using cell line models, and our findings should currently be considered only as proof-of-concept observations. Additionally, these combinations first need to be validated across additional IBC cell lines. Further, prior to any consideration of clinical translation, combinations would need to be tested in animal models to assess  in vivo  efficacy, pharmacokinetics, and toxicity.

This study provides experimental in vitro validation of our computational LWAS- and GRR-derived drug repurposing predictions for a rare form of breast cancer, IBC. Among the LWAS-predicted drugs, we identified several agents with known relevance to breast cancer and IBC. For the GRR-predicted drugs, we identified targeted agents and combinations that showed activity in the SUM149 2D and 3D IBC models, with the most active GRR-derived combinations affecting IGF-1R/IR, EGFR, Akt, and mTOR signaling, and partially reversing the IBC-associated gene-expression signature in SUM149 cells. These findings support further testing of clinically tractable inhibitors for these pathways in IBC  in vivo  models and patient-derived systems to more broadly assess efficacy, dosing, resistance mechanisms, and toxicity.

This study bridges the gap between computational predictions and experimental validation in drug repurposing. Our approach of using LWAS-based text mining and gene-reversal analysis to predict potential drugs, then assessing them in lab-based models for efficacy, should be a generally applicable strategy for identifying possible therapies for a range of understudied rare diseases with limited treatment options.

## Characterizing the Objective Time Spent on Health Care Activities in Clinic and at Home for Patients With Cancer.

**PMID**: 42747975 · **Journal**: Cancer medicine · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1002/cam4.72277 · **PMCID**: PMC13580835

**Authors**: Rocque Gabrielle B, Henderson Nicole Lynne, Parsons Helen M, Brown Katherine, Huang Zuofu, Gupta Arjun, Teoh Deanna, Fan Yingling, Blaes Anne, Odom J Nicholas, Arend Rebecca, Wolfson Julian, Vogel Rachel I

**Types**: Journal Article

**BACKGROUND**: While the time burden of cancer care is increasingly recognized in oncology, existing research lacks the granularity needed to identify intervention targets. This study characterized time spent on cancer care at home and in-clinic, including travel, waiting, and clinical tasks, assessing variations by treatment modality.

**METHODS**: We conducted a secondary analysis of two longitudinal cohorts. Cohort 1 included patients with metastatic breast or advanced ovarian cancer (n = 55) and Cohort 2 included patients with any cancer (n = 55) receiving systemic anti-cancer therapy. Participants used a mobile application for 28 days that collected GPS and motion sensor data to infer locations. Daily surveys characterized activities and captured time spent on home-based tasks.

**RESULTS**: The study population (N = 110) was predominantly female and White, receiving a mix of infusion and oral treatments. Participants recorded 597 out-of-home healthcare episodes. While median time receiving care per episode for lab-only visits was short (10 min), visits combining labs and treatment had a median duration of 162 min (compared to treatment alone, median duration of 68 min). Patients on infusion therapies experienced higher time burdens per episode both in-facility (median 125 min vs. 50 min for oral therapy) and at home for scheduling and symptom management (median 188 min vs. 102 min).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Patients face substantial time burdens that extend beyond the clinical encounter. Waiting between stages, such as labs and treatment, makes combined out-of-home healthcare episodes disproportionately time-consuming. These data facilitate a deeper understanding of the trade-offs between different treatment modalities and care delivery models.

The oncology community increasingly recognizes that patients spend substantial amounts of time on cancer care and associated out‐of‐home healthcare services [ 1 ,  2 ]. Early work evaluating time burden related to cancer, sometimes called time toxicity [ 3 ], found that while oncologists spend on average 20 min with an individual, women with metastatic breast cancer spent over on average 3.5 h on a typical healthcare episode and over 60 h in the initial 3 months traveling to and receiving routine cancer care [ 4 ]. In a broader cancer population, median total time spent on receiving outpatient care was 3.3 h per visit [ 5 ]. This time commitment is exacerbated when patients have to be seen with the health system at increasing frequencies, receive complex treatment regimens, or need multimodal care [ 4 ,  6 ]. When considering healthcare contact days with the health system, defined as days with in‐person healthcare outside the home (e.g., outpatient encounters such as blood draws, infusions, clinician visits, urgent care or emergency department visits, and inpatient stays in acute care hospitals and nursing and rehabilitation facilities), women with metastatic breast cancer spent approximately 30 days within their first year of treatment [ 7 ,  8 ], while patients with metastatic gastrointestinal cancer spent over 25% of their time in contact with the healthcare system [ 6 ].

This time spent on cancer care is burdensome for patients, with almost half of patients reporting a desire to minimize time burdens [ 9 ]. Patients express that while healthcare facility‐based care is often more burdensome than home‐based care, in‐person visits may be perceived as “value added” due to interaction with clinical teams. However, home‐based care can also be burdensome when time needed to complete tasks is unpredictable and/or when it adversely impacts care partners [ 3 ]. Importantly, time demands are often a key consideration when selecting treatment, particularly when considering clinical trials or treatments with marginal benefit [ 3 ,  10 ,  11 ]. Time considerations may also be particularly pertinent for individuals living a substantial distance from care, which has known adverse impacts on cancer stage at diagnosis, treatments received, quality of life and other outcomes [ 12 ]. In a study at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, 25% of patients lived greater than 1 h from their cancer care provider [ 13 ]. The need to travel is exacerbated in rural communities, where 20% of Americans live greater than 60 miles from a medical oncologist [ 14 ].

Despite this increasing recognition of the importance of time burdens in cancer care, data on time spent is often broad (e.g., days with healthcare contact, total hours) and does not provide the granularity needed to understand how the time spent on components of care (e.g., visits, labs, infusion) may be modified or coordinated. There are potential targets for minimizing time toxicity, such as improving coordination of care, selecting treatment modalities associated with more limited need for in‐person care, and transitioning delivery to a local healthcare center or the home. However, further evaluation with nuanced consideration of time spent on cancer care activities is needed to frame future strategies to mitigate time toxicity. The objective of this study was to leverage high‐resolution sensor and self‐reported survey data collected via a mobile application to characterize the granular components of time spent on cancer care, including travel, waiting, and clinical activities, both within healthcare facilities and in the home setting, and to identify how these time burdens vary by service type (e.g., labs, treatments) and treatment modality.

This analysis combines participants from two longitudinal cancer patient cohorts that both assessed the objective time spent on various healthcare activities using a mobile application (Daynamica, described below). The two cohorts were established with distinct primary objectives: Cohort 1 focused on validating a mobile application's utility as a research instrument for capturing time burden; Cohort 2 prioritized assessing the feasibility and patient‐centered acceptability of the mobile application. Details of the approach to capture time and methods for Cohort 1 are described elsewhere [ 15 ]; methods for Cohort 2 are similar unless otherwise stated. In brief, participants completed a baseline survey to report demographic and treatment characteristics. Subsequently, they used the mobile application for 28 days, which leverages sensor data with daily surveys to capture time spent on cancer care. These data were analyzed to assess differential time by healthcare activity to generate hypotheses for future interventions that could reduce time. The Cohort 1 study was approved by the University of Minnesota Institutional Review Board (STUDY00016834) and the Cohort 2 study was approved by Advarra (SSU00246429); both were registered with  ClinicalTrials.gov  ( NCT05708703 ,  NCT06322992 , respectively).

Two study populations were included in this analysis. Cohort 1 included adults (age 18+) with a diagnosis of metastatic (Stage IV) breast cancer or advanced (Stage III or IV)/recurrent ovarian, primary peritoneal, or fallopian tube cancer receiving systemic anti‐cancer therapy within the University of Minnesota M Health Fairview system or the University of Alabama at Birmingham. Eligible patients were approached at the time of a scheduled clinic visit by dedicated research staff in collaboration with their healthcare provider between December 2023 and September 2024. Cohort 2 included adult (aged 18+) patients currently receiving treatment for any type and stage of cancer within the University of Minnesota M Health Fairview system. These participants were recruited via electronic medical record messages between May and September 2024 and completed an electronic consent process over the phone with a study coordinator. For both cohorts, participants were required to be able to read and write English. A smartphone was provided by the study team to participants who did not own a smartphone for the duration of the study. Participants were eligible at any point after their original diagnosis. Participants were compensated $180 for participation in Cohort 1 and $200 for participation in Cohort 2.

After study enrollment and consent, participants were asked to install the mobile application on their smartphone and use it for 28 days. The mobile application, Daynamica, is an established, publicly available application that leverages GPS location data, as well as data from other phone sensors (e.g., accelerometer, gyroscope) to infer a user's location and activity type. The app distinguishes (1) activities (e.g., picking up medications from the pharmacy), which take place at a specific location, and (2) trips, during which individuals move between activities. Participants label locations for the initial time at a given location (e.g., Home). From locations provided by the participant, the “Activity type” is inferred and the mode of transport for trips between locations was identified (car, walk, bike, etc.). Repeated visits to the same care location were automatically recognized and labeled.

When an individual is away from home, the activities are grouped into an episode. Each episode is labeled as being cancer‐related (“facility‐based” out‐of‐home or home‐based healthcare episodes) or not cancer related. For those cancer‐related, the app prompts participants to further clarify the type of care received by selecting all that apply: labs, treatment, clinic visit, research, pharmacy, imaging, other, and to estimate time spent waiting during that episode (no wait, < 15, 15–30, 30–60, > 60 min). These included both ambulatory and in‐patient encounters. At the end of each day, participants were asked to review, correct, and label any unlabeled episodes at the end of each day. Participants were also asked daily to complete a short (< 5 min) survey documenting the amount of time spent on any cancer‐related phone calls or activities (e.g., scheduling appointments, arranging help) during that day that were not otherwise reported.

This analysis included only participants who engaged with the application for at least 7 days (including both activity data collection and end‐of‐day surveys) and recorded at least one out‐of‐home cancer healthcare related episode. We additionally excluded individuals who were participating in a therapeutic clinical trial and those from Cohort 2 who were not receiving systemic anti‐cancer therapy (such as those undergoing surgery or radiation alone). The consort diagram is shown in Figure  S1 . The outcomes of interest for this analysis were time spent on out‐of‐home healthcare activities including labs, imaging, clinic visits for cancer care, clinic visits for non‐cancer care, cancer treatment, non‐cancer treatments, hospitalizations, and waiting for services either alone or in combination with other services. We also evaluated time spent at home on healthcare including telehealth appointments, taking medications, symptom management, scheduling appointments, managing medical bills, and arranging for additional help related to cancer care. We combined time across care activities to identify total out‐of‐home care time (including waiting time), travel time, and total time spent on tasks at home per week for all weeks in which participants had data (all had at least 1 week of data).

Participant demographic and clinical characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Activity data for each participant were generated by combining episodic data with the daily survey responses. We used descriptive statistics and visualizations to provide a detailed breakdown and analysis of time spent on out‐of‐home and at‐home cancer‐related tasks.

Of the 144 participants enrolled in Cohort 1 and Cohort 2, the analytic sample for this study included 110 patients (55 from each Cohort). The median age of participants was 58 years old (range 26–85 years). The majority were female (80.0%), White (78.2%), and privately insured (57.3%). Almost half were working at the time of participation. Cancer types varied, with breast and ovarian being the most prominent cancer type. The cohorts differed in that Cohort 1 had a greater proportion of women (100% vs. 60%) due to being exclusively comprised of patients with breast and ovarian cancer, as well as having a greater proportion of Black participants (18.2% vs. 3.6%), individuals without any college education (30.9% vs. 16.4%), and governmental insurance coverage (Medicare, Medicaid, or TRICARE; 54.5% vs. 29.1%) than Cohort 2 (Table  1 ). Cohort 1 also had more patients treated for recurrent/progressive disease with infusion (intravenous or intramuscular) treatments. Compared to those on oral therapies, individuals on infusion therapies in this sample included a higher proportion of patients who were Black (14.3% vs. 0%), lacked college education (27.4% vs. 11.5%), unemployed (52.4% vs. 42.3%), and on governmental insurance (47.6% vs. 23.1%) (Table  S1 ).

The 110 participants had 597 out‐of‐home healthcare episodes. Care time per episode ranged from 0 to 108 h, with the longest episodes including multi‐day hospitalizations. Figure  1  is a stacked bar plot that summarizes total time spent in each of the 597 episodes, decomposed into three components of the care process: (1) travel to and from appointments, (2) waiting for care, and (3) time receiving care. The median episode length was 112 min (1.9 h). Qualitatively, while there were outliers in individual components (e.g., greatest round‐trip travel time was 11 h; 13% of episodes included waits of > 60 min), these components were relatively consistent compared to the wider variability in treatment time. The individuals with the highest total time predominantly had increased treatment time as the largest component of total time.

When considering individual components, median care time varied by type of service per healthcare episode. The median care time was least for lab only visits (10 min), followed by cancer clinic visits (43 min), imaging (49 min) or treatment only visits (i.e., no lab or imaging, 68 min) (Table  2 ). The median wait time for single types (e.g., lab only, imaging only) of out‐of‐home healthcare episodes was 8 min (e.g., most participants reported waiting < 15 min). Importantly, when visits were combined, the time increased beyond what would be additive for individual components. This was particularly notable where labs were added to another out‐of‐home healthcare episode type: combined visits with labs + cancer clinic visits had a median duration of 75 min, labs + treatment visits 162 min, and labs + cancer clinic visit + treatment visit 191 min. In contrast, the median reported wait time for multi‐component visits only modestly increased.

Patients within this study also spent substantial time on healthcare activities at home (median 164 min). For the 49 patients who accessed telehealth ( n  = 108 telehealth visits), 22% were between 0 and 15 min, 32% between 15 and 30 min, 32% between 30 and 60 min, and 14% greater than 60 min. In addition to formal telehealth visits, patients spend substantial time at home on other cancer‐related healthcare activities. The median amount of time spent per week taking medicine was 60 min, managing symptoms was 55 min, and scheduling appointments was 8 min.

When considering mode of therapy, patients on infusion therapy spent more time on cancer‐related healthcare activities both out‐of‐the‐home (median 125 min per week) and at home (median 188 min per week) compared to those on oral therapies (median 50 and 102 min per week, respectively). Modest differences in these categories were observed with patients on infusion therapy having more travel time (median 45 vs. 28 min), time on symptom management (65 min vs. 37 min), and scheduling appointments (9 vs. 7 min) per week (Table  3 ). Findings were similar amongst the breast cancer only cohort, which was the most common cancer type in the dataset (data not shown).

This analysis provides detailed estimates on both facility‐based and home‐based time spent managing and receiving cancer‐related healthcare activities. We demonstrated that the selection of treatments with less frequent schedules and use of oral therapies instead of IV therapies could influence time spent on healthcare, which should be considered in the context of other potential considerations such as toxicity and efficacy. This study found home‐based time burden might be greater for those on infusion‐based therapies overall due to symptom management and scheduling needs that appeared more time intensive than for those oral therapies. This provides further support that pharmaceutical developers should consider the potential for time toxicity and ability to administer medications at home in treatment development.

Our data highlight potential tradeoffs that can guide future interventions to minimize time toxicity. For example, there are choices about whether to do all out‐of‐home healthcare activities (laboratory and imaging tests, appointment, infusion visits) on the same day or spread across multiple days. Consolidation of the schedule has potential to minimize drive time but also may be associated with substantial wait time between activities as they may be scheduled at different times throughout the day and tests may require results to be posted prior to an appointment or infusion, resulting in substantial wait times. This likely contributes to the observed more‐than‐additive time increase for the addition of labs to other care components. Another potential burden‐reducing approach is to conduct laboratory and imaging tests locally to minimize travel time and clinic wait time in high volume cancer centers. Furthermore, this may avoid unnecessary travel for canceled treatment due to abnormal lab or imaging results. At the same time, this approach may lead to visits spread over multiple days or increase time spent traveling. Minimizing time toxicity through tailored scheduling will require a deeper understanding of patients' priorities and competing time demands.

The option for home‐based healthcare presents an additional option to minimize time toxicity. Our data supports the use of telehealth as a home‐based solution that can minimize drive and wait time. The use of telehealth is currently threatened by policy changes [ 16 ], and advocacy is needed to continue this option for patients. While telehealth and home‐based care are important options, some patients may prefer facility‐based care. There may be shifts in the perception of the quantity and quality of time spent face‐to‐face with their clinical team. In addition, touchpoints with the broader care team (e.g., social work, care coordinators) that benefit patients are often missing from telehealth appointments. Finally, receipt of care in the home setting can shift burden to caregivers, who fill in additional roles managing symptoms and treatments. Both patients and caregivers need education and support for successful home‐based care delivery, including the use of technology for video visits, management of symptoms, treatment administration, and navigating financial concerns. Furthermore, these activities can be time‐consuming, and interventions to simplify home‐based care to minimize burden are needed as well [ 17 ].

This study has several limitations. The participants were receiving care at only two institutions. Other cancer centers may have different workflows that would impact how long patients spend receiving services. Different catchment areas require patients to travel varying distances to receive care. However, this analysis does highlight potential tradeoffs that could be considered in new contexts. There is a possibility of measurement error if participants do not consistently carry their phones when leaving their home, resulting in missing data. Another limitation is that we do not analyze the perceived burden of these different types of time commitments. Understanding the perception of time spent in cancer‐related care is critical to inform interventions to minimize time burdens. The study was also only available to participants who spoke English, and those with a need for language translation may have different time burdens. Finally, due to the small sample size and study duration, we are not able to look at either time demands for individual medications or for the trajectory of a cancer journey.

Patients spend substantial time on their cancer care both within facilities and at home. Granular estimates of components can facilitate consideration of tradeoffs in where time is spent including same day vs. different day services, use of telehealth, and choice of oral vs. infusion therapies. Additional work is needed to develop and test interventions to reduce time toxicity.

## Association between cumulative symptom burden and cognitive impairment among breast cancer survivors: a cross-sectional study.

**PMID**: 42747658 · **Journal**: Breast cancer research and treatment · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1007/s10549-026-08064-7 · **PMCID**: PMC13582376

**Authors**: Li Xiaotong, Lampson Kaitlin, Liou Kevin T, Li Yuelin, Li Susan Q, Ahles Tim, Root James, Mao Jun J

**Types**: Journal Article

**BACKGROUND**: Cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) is a multifaceted symptom associated with various comorbid conditions, complicating management. This study aims to evaluate cumulative symptom burden and its impact on both subjective and objective CRCI in breast cancer survivors.

**METHOD**: Enrollment data were analyzed from a randomized clinical trial involving women with stage 0-III breast cancer, free of oncology disease, reporting moderate or greater CRCI and insomnia. Subjective CRCI was measured using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Cognitive Function (FACT-Cog), and objective CRCI with the Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised (HVLT). Comorbid symptoms (insomnia, fatigue, pain, anxiety, depression) were assessed with validated self-report tools. A Cumulative Symptoms Score (CSS) was calculated to quantify symptom burden. Multivariable linear regression was used to examine associations with CRCI, adjusting for co-variables.

**RESULTS**: Among 260 participants (mean age 56.6 years), 21% were non-White and 10% Hispanic. Fatigue (90%) was the most common, followed by insomnia (70%), pain (45%), anxiety (35%), and depression (12%). Higher CSS was significantly associated with worse subjective CRCI after adjustment for age and chemotherapy (Coef. = -3.0, 95% CI: -3.6 to -2.4, p < 0.001). Each comorbid symptom was correlated with subjective CRCI (all p < 0.001). CSS was not associated with objective cognitive performance (p = 0.58), although insomnia correlated with HVLT scores (r = -0.20; p < 0.001).

**CONCLUSION**: Cumulative symptom burden was associated with subjective but not objective CRCI. Comprehensive symptom management has the potential to improve subjective appraisal of CRCI. Sleep disturbance may be a therapeutic target for improving objective outcomes.

Cancer related cognitive dysfunction (CRCI), involving symptoms such as memory loss, attention deficits, slowed processing speed, and executive function difficulties [ 1 ,  2 ], affects 60–75% of breast cancer survivors [ 1 ,  3 ]. Over half of breast cancer survivors experience persistent CRCI [ 1 ,  4 ,  5 ], lasting over 10–20 years after treatment completion [ 6 ,  7 ]. This negatively impacts the quality of life among breast cancer survivors, particularly in their daily tasks and social relationships [ 2 ,  6 ]. Of more concern, CRCI is associated with an up to 40% increase in risk for the discontinuation of hormonal therapy in breast cancer survivors [ 8 ], increasing the risk of cancer recurrence and mortality [ 9 ,  10 ]. However, CRCI still remains inadequately managed and insufficiently discussed among clinicians and patients [ 11 ], primarily due to limited knowledge, challenges in diagnosis, and the lack of evidence-based interventions [ 12 ].

Effectively addressing CRCI requires recognizing its complex and multifaceted nature [ 13 ], as it may be influenced by and frequently coexist with other cancer-related symptoms, such as insomnia, fatigue, pain, anxiety, and depression. Among these, insomnia is a prominent comorbidity [ 14 ], affecting up to 62% of breast cancer survivors [ 15 ]. A recent study ( N  = 1072) demonstrated a significant association between CRCI and insomnia in breast cancer survivors, with 72% of participants with severe insomnia reporting moderate or greater cognitive impairment [ 16 ]. CRCI is considered a major consequence of insufficient sleep, impacting psychomotor and cognitive speed, vigilance and executive attention, working memory, and executive abilities [ 17 ]. Additionally, other physical and psychological symptoms, such as pain, fatigue, anxiety, and depression are all common among breast cancer survivors and have been shown to be associated with both cognitive impairment and sleep problems independently [ 15 ,  18 ,  19 ].

Although associations between CRCI and individual symptoms have been reported, less is known about the cumulative impact of these co-occurring symptoms on cognitive outcomes. Furthermore, current epidemiological studies evaluating CRCI and its accompanying symptoms have largely been conducted in the general breast cancer survivor population, rather than among patients who report clinically significant insomnia and cognitive impairment, a subgroup that may experience particularly high symptom burden and is more likely to seek clinical care. In addition, limited research has evaluated the relationship between cumulative symptom burden and both subjective and objective measures of cognition within this population.

Evaluating cognitive conditions and symptom burden among breast cancer survivors reporting insomnia and CRCI is crucial for identifying symptom profiles within this population and improving the efficiency of CRCI diagnosis through targeted symptom screening [ 20 ]. Furthermore, exploring the impact of comorbid symptoms on CRCI may help clinicians leverage existing interventions that target co-occurring symptoms to indirectly alleviate cognitive complaints. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the prevalence of both subjective and objective CRCI, as well as comorbid symptoms, among breast cancer survivors with self-reported insomnia and CRCI. Additionally, we sought to assess the impact of cumulative symptom burden on subjective and objective CRCI. Our findings may contribute to identifying distinct symptom profiles within this population and to the development of novel, targeted interventions for managing CRCI.

The current study was conducted using enrollment data from an ongoing 3-arm parallel randomized controlled trial ENHANCE (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier  NCT04837820 ; Registration Date: April 2021), which started in 2021. It compares acupuncture against sham acupuncture and a wait list control among breast cancer survivors with insomnia related CRCI. The institutional review board at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center approved this trial (IRB number: 20–124).

Adult survivors with a diagnosis of stage 0 to III breast cancer were eligible to participate if they met the following criteria: (1) English-speaking; (2) free of oncologic disease by clinical examination or history (3) reported moderate or greater perceived CRCI as indicated by a score of “quite a bit” or “very much” on at least one of the two items that specifically assess concentration and memory problems on the EORTC QLQ-C30 [version 3.0]) [ 21 ]; (4) reported a worsening of cognitive function since their cancer diagnosis by answering “Yes” to all of the following questions: a) Do you think or feel that your memory or mental ability has gotten worse since your cancer diagnosis? b)Do you think your mind isn’t as sharp now as it was before your cancer diagnosis? c) Do you feel like these problems have made it harder to function on your job or take care of things around the home? (5) reported insomnia symptoms, identified as a score of eight or greater on the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) [ 22 ].

We excluded patients if they (1) completed active cancer treatment (surgery, chemotherapy, and/or radiation therapy) within one month prior to study enrollment; (2) had their most recent breast cancer diagnosis more than 10 years ago; (3) were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, Parkinson disease, or other organic brain disorders; (4) had a score of ≥ 10 on the Blessed Orientation-Memory-Concentration (BOMC) screening instrument [ 23 ]; (5) had pre-existing, uncorrectable visual or auditory impairment that would preclude ability to complete the assessments; (6) reported a primary psychiatric disorder not in remission; (7) changed their hormonal or targeted therapies for the past 4 weeks or planned to initiate or change them in the coming 8 weeks; (8) altered the dose of somnogenic medications (e.g., hypnotics, sedatives, antidepressants) in the past 8 weeks prior to study enrollment.

After the initial screening, trained research staff conducted interviews with potential participants to confirm their eligibility. Eligible participants provided informed consent and completed enrollment assessments, which included demographics (e.g., age, race, education), clinical characteristics (e.g., cancer stage, years since diagnosis, cancer treatments), and symptom burden measures (e.g., insomnia, CRCI, pain). This analysis included 260 participants who completed enrollment assessment.

Patient-reported subjective cognitive impairment : We used the perceived cognitive impairment (PCI) subscale from the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Cognitive Function (FACT-Cog), version 3, to assess CRCI by patient self-report. FACT-Cog is one of the most widely recognized and commonly used self-reported instruments in both research and in clinical settings to evaluate cognitive function in adult cancer patients [ 24 ,  25 ]. The FACT-Cog’s 37 items yield four subscales: perceived cognitive impairment, perceived cognitive abilities, impact on quality of life, and comments from others [ 25 ,  26 ]. Each item is rated on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 0 “Never” or “Not at all” to 4 “Several times a day” or “Very much” over the past 7 days. For this analysis, we focused on the total score of the PCI subscale (Cronbach’s α 0.94) [ 27 ], which ranges from 0 to 72, with lower score indicating greater perceived cognitive impairment. A clinically meaningful cutoff score suggesting potential perceived cognitive impairment in female breast cancer survivors is below 54 [ 28 ] (subjective CRCI).

Standardized objective cognitive performance : The Hopkins Verbal Learning Test – Revised (HVLT-R) [ 29 ] was used to provide a standardized measure of cognitive performance. The HVLT-R is a widely-used verbal learning and memory test that is recommended by the International Cognition and Cancer Task Force (ICCTF) guidelines and has high validity and test-retest reliability [ 30 ,  31 ]. The HVLT-R assesses participants’ free-recall of a list of 12 words from three semantic categories and thus provides a more objective assessment of CRCI thought to be unaffected by patients’ appraisal of their cognitive lapses. Participants repeat this free-recall activity for three subsequent trials, and then once again after a delay period of 20–25 min. The test has six equivalent forms available; to mitigate practice effects, three different forms were selected for this trial and administered at the following timepoints: Week 0, Week 10, and Week 26. For this analysis, we focused on the “Delayed Recall” score (range: 0–12; Cronbach’s α 0.94) [ 32 ,  33 ], which is the number of words recalled in the single delay trial. We used published norms[ 34 ] provided in the HVLT-R/BVMT-R Software Portfolio (Version 1.10.031; Psychological Assessment Resources, Lutz, FL) to convert raw Delayed Recall scores to age-matched T-scores. T-scores below 40 were considered to indicate below average cognitive performance (objective CRCI).

Insomnia – Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) : The ISI, a 7-item self-report screen for insomnia, was used to assess patient sleep difficulties with Cronbach’s α of 0.90 [ 35 ]. The ISI has been validated in cancer populations [ 35 ], and clinically-meaningful cutoffs have been established for scores, which range from 0 to 28: no or mild insomnia: 0–14; moderate insomnia: 15–21; and severe insomnia: 22–28 [ 36 ].

Fatigue – Brief Fatigue Inventory (BFI) Worst Fatigue : The BFI is a valid self-report questionnaire with Cronbach’s α of 0.96 [ 37 ]. It consists of 9 items, including one item that assesses a participants’ worst fatigue over the past 24 h on a scale of 0 (no fatigue) to 10 (as bad as you can imagine) [ 37 ]. The BFI Worst Fatigue score (range:0–10) is a commonly-used proxy for patient fatigue severity, and is recommended by the recent American Society of Clinical Oncology [ 38 ] and Society for Integrative Oncology guidelines for the assessment of cancer-related fatigue [ 39 ]. Clinically meaningful cutoffs have been established: no or mild fatigue: 0–3; moderate fatigue: 4–6; and severe fatigue: 7–10 [ 37 ].

Pain: Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System – Global Health (PROMIS – Global Health) Pain Item : The PROMIS Global Health scale is a 10-item scale that includes a single-item measure for pain intensity. The pain item asks participants to rate their average pain over the past 7 days on a scale from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable), with the following cutoffs: 0–3 (none to mild), 4–6 (moderate), and 7–10 (severe). This item has been validated for use in diverse populations, [ 40 ] demonstrates good test-retest reliability, [ 41 ] and has shown adequate responsiveness in detecting clinically meaningful changes in pain in longitudinal studies [ 42 ].

Anxiety – Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale – Anxiety (HADS-A) : The HADS scale, which has been validated in several populations, including cancer patients. It is a widely-used self-report questionnaire that assesses anxiety and depression with Cronbach’s α of 0.83 (anxiety subscale) and 0.79 (depression subscale) [ 43 ,  44 ]. The HADS-A subscale consists of 7 items and is scored from 0 to 21. Clinically meaningful score cutoffs have been established: no or mild anxiety: 0–7; moderate anxiety: 8–10; severe anxiety: 11–21 [ 45 ].

Depression – Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale – Depression (HADS-D) : The HADS-D subscale is a 7-item questionnaire (score range: 0–21) that has been validated for assessing depression in the cancer population [ 46 ]. The clinically meaningful cutoffs for this subscale are: no or mild depression: 0–7; moderate depression: 8–10; and severe depression: 11–21 [ 45 ].

Cumulative Symptom Burden– Cumulative Symptoms Score (CSS) : The CSS was calculated based on the severity of the five comorbid symptoms described above: insomnia, fatigue, pain, anxiety, and depression. A score was assigned to each symptom based on the cutoff values for severity as described above: 0 = no or mild, 1 = moderate, and 2 = severe. For each patient, we calculated a total score by summing the severity scores of their individual comorbid symptoms, which reflects the patient’s cumulative symptom burden. The cumulated symptom score ranges from 0 to 10 with higher scores indicating a greater symptom burden.

Demographic and Clinical Factors : We collected demographic and clinical data at enrollment from patients to characterize the study population and identify potential confounders. Demographic variables included age, race, ethnicity, education, employment, and marital status. Clinical variables included cancer stage, years since cancer diagnosis, the history of chemotherapy and radiation, and the current use of hormone therapy.

Prior to data modeling, descriptive analyses were performed to summarize patients’ subjective cognitive impairment, objective cognitive performance, and other comorbid symptoms. Pearson correlations were used to examine the relationship between each comorbid symptom and cognition. The strength of correlation was interpreted using the following cut-off points: 0.0 to 0.1 indicates a negligible correlation, 0.1 to 0.39 a weak correlation, 0.4 to 0.69 a moderate correlation, 0.7 to 0.89 a strong correlation, and 0.9 to 1.0 a very strong correlation [ 47 ].

A central concept in this study is the use of the CSS cumulative symptom scores which represents the cumulative severity of five common comorbid symptoms, as an important covariate cognitive outcomes. The rationale for using the CSS, rather than individual symptoms one at a time, rests on a common finding in the symptom cluster literature[ 48 – 50 ] that comorbid symptoms typically cooccur at a high prevalence in cancer survivors. Our own descriptive analyses also showed the same pattern. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participant characteristics. Differences in subjective and objective cognitive outcomes across demographic and clinical characteristics were evaluated using independent-samples t-tests for binary variables and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for variables with more than two categories. Univariate linear regression models were fitted by regressing the cognitive outcomes on the cumulated symptom score as the covariate. Additionally, multivariate regression models were fitted to include potential covariates, including clinical variables (e.g., previous cancer treatments and cancer stage) and other characteristics (e.g., age and ethnicity) at enrollment. These covariates were identified a priori in the ENHANCE study protocol based on their potential associations with cognitive outcomes in breast cancer survivors. Characteristics associated with cognitive outcomes at a significance level of  p  < 0.2 in univariable analyses were considered for inclusion as independent variables in the multivariable linear regression model. Clinical judgment was also applied in the selection process to account for collinearity; for example, when two characteristics were highly associated (e.g., cancer stage and chemotherapy usage), only one was included in the model. A sensitivity analysis additionally included education as a covariate in the multivariable model for objective cognitive performance. All analyses were two-sided with a p-value of less than 0.05 for statistical significance. Cytoscape software[ 51 ] was used to visualize the prevalence and correlations of the symptoms. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS (version 26; IBM Corp).

Participants’ demographic and clinical characteristics are presented in Table  1 . Among the 260 participants, the mean age was 56.6 years (standard deviation [SD] = 10.4). The majority were White (203, 79.0%), non-Hispanic (233, 90%), and had at least a college education (195, 77.0%). More than half (134, 52.8%) were employed full-time at enrollment. A total of 59.2% of participants had stage 0–I breast cancer, with a mean time since diagnosis of 4.7 years (SD = 2.8). Additionally, 53.5% had undergone chemotherapy, 69.2% had received radiation therapy, and 62.7% were receiving hormonal therapy (tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors) at the time of enrollment.

All 260 participants completed the FACT-Cog PCI assessment, with a mean PCI score of 36.0 (SD = 14.0). A total of 230 participants (88.5%) had a PCI score below 54, indicating subjective CRCI that met clinical significance. The HVLT delayed recall assessment was completed by 241 participants, with a mean score of 46.0 (SD = 12.7). Among them, 73 participants (30.3%) had a delayed recall T score below 40, indicating objective CRCI. There was no significant difference in PCI scores between participants with objective CRCI (PCI = 36.2, SD = 13.1) and those without (PCI = 35.8, SD = 15.5) ( p  = 0.84).

Among the 241 participants who completed both the FACT-Cog PCI and HVLT delayed recall assessments, 65 (27.0%) met criteria for both subjective and objective CRCI, while 148 (61.4%) met criteria for subjective CRCI only. Eight participants (3.3%) demonstrated objective CRCI without clinically significant subjective CRCI, and 20 (8.3%) met criteria for neither subjective nor objective CRCI.

Among all participants, fatigue was the most common comorbid symptom, with 90.0% reporting moderate to severe severity. More than half of the participants experienced moderate to severe insomnia (70.0%), followed by pain (45.2%), anxiety (35.4%), and depression (11.5%).

All comorbid symptoms were significantly correlated with subjective CRCI (Fact-Cog PCI scores) (all  p  < 0.001). Among them, fatigue ( r  = -0.40), insomnia ( r  = -0.41), and depression ( r  = -0.40) showed a moderate negative correlation, while anxiety ( r  = -0.39) and pain ( r  = -0.25) indicated a weak, negative correlation. However, only insomnia was significantly correlated with objective CRCI (HVLT delayed recall), showing a weak negative correlation ( r  = -0.20,  p  = 0.001). Figure  1  visualized the prevalence of these symptoms and their correlation with cognition.

A total of 259 participants completed all assessments of comorbid symptoms, allowing for the calculation of a CSS score. Among them, the mean CSS was 4.6 (SD = 2.3).

Univariable linear regression analysis revealed a statistically significant association between CSS and FACT-Cog PCI (Coef. = -3.3, 95% CI = -3.9 to -2.7,  p  < 0.001). To explore potential demographic and clinical factors affecting FACT-Cog PCI, univariable analyses (Table  1 ) identified possible differences in FACT-Cog PCI based on age, ethnicity, years since cancer diagnosis, cancer stage, chemotherapy history, and current hormonal therapy (all  p  < 0.20). In multivariable linear regression models including these factors, age and chemotherapy were significantly associated with FACT-Cog PCI (both  p  < 0.05), indicating that these patient characteristics may impact subjective cognitive function (Table  2 ).

After adjusting for age and chemotherapy in the multivariable linear regression model with CSS, the association between CSS and FACT-Cog PCI remained significant. A higher CSS was significantly associated with a lower FACT-Cog PCI (Coef. = -3.0, 95% CI = -3.6 to -2.4,  p  < 0.001) (Table  3 ). Additionally, older age was significantly associated with higher FACT-Cog PCI (Coef. = 0.2, 95% CI = 0.1 to 0.4,  p  = 0.001).

However, in contrast to FACT-Cog PCI, univariable linear regression showed that the CSS score was not significantly associated with the HVLT-R delayed T-score (Coef. = -0.20, 95% CI = -0.90 to 0.51,  p  = 0.58). The association remained non-significant after adjusting for additional potential factors that could impact the HVLT-R delayed T-score ( p  < 0.20 in Table  1 ), including age, ethnicity, and cancer stage, in multivariable linear regression models (Coef. = − 0.17, 95% CI: − 0.88 to 0.55,  p  = 0.64). In a sensitivity analysis, education was additionally included as a covariate because the HVLT-R normative data are adjusted only for age but not education. The association between CSS and HVLT-R delayed T-scores remained non-significant (Coef. = − 0.06, 95% CI: − 0.78 to 0.67,  p  = 0.88), and education was not significantly associated with objective cognition ( p  = 0.46).

Cancer-related cognitive impairment remains a common and challenging problem for cancer survivors and evidence-based solutions are still limited. While insomnia has been previously found to be associated with CRCI, this study also evaluated the influence of additional comorbid symptoms among breast cancer survivors with self-reported insomnia and cognitive impairment who seek care through a clinical trial. Results showed that cumulative symptom burden was significantly associated with subjective—but not objective—CRCI, suggesting that managing comorbid symptoms may be a promising strategy to improve perceived cognitive function. Given that only insomnia was corelated with objective CRCI, targeted treatment of insomnia has the potential to improve objective cognitive functions in women with breast cancer.

Our study contributes to the growing body of literature showing CRCI is a multifactorial symptom. We identified a high symptom burden: all comorbid symptoms assessed—fatigue, insomnia, pain, anxiety, and depression—were common, with prevalence rates two to four times higher than those reported in the general breast cancer survivors [ 52 ]. Each of these symptoms was strongly associated with subjective CRCI, consistent with previous findings [ 12 ,  53 ]. Notably, we also assessed cumulative symptom burden to evaluate its overall impact on cognitive function—a novel approach in this context—which also showed a strong association with subjective CRCI. Previous research suggests that psychological and physical symptoms may increase the mental effort required for daily tasks for cancer patients, thereby negatively affecting patients’ perception of their cognitive functioning [ 54 ]. These findings highlight that not only individual symptom but also the overall comorbid symptom burden significantly shapes subjective cognitive experience in this cohort of breast cancer survivors with co-occurring CRCI and insomnia.

We also observed that older age was associated with better subjective cognitive function, a finding that is consistent with some previous studies and may reflect differences in symptom perception across age groups [ 55 ,  56 ]. Older survivors may be more likely to attribute cognitive changes to normal aging, whereas younger survivors often face greater work and family demands and may therefore be more aware of cognitive difficulties [ 55 ]. Interestingly, chemotherapy was no longer associated with subjective CRCI after accounting for cumulative symptom burden, suggesting that cognitive complaints may be influenced by the broader burden of co-occurring symptoms beyond the direct effects of chemotherapy alone. Similarly, hormonal therapy was not associated with cognition in our cohort. Although endocrine therapy has been linked to cognitive symptoms in some studies, findings have been inconsistent, and the magnitude of cognitive effects may vary according to treatment type, duration, and patient characteristics [ 57 ].

In contrast, no significant association was observed between symptom burden and objective CRCI; only insomnia showed a significant correlation. Our findings differ from the only study we identified that examined the influence of accumulated indicators on CRCI, which reported a significant association with objective cognition [ 58 ]. Notably, that study used the Deficit Accumulation Frailty Index (DAFI) to measure accumulated indicators, which primarily includes items related to chronic diseases (e.g., diabetes), functional impairments (e.g., difficulty walking), and clinical abnormalities, in addition to some symptoms [ 59  ]. These indicators tend to reflect long-term physiological vulnerability or biological aging rather than patient-reported symptom experience, which may account for their different associations with objective CRCI. However, consistent with previous research, [ 16 ,  60 ] insomnia appears to play a significant role in objective cognitive function. Sleep is essential for normal cognitive processes, such as memory consolidation [ 61 ,  62 ]. Neurobiological studies suggest that insomnia may increase the risk of cognitive decline by contributing to reduced gray matter volume and compromised white matter integrity in the brain—factors associated with impairments in attention, memory, visuospatial ability, executive function, and verbal memory [ 63 ]. The distinct contributors to subjective and objective CRCI highlight the need for tailored approaches in their assessment and management.

Our study also confirms previous research showing that only a subset of patients with subjective cognitive complaints exhibits objective, and that the severity of these two are often not related [ 12 ]. This discrepancy may partly stem from the way each type of cognition is assessed [ 64 ]. Subjective cognitive measures typically reflect the everyday cognitive challenges patients face. In contrast, objective cognition is evaluated through structured, time-limited neuropsychological tests conducted under optimal conditions, that may reduce the influence of real-life stressors [ 65 ]. Furthermore, many neurocognitive batteries were originally designed to detect more severe impairments, such as dementia, which affect functional independence. [ 65 ,  66 ] While cancer survivors with sufficient cognitive reserve may still score within the normal range on these tests, even experiencing real-life difficulties. Additionally, brain imaging studies have shown that some treatment-related abnormalities—such as reduced fractional anisotropy associated with cognitive decline—can return to baseline levels within 3–4 years after treatment [ 67 ]. However, comorbid symptoms often persist for many years and may continue to contribute to subjective CRCI [ 52 ], independent of measurable changes in cognitive function. It is important to note that both subjective and objective measures are valuable when evaluating CRCI, as they assess different aspects of cognitive functioning and are influenced by distinct factors.

Our study provides valuable insights into both research and clinical practice. First, to adequately recruit patients with objectively measured CRCI for future studies, researchers may need to screen approximately three times as many patients with self-reported moderate to severe cognitive concerns. Second, the symptom patterns identified in our study suggest that CRCI requires a multicomponent management approach. Given the high prevalence of comorbid symptoms—and their strong association with subjective cognitive impairment— evidence-based comprehensive strategies (such as cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia [CBT-I], exercise interventions for fatigue) that target co-occurring symptom clusters may help alleviate perceived cognitive impairment, especially in the absence of definitive treatments[ 68 ]. Third, since only insomnia was significantly correlated with objective CRCI, addressing sleep disturbances may offer a promising approach to improving objective cognitive function—this warrants further investigation.

Our study has several limitations. First, the data were drawn from the enrollment visit of a clinical trial evaluating an intervention for CRCI, so the recruited population may have reported more cognitive complaints and comorbid symptoms than those in population-based surveys. However, this cohort represents the patients most in need of care and is commonly seen in clinical practice. Second, our study sample included individuals with insomnia and CRCI, so findings may differ from those with CRCI alone. However, both insomnia and CRCI are highly prevalent and closely associated in breast cancer survivors [ 16 ]. Third, most participants had a college-level education or higher. Given that higher education levels may influence neurocognitive test performance [ 69 ], results should be interpreted with caution when applied to populations with lower educational level. Fourth, we included only the HVLT-R as a measure of objective cognitive function. Although this is a well-established and validated test, future studies should consider incorporating additional objective assessments to evaluate other objective cognitive domains. Fifth, multiple comparisons were performed when evaluating associations between individual symptoms and cognitive outcomes. Although most statistically significant findings remained highly significant ( p  < 0.001), these results should be interpreted cautiously and warrant confirmation in future studies. Sixth, the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions regarding the direction of the association between cumulative symptom burden and subjective CRCI. Shared underlying distress or other unmeasured factors may contribute to both symptom burden and perceived cognitive impairment. Future longitudinal studies are needed to clarify these relationships. Seventh, the evaluation of symptom burden is complex. In this study, we used a simple summative score to reflect the cumulative severity of symptoms, which may not fully capture the complexity of symptom burden. Finally, this study was conducted at a large, urban, well-resourced academic cancer center. All participants were English-speaking, and most were white and not Hispanic. As such, our findings may not be generalizable to other settings or patient populations.

Despite these limitations, this study extends previous research by evaluating subjective and objective cognitive function in relation to symptom burden among breast cancer survivors with co-occurring CRCI and insomnia. By focusing on this highly symptomatic cohort, our findings are directly relevant to patients who actively seek clinical care and may be most likely to benefit from interventions targeting symptom clusters. The findings underscore the distinct influences of comorbid symptoms on perceived versus objective cognitive function, highlighting the importance of individualized, symptom-informed approaches to care. These insights can inform the development of more targeted interventions and guide future research aimed at improving both subjective and objective cognitive outcomes in women with breast cancer.

## Efficacy, safety and circulating tumor cell dynamics in patients treated with Eribulin for HER2-negative advanced breast cancer - results from the phase II DETECT IVb trial.

**PMID**: 42747616 · **Journal**: Breast cancer research and treatment · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1007/s10549-026-08069-2 · **PMCID**: PMC13582096

**Authors**: Schochter F, Friedl T W P, Schäffler H, Meier-Stiegen F, Pfister K N, Riethdorf S, Wiesmüller L, Neubauer H, Müller L, Wimberger P, Fasching P A, Lorenz R, Hempel T, Heublein S, Hartkopf A, Pantel K, Rack B, Müller V, Fehm T, Janni W, Cieslik J P

**Types**: Journal Article, Clinical Trial, Phase II

**BACKGROUND**: Eribulin is a non-taxane microtubule inhibitor that showed survival benefits for pretreated metastatic breast cancer (MBC) patients. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are a prognostic marker, but their role in predicting response to specific MBC treatments is less clear. In this trial, we assessed the clinical outcome and its association with CTC-dynamics in HER2-negative MBC treated with eribulin.

**PATIENTS AND METHODS**: HER2-negative MBC-patients were screened for CTCs within the DETECT study program using the CellSearch® technology (Menarini Silicon Biosystems; Bologna, Italy). Patients with HER2-negative CTCs were eligible for the single-arm DETECT-IVb study treatment with eribulin. Primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), and secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), CTC-clearance rate and safety.

**RESULTS**: Median PFS and OS were 4.6 months and 13.4 months, respectively. Multivariable adjusted analyses showed that patients with CTC-clearance at first follow-up (34.7%) had significantly improved PFS (p = 0.043) but not OS (p = 0.192) compared to patients with at least 1 CTC. Likewise, patients with CTC-clearance at the end of the treatment (23.1%) achieved a significantly better PFS (p = 0.015) but not OS (p = 0.218). Neutropenia, leukopenia, anemia and fatigue were the most common adverse events and no new or unexpected safety signals were obtained.

**CONCLUSION**: In this trial, we could confirm eribulin as an effective treatment option in high-risk HER2-negative MBC. CTCs proved their role as a prognostic marker and our results support the potential role of CTC dynamics as an early biomarker of treatment response to eribulin.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: EudraCTNo2013-001269-18 http://ClinicalTrials.gov , TRN NCT02035813, Registration date 2014-01-12.

Therapies in incurable metastatic breast cancer (MBC) focus on prolonging survival and maintaining quality of life. According to current guidelines, single-agent chemotherapy is the preferred treatment option if chemotherapy is indicated [ 1 ]. Eribulin is a non-taxane, microtubule dynamic inhibitor with both antimitotic activities and non-mitotic effects on tumor biology, tumor environment, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) [ 2 – 5 ], which significantly improved overall survival (OS) in pretreated MBC patients [ 6 – 8 ]. Given the role of eribulin in the therapy of MBC, it is important to further investigate the molecular mechanisms and to identify biomarkers predictive of eribulin response.

Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) showed their prognostic value in several MBC studies [ 9 ]. Although there is some evidence that repeated CTC measurements can predict therapy response [ 10 – 12 ], until now no clinical trial using CTC-enumeration as a decision tool for therapeutic interventions has succeeded. The DETECT study program uses an alternative approach, where not only the number but also phenotypic characteristics of CTCs are considered for the choice of individualized treatment options [ 13 ,  14 ].

The DETECT IVb study reported here focuses on MBC patients with HER2-negative disease according to both primary tumor histology and CTCs and evaluates treatment efficacy of eribulin in these patients. A particular interest was to analyze outcome in relation to CTC prevalence, dynamics and clearance rates under therapy to assess the utility of CTCs as an early treatment monitoring tool for MBC patients receiving eribulin.

The phase II DETECT IV trial (EudraCT Number 2013-001269-18, ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier  NCT02035813 ) is part of the prospective, multicenter DETECT study program for patients with MBC [ 14 ]. The DETECT study program involves an initial CTC-screening to determine presence and HER2-status of CTCs in patients with HER2-negative MBC, who could not be treated by surgery or radiotherapy alone. CTC-positive patients (at least one CTC in 7.5 m of blood) with only HER2-negative CTCs could be recruited in the DETECT IV trial, which comprises two cohorts (DETECT IVa and DETECT IVb) that represent two separate and independent single-arm studies. In DETECT IVb, which is reported here, patients with either triple-negative tumors or hormone receptor positive tumors and indication for chemotherapy received single-agent chemotherapy with eribulin (HALAVEN ® ). The DETECT IV trial was performed in accordance to the Declaration of Helsinki, adhered to good clinical practice and was approved by the responsible sponsor’s ethics committee (MC-LKP-668).

CTC assessments in the DETECT study program were performed using the CellSearch technology (Menarini Silicon Biosystems, Bologna, Italy) as described in Riethdorf et al. [ 15 ]. Peripheral blood samples of 7.5 ml were collected into CellSave Tubes and sent to CTC laboratories, where they were analyzed within 96 h. HER2 expression was categorized based on an immunohistochemistry (IHC) score as negative (IHC 0), weak (IHC 1+), moderate (IHC 2+) or strong (IHC 3+) according to Riethdorf et al. [ 16 ]. To be eligible for inclusion in the DETECT IVb study, patients had to be CTC-positive with all CTCs showing HER2-negativity (defined as IHC score 0, 1 + or 2+).

Patients were recruited from March 2015 to October 2019 and provided written informed consent. Eribulin doses are administered according to the European prescribing information 1.23 mg/m 2  with possible dose reductions to 0.97 or 0.62 mg/m 2 ; these are equivalent to 1.4, 1.1, and 0.7 mg/m² eribulin mesylate as used in the US prescribing information. Treatment duration was up to 12 months, with a 24-month follow-up. Study visits were scheduled every six weeks, radiological tumor evaluation per RECIST 1.1 every 12 weeks. Blood sampling for CTC-analysis was recommended at tumor evaluations and at the end of the treatment period.

Safety was evaluated by the frequency of adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) graded according to international Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 4.0.

The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS); secondary end points included overall survival (OS), CTC clearance rate, and safety. CTC clearance rate was defined as proportion of patients with no evidence of detectable CTCs (0 CTCs/7.5 mL blood) during follow-up among all patients (CTC positivity at baseline was one of the inclusion criteria; see above). CTC counts were further categorized according to the established prognostic cutoff described by Cristofanilli et al. (< 5 vs. ≥5 CTCs/7.5 mL blood), defining low and high CTC burden, respectively [ 17 ]. CTCs were assessed at two follow-up timepoints: first on-treatment follow-up (≥ 21 days after registration) and at the end of study treatment. Baseline characteristics were summarized using absolute and relative frequencies for categorical and ordinal variables, and using median and range for continuous variables. Associations between CTC status and categorical clinical parameters were assessed using chi square tests; in case of expected frequencies of less than 5 in 2 × 2 contingency tables, Fisher’s exact test was used instead. PFS and OS were calculated from registration to progressive disease or death, respectively, with patients without known events being censored at the date of last adequate follow-up. Survival outcomes were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared by log-rank tests. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for predefined prognostic factors including metastatic treatment line (first vs. second vs. third or higher), metastasis-free interval (≤ 12 months, including de novo metastatic disease vs. > 12 months), and site of first metastasis (bone, no visceral vs. visceral, no bone vs. bone and visceral vs. other). To test whether the addition of the variable CTC status (at baseline and/or during follow up) significantly improved the model, we added CTC status to the multivariable Cox regression model and used the likelihood-ratio test to assess changes in model fit. There was no significant time-by-variable interaction for any of the included variables (all  p  > 0.10), indicating that the proportional hazard assumption was not violated. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 26 (IBM Corp, Armonk, New York, USA). All tests were two-sided with a significance level α of  p  < 0.05, and no adjustments of the significance level for multiple testing were made.

Overall, 1091 patients with HER2-negative MBC were screened for CTCs within the DETECT study program starting in December 2014. Due to low recruitment rate, enrollment for DETECT IVb was terminated prematurely in October 2019. Rather than the planned 120 patients, the final intention-to-treat (ITT) population for DETECT IVb comprised 109 registered patients. (CONSORT flow diagram, Supplementary Fig. 1).

The median age of enrolled patients was 62 years, and 87.2% of patients were postmenopausal. Most patients (75.2%) had hormone receptor-positive (luminal-like) tumors, while 20.2% had triple-negative disease. A metastasis-free interval of more than 12 months was observed in 84.4% of patients. Eribulin was administered as first-line treatment for MBC in 28.4% of patients. Detailed baseline characteristics are summarized in Table  1 .

Study treatment with eribulin was discontinued in 98 patients (89.9%). The most frequent reason for treatment discontinuation was progress (71 patients), followed by non-haematological toxicity (7 patients), patient withdrawal (6 patients), treatment delay (5 patients), death (4 patients), haematological toxicity (2 patients) and other reasons (3 patients).

Disease progression occurred in 87 patients (79.8%). Median PFS was 4.6 months (95% CI 3.3–6.0 months), with 1-year and 2-year PFS rates of 10.4% and 3.5%, respectively (Fig.  1 A). Overall, 88 patients (80.7%) died. Median OS was 13.4 months (95% CI 10.7–16.1 months); the 1-year and 2-year OS rates were 53.4% and 26.0%, respectively (Fig.  1 B). One patient with disease progression was censored for OS at the date of last contact because the exact date of death was unknown.

Fig. 1 Kaplan-Meier survival plots for progression-free survival ( A ) and overall survival ( B )

Log-rank tests, univariable and adjusted multivariable Cox proportional hazard models showed that only metastatic treatment line but not metastasis-free interval, site of first metastatic disease, patient age and tumor subtype significantly affected PFS and OS in our patient cohort (Supplementary Results 1, Supplementary Tables 1, 2).

In total, 1343 adverse events (AEs) of any grade and 181 AEs of grade ≥ 3 were observed during the study. Two patients did not receive study treatment because of withdrawal (one case) or death (one case) before the first study visit. Overall, 105 (96.3%) patients had at least one AE of any grade and 73 patients (67.0%) had at least one grade 3–5 AE. Adverse events occurring in ≥ 10% of patients (any grade) and AEs grade ≥ 3 occurring in ≥ 2% of patients are presented in Table  2 .

The most frequent AEs of any grade observed in more than 25% of patients were fatigue (54.1%), alopecia (46.8%), peripheral sensory neuropathy (34.9%), nausea (30.3%), neutropenia (29.4%), constipation (28.4%), and anemia (24.8%). The most common grade ≥ 3 or higher observed in more than 10% of patients were neutropenia (21.1%) and leukopenia (15.6%).

Overall, 71 serious adverse events (SAE) were reported in 49 patients. Most frequently reported SAEs were dyspnea (5 patients), pleural effusion (5 patients), febrile neutropenia (3 patients) and febrile leukopenia (1 patient). A possible relationship to eribulin treatment was reported for 25 SAEs, and no suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction (SUSAR) occurred.

There were 89 deaths, predominantly due to disease progression (81 cases). In six cases, the cause of death was unknown. Two deaths (stroke and subdural hemorrhage) were assessed as not related to study treatment.

At baseline, the median CTC count was 5 CTCs (range 1–482), consistent with the inclusion criterion for this study; 59 patients had ≥ 5 CTCs. Baseline CTC status (< 5 CTCs/≥ 5 CTCs) did not differ significantly according to tumor subtype ( p  = 0.170), metastatic treatment line ( p  = 0.222), metastasis-free interval ( p  = 0.915), or site of first metastatic disease ( p  = 0.966).

Baseline CTC status (≥ 5 CTCs vs. 1–4 CTCs) was not significantly associated with PFS in univariable analysis (HR 1.31, 95% CI 0.85–2.01; Supplementary Fig. 2A) but significantly associated with OS (HR 1.72, 95% CI 1.12–2.65; Supplementary Fig. 2B). Inclusion of baseline CTC status in the multivariable Cox regression model - adjusted for metastatic treatment line, metastasis-free interval, site of first metastatic disease, tumor subtype and patient age - significantly improved model fit for both PFS ( p  = 0.041) and OS ( p  = 0.001). Baseline CTC status (≥ 5 CTCs vs. 1–4 CTCs) remained independently associated with outcome, with hazard ratios of 1.63 (95% CI 1.02–2.62) for PFS and 2.25 (95% CI 1.36–3.74) for OS (Tables  3  and  4 ).
