<!-- ===== PMID 42745462 ===== -->
## Epidemiological and Clinical Risk Factors for Breast Cancer-Related Lymphedema: A Case-Control Study From Hamadan, Western Iran.

**PMID**: 42745462 · **Journal**: BioMed research international · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1155/bmri/8099570 · **PMCID**: PMC13578934

**Authors**: Rahbar Soulmaz, Radinmehr Hojjat, Asadi Mohammad Reza, Roghani Tayebeh, Tabatabaei Azade, Sedighi Pashaki Abdolazim, Ayubi Erfan

**Types**: Journal Article

**BACKGROUND**: Breast cancer-related lymphedema (BCRL) is one of main issues following treatments in patients with breast cancer (BC). The current study is aimed at evaluating epidemiological and clinical risk factors for BCRL in female patients with BC.

**METHODS**: In a case-control study design from October 2024 to March 2025, female BC patients with and without BCRL were recruited from the Lymphedema Physiotherapy Clinic and the Cancer Therapeutic and Diagnosis Imaging Center in Hamadan, Western Iran. Patient, tumor, and treatment characteristics were gathered via interview and reviewing medical and pathology records.

**RESULTS**: Overall, 230 patients (127 cases and 103 controls) were included. The multivariable analysis revealed several potential risk factors for BCRL: older age at diagnosis (odds ratio [OR] = 1.05; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.00, 1.10), urban residency (4.76; 1.20, 20.00), axillary lymph node dissection number of 6-9 compared to ≤ 5 (2.54; 0.99, 6.49), pathology grade of 2 (7.11; 1.47, 34.27) and 3 (6.53; 1.32, 32.32) compared to Grade 1, mastectomy versus lumpectomy (2.86; 1.23, 6.67), receiving chemotherapy (9.55; 1.23, 73.95), and positive progesterone receptor (PR) status (2.56; 1.16, 5.55).

**CONCLUSION**: The combination of patient, tumor, and treatment characteristics may be associated with BCRL, highlighting the close monitoring of high-risk patients (older age, high-grade tumors, mastectomy, and PR-positive) in Western Iran.

Globally, female breast cancer (BC) is second in new case numbers among all cancers and ranks fourth in the number of deaths [ 1 ,  2 ]. In 2020, over 2.3 million new cases and 685,000 deaths from female BC were reported worldwide. However, the cancer burden projections show that the incident cases and deaths will exceed 3 million and 1 million, respectively, by 2040 [ 3 ]. Therefore, early diagnosis, immediate start of treatment, and improving survival are pivotal aspects in the management of female BC.

A delayed diagnosis of the BC can necessitate the application of more aggressive treatment procedures, which can result in complications such as lymphedema [ 4 ,  5 ]. Breast cancer‐related lymphedema (BCRL) is a chronic condition resulting from impaired lymphatic drainage, so protein‐rich lymphatic fluid abnormally accumulates in the interstitial tissues, and limbs become swollen [ 6 ]. Pain, redness, tightness, heaviness, paresthesia, fibrosis, and impaired function are common symptoms and complications due to swelling in the limbs. BCRL can along with psychological and physical consequences, which can reduce patients′ quality of life [ 7 ]. On the other hand, prospective surveillance programs with prompt intervention can reduce risk of BCRL [ 8 ].

Although treatment‐related factors are suggested as leading risk factors for the BCRL, there was evidence regarding the role of demographic, anthropometric, physiological, and biochemical factors in the development of BCRL [ 9 – 11 ]. There is still controversy on well‐established risk factors of the BCRL in terms of direction and strength of association because the results of previous clinical prediction models are function of study population, candidate predictors, and type of model development [ 11 ]. In other words, the risk factors of BCRL may vary across different populations. Developing clinical prediction models in independent populations can guide interventions within those populations effectively.

In Iran, BC is first rank in incidence and mortality rates among women [ 1 ,  2 ]. Female BC is one of the three cancers that has seen the greatest increase in recent years [ 12 ]. There is spatial inequality in the distribution of female BC within Iran and the trend in incidence and mortality rates varies across the provinces of Iran. For example, Hamadan province was among those with a higher percentage change in incidence rates [ 13 ]. Although the epidemiology of female BC is well understood, there is still a lack of knowledge regarding other important aspects, such as complications following BC treatments, for example, BCRL [ 14 ]. Considering the above issues, the current study is aimed at evaluating epidemiological and clinical risk factors for BCRL in female patients with BC in Hamadan, Western Iran.

In this case‐control study, female patients with BC were included from October 2024 to March 2025. Patients aged 18 and over and with surgical history were enrolled into the study after obtaining informed consent. Patients with a history of trauma or limb surgery, as well as those with conditions that can cause edema or swelling such as myocardial infarction, renal disease, or gastrointestinal disorders were excluded. Female BC patients with BCRL, as the case group, were selected from those referred to the lymphedema physiotherapy clinic affiliated with the Rehabilitation Faculty, Hamadan University of Medical Sciences. Those without BCRL, as control group, were selected from patients who had visited the Mahdieh Therapeutic and Diagnosis Imaging Center in Hamadan for therapeutic process. All patients were female BC survivors, defined according to the National Cancer Institute as individuals from the time of cancer diagnosis through the remainder of life [ 15 ]. Patients who were alive and available for interview during the study period were included, and clinical data were extracted from medical records.

Circumferential assessment of both the affected and unaffected upper limbs was conducted at seven standardized anatomical landmarks. These landmarks included Point 1, located at the base of the fingers along the little finger; Point 2, at the base of the thumb; Point 3, at the wrist; Point 4, positioned midway between the wrist and the elbow crease; Point 5, at the elbow crease; Point 6, located halfway between the elbow crease and the axillary fold; and Point 7, situated 2 cm distal to the axillary fold. To identify the presence of lymphedema, circumferential measurements of the affected limb were compared with those of the contralateral unaffected limb by narrow tape. Lymphedema was diagnosed when the interlimb difference exceeded 2 cm or was ≥ 2 cm at any single measurement site, or when the cumulative difference across all measurement sites exceeded 5 cm or was ≥ 5 cm [ 16 ]. The stage of BCRL was defined according to the International Society of Lymphology (ISL) guidelines [ 17 ].

To determine the sample size, the assumed proportion of mastectomy in the BC without BCRL was considered 52% based on previous study [ 14 ]. Considering a minimum detectable odds ratio (OR) of at least 2.25, two‐sided confidence interval (CI) of 95% ( α  = 0.05), a power of 80% ( β  = 0.20), and a case‐to‐control ratio of 1, the minimum sample size was estimated to be 105 per group.

Patient characteristics, including age at the time of BC diagnosis, marital status, education level, place of residence, type of insurance coverage, number of children, smoking status, family history of BC, and comorbidity with other chronic diseases, were gathered via interview with the patients. Height was measured in a standing position (e.g., without shoes, upright, feet together, heels, and shoulders) against the wall using a tape meter. Weight was measured using a digital electronic weighing scale while wearing minimal clothing and without shoes. Tumor and treatment characteristics were extracted from medical and pathology records. These characteristics involved tumor size, number of axillary lymph node dissection (ALND), number of involved lymph nodes, metastasis, pathological grade, status of hormone receptors, type of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy.

The characteristics were compared between the two study groups using independent  t  test and chi square test, as appropriate. Variables with a  p  value ≤ 0.10 in univariate analysis were considered potential predictors and were retained for multivariable analysis, in line with the recommendations of Steyerberg and Van Calster [ 18 ], who demonstrated that using conventional low  p  value thresholds (e.g., 0.05) for variable selection in prognostic models leads to testimation bias, the exaggeration of effect estimates. The multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to estimate the adjusted associations. A  p  value ≤ 0.05 was considered as statistical significance in the multivariable analysis. The results were presented as OR with 95% CI. The discriminatory ability of the multivariable analysis was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC‐ROC). As a limited sample size is expected in the combination of risk factors and BCRL levels, a sensitivity analysis using penalized logistic regression via data augmentation with a plausible prior interval for the true effect (OR between 1/40 and 40) was performed to shrink unstable estimates and reduce bias due to sparse data [ 19 ]. All statistical analyses were performed using Stata software Version 14.

Overall, 230 patients (127 cases, 103 controls) were included in the analysis. The median (Quartile 1–Quartile 3) time from surgery to study enrollment of cases and controls was 30 (21–50) and 17 (9–50) months, respectively. Among patients with BCRL, the median time from surgery to lymphedema onset was 11 months (Quartile 1–Quartile 3: 5–25 months; range: 1–72 months), and the median lymphedema duration was 16 months (Quartile 1–Quartile 3: 5–32 months; range: 1–72 months). The left arm was the most affected side (68, 53.5%), and most patients had Grade 2 lymphedema (70, 55.12%). Regarding observed signs, the most frequent sign was fibrosis (50, 39.37%), and 61 patients (48.03%) had no observable signs. Concerning treatment received for BCRL, the most common treatments were massage (45, 35.43%) and lymphotherapy (17, 13.39%). Additionally, 24 patients (18.90%) received complementary and alternative medicine, including leech therapy and cupping, whereas 35 patients (27.56%) received no treatment (Table  1 ).

Table  2  demonstrates the comparison of patient characteristics between the two study groups. The patients with BCRL were older at time diagnosis (49.86 vs. 46.68,  p  = 0.01), mostly living in urban areas (96.85% vs. 85.44%,  p  = 0.002) compared to those without BCRL. The percentage of employed was higher in patients without BCRL, whereas the percentage of retired was higher in those with BCRL ( p  = 0.06). The mean of BMI in patients with BCRL was more than those without BCRL (mean difference = 1.16,  p  = 0.07).

As shown in Table  3 , the patients with BCRL had higher percentage of involved lymph nodes in advanced stages (e.g., for N3: 28.81% vs. 3.49%,  p  = 0.01), the percentage of ALND (e.g., for ≥ 10: 37.40% vs. 32.58%;  p  = 0.07), compared to those without BCRL. The distribution of pathology grade was significantly between the two studied groups. The percentage of Grade 3 in patients with BCRL was 36.13%, whereas this figure in another group was 31.76% ( p  = 0.004). The progesterone receptor (PR) positivity in patients with BCRL was about 14% higher than those without BCRL (75.41% vs. 61.63%,  p  = 0.03). Mastectomy surgery is more frequently performed in the case group compared with control group (34.13% vs. 21.57%,  p  = 0.03). The percentage of chemotherapy among patients with BCRL (97.64%) was higher than those without BCRL (92.23%) ( p  = 0.05). No significant differences were observed regarding radiotherapy treatment.

The multivariable analysis showed that each 1‐year increase in age at diagnosis was associated with 5% higher odds of lymphedema (OR = 1.05; 95% CI, 1.00, 1.10;  p  = 0.016). Patients residing in rural areas had 79% lower BCRL compared to those in urban areas (0.21, 0.05, 0.83;  p  = 0.026). The odds of BCRL for patients with ALND 6–9 was 2.54 times higher compared to those with ALND ≤ 5 ( p  = 0.052). Pathology Grades 2 and 3 were associated with higher odds of BCRL compared to grade 1 (OR = 7.11 and 6.53, respectively;  p  < 0.05). The odds of BCRL were approximately 2.86 times higher after mastectomy compared to lumpectomy ( p  = 0.014). PR positivity was associated with 2.56‐fold higher odds of BCRL ( p  = 0.02). Chemotherapy was also associated with increased odds of BCRL ( p  = 0.031) (Table  4 ). The predictive power of the multivariable model was 80% (AUC‐ROC [95% CI] = 0.78 [0.72, 0.82]) (Figure  1 ).

The sensitivity analysis using penalized logistic regression showed that chemotherapy, ALND 6–9, and pathology Grade 3 were no longer statistically significant, suggesting degree of precision uncertainty in their initial estimates. However, age at diagnosis, rural residence, pathology Grade 2, mastectomy, and PR positivity remained robust, supporting their independent association with BCRL (Table  4 ).

Our results showed older age at diagnosis, urban residency, greater number of ALND, higher pathology grade, mastectomy, chemotherapy, and PR positivity may be associated with BCRL.

The systematic reviews on the previous studies identified that common characteristics for predicting BCRL were BMI, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, mastectomy, and ALND [ 9 – 11 ,  20 ]. In our multivariable model, pathology grade, place of residence, ALND, PR, surgery type, chemotherapy, and age at diagnosis remained significant predictors, showing the strongest associations and making the largest contributions to the prediction. BMI, lymph node, and occupation were not significantly associated with risk of BCRL. One study in Iran showed that characteristics such as the lymph node involvement ratio, the number of removed lymph nodes, heaviness, and undergoing radiotherapy are the main and important predictors for BCRL [ 14 ]. An Australian study identified ALND, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and BMI as significant predictors of BCRL, whereas mastectomy, age, and smoking showed no significant association [ 21 ]. A longitudinal study on the population of Latin America identified radiotherapy, obesity, seroma formation after surgery, chemotherapy infusion in the affected limb and advanced staging as significant predictors [ 5 ]. A study in China found that older age, lower income, mastectomy, postsurgical wound infection, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy significantly increased the risk of BCRL [ 22 ]. Another study on a European population identified ALND, lymph node involvement, complications following surgery, BMI, and number of dissected lymph nodes as significant predictors [ 23 ].

Our model can discriminate between female BC with and without BCRL with 78% accuracy. One study found that the application of a saturated model incorporating a combination of demographic, clinical, and lymphedema‐specific characteristics with an ensemble machine learning method yielded 91% accuracy [ 14 ]. A comprehensive review showed that the predictive power of models for predicting BCRL ranged from 68% to 91% [ 11 ]. This indicates that in order to increase the predictive ability, future studies should focus on identifying new predictors, combining biological and clinical data, and applying advanced techniques for model development and validation, such as machine learning and deep learning algorithms.

Our finding showed that PR positivity was associated with increased risk of BCRL. In the univariate analysis, there was a borderline association between PR positivity and BCRL ( p  = 0.063). Although this value did not reach the conventional threshold of 0.05, however, the PR has been included in the multivariate analysis according to a previous recommendations that variables with  p  value ≤ 0.10 or 0.20 in univariate analysis be retained for multivariable adjustment to avoid exaggeration of effect estimates [ 18 ]. Interestingly, the multivariable analysis showed a significant association for PR positivity ( p  = 0.02). However, given the borderline nature of the univariate finding, this result should be interpreted with caution and considered as hypothesis‐generating rather than conclusive. One possible explanation is that PR‐positive patients are more likely to receive adjuvant chemotherapy, which may be associated with more extensive ALND and consequently a higher risk of BCRL. Our finding is partially consistent with a recent Iranian study [ 24 ], which reported a higher odd of advanced BCRL stage among PR‐positive patients, although the association did not reach statistical significance. The directionality of both studies is similar, suggesting that PR positivity might play a role in BCRL pathogenesis, but the marginal significance underscores the need for larger, multicenter studies to confirm this relationship. The discrepancy between our findings and a previous Italian study [ 25 ], which reported a nonsignificant protective effect for PR positivity, may be attributed to differences in study design, patient characteristics, and unmeasured confounders such as hormonal therapy. Future studies specifically designed to evaluate the interplay between hormone receptor status, treatment choices, and lymphatic function are warranted to clarify this association.

Consistent with findings in previous studies [ 5 ,  26 ,  27 ], our study provides evidence regarding the impact of mastectomy and ALND on development of BCRL. However, in contrast to previous studies [ 28 – 30 ], our study was unable to identify radiation therapy as risk factor. The BCRL is a long‐term complication of BC treatments such as radiotherapy [ 31 ,  32 ]. It is likely that the association between radiotherapy and BCRL would be more easily detected if a higher percentage of patients with longer BCRL duration were included.

In this study, the relationship between BMI and BCRL was not statistically significant. The main reason is that number of patients with high BMI (e.g., > 30) was low in our study, as the mean BMI in both groups fell within the overweight category (25 < BMI < 30), and the standard deviation was less than five. The previous studies argued that BMI has a threshold effect on the risk of BCRL. For example, BMI above 30 can significantly increase the risk of BCRL [ 5 ,  21 ,  33 ].

Previous studies have found that BCRL is less likely to be diagnosed in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas [ 21 ,  34 ]. In contrast to previous studies, our study showed that the percentage of BCRL in patients residing in urban areas is higher than that of those in rural areas. It should be noted that accessibility to screening, care and diagnosis services is greater in urban areas, which increases the likelihood of detecting outcomes such as BCRL. Therefore, potential biases including surveillance bias, detection bias, and volunteer bias should be carefully considered when interpreting these results.

Our findings were consistent with previous Iranian studies. A study in Shiraz, Southern Iran, reported that modified radical mastectomy, number of excised lymph nodes, radiotherapy, and BMI ≥ 25 were significant predictors of BCRL [ 35 ]. Another study on patients from Tehran (Central Iran) and Mashhad (Northeast Iran) found that each unit increase in BMI and each additional involved lymph node significantly increased BCRL risk [ 36 ]. Furthermore, a multicenter study provided evidence regarding the potential impact of mastectomy, radiotherapy, and supraclavicular radiation on BCRL, further supporting the role of treatment intensity [ 37 ]. Our findings on patient, tumor, and treatment characteristics were relatively consistent with these reports. However, our study extends the existing literature by providing a risk profile for Western Iran, highlighting urban/rural disparities, and identifying PR positivity as a potential biological predictor of BCRL.

Although our sensitivity analysis did not confirm the statistical significance of some variables such as chemotherapy, ALND 6–9, and pathology Grade 3, these factors should not be ignored as clinically unimportant. It is crucial to distinguish between statistical significance and clinical importance, particularly in the context of limited sample sizes. The wide CIs and unstable estimates observed in our study likely reflect insufficient statistical power rather than a true absence of effect. Therefore, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously, the potential clinical relevance of these risk factors remains, and their role should be further investigated in larger prospective cohorts with adequate power to detect modest but clinically meaningful associations.

There were several limitations that should be considered. First, modeling without validation adds nothing; therefore, it is still necessary to externally validate the developed model using independent datasets. Second, BCRL was measured in dichotomous scale. The categorization of variable can lead to loss of information. Considering other forms of the BCRL, such as its severity or volume, can reveal more accurately and precisely the effects of tumor, treatment and patient risk factors on BCRL. These two limitations have not been addressed because of limited sample size. For example, there was not enough data to apply  k ‐fold cross‐validation to assess the model′s validity. Third, there was limited precision for some risk factors, such as chemotherapy, ALND 6–9, and pathology Grade 3, likely due to sparse data bias. Therefore, larger prospective studies are warranted to provide more precise estimates of these associations. Fourth, the multivariable prediction model for BCRL still needs to be enhanced by incorporating additional risk factors such as BC diagnosis (e.g., ductal carcinoma in situ and invasive lobular carcinoma), mammographic breast density, treatment features (e.g., hormones therapy and number of chemotherapy sessions). Fifth, missing data for some characteristics may have introduced bias, although the small proportion and random nature of missingness (due to incomplete records) suggest minimal impact on the findings. Finally, although both centers for selection of cases and controls are affiliated with Hamadan University of Medical Sciences, serve the same geographic catchment area, and utilized consistent eligibility criteria, the degree of selection bias should still be considered. However, we believe that the potential impact of this bias on our results might be limited. Although we observed differences in age, residency, and occupation—which were adjusted for in multivariable analysis—there were no significant differences in other baseline characteristics such as marital status, education, family history, and comorbidity, supporting the overall comparability of the groups. Additionally, any residual selection bias would likely attenuate the observed associations (i.e., bias towards the null) because controls recruited from the radiology center are likely to have a higher prevalence of aggressive treatments (e.g., ALND, mastectomy, chemotherapy) compared to the general population of BC survivors, as evidenced by the high proportions of controls who had received chemotherapy (92.23%), radiotherapy (97.09%), and ALND with ≥ 10 nodes dissected (32.58%). This would reduce the contrast between cases and controls, leading to an underestimation of the true associations. Therefore, any significant associations we observed are likely conservative estimates of the true effects. Future population‐based or prospective studies are warranted to confirm these results.

Our findings confirm that some well‐known treatment‐related factors remain important predictors of BCRL. However, the results observed in the current study highlight several clinical implications for the Iranian healthcare system. The urban/rural disparity in BCRL suggests the presence of surveillance/detection bias, implying that the true burden of BCRL in rural areas may be underestimated. Consequently, this calls for enhanced outreach and screening programs in underserved regions. The independent role of PR positivity, alongside pathological grade, highlights that tumor biology—not just treatment intensity—may contribute to lymphatic vulnerability. This finding encourages future research into hormonal influences on fluid homeostasis and tissue fibrosis. Finally, the developed risk model provides a simple, accessible tool for clinicians in Western Iran to identify high‐risk patients (older age, high‐grade tumors, mastectomy, and PR‐positive) who would benefit most from prospective surveillance and early physiotherapy interventions, ultimately reducing the morbidity and healthcare costs associated with chronic lymphedema.

Soulmaz Rahbar and Erfan Ayubi conceptualized and supervised the study. Soulmaz Rahbar, Hojjat Radinmehr, Mohammad Reza Asadi, and Abdolazim Sedighi Pashaki participated in data collection and data curation. Soulmaz Rahbar, Tayebeh Roghani, Azade Tabatabaei, Abdolazim Sedighi Pashaki, and Erfan Ayubi contributed to methodology development and data interpretation. Soulmaz Rahbar and Erfan Ayubi performed the statistical analysis. Soulmaz Rahbar and Erfan Ayubi drafted the manuscript.

This work was supported by the Hamadan University of Medical Sciences,  10.13039/501100004697 , 140303292698.

All authors critically reviewed and revised the manuscript, approved the final version, and agreed to be accountable for all aspects of the work.

The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Hamadan University of Medical Sciences (IR.UMSHA.REC.1403.192).

The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

<!-- ===== PMID 42744385 ===== -->
## Spiritual wellbeing in advanced cancer patients receiving palliative care in a tertiary cancer centre in northern Kerala, India: a qualitative study.

**PMID**: 42744385 · **Journal**: BMJ open · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1136/bmjopen-2026-118373 · **PMCID**: PMC13583880

**Authors**: Biji M S, Kc Rajasree, Nair Shoba, Shenoy Praveen Kumar, Spruyt Odette, Venkateswaran Chitra, B Satheesan, Vijayakumar Dehannathparambil Kottarathiil

**Types**: Journal Article

**OBJECTIVES**: Spiritual well-being is an essential component of holistic palliative care. However, patients' lived experiences of spirituality in advanced cancer remain underexplored in low- and middle-income settings. This study aimed to explore spiritual well-being from the perspectives of patients with advanced cancer receiving palliative care in a tertiary cancer centre in Kerala.

**DESIGN**: Qualitative descriptive study using face-to-face, in-depth, semistructured interviews and conventional content analysis conducted between November 2022 and December 2024.

**SETTING**: Outpatient palliative care services of a tertiary cancer centre in Kerala, India.

**PARTICIPANTS**: 20 adults with advanced cancer receiving palliative care were recruited using purposive sampling. Interviews were conducted in Malayalam. Data were audiorecorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using conventional qualitative content analysis as described by Graneheim and Lundman. Data collection continued until saturation was achieved. Trustworthiness was ensured through credibility, dependability, confirmability and authenticity.

**RESULTS**: A total of 127 codes were identified and organised into 18 subthemes and four overarching themes: (1) multidimensional suffering and reflection in advanced cancer, encompassing physical suffering, psycho-existential distress, social concerns, financial burden and moral reflection; (2) healing through social support and relationships, emphasising the supportive roles of family, community and healthcare professionals; (3) coping mechanisms and inner strength, including acceptance, peer inspiration, prior life experiences and adaptive psychological and physical strategies and (4) spiritual beliefs and practices, where faith, prayer, rituals and spiritual questioning contributed to meaning-making and emotional regulation.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Spiritual wellbeing in advanced cancer extends beyond religious practices and is shaped by interconnected experiences of illness, relationships, spiritual beliefs and cultural context. Addressing these dimensions through holistic and culturally sensitive palliative care may enhance emotional resilience and overall quality of life.

Cancer remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. 1  In India, including Kerala, where awareness and healthcare access are relatively high, a substantial proportion of patients continue to present with advanced disease, for whom curative treatment may no longer be feasible. In such situations, palliative care plays a critical role not only in symptom management but also in addressing the psychological, social and spiritual dimensions of suffering. 2

Spiritual well-being is increasingly recognised as a key component of quality of life in advanced cancer and those receiving palliative care. 3  In this study, spiritual well-being is understood as a multidimensional aspect of human experience that relates to the way individuals seek and express meaning, purpose and connectedness and the way in which they experience relationships with themselves, others, nature or the sacred. This understanding is consistent with the definition proposed in the international consensus on spiritual care in palliative care. 4  Accordingly spiritual well-being is conceptualised as something more than a coping strategy or source of social support, encompassing existential, relational and faith related dimensions that influence how a person interprets his or her sufferings. While spiritual concerns are often viewed as end-of-life issues, evidence suggests that they may emerge at any point following diagnosis, influencing adjustment throughout the illness trajectory. 5 
 6  This study explores how patients with advanced cancer experience and express these dimensions within their sociocultural and religious context.

A growing body of literature demonstrates that higher levels of spiritual well-being are associated with lower anxiety and depression, improved coping and better overall quality of life among patients with advanced cancer. 7  Conversely, unmet spiritual needs have been linked to poorer satisfaction with care and increased healthcare utilisation at the end of life. 8 
 9  Studies have also shown associations between spiritual distress and symptom burden, including pain, fatigue, anxiety and depression in patients with serious illness. 10 – 12  In an Indian study exploring spiritual concerns among patients receiving palliative care, commonly reported issues included faith in God, acceptance of illness, belief in karma and rebirth, concern about the future and existential questioning such as ‘Why me?’. 13

Although evidence supports the role of spiritual care, it remains insufficiently addressed in routine clinical practice, particularly in non-Western contexts. 13 
 14  In these settings, spiritual well-being is strongly shaped by cultural, religious and relational worlds, which may not be adequately reflected in assessment tools developed in Western healthcare systems.

In Kerala (a southern state of India where Malayalam is the primary official and vernacular language), recent efforts to linguistically validate spiritual well-being measures, such as the Malayalam version of the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Spiritual-Well-being-Expanded, highlight a growing recognition of the need for culturally appropriate assessment. 15  However, quantitative tools alone may not fully capture the nuanced, contextual and deeply personal experience of spiritual well-being in advanced illness. Qualitative research offers rich insights into patients’ lived experiences, bringing to light aspects of spirituality that are difficult to measure, such as culturally rooted beliefs and rituals, moral reflections, relationships and existential concerns. 6

To date, there is limited qualitative research exploring how patients with advanced cancer in Kerala understand and experience spiritual well-being within the context of palliative care. Addressing this gap is important for developing culturally sensitive spiritual care and strengthening holistic palliative care practice.

This qualitative study forms part of a larger mixed-method PhD research project assessing the spiritual well-being among patients with advanced cancer receiving palliative care. This study builds on the previous quantitative part, which found that higher spiritual well-being was associated with better quality of life. 16  However, the quantitative findings did not explain how patients understood and experienced spiritual well-being. This study aimed to explore spiritual well-being from the perspectives of patients with advanced cancer receiving palliative care in a tertiary cancer centre in Kerala.

Study design: A qualitative descriptive study design was used. 17

Study setting: he study was conducted at the outpatient palliative care services of a tertiary-level autonomous cancer centre under the Government of Kerala, located in Thalassery, South India.

The palliative care service follows a holistic approach addressing physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs. Spiritual concerns are explored when relevant during clinical interactions, with supportive listening and discussion of patients’ beliefs, values, sources of meaning and concerns related to illness and suffering. Patients may be supported in accessing family, community or faith-based resources according to their preferences.

Purposive sampling was used to recruit participants who could provide relevant information about their spiritual well-being. The sampling technique allowed selection of participants with varying age, diagnosis, socioeconomic status and treatment status to capture a range of experiences.

Eligible participants were recruited from patients attending the palliative care outpatient services of the centre. Inclusion criteria were: (1) adults aged 18 years or older; (2) diagnosis of advanced cancer, defined as metastatic, recurrent or progressive malignant disease; (3) receiving palliative care and (4) ability to read and comprehend Malayalam.

Patients were excluded if they had cognitive impairment or communication difficulties that prevented meaningful participation in the interview, were clinically unstable as determined by the investigator (including those requiring hospitalisation or intensive care) or were unwilling to participate due to time constraints.

Potential participants were approached by the first author (MSB) who explained the purpose and procedures of the study in detail. Some participants may have been familiar with MSB through clinical care at the palliative care service. However, no specific relationship was established prior to recruitment for the study. Written informed consent, including consent for audiorecording of the interviews, was obtained prior to participation. Participants were assured that their information would remain confidential and that they could withdraw from the study at any time without any impact on their care.

In-depth interviews were conducted between November 2022 and December 2024.

Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics, including age, gender, diagnosis, performance status, type of treatment received and time since completion of primary treatment, were extracted from medical records and recorded in a structured data collection sheet ( online supplemental file 1 ). Additional information, including marital status, religion, family structure and participants’ awareness of their disease and prognosis, was obtained through direct interviews and documented in the same form. Socioeconomic status was assessed using the ‘Modified Kuppuswamy Socioeconomic Scale’. 18

Data were collected through individual, face-to-face, in-depth, semistructured interviews using an interview guide ( online supplemental file 2 ) developed by the research team based on relevant literature and clinical expertise. 13 
 19  The guide was used flexibly to ensure consistency but at the same time allowed participants to elaborate on issues of importance to them. Interviews were conducted in Malayalam, the native language of both the interviewer and participants, by the first author (MSB), a female PhD candidate in palliative medicine. She is a palliative care clinician with more than 20 years of clinical experience in palliative care, particularly in symptom management and has undergone training in qualitative research methods.

Interviews were conducted in a private room within the outpatient palliative care service to ensure confidentiality and minimise interruptions. Caregivers were permitted to be present only at the participant’s request for support and did not participate in the interviews. Interviews lasted for 45–60 min, were audiorecorded with participants’ consent and field notes taken to document contextual details and non-verbal cues. No repeat or follow-up interviews were done in any of the participants.

All interviews were transcribed verbatim within 48 hours. Transcripts were translated into English and back-translated to Malayalam by the first author to ensure accuracy and preserve participants’ meanings. Interviews continued until data saturation was achieved, defined as the point at which no new codes or concepts emerged from successive interviews, as determined by the research team.

Audiorecorded interviews and field notes were checked for accuracy and de-identified prior to analysis. The research data were managed and analysed using QDA Miner Lite V.3.0.8 (MSB). 20  Qualitative content analysis was conducted using a conventional approach as described by Graneheim and Lundman, which enables interpretation of both manifest and latent content across increasing levels of abstraction. 21

Analysis was conducted on the translated English transcripts. First, transcripts were imported into QDA Miner Lite and read repeatedly to achieve familiarity with the data. Meaning units relevant to the study aim were then identified, condensed and assigned codes (MSB). An inductive approach was used, allowing codes to directly emerge from the data. Coding initially focused on participants’ experiences of suffering and the way in which they overcame these sufferings. The codes were exported from the software for manual sorting and grouping into subthemes based on the similarities in content (MSB, PKS). The resulting subthemes were organised into overarching themes representing the latent meaning of the text. 21  Data analysis was iterative and reflective, requiring movement back and forth between the data, codes and emerging themes, with revisions made when new insights emerged. The final codes, subthemes and themes were reviewed and discussed among the research team (BSM, PKS, RKC, SN, OS and CV) until consensus was reached.

A total of 127 codes were generated and subsequently organised into 18 subthemes and four overarching themes.

The trustworthiness of the study was ensured by addressing credibility, dependability, transferability, confirmability and authenticity, in line with established qualitative criteria. 21  Credibility was improved by doing the interviews in a supportive setting where participants felt comfortable sharing openly, by using their exact words to show their experiences of spiritual well-being and through repeated discussions among the research team during analysis. Transcripts were not returned to participants for comment or correction and participants did not provide feedback on the preliminary findings. Dependability was strengthened by keeping clear records of how we analysed the data and having the research team check the codes and themes. Transferability was supported by clearly describing the study setting, participant characteristics and research procedures. Confirmability was supported by reflexive notes and an audit trail. Authenticity was strengthened by including at least one quotation for each subtheme and by presenting views from different participants.

The first author is a palliative care clinician with a long-standing interest in spiritual well-being, and this background could have influenced how the data were collected and interpreted. For example, while interviewing one participant (P19) the interviewer asked “Is it because your faith was low before your illness and has increased now?” This question contains an implicit assumption that illness may lead to stronger faith. However, the participant immediately rejects this assumption (“No”) showing that the participant was able to express views that differed from those anticipated by the interviewer. To address this, reflexive notes were written after each interview, and interpretations were regularly discussed with co-researchers. These steps helped examine assumptions and ensured that the findings reflected participants’ accounts as much as possible rather than the researcher’s own views.

This qualitative study was reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guidelines. 22  A completed COREQ checklist is provided as  online supplemental file 3 .

Patients or the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of our research.

20 participants with advanced cancer were interviewed. Data saturation was achieved by the 20th interview, as no new codes or concepts emerged in the final interviews. The median (IQR) age was 51.5 (45–55.75) years. Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics are summarised in  table 1 . An example of the content analysis, including coding, subthemes and theme is presented in  table 2 . Analysis of spiritual well-being yielded 127 codes, categorised into 18 subthemes under four overarching themes ( online supplemental table 1 ).

The four main themes were:

Participants described how the diagnosis and progression of cancer affected their daily functioning, emotional state, relationships and sense of self. Physical symptoms such as pain, fatigue and reduced mobility were common. One participant described the persistent nature of the pain:

Despite these challenges, many participants described adapting to their limitations through practical adjustments and a determination to maintain independence. For example, one participant living with stoma explained,  “ The main difficulty I face is having this stoma bag… I always carry a spare stoma bag—you never know when it will leak .”  (P10, male, 50–59 years)

Alongside physical symptoms, participants described fear, uncertainty and emotional distress, especially at diagnosis. One participant reflected,  “ When I realized the severity of this disease, a sudden fear came over me, and I did not know what to do .”  (P07, female, 40–49 years). Illness also affected participants’ social lives and relationships. Some expressed sadness about reduced social participation while others experienced losing previous roles.

Financial hardships emerged as another important source of distress. The cost associated with treatment, travel and loss of income placed considerable strain on patients and families.  “ Monthly check-ups require a lot of money for travel. That is my main difficulty .”  (P15, Female, 40–49 years)

Many participants were worried about becoming a burden to their loved ones. Dependence on family members for physical, emotional and financial support often generated feelings of guilt and concern.

Alongside these experiences of suffering, participants engaged in deep inner questioning about past actions, regrets or life purpose.

Over time many participants described a gradual process of acceptance and adaptation. Rather than remaining focused on their illness, they sought ways to continue living meaningfully and move forward with their lives.

Participants consistently described relationships as an important source of strength, comfort and healing throughout their illness journey. Support extended beyond immediate family to include friends, neighbours, religious communities, support groups and healthcare professionals. Many participants valued the practical and emotional support they received from their wider social networks.

Family relationships were particularly important. Participants frequently described spouses, children, siblings and extended relatives as their primary source of emotional, physical and financial support contributing to a sense of security and hope.

Many participants explained that being able to talk, express feelings and be listened to provided emotional relief. Feeling heard made them feel valued.

Positive interaction with healthcare professionals further contributed to participants’ well-being. Trust, reassurance, kindness and clear communication helped patients feel emotionally comfortable and safe.

Participants used a variety of internal and external strategies to cope with illness and its challenges. Many found strength by observing how others managed similar or even more difficult circumstances. Some compared themselves positively with others who were more ill.

Previous life experiences also served as a source of resilience. Participants reflected on past hardships, caregiving responsibilities and personal challenges that had prepared them to face their present condition.

Many participants coped by maintaining daily routines and engaging in meaningful activities that provided a sense of normalcy and purpose. Practical strategies such as exercise, relaxation techniques, household tasks and gardening helped distract from suffering and promoted a sense of well-being.

Participants also described cognitive and emotional strategies that helped them maintain stability in the face of uncertainty. Acceptance, positive thinking, distraction and consciously avoiding excessive worry were commonly used to manage distress and preserve inner peace.

Spiritual beliefs and practices played an important role in how patients understood and responded to their illness. Many participants described faith in God as a source of strength, comfort and hope during periods of uncertainty. Religious practices such as prayer, visiting places of worship and reading religious texts were commonly used to cope with emotional distress and maintain a sense of inner peace.

Participants frequently described prayer as providing relief from fear, worry and suffering. For some, prayer created a sense of calm and temporary escape from illness-related concerns, while others felt it helped reduce their experience of physical suffering.

At the same time, spirituality was not always experienced as a source of comfort. Some participants engaged in spiritual questioning as they tried to understand the meaning of their illness and suffering. They reflected on the divine purpose of their disease, questioned divine intentions and at times expressed doubts about their faith.

This qualitative study explored spiritual well-being among patients with advanced cancer receiving palliative care and identified four interrelated themes: multidimensional sufferings and reflection in advanced cancer, healing through social support and relationships, coping mechanisms and inner strength and spiritual beliefs and practices. The findings show that spiritual well-being is dynamic and shaped by physical suffering, emotional distress, relationships with others, meaning-making and cultural spiritual practices. 23 
 24

The present findings complement our previous quantitative study by explaining how spiritual well-being is experienced and shaped within the personal, social, cultural and existential context of advanced cancer. 16

Participants’ narratives suggest that spiritual well-being cannot be understood separately from the broader experience of living with advanced cancer. Physical symptoms, functional decline, uncertainty about the future, social stigma, financial hardship and concerns about burdening family members were closely interconnected and often contributed to psychological and existential distress. These findings support the concept of ‘total pain’, which recognises suffering as a multidimensional experience encompassing physical, emotional, social and spiritual distress. 25  This interpretation is further supported by a systematic review, which describes cancer-related suffering as extending beyond physical symptoms to include existential, relational and spiritual dimensions. 26  At the same time, participants demonstrated considerable resilience through acceptance, positive reframing, relying on past life experiences, engaging in meaningful activities and maintaining social connections. Together, these findings suggest that spiritual well-being is not simply the absence of distress but a dynamic process through which individuals seek meaning, maintain hope and adapt to the challenges of advanced illness. Similar observations have been reported in studies of patients with life-limiting illnesses, where meaning-focused coping and resilience were associated with reduced existential distress and improved spiritual well-being 27 
 28

Another important finding was the central role of relationships and spirituality as sources of strength and meaning. Family members, relatives, community networks and healthcare professionals provided emotional reassurance, practical assistance and a sense of belonging. These relational resources were closely intertwined with participants’ spiritual lives, reflecting a view of spirituality that extended beyond individual religious belief. Faith in God, prayer and rituals provided comfort, peace and temporary relief from suffering, consistent with previous studies in advanced cancer and palliative care settings. 4 
 27 
 29  However, spirituality was not experienced solely as a source of comfort. Some participants expressed spiritual questioning and doubts regarding divine purpose and justice leading to spiritual struggle or distress. This varying spiritual response seen in advanced cancer patients highlights the need to recognise spiritual distress as well as spiritual strengths. 23 
 30

Cultural and contextual considerations:

The findings must be interpreted within the Indian sociocultural context, where strong family ties, community involvement and religious practices are commonly part of everyday life. 31 
 32  In this study, participants rarely described spiritual well-being as a personal experience. Instead, it was closely intertwined with community connectedness, family relationships, religious practices and concerns about loved ones. This relational understanding of spiritual well-being is similar to the observations from Indian and other Asian cultures where the self is understood in relation to one’s family and community rather than as the individual alone. 33

These findings suggest that spiritual care in Kerala may need to extend beyond individual beliefs and acknowledge relational and family-centred dimensions of suffering and meaning.

Concerns about healthcare costs and being a burden to family members significantly influenced emotional experiences and treatment-related decisions. 34 
 35  These challenges are common in low- and middle-income settings and should be considered when providing culturally sensitive palliative care and spiritual care. 36 
 37

The findings add to the evidence that spiritual concerns are many and addressing these is a necessary part of palliative care. Healthcare professionals should proactively assess spiritual distress, create opportunities for emotional expression, support family and community involvement and respect patients’ spiritual and religious beliefs. 4 
 24

Economic distress is a major but often overlooked source of spiritual and existential suffering, particularly in settings where patients and families bear the cost of care. Spiritual care should therefore acknowledge financial suffering, facilitate access to social support and address the moral distress among healthcare providers arising from overwhelming poverty and uncertainty to enable truly holistic palliative care. 24 
 34

A key strength of this study is the in-depth exploration of patients’ lived experiences, providing rich insights into spiritual well-being from the patients’ own perspectives using a rigorous qualitative content analysis approach. 21  As all participants were recruited from a single palliative care unit, perspectives may reflect institution-specific approaches to spiritual care. The predominance of female participants, largely due to the high proportion of breast cancer patients, may have limited the representation of male perspectives particularly regarding family relationships, caregiving roles, emotional expressions and spiritual coping.

In addition, the religious composition of the study sample did not fully reflect the religious diversity of Kerala. 38  Hindu participants were over-represented, with limited representation from Christian participants and no representation from the Muslim community. The themes that emerged in this study may primarily reflect the Hindu cultural and spiritual perspectives prevalent in Kerala. As spiritual beliefs, practices and interpretation of illness are often shaped by religious traditions, these findings may not be fully transferable to people from different religious backgrounds. 39 
 40

Future research should explore spiritual well-being in gender-balanced and religiously diverse populations, examine caregivers’ perspectives and longitudinal changes in spiritual well-being across the illness trajectory and evaluate structured spiritual care interventions in palliative care settings especially in low- and middle-income settings. Further cross-cultural studies may deepen understanding of how spirituality is experienced and expressed in different socioeconomic contexts. 36 
 41

Spiritual well-being in advanced cancer extends beyond religious practices and is shaped by interconnected experiences of illness, relationships, coping strategies and spiritual beliefs. Addressing these dimensions through holistic and culturally sensitive palliative care may enhance emotional resilience and overall quality of life. 4 
 23 
 24

<!-- ===== PMID 42744377 ===== -->
## Feasibility of an N-of-1 trial using a crossover design to evaluate music therapy in patients with breast cancer undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy: a multicentre pilot study protocol in two Italian centres (IMPACT-CASTA DIVA).

**PMID**: 42744377 · **Journal**: BMJ open · **Year**: 2026 · **DOI**: 10.1136/bmjopen-2026-122143 · **PMCID**: PMC13583835

**Authors**: Giordano Filippo, Baroni Mariagrazia, Zingarelli Marzia, Scarlata Elide, Pelazza Carolina, Mazzucco Riccardo, Santi Marco, Albini Giovanni, Visconti Mauro, Rossi Maura, Blasi Livio, Santinon Patrizia

**Types**: Journal Article, Clinical Trial Protocol

**INTRODUCTION**: Breast cancer is often accompanied by significant psychological and physical symptoms during chemotherapy, which have a considerable impact on quality of life. Music therapy is a non-pharmacological intervention that can support psychological well-being but the way individuals respond to the treatment can vary considerably. Traditional group-based studies do not allow such variability to be captured. N-of-1 trials, which are based on repeated intra-individual comparisons, offer an innovative way to assess personalised effects. This pilot study aims to evaluate the feasibility of this approach in patients with breast cancer.

**METHODS AND ANALYSIS**: This multicentre pilot study uses an N-of-1 design combined with a crossover design involving 24 patients with breast cancer who are undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy. Participants will be randomised into alternating sequences of phases with and without music therapy each lasting 4 weeks. The intervention consists of weekly 60-minute group sessions incorporating receptive and active techniques as well as personalised playlists. The primary outcomes focus on feasibility, including dropout rate and missing data as well as acceptability. The secondary outcomes include measures of psychological and physical well-being as assessed using validated instruments (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, Self-Rating Depression Scale, Quality of Life, Emotion Thermometers, Visual Analogue Scale and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). The analysis will be primarily descriptive, exploring individual trajectories and intra- and inter-patient variability using mixed-effects models.

**ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION**: The study protocol was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of AOU Maggiore della Carità Novara (Protocol No. 590/CE/2025) and the Research Ethics Committee of Palermo 2 (Protocol No. 137/2025) and will be conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants. The results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed scientific publications and presentations at national and international scientific conferences.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER**: NCT07549685.

Cancer is a major social, public health and economic challenge of the 21st century, accounting for almost one in six (16.8%) deaths worldwide and one in four (22.8%) deaths from non-communicable diseases worldwide. 1

In 2020, approximately 2.3 million new cases of breast cancer (BC) were recorded worldwide, accounting for almost a quarter of all cancers in women, with age-standardised incidence and mortality rates of 47.8 and 13.6 per 100 000, respectively. 2

In Italy, it is estimated that there will be around 53 686 new diagnoses in 2024, with the vast majority occurring in women, across all age groups. 3

Early diagnosis, together with increasingly effective treatment strategies, has contributed to improved survival rates, which currently reach approximately 87% at 5 years after diagnosis.

Despite these advances, patients with BC frequently experience a substantial burden of physical and psychological symptoms throughout the disease trajectory. During diagnosis and treatment, women may experience symptoms related to disease uncertainty, treatment-related side effects and the overall life-threatening nature of cancer.

Anxiety can influence both the surgical experience and the perception of pain, 4 – 6  exposing women to high levels of psychological distress. 7

For instance, physical symptoms such as gastrointestinal problems, fatigue and neurological effects are common during chemotherapy, along with psychological symptoms including anxiety (reported in 26.9%–41.55% of patients) and depression. 8  These symptoms can drastically reduce quality of life and negatively affect treatment adherence. 9

Furthermore, the experience of chemotherapy-induced side effects, such as nausea and vomiting, 10  varies widely among patients receiving the same cytotoxic agents, 11  suggesting that non-pharmacological factors may play an important role in symptom perception and management. 12

Therefore, the management of BC requires an integrated, interdisciplinary approach that addresses not only clinical outcomes but also psychological, social, spiritual and patient needs. 13

Music therapy (MT), unlike other music-based approaches, is defined as the clinical and evidence-based use of musical interventions by a qualified music therapist to achieve personalised goals within a therapeutic relationship. 14 
 15  It represents a promising non-pharmacological intervention to address these needs.

Previous evidence suggests that MT may reduce anxiety, stress and depression symptoms while improving overall well-being in patients with BC. 16 
 17

In oncology settings, MT has been shown to improve symptom management and patient-reported outcomes using both receptive and active approaches. It can also be integrated into surgical procedures to manage preoperative and postoperative anxiety effectively. 18 
 19

Group-based MT interventions have demonstrated reductions in anxiety and improvements in mood as well as enhanced social cohesion among hospitalised patients with cancer. 20 – 22

However, responses to MT may vary substantially between individuals, highlighting the need for more personalised approaches to evaluate treatment effects. 23

To date, most studies have assessed MT using conventional group-based designs, 24  which may overlook intra- and inter-individual variability in response.

N-of-1 trials, characterised by repeated crossover comparisons within individual patients, provide a methodological framework to evaluate personalised treatment effects and variability at the individual level.

Nevertheless, the feasibility of applying N-of-1 trial designs to MT in oncology has not yet been investigated. 25

For this reason, a pilot study was considered a necessary methodological step before undertaking a definitive effectiveness trial in women undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy for BC. This study will determine whether the proposed study procedures can be successfully implemented within routine oncology care. As MT is a complex intervention involving multiple interacting clinical and contextual components, this approach is consistent with the current recommendations for the evaluation of complex interventions. 26

The primary aim of this pilot study is to assess the feasibility of using an N-of-1 design to evaluate the effects of MT on psychological well-being in patients with BC undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy. In addition, the study will estimate intra- and inter-patient variability to inform future adequately powered trials.

This multicentre, non-profit, interventional pilot study is designed as a series of combined N-of-1 trials. This protocol was prepared in accordance with the SPENT (SPIRIT Extension for N-of-1 Trials) reporting guideline (2019). In this design, participants will alternate between periods during which they receive MT and periods during which they do not receive MT, allowing within-patient comparisons across repeated treatment and non-treatment phases. The study will be conducted at two Italian oncology centres: the SS Antonio e Biagio e C. Arrigo University Hospital in Alessandria and the Civico Di Cristina Benfratelli Hospital in Palermo, between November 2025 and June 2026.

Participants will be eligible for inclusion if they meet all the following criteria: (1) women aged 25–75 years; (2) histologically confirmed diagnosis of BC; (3) undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy following surgery; (4) Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0–1; (5) ability to understand the Italian language and comply with study procedures; (6) provision of written informed consent for study participation.

Participants will be excluded if they meet any of the following criteria: (1) active neurological disorders; (2) active psychiatric disorders; (3) current or past substance abuse; (4) significant uncorrected visual, auditory or speech impairments; (5) primary or metastatic brain tumours, as confirmed clinically or radiologically; (6) any condition that, in the opinion of the investigators, may interfere with participation in the study.

The following reasons will result in discontinuation of patients from the study: (1) failure to meet the inclusion or exclusion criteria; (2) poor compliance with study procedures or failure to comply with study procedures; (3) incomplete medical records; (4) voluntary withdrawal from the study; (5) serious deterioration of disease, severe complications or other clinically relevant physiological changes. Participants may also withdraw if the investigator considers them unsuitable to continue the study.

Participants will be recruited from the oncology departments of the participating centres. Eligible patients will be identified by the clinical staff and informed about the study during routine clinical visits. A brief description of the study’s objectives, requirements and methods will be provided during these visits. Patients who express interest in participating will undergo screening to verify eligibility according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria.

All participants will receive detailed information about the study objectives, procedures, potential risks and benefits prior to enrolment. Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants before any study-related procedures are performed ( online supplemental material 1 ). Participation in the study will be entirely voluntary, and participants will be free to withdraw at any time without affecting their standard clinical care. Personal information will be handled in accordance with applicable data protection regulations. Participants will be assigned a unique study identification code, and access to identifiable information will be restricted to authorised study personnel.

Participants will be allocated in a 1:1 ratio to one of two sequence groups (GR1 and GR2) using a computer-generated block randomisation scheme, stratified by study centre to ensure balanced group sizes within each site. Given the group-based nature of the MT intervention, randomisation will be performed after enrolment of the planned number of participants at each centre, allowing the formation of balanced groups. Allocation will be concealed using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes.

The randomisation sequence will be generated by an independent statistician not involved in participant recruitment, assessment or intervention delivery.

Patients and the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of this study.

MT will be provided in group sessions lasting approximately 60 min, on a weekly basis. Sessions will include both receptive (eg, guided listening and music imagery) 27  and active techniques (eg, instrumental or vocal improvisation, songwriting). 10  All the sessions will be conducted by qualified music therapists affiliated with the ‘Antonio Vivaldi’ Conservatory of Music in Alessandria and the ‘Alessandro Scarlatti’ Conservatory of Music in Palermo, with support from trained doctoral students when required. At the end of each session, participants receiving MT will be provided with customised playlists prepared by the music therapist. Each playlist will last approximately 20 min and will be designed to support relaxation and improve sleep quality. Participants will be encouraged to listen to the playlists independently between sessions, according to their preferences and clinical needs. Although the intervention follows a common clinical framework, the specific MT methods, musical materials and balance between receptive and active techniques will be individualised and continuously adapted according to each participant’s therapeutic needs, preferences, clinical condition and responses throughout the intervention.

The study consists of four consecutive phases (A-1, B-1, A-2 and B-2), each lasting 4 weeks. Participants will be randomly assigned to two groups (GR1 and GR2), which will alternate between periods with MT and periods without MT according to a crossover design. During MT phases, participants will attend 1 weekly 60 min MT group session. During non-MT phases, participants will not receive any specific intervention but will undergo the same assessments at the same time points ( figure 1 ).

All study assessments will be administered according to a standardised study schedule. Assessments requiring participants’ attendance at the participating centres will be conducted by trained research personnel, whereas remote patient-reported outcome measures will be completed using the REDCap platform.

At enrolment, eligibility criteria will be verified, and a clinical psychologist will explain the nature of the study to participants and obtain their written informed consent. Demographic and clinical data will be collected, including age, ethnicity, disease stage, comorbidities, current oncological treatments and relevant concomitant therapies.

All participants will be required to complete the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-Y1/Y2), 28 
 29  Self-Rating Depression Scale, 30  Quality of Life (QoL), 31  Emotion Thermometers (ET), 32  Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) 33  and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, 34  which will serve as baseline measures for subsequent within-patient comparisons.

During MT phases (A-1 and B-1), participants assigned to the intervention group will attend weekly sessions. Questionnaires (short STAI version, ET and VAS) will be administered approximately 30 min before and 5 min after each session to evaluate immediate changes associated with the intervention

During non-intervention phases, participants will not receive MT but will complete the same assessments remotely using the secure Research Electronic Data Capture 35  platform according to the predefined study schedule. No additional visits to the participating centres will be required during these phases.

Scheduled assessments will be conducted at the end of each phase: T1 (4 weeks); T2 (8 weeks); T3 (16 weeks, end of study). At each time point, participants will complete the same set of questionnaires administered at baseline. At the end of the study, qualitative data will be collected through semi-structured interviews and/or focus groups to explore participants’ experiences and perceptions of the intervention. The interviews will explore the acceptability of the intervention and study procedures, participants’ perceived benefits and challenges, and their overall experience of participating in the study. A draft semi-structured interview guide is provided as  online supplemental material 2 .

The primary outcome of this study is the feasibility of using an N-of-1 trial design to evaluate MT in patients with BC undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy.

Feasibility will be assessed using multiple complementary indicators. These include the dropout rate, defined as the proportion of participants who discontinue the study for reasons not attributable to clinical conditions; the completeness and consistency of patient-reported outcome data collection; the occurrence of any interference between the intervention procedures and routine clinical activities of the oncology units or healthcare staff; and participants’ acceptability of the intervention and study procedures, which will be explored through semi-structured interviews conducted at the end of the study.

Secondary outcomes will include changes in psychological and physical well-being, assessed using validated patient-reported outcome measures ( table 1 ).

In addition, intra- and inter-patient variability in these outcomes will be explored to inform the design of future adequately powered studies.

Given the pilot nature of the study, no formal hypothesis testing is planned for feasibility outcomes.

To guarantee the quality and the accuracy of the study procedures and data collection, research assistants will regularly review study documents, informed consent forms, case report forms (CRFs) and data records. These reviews will verify the completeness and accuracy of informed consent documentation, the completeness of CRFs, the consistency between source documents and recorded data, adherence to the study protocol and the timely identification and resolution of missing or inconsistent data. Any discrepancies identified during these reviews will be discussed with the study investigators and corrected where appropriate.

The CRFs and scales will be reviewed by the principal investigator and research assistant before they are handed over to the data management staff for data entry and administration. The Department of Oncology at Alessandria will be storing the original CRFs and all scales (including consent forms). The Data and Safety Monitoring Board in Alessandria Hospital will review study conduct and participants’ safety monthly. Access to the final study dataset will be restricted to the principal investigator and authorised members of the research team involved in data analysis. No contractual agreements will limit investigators’ access to the final dataset.

This study is designed as a pilot feasibility study. A total of 24 participants will be enrolled, with 12 participants from each centre. Due to the exploratory nature of the study, and in accordance with current methodological recommendations for pilot and feasibility studies, a formal sample size calculation was not performed. Instead, the target sample size was determined based on both methodological and pragmatic considerations. Specifically, enrolling 12 participants per centre was considered appropriate to estimate key feasibility parameters while ensuring the organisational feasibility of delivering the intervention across the two participating centres within the available project resources and study timeline.

From a methodological perspective, the selected sample is intended to provide preliminary estimates of recruitment, retention, data collection completeness, intervention acceptability and within- and between-patient variability in patient-reported outcomes 36 – 38  rather than to detect treatment effects.

The results of these estimates will inform the optimisation of study procedures and the design and sample size calculation for future studies with adequate statistical power. As this is a pilot study, the emphasis is on feasibility rather than formal hypothesis testing. This approach is consistent with the primary purpose of pilot studies, which is to generate feasibility data to inform the design of a future definitive trial rather than to formally evaluate treatment efficacy.

Descriptive statistics will be used to summarise the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics. Continuous variables will be reported as the mean and SD or the median and IQR depending on their distribution. Categorical variables will be presented as frequencies and percentages. Feasibility outcomes will be analysed descriptively. Dropout rates and the proportion of missing data will be calculated relative to the number of enrolled participants. Participants’ acceptability will be summarised using qualitative and descriptive approaches.

The effects of MT will be explored by graphically representing individual patient trajectories and comparing outcome measures during intervention and non-intervention periods.

Intra- and inter-patient variability in treatment effects will be analysed using mixed-effects models that account for repeated measures within individuals and the crossover design. These analyses will be exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

All analyses will be performed using standard statistical software (eg, R, Stata or SPSS version 32).

The study will be conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Ethical Guidelines for Clinical Research. Ethical approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee of AOU Maggiore della Carità Novara (Protocol No. 590/CE/2025) and the Research Ethics Committee of Palermo 2 (Protocol No.137/2025). Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants before enrolment. The study findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and presentations at national and international scientific conferences regardless of the study outcomes.

This study is one of the first to use an N-of-1 trial design to evaluate MT for patients with BC undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy. It focuses on a methodological approach centred on tailoring support interventions. This makes it possible to explore individual responses to MT in a systematic and longitudinal manner. This study addresses an important gap in personalised supportive care research. The multicentre design increases the feasibility and generalisability of the study across different clinical settings. Additionally, repeated within-patient measurements enable a thorough evaluation of variability in treatment response at the individual and group levels, a dimension that traditional group-based study designs fail to capture. Our approach enables the incorporation of intra-individual variability into clinical assessment models, contributing to the development of more sensitive approaches to individual response trajectories. Providing MT in a group setting reflects routine clinical practice and improves the intervention’s ecological validity. At the same time, it strikes a balance between personalisation and the organisational sustainability of the intervention in real-world settings. 39

However, as a pilot study with a relatively small sample size, it is not adequately powered to detect definitive treatment effects. Therefore, the results will primarily be interpreted in terms of feasibility and hypothesis generation rather than clinical efficacy. 40

Additionally, the absence of blinding may introduce bias in patient-reported outcomes. These aspects are inherent to pragmatic studies and must be carefully considered when interpreting the collected data.

The complexity of the N-of-1 crossover design may affect participant adherence and data completeness.

From a practical standpoint, implementing this study could present several operational challenges. First, coordinating participants’ schedules for the group MT sessions can be challenging for patients undergoing chemotherapy due to treatment-related fatigue, clinical appointments and potential side effects.

Second, it can be difficult for participants to maintain adherence across multiple phases, particularly given the repeated assessments and the length of the study. Completing multiple patient-reported outcome measures at different time points may also impact data completeness. These challenges are key factors in assessing feasibility, and they may also provide useful insights for optimising future, larger-scale studies.

Furthermore, the multicentre design requires careful coordination between centres to ensure consistency in intervention delivery, data collection procedures and adherence to the study protocol. Variability in clinical settings and organisational workflows may affect the feasibility of implementing a standardised intervention. However, this diversity reflects the real-life conditions of clinical practice, thereby reinforcing the practical relevance of the findings.

Finally, as MT is delivered in a group setting, individual preferences and group dynamics may influence engagement and perceived benefit, introducing further variability that must be considered when interpreting results. This variability is not just a limitation: it also provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying responses to MT in complex settings. Overall, this study offers preliminary insights into the feasibility and usefulness of an N-of-1 design for evaluating MT in BC. This could contribute to the development of more patient-centred research models that are aligned with personalised medicine.
